2. Why a robot needs a map


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A map (G-2331)Map: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in §2.1 What a map is for. is the robot’s model of its surroundings: a list of the objects that matter, with where they are. Localization compares readings with it, and planning searches it for routes.


2.1 What a map is for
A reading such as “the pink pole is 2.236 m away, to the left” says where things are relative to the robot. To turn it into “where am I?”, the robot needs to know where those things are in the room. A map gives exactly that: the robot compares what it sees with the map and keeps the poses where the two agree. Planning needs the map too: a route to the door must go round the table.
A map (G-2331)Map: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in §2.1 What a map is for. is a list of the objects in the environment that matter to the robot, with their positions and properties (Thrun et al. 2005 §6.2). We write it as a list of objects:

m_i is object number i of the map, such as the pink pole at (1 m, 3 m);
N is the number of objects, 2 when the map holds only the two poles (Section 3);
m is the whole map, the list of all N objects.

m = \lbrace m_1,\ m_2,\ \dots,\ m_N \rbrace
Fixed things, such as walls and furniture, belong in the map; things that move, such as people, belong in the robot’s state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §4.1 State: from one number to many, the quantities it keeps track of, instead. What goes in the map is settled; how much of the room it records is not.

4.2 Half-plane: one side of a line
Every edge of the table lies on a line, which we can write in the general form of a lineExplained in: The Equation of a Hyperplane, §3.1 The general form of a line. For a point on the floor:

x is the point’s x coordinate, in m;
y is its y coordinate, in m;
a is the number that multiplies x, set by the line’s direction (1.5 for the table’s right edge below);
b is the number that multiplies y (−0.5 for the right edge);
c is the constant that shifts the line into place (−7 for the right edge);
f(x, y) is the line’s function: 0 on the line, negative on one side and positive on the other.

f(x, y) = a x + b y + c = 0
The vector (a, b) is the line’s normal vector (G-1346)Normal vector: A vector perpendicular to a line, plane or hyperplane; for w^{\mathsf T}x + w_0 = 0 it is w. Explained in: The Equation of a Hyperplane, §6.1 The argument, a direction square to the line, and points towards the positive side. All the points on one side of a line, together with the line, form a half-plane (G-2336)Half-plane: All points on one side of a line, together with the line: the points where a x + b y + c \le 0; one sign test, used as a building block for polygon obstacles. Explained in §4.2 Half-plane: one side of a line. (LaValle §3.1.1):

H is the half-plane on the negative side: the set of floor points (x, y) where f is 0 or less; in the braces below, the colon reads “such that”.

H = \lbrace(x, y) : f(x, y) \le 0 \rbrace
Worked example: the right edge of the table. It runs from (5, 1) to (5.5, 2.5), so its direction is (0.5, 1.5). The corners run counter-clockwise, so the table always lies on the left of each edge as we walk along it. Turning the direction a quarter turn clockwise therefore gives a normal that points to the right of the edge, out of the table:
(a, b) = (1.5,\ -0.5)
The line passes through (5, 1), where f must be 0:
1.5 \times 5 - 0.5 \times 1 + c = 0
c = -7
Doubling every number gives whole numbers and the same line, with the same signs. We call this right-edge function f_2:
f_2(x, y) = 3x - y - 14
One edge gives one half-plane; the table has four edges.

Triangles are popular because graphics hardware is built to draw them (LaValle §3.1.3).                   Key point 
                  
                

A scan of 360 distances is mostly wall. Feature extraction (G-2341)Feature extraction (from sensor data): Pulling a few distinctive objects out of raw sensor data, such as two poles out of a 360-beam laser scan; it shrinks hundreds of numbers to a short list that is easy to match with a map. 6.1 Why extract features
The other half of the comparison is the reading itself. A laser scanner on our robot at (2, 1) measures 360 distances, one per degree. Comparing all 360 with a map (G-2331)Map: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in §2.1 What a map is for., the robot’s model of the room, is possible (the range-sensor Notes later in this chapter do it), but most of the numbers describe plain wall, which looks the same all along the room. A few distinctive objects carry most of the information about where the robot is. Pulling such objects out of raw sensor data, so that a scan of hundreds of numbers becomes a short list of objects, is feature extraction (G-2341)Feature extraction (from sensor data): Pulling a few distinctive objects out of raw sensor data, such as two poles out of a 360-beam laser scan; it shrinks hundreds of numbers to a short list that is easy to match with a map. Explained in §6.1 Why extract features. (Thrun et al. 2005 §6.6, as in the Freiburg sensor-model slides).
An object makes a good landmark (G-2342)Landmark: An object the robot can detect reliably and tell apart from the others, such as a coloured pole or a door; its known position in the map lets readings of it fix the robot’s pose. Explained in §6.1 Why extract features. when two things hold:

the robot can detect it reliably, such as a pole that stands out in a laser scan or a coloured marker in a camera image;
the robot can tell it apart from the other landmarks: tree 1 from tree 2, the pink pole from the green one.

Landmarks can be natural objects (trees, doors, road signs) or artificial ones put there for the robot (coloured markers, reflectors). Some are passive, only seen; others are active and send a signal, such as a radio beacon (Freiburg sensor-model slides). The two poles of our room are passive landmarks; the next step finds them in the scan.
6.2 Finding the poles in a scan
Our robot at (2, 1) facing 30° takes a simulated scan: 360 beams, one per degree, each with 1 cm of range noise. The beams hit the walls, the near side of the table, and two small clusters.
A pole shows up as a few neighbouring beams that are much shorter than the beams on both sides, which pass it and hit the wall behind. So the extraction rule, applied to the scan in order, is:

cut the scan wherever the range jumps by more than 0.3 m between neighbouring beams;
keep a piece that is narrower than 0.35 m and nearer than the beams on both sides of it;
report its bearing (G-2344)Bearing: The angle from the robot’s heading to a sensed landmark, positive to the left, such as 86.6 degrees; together with the range it fixes where the landmark is relative to the robot. Explained in §6.3 Range, bearing and signature., its direction measured from the robot’s heading, as the average direction of its beams, and its range (G-2343)Range (of a landmark reading): The distance from the robot to a sensed landmark, such as 2.236 m; together with the bearing it fixes where the landmark is relative to the robot. Explained in §6.3 Range, bearing and signature., its distance, as its nearest beam’s range plus the pole’s radius of 0.1 m, so that the range is to the pole’s centre.

Figure 8 applies the rule to the scan, one beam after another. Watch each reading land as a grey dot, the orange jump at each cut, and the test of each piece when the next cut closes it: only a 3-beam piece and a 5-beam piece pass, and they become the green and the pink pole.

Figure 8: Animation: from the robot at (2, 1) facing 30 degrees, a blue cursor reads the 360 beams in order and each reading lands as a grey dot; at each cut, where the range jumps by more than 0.3 m, an orange line shows the jump, and the piece that the cut closes is tested: narrower than 0.35 m and nearer than the beams on both sides. Beams through the door read 8 m and leave the picture. Only two pieces pass: 3 beams, the green pole at range 4.004 m and bearing −33.0 degrees, and 5 beams, the pink pole at range 2.232 m and bearing 87.0 degrees. The last frame shows all 360 scan points in grey and the two extracted poles, each labelled with its range r and bearing φ
The rule finds exactly the two poles:

The table’s corners pass step 2 only if they are narrow and stand in front of something farther away, which they do not here; real extractors add more tests for such cases.
6.3 Range, bearing and signature
Each extracted landmark (G-2342)Landmark: An object the robot can detect reliably and tell apart from the others, such as a coloured pole or a door; its known position in the map lets readings of it fix the robot’s pose. Explained in §6.1 Why extract features. is reported as three numbers (Thrun et al. 2005 §6.6, as in the Brown CS148 tutorial), shown in Figure 9:

its range (G-2343)Range (of a landmark reading): The distance from the robot to a sensed landmark, such as 2.236 m; together with the bearing it fixes where the landmark is relative to the robot. Explained in §6.3 Range, bearing and signature. r: the distance from the robot to the landmark, in m (2.236 m for the pink pole, worked out below);
its bearing (G-2344)Bearing: The angle from the robot’s heading to a sensed landmark, positive to the left, such as 86.6 degrees; together with the range it fixes where the landmark is relative to the robot. Explained in §6.3 Range, bearing and signature. \varphi: the angle from the robot’s heading to the landmark, positive to the left, negative to the right, in degrees (86.6° for the pink pole);
its signature (G-2345)Signature (of a landmark): A label that says what kind of landmark was sensed, such as its colour or ID number; it tells the robot which landmark in the map a reading belongs to. Explained in §6.3 Range, bearing and signature. s: what kind of landmark it is, such as its colour (pink) or an ID number.


Figure 9: A landmark reading: from the robot at (2, 1) facing 30 degrees, the pink pole at (1, 3) is at range r = 2.236 m and bearing phi = 86.6 degrees from the heading; its signature is pink
For the pink pole, the true values follow from the map (G-2331)Map: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in §2.1 What a map is for.. The pole is 1 m back in x and 2 m up in y from the robot:
r = \sqrt{1^2 + 2^2} = 2.236 \text{ m}
The pole’s direction in the room comes from atan2 (G-2325)atan2: A function atan2(rise, run) that returns the direction of a line over the full circle from its rise and run given separately; needed because the plain inverse tangent of the ratio cannot tell opposite directions apart. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §4.2 Turn, drive, turn, which turns the rise and the run into an angle over the full circle:
\text{atan2}(2,\ -1) = 116.6^\circ
The bearing is measured from the heading, 30°:
\varphi = 116.6^\circ - 30^\circ = 86.6^\circ
So the reading of the Overview, with its bearing and signature, is one landmark reading:

z is the reading: its range, bearing and signature together.

z = (2.236 \text{ m},\ 86.6^\circ,\ \text{pink})
Why each of the three numbers is needed:

Range and bearing fix where the landmark is relative to the robot. Range alone puts it anywhere on a circle around the robot; bearing alone, anywhere along a ray from it.
The signature says which landmark of the map the reading belongs to. Without it, two identical poles would leave the robot with two explanations of every reading, like the three identical doors of the hallwayExplained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §3.1 Why one reading fits many places; with it, the reading “pink” can only be the pole at (1, 3).

In localization the map is known and the pose is not. Then a single landmark reading cannot fix the pose; with the range alone it only says the robot stands somewhere on a circle of radius r around the landmark, and two or three landmarks together pin it down. The landmark measurement model (G-2401)Landmark measurement model: The density of a landmark reading (range, bearing) given a pose and the map: a Gaussian of the range error times a Gaussian of the bearing error, with the errors taken as independent; it scores how well a guessed pose explains what the robot saw. Explained in: Landmark Measurement Model, §4.1 Two Gaussians, multiplied builds that step.

Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §7. Ruling out poses inside walls needs to keep sampled poses out of walls.
A half-plane (G-2336)Half-plane: All points on one side of a line, together with the line: the points where a x + b y + c \le 0; one sign test, used as a building block for polygon obstacles. Explained in §4.2 Half-plane: one side of a line. is one sign test: the function f of the line through an edge is at most 0; a convex obstacle is where all its edge tests pass, so the table’s inside test is four multiplications and sums (−1, −4, −7, −3 for (4, 2)).
Non-convex obstacles are unions (G-2045)Union (A ∪ B): The set of elements in A or B (or both), such as the points inside either of two convex pieces of an obstacle; for events, the event that A or B (or both) happens. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Mutually Exclusive Events, §5. The addition rule: where mutual exclusivity pays off of convex pieces, because the overlap of half-planes is always convex; the cabinet’s notch point (6.2, 3.0) fails both rectangles and is free.
Triangle meshes (G-2338)Triangle mesh: A set of triangles, each given by three corner points in space, that together cover an object’s surface (a table as 12 triangles on 8 corners); fast to draw in 3D, but it does not say what is inside. Explained in §5.1 Triangle meshes. suit 3D graphics, because graphics hardware is built to draw triangles, but do not define an inside; bitmaps are simple, but 0.5 m cells inflate the obstacles from 5.13 m² to 11.75 m², because a cell turns black when any part of it is covered, and 0.1 m cells cost 25 times as many cells.
An occupancy grid (G-2340)Occupancy grid: A grid map that stores in each cell a number between 0 and 1, such as the probability that the cell is occupied, instead of a hard 0 or 1; the standard grid map of robotics, since sensors are never sure. Explained in §5.2 Bitmaps and occupancy grids. stores a number between 0 and 1 in each cell, such as the probability that an obstacle is there; with each 0.5 m cell holding the share of it that is covered, the shares add up to the true 5.13 m², because each share times the cell’s area is the obstacle area inside it.
Feature extraction (G-2341)Feature extraction (from sensor data): Pulling a few distinctive objects out of raw sensor data, such as two poles out of a 360-beam laser scan; it shrinks hundreds of numbers to a short list that is easy to match with a map. Explained in §6.1 Why extract features. turns 360 scan distances into two landmarks, because a few distinctive objects carry most of the information about the pose; each landmark is reported as range, bearing and signature, and the signature says which map landmark it is.

The robot can now hold its room as a map and turn a scan into readings such as (2.236 m, 86.6°, pink). Still missing: how likely is a reading if the robot stood at a guessed pose? The beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture answers that for each beam of a laser scan.

Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Normal distributionNormal distribution: A symmetric, bell-shaped distribution: most values sit near the mean and they get rarer the further out we go; its mean and standard deviation set its centre and width. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is; Uniform distributionUniform distribution: A distribution in which every outcome in a range is equally likely. Explained in: Uniform and Log-normal Distributions, §2. The uniform distribution; Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE): Fitting parameters by making the likelihood of the observed data as large as possible. Explained in: Maximum Likelihood Estimation, §7. The likelihood function and the MLE; Exponential distributionExponential distribution: The pattern of waiting times between random events: short waits are common and long waits rare (a right-skewed continuous distribution). Explained in: MLE for the Binomial, Exponential and Normal Distributions, §3.1 The distribution of waiting times; Gaussian mixture model (GMM)Gaussian mixture model (GMM): A model for data made of several overlapping groups: one normal curve per group, combined as a weighted sum \sum_k \pi_k N(x \mid \mu_k, \sigma_k^2). Each point is shared among the curves by probabilities instead of being given to one group. Explained in: Gaussian Mixture Models, §6. The mixture density; Expectation maximization (EM)Explained in: The Expectation Maximization (EM) Algorithm, §3. The two steps and the algorithm; Maps and landmarksMap: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §2.1 What a map is for.
Leads to: Likelihood field modelLikelihood field model: A measurement model for range finders that scores each reading by how close its beam endpoint lands to an obstacle in the map (a Gaussian of that distance plus a small uniform part p_{\text{rand}}, so no reading scores 0); it is fast and smooth because it skips ray casting, but it ignores what lies along the beam. Explained in: Likelihood Fields and Scan Matching, §3. The likelihood field model; BeliefBelief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition.
Compare with: Likelihood field modelLikelihood field model: A measurement model for range finders that scores each reading by how close its beam endpoint lands to an obstacle in the map (a Gaussian of that distance plus a small uniform part p_{\text{rand}}, so no reading scores 0); it is fast and smooth because it skips ray casting, but it ignores what lies along the beam. Explained in: Likelihood Fields and Scan Matching, §3. The likelihood field model.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A robot judges a guess about its pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, where it stands and which way it faces, by asking how likely its laser readings would be from there. The beam model gives that number for one reading as a mix of four causes, so that a person walking past does not make the right pose look impossible.


So far the robot has a grid map (G-2335)Location-based map (grid map): A map that splits space into cells and stores a value for every cell, occupied or free, free space included (2800 cells for a 7 m by 4 m room at 0.1 m); larger, but it answers at once whether a pose is free. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §3. Feature-based and grid maps of its room: the room split into small cells, each marked free or occupied. The map does not say where the robot is on it; the robot can only guess poses and test each guess against what its sensors report. Figure 1 shows where that test breaks: watch the four beams leave the robot one by one, and see which one stops short of the wall.

Figure 1: Animation: a 5 m by 4 m room seen from above. The robot at (2, 2), facing along x, fires four laser beams one by one, at 0°, 90°, 180° and 270° from its heading. Each beam travels out and stops at the first surface it meets: the forward beam at a person 1.00 m ahead, although the wall is 3 m away (dashed blue line); the other three at the walls, after 1.97, 2.04 and 1.99 m. The readings fill in beside the room, and the last frame holds the whole scan
The robot stands at pose (2, 2, 0) in a 5 m by 4 m room; its laser measures the distance to the nearest surface in four directions. A person stands 1 m in front of it, so the forward beam reads 1.00 m, although the map says the wall is 3 m away. Is the robot at (2, 2, 0), or one metre further along at (3, 2, 0)? This Note adds the rule that answers it.
The room is smaller and emptier than the 7 m by 4 m room with poles and furnitureExplained in: Maps and Landmarks, §1. Overview used for maps: a laser needs only walls, and bare walls keep every expected range (G-2375)Expected range z^{\ast}: The distance a beam would read with a perfect sensor, if the robot were at a given pose in the map; the measurement model compares each real reading with it. Explained in §2.2 Why we need a measurement model., the distance a beam should read according to the map, a round number we can check by hand.
A sensor reading is a measurement (G-2317)Measurement z_t: What a robot’s sensors report about the world at time t, such as “door”, a laser scan or a camera image; it does not change the state but tells the robot something about it, which narrows its distribution. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §5.1 Measurements and controls: what the sensors report about the world at one moment. To test a guessed pose we need a rule that answers one question: how likely are these four readings if the robot stood at that pose? This Note builds the standard rule for range sensors:

what a range sensor reports, and why the question above is the one to ask (Section 2);
why a Gaussian around the expected range is not enough (Section 3);
the four causes of a reading and the shape each one gives, with the reason for every shape (Section 4);

2. What a range sensor measures


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A range sensor reports, for each direction, the distance to the first surface the beam meets. A measurement model scores a guessed pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, a position and heading, by how likely those distances are from there.


2.1 Range finders and scans
The four numbers of Figure 1 come from a range finder (G-2371)Range finder: A sensor that measures the distance to the nearest surface in one direction, for example by timing a laser or sound pulse; robots use it to compare what they see with a map. Explained in §2.1 Range finders and scans., which measures the distance to the nearest surface in one direction. A laser range finder, or LiDAR (G-1083)LiDAR: A sensor that measures distances to nearby objects with laser light. Explained in: Types of Neural Networks, History and Applications of Deep Learning, §4.1 Mainstream applications, sends a short pulse of light and times its return. The pulse travels to the surface and back, so the time of flight multiplied by the speed of light is twice the distance; halved, it is the distance. A sonar does the same with a sound pulse (LaValle §11.5.1).
A scanning laser turns, so one sweep gives many readings, for example one every half degree. The list of readings from one sweep is a range scan (G-2372)Range scan: The list of readings from one sweep of a scanning range finder, one distance per beam direction, such as z = (1.00, 1.97, 2.04, 1.99); it is the measurement a laser-based robot tests poses against. Explained in §2.1 Range finders and scans.. 2.2 Why we need a measurement model
Suppose the robot is unsure whether it is at pose A, (2, 2, 0), or at pose B, (3, 2, 0): one metre further along the room. To decide, it compares its readings with what each pose would predict. The map predicts, for each pose and each beam, the distance the beam should travel before it meets a wall: the expected range (G-2375)Expected range z^{\ast}: The distance a beam would read with a perfect sensor, if the robot were at a given pose in the map; the measurement model compares each real reading with it. Explained in §2.2 Why we need a measurement model., written z^{\ast}.
We find it by ray casting (G-2376)Ray casting: Finding the expected range by walking along a beam’s direction through the map until the first occupied cell; it turns a guessed pose and a map into the readings the robot should see. Explained in §2.2 Why we need a measurement model.: start at the robot, walk along the beam’s direction in small steps, and stop at the first occupied cell of the grid map (Figure 3). The distance walked is z^{\ast}. For the forward beam:

z_{A}^{\ast} is its expected range from pose A, in m;
z_{B}^{\ast} is its expected range from pose B, in m.

z_{A}^{\ast} = 3.0 \text{ m}
z_{B}^{\ast} = 2.0 \text{ m}
In Figure 3, watch the counter as each ray checks one cell after another: the walk ends when the ray enters a wall cell, after 3.0 m from pose A and after 2.0 m from pose B.

The reading was 1.00 m, which matches neither 3.0 nor 2.0. We need a number for “how well does a reading of 1.00 m fit an expected range of 3.0 m?”, one that tolerates small sensor errors and an odd reading now and then. That number is the measurement model (G-2374)Measurement model p(z \mid \mathbf{x}, m): The density of getting sensor readings z if the robot were at pose \mathbf{x} in map m (also sensor or observation model); read over poses it is a likelihood that tells a filter which poses fit the readings. Explained in §2.2 Why we need a measurement model., also called the sensor model or observation model (Thrun §6.1). For one scan and one guessed pose:

z is the scan, the four readings (1.00, 1.97, 2.04, 1.99) m;

m is the map, the grid map of the room;
the bar \mid reads “given”.

p(z \mid \mathbf{x}, m)
In words: the density of getting the readings z, given that the robot is at pose \mathbf{x} and the world looks like map m. The pose \mathbf{x} is the pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading of a floor robot, position and heading:

its first entry x is the position along the room, in m (2 m at pose A);
y is the position across the room, in m (2 m at pose A);
\theta is the heading, in degrees (0° at pose A, facing along x).

\mathbf{x} = (x,\ y,\ \theta)
For a fixed set of readings, p(z \mid \mathbf{x}, m) read as a function of the pose is the likelihood (G-1086)Likelihood: How probable the observed data is under given parameter values; read as a function of the parameters with the data fixed. Explained in: Probability vs Likelihood, §2.2 Likelihood: from the event back to the parameter of that pose: the poses under which the readings are more likely score higher. A localization filter uses the model this way: the Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm multiplies its belief by this likelihood in its correction step.
A range reading is a continuous quantity, so p(z \mid \mathbf{x}, m) is a probability density (G-1569)Probability density: The height of a continuous distribution’s curve; compares how likely nearby values are. Explained in: Probability Density Function and the CDF of a Continuous Variable, §5. What the density at a point means, not a probability: per metre for one reading, per m⁴ for our scan of four readings. A density can be larger than 1; only areas under it are probabilities.
2.3 Why a whole scan is a product of beams
A scan has many beams, and writing one density for all of them at once is hard. We split it into one density per beam and multiply. With the symbols of Section 2.1 and Section 2.2:

z^k is the reading of beam k, in m;
K is the number of beams, 4;
\mathbf{x} is the guessed pose, such as A;
m is the map;
\prod means “multiply the terms for k = 1 to K“.

p(z \mid \mathbf{x}, m) = \prod_{k=1}^{K} p(z^k \mid \mathbf{x}, m)
Multiplying is allowed when the beams are independent: knowing one beam’s error tells us nothing about another’s. Independence does not hold in general, but it nearly holds once the pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading and the map are known (Thrun §6.3.1):

Without a map, beams are linked: if one beam hits something at 2 m, the beam half a degree away probably hits the same object at about 2 m.
With the map and the pose given, that shared object is already in the map, so each beam’s remaining error is its own sensor noise, and the beams are close to independent.

Independence that holds only once a third thing is known is conditional independence (G-443)Conditional independence: Independence that holds once a third variable is known: given the class, knowing one feature tells nothing more about another. Naive Bayes assumes it so it can multiply one probability per feature. Explained in: Naive Bayes: The Mathematics, §5. Step 3: the naive assumption, the same assumption Naive Bayes makes for features given the class.


                  
                  Extra 
                  
                

The assumption is not exact. A person blocks several neighbouring beams at once, and their errors are then linked. The product then counts that one person several times, which makes the model overconfident (Freiburg sensor-model slides, “Summary beam-based model”). Implementations therefore use only a subset of the beams of each scan: the ROS localization package AMCL uses 30 evenly spaced beams per scan by default (ROS amcl, laser_max_beams).


So scoring a pose comes down to one density per beam; what is still missing is the shape of that density.
3. Why a Gaussian alone fails


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A narrow Gaussian around the expected range gives a reading caused by a passer-by a density of practically zero, and the product then rejects the true pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, the robot’s real position and heading, outright.


The first rule that comes to mind fails on the person’s 1.00 m reading of Figure 1. The rule says the reading should be the expected range (G-2375)Expected range z^{\ast}: The distance a beam would read with a perfect sensor, if the robot were at a given pose in the map; the measurement model compares each real reading with it. Explained in §2.2 Why we need a measurement model., the distance the map predicts, plus a small sensor error, and small errors follow a Gaussian distribution (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is. A good laser’s readings typically lie about 0.05 m from the true distance: its standard deviation (G-1870)Standard deviation of a random variable: The square root of a random variable’s variance, in the units of X; it says how far values typically fall from the expected value. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4.1 Variance term by term is \sigma = 0.05 m. For one beam:

z is the beam’s reading, in m (1.00 m for the forward beam);
z^{\ast} is its expected range, 3 m for the forward beam at pose A;
\sigma is the sensor’s standard deviation, 0.05 m;
\mathcal{N}(z;\ z^{\ast}, \sigma^2) is the Gaussian density of the reading, with mean z^{\ast} and variance \sigma^2, in per m.

\mathcal{N}(z;\ z^{\ast}, \sigma^2) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\ e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{z - z^{\ast}}{\sigma}\right)^2}
Figure 4 draws it for the forward beam at the true pose A, where z^{\ast} = 3 m. Now put the person’s reading, 1.00 m, into it. The distance from the expected range, in units of \sigma:
\frac{1.00 - 3.00}{0.05} = -40
The exponent:
-\tfrac{1}{2} \times 40^2 = -800
The factor in front of the exponential:
\frac{1}{0.05 \times \sqrt{2\pi}} = 7.98
The density:
7.98 \times e^{-800}
\approx 0
The number e^{-800} is so small that a computer stores it as exactly 0 (the notebook checks). In Figure 4, the reading of 1.00 m sits 40 standard deviations left of the peak, where the curve lies flat on the axis.

Because the scan density is a product, one zero beam makes the whole scan density zero, whatever the other beams say. So the true pose A gets 0. The wrong pose B fits the backward beam far worse but escapes the zero: its forward beam expects 2 m, and its backward beam expects 3 m but reads 2.04 m. Those two densities are tiny but not zero, and B ends up with a scan density of about 4 \times 10^{-164}. A Gaussian alone would prefer the wrong pose, only because a person stepped in front of the robot.
The cure is not a wider Gaussian: that would make every reading near the wall less informative too. Instead we list the other ways a reading can come about, and give each its own shape.
4. The four causes of a reading


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A reading is one of four things: a correct hit with small noise; a hit on something not in the map; a failure, which reports the sensor’s longest distance, its maximum range (G-2373)Maximum range z_{\max}: The longest distance a range sensor can report, such as 5 m; when no pulse returns, the sensor reports this value, so a reading of z_{\max} usually means a failure, not a wall. Explained in §2.1 Range finders and scans.; or a random reading with no modelled cause. Each cause has its own density shape, and each shape follows from how that cause works.


The person’s reading is one of four ways a beam can come back. 4.2 Unexpected objects: why the curve falls off, and why it stops
A person, a chair or an open door that is not in the map can block the beam first. The reading is then shorter than z^{\ast}. Such a blocker is an unexpected object (G-2379)Unexpected object (p_{\text{short}}): Something not in the map, such as a person, that blocks the beam before the mapped surface and gives a short reading; modelled as an exponential from 0 up to z^{\ast}, because only the first blocker counts. Explained in §4.2 Unexpected objects: why the curve falls off, and why it stops., and its reading a short reading. Figure 5 shows its shape: high at 0, falling off, and zero after z^{\ast}. Both features have a reason.
Why it stops at the expected range. An object behind the wall cannot block the beam: the wall is hit first. So a short reading is always shorter than z^{\ast}, and the density is 0 beyond it.
Why it falls off. Only the first object along the beam matters; anything behind it is hidden. Cut the beam into 4 equal cells and let each cell be either blocked (1) or free (0), all 16 patterns equally likely. Figure 8 sorts the 16 patterns by the first blocked cell:

The count halves with each cell, because each extra free cell in front is one more condition the pattern must meet.
The same holds for any blocking chance. Let each cell be blocked independently of the others:

j is a cell’s number along the beam, counted from the robot (1, 2, 3, …);
P(\text{first stop at cell } j) is the probability that the beam stops at cell j and not before.

For the beam to stop at cell j, the j - 1 cells before it must be free and cell j blocked:
P(\text{first stop at cell } j) = (1 - b)^{j - 1}\ b
Each further cell multiplies the chance by the same factor 1 - b. With cells of 0.1 m and b = 0.2:
P(\text{cell } 1) = 0.2
P(\text{cell } 2) = 0.8 \times 0.2 = 0.16
P(\text{cell } 3) = 0.8^2 \times 0.2 = 0.128

z is the reading, in m;
z_{\max} is the maximum range, 5 m;
p_{\max}(z) is the failure part of the model.

p_{\max}(z) = 1 \text{ if } z = z_{\max}, \text{ else } 0
A distribution that puts all its probability on one value is a point mass (G-2383)Point mass: A distribution that puts all its probability on one value, such as a reading of exactly z_{\max}; it has no density height, so code draws it as a very narrow box of area 1. Explained in §4.3 Failures: a spike at the maximum range.. A point mass has no height, only a probability, so it cannot be added to densities as it stands. Readings of exactly 5 m now have a cause; a stray reading such as 4 m, behind the wall at 3 m, still has none.
4.4 Random readings: the uniform part
Some readings have no cause we can model: cross-talk between sonars, reflections that come back by a strange path, electronic glitches (Thrun §6.3.1; Freiburg slides). In Figure 12, watch such stray readings of the forward beam land anywhere from 0 to 5 m, even beyond the wall at 3 m, and their histogram fill in evenly into a flat floor.

We know nothing about where such a random measurement (G-2381)Random measurement (p_{\text{rand}}): A reading with no modelled cause, such as cross-talk or a stray reflection; modelled as a uniform density 1/z_{\max} (the uniform part p_{\text{rand}}) so that no reading ever has density 0. Explained in §4.4 Random readings: the uniform part. lands, so we give every value from 0 to z_{\max} the same density, a uniform distribution (G-2043)Uniform distribution: A distribution in which every outcome in a range is equally likely. Explained in: Uniform and Log-normal Distributions, §2. The uniform distribution:

z is the reading, in m, anywhere from 0 to z_{\max};
z_{\max} is the maximum range, 5 m;
p_{\text{rand}}(z) is the density of a random reading, in per m.

p_{\text{rand}}(z) = \frac{1}{z_{\max}}
= \frac{1}{5} = 0.2 \text{ per m}
The uniform part p_{\text{rand}} has a job: no reading between 0 and 5 m ever gets a density of exactly 0, so one strange reading can never wipe out a whole scan.
5. The beam model: one mixture of four shapes


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The beam model adds the four densities with weights that sum to 1. With it, the person’s reading costs pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading A, the robot’s true position and heading, a factor, not everything, and A wins.


5.1 The mixture
We do not know whether the forward beam’s 1.00 m came from the person or from a random reading, only how often each cause happens. So the density of a reading is the weighted sum of the four densities, a mixture densityExplained in: Gaussian Mixture Models, §6.1 The formula like a Gaussian mixture, but with parts of different shapes. For one beam k:

p(z^k \mid \mathbf{x}, m) is the density of beam k‘s reading z^k, given the pose \mathbf{x} and the map m, in per m;
p_{\text{hit}} is the Gaussian around the expected range (Section 4.1);
p_{\text{short}} is the falling exponential of unexpected objects (Section 4.2);
p_{\max} is the failure spike at 5 m (Section 4.3);
p_{\text{rand}} is the uniform part, 0.2 per m (Section 4.4);
w_{\text{hit}} is the share of readings that are hits, 0.75;
w_{\text{short}} is the share caused by unexpected objects, 0.12;
w_{\max} is the share of failures, 0.05;
w_{\text{rand}} is the share of random readings, 0.08.

p(z^k \mid \mathbf{x}, m) = w_{\text{hit}}\ p_{\text{hit}} + w_{\text{short}}\ p_{\text{short}}
\qquad + w_{\max}\ p_{\max} + w_{\text{rand}}\ p_{\text{rand}}
The mixture weights (G-1238)Mixture weight \pi_k: How big a share of a mixture one component k gets; the weights are non-negative and add up to 1. Explained in: Gaussian Mixture Models, §6.1 The formula are the shares of readings each cause produces. They are not negative and add up to 1, so the mixture’s area is 1 too. Thrun writes them z_{\text{hit}}, \dots; we write w so that z always means a reading. This weighted mixture of four densities is the beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in §5.1 The mixture. of a range finder (G-2371)Range finder: A sensor that measures the distance to the nearest surface in one direction, for example by timing a laser or sound pulse; robots use it to compare what they see with a map. Explained in §2.1 Range finders and scans., a distance sensor such as our laser; it is also called the beam-based proximity model (Thrun §6.3; Freiburg slides). def beam_model(readings, expected):  # metres

6. Learning the model’s numbers from data


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Record many readings of a wall at a known distance and choose the weights and widths that make those readings most likely. The causes are hidden, so EM finds them by alternating “which cause made each reading?” with “refit each cause”.


6.1 Why the numbers must be learned
The answer of Section 5.2, the scan about 215 times more likely from pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading A (the robot’s true position and heading) than from pose B, rests on six numbers we chose: the four weights, the standard deviation of the hits \sigma_{\text{hit}} (0.05 m) and the rate of short readings \lambda_{\text{short}} (2 per m). The six numbers are the model’s intrinsic parameters (G-2384)Intrinsic parameters (of a sensor model): The numbers that describe a sensor and its surroundings rather than the pose, such as the beam model’s four weights, \sigma_{\text{hit}} and \lambda_{\text{short}}; they are learned from recorded readings. Explained in §6.1 Why the numbers must be learned.: they belong to the sensor and its surroundings, not to the pose (Thrun §6.3.4). A sonar is noisier than a laser, and a busy hall has more short readings than an empty lab, so no textbook value fits every robot. We measure them.
The experiment: place the robot 3 m from a wall and record 1000 readings of the beam that faces it while people walk past (Freiburg slides, “Raw sensor data” for an expected distance of 300 cm). Figure 15 shows the result as counts per 0.05 m bin. Look for the four causes in it: the tall peak at the wall, the falling pile of short readings near 0, the thin even layer of random readings, and the bar at 5 m. We built these readings in the notebook from the model of Section 5, so that we can check the fit against known values; real recordings look the same (Freiburg slides, “Raw sensor data”).

Some numbers are easy. With nobody around, the readings scatter only by measurement noise (G-2378)Hit part p_{\text{hit}} (measurement noise in the beam model): The small scatter of a reading around the true distance when the beam does hit the mapped surface; modelled as a Gaussian around z^{\ast} cut to [0, z_{\max}]. Explained in §4.1 Measurement noise: a Gaussian around the expected range., and \sigma_{\text{hit}} is their standard deviation (G-1870)Standard deviation of a random variable: The square root of a random variable’s variance, in the units of X; it says how far values typically fall from the expected value. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4.1 Variance term by term, their typical distance from 3 m, as given by the MLE of a normal distribution (G-1242)MLE of a normal distribution: The normal curve that makes the data most likely: its mean is the sample mean and its variance the average squared distance from that mean (dividing by n), \hat\mu = \bar{x} and \hat\sigma^2 = \sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2/n. Explained in: MLE for the Binomial, Exponential and Normal Distributions, §4.4 The MLE of the standard deviation. The weights cannot be read off like that: a reading of 2.95 m could be a hit or a short reading, and nothing in the reading says which.
6.2 Maximum likelihood, and why it needs a search
The principle is maximum likelihood estimation (G-1191)Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE): Fitting parameters by making the likelihood of the observed data as large as possible. Explained in: Maximum Likelihood Estimation, §7.2 The maximum likelihood estimate: choose the six numbers that make the 1000 recorded readings most likely. With the log-likelihood (G-1113)Log-likelihood: The logarithm of the likelihood, which turns the product of probabilities into a sum of log probabilities; it peaks at the same parameters as the likelihood and is easier to compute and maximise. Explained in: Logistic Regression: Maximum Likelihood and the Log Loss, §4.2 Taking logs, we maximise a sum over the readings:

z_i is recorded reading number i, in m;
n is the number of readings, 1000;
z^{\ast} is the expected range, the wall’s distance, 3 m;
p(z_i \mid z^{\ast}) is the mixture of Section 5 at reading z_i, in per m;
\ell is the log-likelihood, the sum of the logs of those densities.

\ell = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log p(z_i \mid z^{\ast})
The log of a sum of four parts does not split into simple pieces, so setting the derivative to zero gives no closed formula, exactly as for a Gaussian mixtureExplained in: Gaussian Mixture Models, §9. Why maximum likelihood has no closed form. The standard way out for mixtures is EM, which guesses which cause made each reading, refits each cause to its readings, and repeats; each of its steps has a simple formula (UW CSE 571 slides; Thrun §6.3.4; De Laet et al. 2008, Algorithm 1).
6.3 EM for the beam model
The hidden piece of information is the cause of each reading, a latent variable (G-1050)Latent variable: A variable in a model that is never observed, such as the component that produced a point. Explained in: Gaussian Mixture Models, §5.2 The latent variable. The EM algorithm (G-675)EM algorithm (expectation maximization): A method for finding the maximum likelihood when some variables are hidden (latent): it repeats two steps, an E-step and an M-step, until the fit settles. Explained in: The Expectation Maximization (EM) Algorithm, §3. The two steps and the algorithm repeats two steps from a starting guess. We start from equal weights 0.25, a standard deviation of the hits \sigma_{\text{hit}} of 0.3 m and a rate of short readings \lambda_{\text{short}} of 0.5 per m.
E-step: share each reading among the causes. For each reading, compute each weighted part and divide by their sum. The shares are the responsibilities (G-1687)Responsibility r_{nk}: In a mixture model, how likely it is that component k produced point n, given that point (the posterior probability). Explained in: Gaussian Mixture Models, §3.2 The standard terms e_{i,c} of cause c for reading i; they add up to 1 over the four causes (E-step (G-654))E-step: The expectation step of the EM algorithm: using the current parameters, give every point its responsibilities (the probability that it came from each component), a soft assignment that the M-step then uses. Explained in: The Expectation Maximization (EM) Algorithm, §3.1 The two steps. With the starting guess, the weighted parts (per m) for three readings:

Each cause is now fitted like a single distribution, with each reading counted by its responsibility (the M-step (G-1139))M-step: The second step of each EM round (maximisation): with the responsibilities held fixed, re-estimate each component’s mean, covariance and weight as responsibility-weighted averages, so the fit to the data improves. The three refits (Thrun §6.3.4; De Laet et al. 2008, Eq. 65–66):


Weights: a cause’s weight is its average responsibility, its share of the readings.
w_c = \frac{1}{n} \sum_i e_{i,c}

\sigma_{\text{hit}}^2 = \frac{\sum_i e_{i,\text{hit}}\ (z_i - z^{\ast})^2}{\sum_i e_{i,\text{hit}}}

With weighted readings, the count becomes the sum of responsibilities:
\lambda_{\text{short}} = \frac{\sum_i e_{i,\text{short}}}{\sum_i e_{i,\text{short}}\ z_i}

7. A catalogue of sensor models


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Every sensor needs its own measurement model p(z \mid \mathbf{x}, m), the density of its reading z given the pose \mathbf{x} (position and heading) and the map m, because each reports a different kind of number. Four kinds cover most mobile robots: landmark, range, boundary and odometry sensors.


The beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. A model is needed for every sensor the robot uses, and its shape follows from what the sensor reports. LaValle collects the common kinds (LaValle §11.5.1); Figure 17 draws four of them in our room.

Explained in: Probability vs Likelihood, §2.2 Likelihood: from the event back to the parameter that a localization filter multiplies into its belief.
A scan’s density is the product of its beams’ densities, because once the pose and map are known the beams are nearly independent; the leftover dependence makes the product overconfident, so implementations use a subset of beams.
A Gaussian alone fails, because one reading caused by a passer-by gets density 0 and the product then rejects the true pose.
The beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in §5.1 The mixture. mixes four causes with weights that add up to 1, so a short reading costs a pose a factor instead of everything; in our scan the readings are 215 times more likely from the true pose than from the wrong one.
The short-reading curve is exponential because the beam stops at the first of many evenly spread blockers, which halves (or shrinks by a fixed factor) the chance with every extra stretch of beam.
The weights and widths are learned by maximum likelihood from recorded readings; the causes are hidden, so EM alternates responsibilities and weighted refits, and it never lowers the log-likelihood (G-1113)Log-likelihood: The logarithm of the likelihood, which turns the product of probabilities into a sum of log probabilities; it peaks at the same parameters as the likelihood and is easier to compute and maximise. Explained in: Logistic Regression: Maximum Likelihood and the Log Loss, §4.2 Taking logs.
Each sensor kind (landmark, range, boundary, odometry) needs its own model, because each reports a different kind of number.

Now the robot can score a guessed pose from a laser scan on a grid map, even with a person in the way. RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-011-.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Normal distributionNormal distribution: A symmetric, bell-shaped distribution: most values sit near the mean and they get rarer the further out we go; its mean and standard deviation set its centre and width. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is; Probabilistic motion modelsMotion model p(\mathbf x_t \mid u_t, \mathbf x_{t-1}): The probability distribution of a robot’s pose after a move, given its pose before and the control (command or odometry); it describes how uncertain motion is, so a filter can score possible end poses or draw them at random. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §2.2 The motion model and its density; Beam modelBeam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture.
Compare with: Beam modelBeam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture; Landmark measurement modelLandmark measurement model: The density of a landmark reading (range, bearing) given a pose and the map: a Gaussian of the range error times a Gaussian of the bearing error, with the errors taken as independent; it scores how well a guessed pose explains what the robot saw. Explained in: Landmark Measurement Model, §4. The landmark measurement model.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The likelihood field model (G-2391)Likelihood field model: A measurement model for range finders that scores each reading by how close its beam endpoint lands to an obstacle in the map (a Gaussian of that distance plus a small uniform part p_{\text{rand}}, so no reading scores 0); it is fast and smooth because it skips ray casting, but it ignores what lies along the beam. Explained in §3.2 From distance to density. scores a laser reading by one look-up: how close does the beam’s end point land to an obstacle in the map? The model gives up some physics for a large gain in speed and smoothness, and the same idea lets a robot match one scan against another to measure how far it moved.


Make interactive
Figure 1: The 5 m by 4 m room with a box in the lower right. The robot at pose A (2, 2, 0) sends 12 laser beams, one every 30 degrees; each beam ends at a red dot on a wall or on the box, except the forward one, which stops at a person 1 m ahead
So far the robot can score a guessed pose from a laser scan with the beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture: it casts every beam through the map and compares each reading with the distance it should have read, and in this room it rated the true pose A 215 times above a pose 1 m off, even with a person in front. What still breaks is that it is slow and jumpy. A localization filter may try hundreds of guessed poses for every scan, and each guess needs a ray cast per beam: 15 million small steps per scan for 1000 poses (Section 2.1). And a 1 cm move can make one beam slip past an edge and change its score 270-fold (Section 2.2). This Note adds a score that looks only at where each beam ends.
We keep the 5 m by 4 m room, pose A and person of the beam model, and add one box (Figure 1) so that a beam has an edge to slip past. The Note covers:

why the beam model is too slow and too jumpy for some uses (Section 2);
the likelihood field model: look only at where each beam ends (Section 3);
how the whole map is turned into a look-up picture once, in advance, and what that picture gives up (Section 4);
scan matching: using a likelihood field (G-2393)Likelihood field: A grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam. Explained in §4.2 From distances to the likelihood field. built from one scan to find how far the robot moved before the next (Section 5);
correlation-based map matching (G-2397)Map matching (correlation-based): Scoring a guessed pose by placing a local map built from the scan on the global map there and computing their correlation, cut at zero; it is cheap but coarse, limited by the cell size. Explained in §6.1 A local map from the scan.: comparing a small map built from a scan with the global map (Section 6).

2. Why the beam model is not enough


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture needs a ray cast for every beam of every guessed pose, and a tiny change of pose can make a beam slip past an edge and change its score 270-fold.


2.1 It is slow
For each guessed pose, the beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture walks every beam through the map until it meets an obstacle (ray casting (G-2376))Ray casting: Finding the expected range by walking along a beam’s direction through the map until the first occupied cell; it turns a guessed pose and a map into the readings the robot should see. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §2.2 Why we need a measurement model. A particle filter, which tries many poses at once, multiplies that work. With 1000 guessed poses, 30 beams each, and up to 500 steps of 1 cm per beam:
1000 \times 30 \times 500
= 15\ 000\ 000 \text{ steps per scan}
In the notebook, scoring the 12-beam scan of Figure 1 at one pose takes about 11 ms with the beam model and 0.045 ms with the likelihood field (G-2393)Likelihood field: A grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam. Explained in §4.2 From distances to the likelihood field. of Section 3: about 250 times faster (plain Python; the exact ratio depends on the machine). The Freiburg slides list “not very efficient” as a weakness of the beam model and “highly efficient, uses 2D tables only” as a strength of the endpoint model of Section 3 (Freiburg slides, “Endpoint model” and “Properties of endpoint model”).
2.2 It jumps at edges
The beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture is “not smooth for small obstacles and at edges” (Freiburg slides, “Endpoint model”). Figure 2 shows why. Take one beam, at 330° (pointing down to the right), with the reading 1.86 m, and slide the robot down the room a centimetre at a time, so that its y coordinate y falls; the table gives the beam’s expected range z^{\ast} at each y:




















Robot at yExpected range z^{\ast}Beam model (per m)1.53 m1.85 m (hits the box)5.881.52 m3.04 m (misses the box)0.0218
One centimetre of movement lets the beam slip under the box’s corner. Its expected range jumps from 1.85 m to 3.04 m, and the density of the same reading drops by a factor of:
5.88 / 0.0218 = 270
Figure 2 plays the slide, with the robot’s y going from 1.70 m down to 1.40 m. Watch the red curve, the beam model’s density of the reading: it holds at 5.88 and then drops to 0.0218 in a single centimetre, while the green curve only bends gently.

Figure 2: Animation: the robot slides down the room 1 cm at a time, its y coordinate falling from 1.70 m to 1.40 m, and one beam at 330 degrees reads 1.86 m. Left: the ray cast from the robot, blue while it meets the box after an expected range z* of 1.85 m, orange from y = 1.52 m, when it slips under the box’s corner and meets the bottom wall after 3.04 m; the green dot is where the reading 1.86 m ends. Right: the density of that reading as y falls: the beam model (red) jumps from 5.88 to 0.0218 per m between y = 1.53 and 1.52 m, while the likelihood field (green) changes smoothly. The last frame shows both beams and both full curves
A score that jumps like this is hard to search: a method that improves a guess by small steps, such as gradient descent (G-862)Gradient descent: Finding the lowest point of a function by repeated small steps downhill. Explained in: Gradient Descent from Scratch, §1. Overview, finds no slope to follow on the flat parts and a cliff at the edge. The green curve in Figure 2 is the likelihood field (G-2393)Likelihood field: A grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam. Explained in §4.2 From distances to the likelihood field. of the next section. The field changes smoothly with the pose, which is the second thing we gain (Freiburg slides, “Properties of endpoint model”).
3. The likelihood field model


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Turn each reading into the point where the beam ended. A reading is likely if that end point lies close to an obstacle in the map; the density is a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is of the distance to the nearest obstacle, plus a small uniform part.


3.1 Look only at where the beam ends
Both problems of Section 2, the ray cast per beam and the jump at the box’s edge, come from following the beam through the map. A correct reading ends on a surface. So instead of following the beam, we can ask a simpler question: does the beam’s end point lie on, or near, a surface in the map (Freiburg slides, “Endpoint model”: “instead of following along the beam, just check the endpoint”)? The point where a beam ends is the beam endpoint (G-2392)Beam endpoint: The point where a beam ends: the robot’s position plus the reading along the beam’s direction, (x + z\cos(\theta + \theta_k),\ y + z\sin(\theta + \theta_k)); the likelihood field model looks only at this point. Explained in §3.1 Look only at where the beam ends.. For beam k:

x is the robot’s x coordinate, in m (2 m at pose A);
y is its y coordinate, in m (2 m at pose A);
\theta is its heading, in degrees (0° at pose A);
\theta_k is the beam’s angle from the heading, in degrees (90° in the worked example below);
z^k is the beam’s reading, in m (1.97 m for the 90° beam);
x_{\text{end}} is the x coordinate of the beam’s end point, in m;
y_{\text{end}} is its y coordinate, in m.

The beam ends at:
x_{\text{end}} = x + z^k \cos(\theta + \theta_k)
y_{\text{end}} = y + z^k \sin(\theta + \theta_k)
The two lines are the cosine and sine shares of a length along a direction, as in the kinematic model (G-2297)Kinematic model: Equations that give how a robot’s configuration changes from its speed inputs alone, ignoring masses and forces, such as \dot{x} = v\cos\theta, \dot{y} = v\sin\theta, \dot{\theta} = \omega; used to predict motion at low speed. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §5.2 The kinematic model. The laser sits at the robot’s centre here; a laser mounted elsewhere adds its offset (UChicago class 05).
Worked example. At pose A, the beam at 90° reads 1.97 m:
x_{\text{end}} = 2 + 1.97 \cos 90^\circ = 2
y_{\text{end}} = 2 + 1.97 \sin 90^\circ = 3.97
The forward beam reads 1.00 m, so it ends at (3, 2). Figure 3 marks both end points and how far each lies from the map’s obstacles:

d is the distance from an end point to the nearest obstacle in the map, in m.

d(2, 3.97) = 0.03 \text{ m (top wall)}
d(3, 2) = 1.0 \text{ m (box corner)}

3.2 From distance to density
An end point 3 cm from a wall is what a good reading looks like; one 1 m away from everything is not. We turn the distance into a density with two parts (Thrun §6.4; Freiburg slides, “Endpoint model”; UChicago class 05):

a Gaussian of the distance: sensor noise scatters end points a little around the surface, so we use a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is of d with mean 0 and standard deviation (G-1871)Standard deviation: How far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n - 1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default). Explained in: Understanding Your Data: Seven First Questions, §7.1 Count, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum \sigma, the typical distance of an end point from the surface;
a uniform part: readings with no modelled cause, such as the person, must not get density 0, so every reading from 0 to z_{\max} gets the same small density, the random measurement part p_{\text{rand}} (G-2381)Random measurement (p_{\text{rand}}): A reading with no modelled cause, such as cross-talk or a stray reflection; modelled as a uniform density 1/z_{\max} (the uniform part p_{\text{rand}}) so that no reading ever has density 0. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §4.4 Random readings: the uniform part of the beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture.

With our numbers:

d is the distance from the beam’s end point to the nearest obstacle, in m;
\sigma is the standard deviation of that distance, 0.1 m;
z_{\max} is the laser’s maximum range, 5 m;
w_{\text{hit}} is the share of readings that end on a surface, 0.9;
w_{\text{rand}} is the share of random readings, 0.1;
\mathcal{N}(d;\ 0, \sigma^2) is the Gaussian density of d with mean 0 and variance \sigma^2, in per m;
\mathbf{x} (bold) is the pose, the three numbers (x, y, \theta) of Section 3.1; plain x is its first number; pose A is (2 m, 2 m, 0°);
m is the map: the room’s walls and box of Figure 1;
p(z^k \mid \mathbf{x}, m) is the density of beam k‘s reading z^k, given the guessed pose \mathbf{x} and the map m, in per m.

p(z^k \mid \mathbf{x}, m) = w_{\text{hit}}\ \mathcal{N}(d;\ 0, \sigma^2) + \frac{w_{\text{rand}}}{z_{\max}}
The standard deviation is wider than the beam model’s 0.05 m, because d also absorbs small errors in the map and the pose. The ROS localization package uses 0.2 m by default (ROS amcl, laser_sigma_hit).
Worked example: the 90° beam, d = 0.03 m. The Gaussian at d = 0 has height 3.989 per m:
\mathcal{N}(0.03;\ 0, 0.1^2) = 3.989 \times e^{-0.045}
= 3.8135
0.9 \times 3.8135 = 3.432
3.432 + 0.1 / 5 = 3.452 \text{ per m}
The person’s beam, d = 1.0 m, ten standard deviations away. The Gaussian part is about e^{-50}, so only the uniform part is left:
0.9 \times 3.989 \times e^{-50} \approx 0
p = 0 + 0.02 = 0.02 \text{ per m}
Two kinds of reading need a rule of their own:

Max-range readings are skipped. Their end point is not on any surface; it only says nothing came back (UChicago class 05; Thrun §6.4).
The whole scan is the product of its beams, as for the beam model, because the beams are close to conditionally independentExplained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §2.3 Why a whole scan is a product of beams given the pose and the map. In practice we add logs instead of multiplying, which gives the same ranking without very small numbers.

This mixture, evaluated at beam end points, is the likelihood field model (G-2391)Likelihood field model: A measurement model for range finders that scores each reading by how close its beam endpoint lands to an obstacle in the map (a Gaussian of that distance plus a small uniform part p_{\text{rand}}, so no reading scores 0); it is fast and smooth because it skips ray casting, but it ignores what lies along the beam. Explained in §3.2 From distance to density., also called the endpoint model (Thrun §6.4; Freiburg slides).

Python: the likelihood field model (G-2391)Likelihood field model: A measurement model for range finders that scores each reading by how close its beam endpoint lands to an obstacle in the map (a Gaussian of that distance plus a small uniform part p_{\text{rand}}, so no reading scores 0); it is fast and smooth because it skips ray casting, but it ignores what lies along the beam. def field_loglik(F, pose, z, angles):
    x, y, th = pose
    keep = z < ZMAX                    # skip max-range readings
    ex = x + z[keep] * np.cos(th + angles[keep])
    ey = y + z[keep] * np.sin(th + angles[keep])
    return np.log(lookup(F, ex, ey)).sum()
F is the precomputed field of Section 4 and lookup reads the grid cell under each end point; both are in RO-011-likelihood-fields-and-scan-matching.ipynb.

Every score still needs the distance d from each end point to the nearest obstacle, and finding it at every guessed pose would bring back the slowness of Section 2.1. Section 4 computes it once, for the whole map.
4. Precomputing the field


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The density depends only on where the end point lands, not on the pose, so we compute it once for every cell of the map and store it. That stored picture is the likelihood field (G-2393)Likelihood field: A grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam. Explained in §4.2 From distances to the likelihood field..


4.1 The distance transform
The ray casts that made the beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture slow (Section 2.1) are replaced here by a table built once. The density of Section 3.2 needs one number per end point: the distance to the nearest obstacle. That number depends only on the end point’s position, never on the pose the beam came from. So we can work it out for every cell of the map once, before the robot moves, and store it.
The stored grid of “distance from this cell to the nearest occupied cell” is the distance transform (G-2394)Distance transform: A grid that stores, for every cell of a map, the distance to the nearest occupied cell (with straight-line distances, the Euclidean distance transform); it lets a likelihood field be built in one pass. Explained in §4.1 The distance transform. of the map, and with straight-line distances the Euclidean distance transform. Image-processing libraries compute it in one pass over a grid of marked and unmarked cells, for example scipy.ndimage.distance_transform_edt (SciPy docs). Figure 5 shows it on a coarse grid of 0.5 m cells, with the box rounded to whole cells. Read it like a table: each number is the distance in metres from that cell’s centre to the nearest grey cell. The numbers grow by about one cell size (0.5 m) per step away from any wall, and the cells between the box and the right wall stay small because two obstacles are near.

Putting each cell’s distance into the density of Section 3.2 gives the density an end point would have in that cell. The grid of these densities is the likelihood field (G-2393)Likelihood field: A grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam. Explained in §4.2 From distances to the likelihood field. of the map (Thrun §6.4; Freiburg slides, “Example”). We build it in three views, from the familiar to the compact.
