The field is computed once per map, so its cost does not grow with the number of poses tried. Scoring a pose then costs one look-up per beam, with no ray casting (G-2376)Ray casting: Finding the expected range by walking along a beam’s direction through the map until the first occupied cell; it turns a guessed pose and a map into the readings the robot should see. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §2.2 Why we need a measurement model, the walk along each beam: this is where the speed-up of Section 2.1, about 250 times, comes from (Freiburg slides: “highly efficient, uses 2D tables only”). The ROS localization package AMCL uses this model by default (ROS amcl, laser_model_type).
4.3 What the field gives up
The model “ignores physical properties of beams” (Freiburg slides, “Properties of endpoint model”): it looks at the end point and ignores what lies between the robot and it. Two consequences follow.
The field sees through walls. Figure 9 shows a guessed pose C, (3.9, 2, −90°), above the box, facing down. Suppose a reading of 1.98 m. Its end point, (3.9, 0.02), lies next to the bottom wall, so the field scores it 3.45 per m, a near-perfect reading. But from C the beam would meet the box after 0.8 m; it could never reach the wall. The beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture knows this and gives the reading 0.016 per m (Thrun §6.4 lists the same drawback).

Figure 9: A guessed pose C above the box, facing down. A reading of 1.98 m would end next to the bottom wall, which the likelihood field scores 3.45 per m; the beam model knows the box blocks the beam after 0.8 m and gives 0.016 per m
The field does not model people. The field has no short-reading part. A person’s reading is scored only by the uniform part of Section 3.2, 0.02 per m, wherever it lands. The cost is mild in practice, because the uniform part still keeps the scan’s product from reaching 0, and the person costs every guessed pose the same.
So the trade is: physics for speed and smoothness. The trade pays when many poses must be scored, as in a particle filter, and when the score is searched by small steps, as in scan matching (G-2395)Scan matching: Aligning two range scans to find the motion between the poses they were taken from, for example by sliding the second scan over a likelihood field built from the first; it corrects drifting odometry. Explained in §5.1 The problem: odometry drifts., lining up two scans to measure the robot’s motion (Section 5) (Freiburg slides, “Properties of endpoint model”).
5. Scan matching: how far did the robot move?


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Build a likelihood field (G-2393)Likelihood field: A grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam. Explained in §4.2 From distances to the likelihood field., the look-up grid of end-point densities, from the first scan’s end points, then slide the second scan over it. The shift that puts the second scan’s end points on the brightest places is the robot’s motion between the two scans.


5.1 The problem: odometry drifts
The smooth score of Section 3, with no 270-fold jump, lets a search slide one scan over another to measure how far the robot moved. Wheel odometry estimates motion by counting wheel turns, and wheels slip, so its estimate drifts (wheel odometry (G-2321): motion measured from wheel turns, with errors that grow as the robot drives)Wheel odometry: Working out a robot’s pose by adding up the wheel motion its encoders measure: ticks to wheel distances, to the robot’s move and turn, to a new pose; accurate over short distances but it drifts, because every error stays in the sum. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §3.1 From encoder ticks to a new pose. A laser sees the same walls before and after a move, and they shift in its view by exactly the robot’s motion. Finding that shift is scan matching (G-2395)Scan matching: Aligning two range scans to find the motion between the poses they were taken from, for example by sliding the second scan over a likelihood field built from the first; it corrects drifting odometry. Explained in §5.1 The problem: odometry drifts.: aligning two scans to find the motion between the poses they were taken from (Olson 2009).
Our test: the robot takes scan 1 at (2, 2, 0), then drives to (2.3, 2.1, 5°). Odometry claims it reached (2.3, 2.0, 0): it missed the 0.1 m sideways slip and the 5° turn. Each scan has 360 beams, one per degree.
5.2 A likelihood field from the first scan
Scan matching needs no map. We treat the end points of scan 1 as the occupied cells of a little map and build its likelihood field (G-2393)Likelihood field: A grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam. Explained in §4.2 From distances to the likelihood field. exactly as in Section 4 (Freiburg slides, “Scan matching (G-2395): extract likelihood field from first scan and use it to match second scan”)Scan matching: Aligning two range scans to find the motion between the poses they were taken from, for example by sliding the second scan over a likelihood field built from the first; it corrects drifting odometry. Explained in §5.1 The problem: odometry drifts.. Scan 2’s end points, placed at the right motion, must then land on the bright ridges of that field.
5.3 Search the candidate motions
A candidate motion is a shift and a turn:

\Delta x is the shift along x, in m (0.3 m for the true motion);
\Delta y is the shift along y, in m (0.1 m for the true motion);
\Delta\theta is the turn, in degrees (5° for the true motion).

To test one, we turn scan 2’s end points by \Delta\theta, shift them by (\Delta x, \Delta y), look up the field of scan 1 under each, and add the logs. That sum is the score of the candidate. We try every candidate on a grid:

\Delta x from −0.1 to 0.7 m and \Delta y from −0.3 to 0.3 m, in steps of 0.02 m;
\Delta\theta from −10° to 10°, in steps of 1°.

The grid holds:
41 \times 31 \times 21
= 26\ 691 \text{ candidates}
The notebook scores them in about one second. Searching a whole grid of candidates and keeping the best is correlative scan matching (G-2396)Correlative scan matching: Scan matching that scores every candidate motion on a grid of shifts and turns and keeps the best, so it needs no good first guess. Explained in §5.3 Search the candidate motions. (Olson 2009). The grid search does not need a good first guess, unlike methods that improve one guess step by step.
Figure 10 plays a few candidates. At the odometry guess, scan 2’s end points sit beside the ridges: the score is 169. The best candidate is the true motion, (0.3, 0.1, 5^\circ), where the points lie along the ridges and the score is 447.

At the odometry guess (0.3, 0, 0) they sit beside the bright ridges, score 169; at the best candidate (0.3, 0.1, 5 degrees) they lie on the ridges, score 447
Because the field is smooth, the score also rises smoothly towards the best candidate, so the search can be refined by small steps, for example by gradient ascent from the best grid point (Freiburg slides: the distance grid “is smooth w.r.t. to small changes in robot position”; Olson 2009).


                  
                  Extra 
                  
                

The field must be dense enough. With 72 beams per scan (one every 5°), scan 1’s end points 3 m away lie about 0.26 m apart, more than twice the field’s standard deviation \sigma of 0.1 m. The field then has dark gaps between the points, and the same search picks (0.28, 0.1, 7^\circ) instead of the true motion (the notebook shows it). Denser scans, a wider \sigma, or a field built from several scans fix it.


Scan matching measures how far the robot moved between two scans, not where it stands in the map; Section 6 compares a scan with the map itself.
6. Correlation-based map matching


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Turn the scan into a small map of marked cells, place it on the global map at a candidate pose, and measure how well the two agree with a correlation coefficient. The placement with the highest correlation is the best pose.


6.1 A local map from the scan
Scan matching (G-2395)Scan matching: Aligning two range scans to find the motion between the poses they were taken from, for example by sliding the second scan over a likelihood field built from the first; it corrects drifting odometry. Explained in §5.1 The problem: odometry drifts. compared one scan with another. A third way to score a pose compares the scan with the global map, again without a ray cast per beam: it compares maps instead of points. We mark, on cells of 0.1 m, every cell that holds an end point of scan 2. This small grid built from the robot’s own readings is a local map (G-2398)Local map: A small grid map built from the robot’s current readings alone, such as the cells holding a scan’s endpoints; map matching compares it with the global map. Explained in §6.1 A local map from the scan.. Placed at a candidate pose, it should line up with the global map’s occupied cells (Freiburg slides, “Map matching: generate small, local maps from sensor data and match local maps against global model”). Comparing the two grids cell by cell to score the placement is map matching (G-2397)Map matching (correlation-based): Scoring a guessed pose by placing a local map built from the scan on the global map there and computing their correlation, cut at zero; it is cheap but coarse, limited by the cell size. Explained in §6.1 A local map from the scan. (Thrun §6.5).
6.2 Multiply and add
The simplest comparison places the local map (G-2398)Local map: A small grid map built from the robot’s current readings alone, such as the cells holding a scan’s endpoints; map matching compares it with the global map. Explained in §6.1 A local map from the scan. on the global map, multiplies matching cells and adds the products (Konolige and Chou 1999: “places the sensor patch on the map, multiplies the corresponding values, and sums them”). A cell adds 1 only where both maps are marked. Take a strip of 8 cells across a corridor, small enough to work by hand, with walls in cells 3 and 7 of the global map:

















































Cell12345678global map g00100010local map, placed off by one01000100local map, placed right00100010
Placed off by one, no marked cells meet, so the sum is 0; placed right, two meet, so the sum is 2. Larger is better.
The raw sum has a flaw: it rewards a local map for marking many cells. In the room of Figure 1, the right placement of scan 2 scores 175, but a local map with every cell marked scores 224, the global map’s whole count. A comparison must not prefer “everything is a wall”.
6.3 Why we normalise: the correlation coefficient
The fix is the Pearson correlation coefficient (G-1474)Pearson correlation coefficient (Pearson’s r): A number from −1 to +1 that measures how closely two numerical columns follow a straight-line relationship (+1: they rise together exactly; 0: no straight-line link), written r; it is the one df.corr() computes. Explained in: Understanding Your Data: Seven First Questions, §9.1 Correlation of the two maps, read cell by cell as two lists of numbers. The coefficient subtracts each map’s mean before multiplying, so cells marked everywhere earn nothing, and divides by the two maps’ standard deviations (G-1871)Standard deviation: How far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n - 1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default). Explained in: Understanding Your Data: Seven First Questions, §7.1 Count, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum, their typical spread about the mean, so the result lies between −1 and +1. For the two maps, read cell by cell:

g_i is cell i of the global map, 1 if marked and 0 if not;
l_i is cell i of the local map (G-2398)Local map: A small grid map built from the robot’s current readings alone, such as the cells holding a scan’s endpoints; map matching compares it with the global map. Explained in §6.1 A local map from the scan., 1 or 0 in the same way;
\bar g is the global map’s mean, the share of its cells that are marked;
\bar l is the local map’s mean;
\sum_i adds the terms over all cells i;
r is the correlation, a number from −1 to +1.

r = \frac{\sum_i (g_i - \bar g)(l_i - \bar l)}{\sqrt{\sum_i (g_i - \bar g)^2\ \sum_i (l_i - \bar l)^2}}
Thrun §6.5 uses this correlation for map matching (G-2397)Map matching (correlation-based): Scoring a guessed pose by placing a local map built from the scan on the global map there and computing their correlation, cut at zero; it is cheap but coarse, limited by the cell size. Explained in §6.1 A local map from the scan..
Worked example: the strip placed off by one. Both maps mark 2 of 8 cells:
\bar g = \bar l = 2 / 8 = 0.25
Each cell’s product (g_i - 0.25)(l_i - 0.25) is one of three values:


both 0 (4 cells):
(-0.25) \times (-0.25) = 0.0625


one marked, one not (4 cells):
0.75 \times (-0.25) = -0.1875


both marked: no such cell.


The top of the fraction:
4 \times 0.0625 = 0.25
4 \times (-0.1875) = -0.75
0.25 - 0.75 = -0.5
Each map’s sum of squares, 2 marked and 6 unmarked cells:
2 \times 0.75^2 + 6 \times 0.25^2 = 1.5
The correlation:
r = \frac{-0.5}{\sqrt{1.5 \times 1.5}}
= -0.5 / 1.5 = -0.333
Placed right, the two lists are identical, so r = 1. A local map with half its cells marked at random gets r = 0.001 against the room, although its raw sum is 113: the correlation sees that it agrees with the walls no better than chance.
The score is used as the likelihood of the reading at that pose, a weight for the pose, and a likelihood cannot be negative. The correlation can be, as the placement off by one shows. Only a positive correlation counts as evidence for a pose; a negative one is treated the same as no correlation at all. So the score of a placement is the correlation cut at zero (Thrun §6.5; Omr et al. 2024):
\text{score} = \max(r,\ 0)
For the strip placed off by one:
\max(-0.333,\ 0) = 0
6.4 Matching scan 2 against the room
Figure 11 slides scan 2’s local map (G-2398)Local map: A small grid map built from the robot’s current readings alone, such as the cells holding a scan’s endpoints; map matching compares it with the global map. Explained in §6.1 A local map from the scan. along x over the room’s map, 2 cm at a time: watch the red cells line up with the grey walls as the correlation climbs to a flat top, then drift off again as it falls. With the turn fixed at 5° and the sideways shift at 0.1 m, the correlation rises from about 0.6 to a flat top of 0.86 to 0.875 for a shift along x, \Delta x, between 0.24 and 0.36 m. Its best value is at 0.28 m, next to the true 0.3 m. Searching all candidates of Section 5.3, the best placement is (0.30, 0.08, 6^\circ) with correlation r = 0.877, against r = 0.872 at the true motion and 0.617 at the odometry guess.

Figure 11: Animation of map matching on 0.1 m cells. Left: the global map (grey cells along the walls and around the box) and the local map of scan 2 (red cells, the cells that hold an end point), placed at a candidate shift along x, dx, with the sideways shift fixed at 0.1 m and the turn at 5°; end points that fall beyond the map’s edge are counted in its edge cells. Right: the correlation r of the two maps, drawn point by point as dx slides from −0.1 to 0.7 m in steps of 0.02 m: about 0.6 at both ends and a flat top near 0.87 between 0.24 and 0.36 m. The last frame keeps the best placement, dx = 0.28 m with r = 0.875, where the red cells cover the walls and the two box faces the robot can see
So map matching found the motion to within one cell (0.1 m) and one degree. The flat top shows its limit: on 0.1 m cells, placements a few centimetres apart mark the same cells, so they cannot be told apart. Smaller cells sharpen it at a higher cost. Map matching is cheap and needs only a grid comparison, but its score is a measure of agreement, not a density derived from how the sensor works; like the likelihood field (G-2393)Likelihood field: A grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam. Explained in §4.2 From distances to the likelihood field., it ignores what lies along each beam (Konolige and Chou 1999: correlation “violates the visibility constraint”).
7. Summary

































ModelLooks atCost per guessed poseSmooth in the poseKnows what blocks a beambeam modelthe whole beam, by ray castinga ray cast per beamno: jumps at edgesyeslikelihood fieldeach beam’s end pointone look-up per beamyesno: sees through wallsmap matchinga local map of the scana grid comparisonin steps of a cellno

The likelihood field fixes both problems of the beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture: scoring the 12-beam scan takes about 0.045 ms instead of 11 ms, and the score of a beam rises smoothly as the robot slides past the box’s edge instead of jumping 270-fold, because each pose needs only one look-up per beam on a field computed once in advance.
The likelihood field model (G-2391)Likelihood field model: A measurement model for range finders that scores each reading by how close its beam endpoint lands to an obstacle in the map (a Gaussian of that distance plus a small uniform part p_{\text{rand}}, so no reading scores 0); it is fast and smooth because it skips ray casting, but it ignores what lies along the beam. Explained in §3.2 From distance to density. scores a reading by the distance from its end point to the nearest obstacle, because a correct reading ends on a surface; the density is a Gaussian of that distance plus a uniform part p_{\text{rand}}, so no reading scores 0.
The distances depend only on where the end point lands, not on the pose, so the whole field is computed once with a distance transform (G-2394)Distance transform: A grid that stores, for every cell of a map, the distance to the nearest occupied cell (with straight-line distances, the Euclidean distance transform); it lets a likelihood field be built in one pass. Explained in §4.1 The distance transform. and every later score is a look-up: about 250 times faster than the beam model in our test.
The field changes smoothly with the pose, because moving the robot moves each end point only a little, so a search by small steps can climb it; the beam model jumps when a beam slips past an edge.
The price is physics: the field ignores what lies along the beam, so it can score a reading that would have to pass through a wall, and it has no part for people.
Scan matching (G-2395)Scan matching: Aligning two range scans to find the motion between the poses they were taken from, for example by sliding the second scan over a likelihood field built from the first; it corrects drifting odometry. Explained in §5.1 The problem: odometry drifts. builds a field from one scan and slides the next scan over it; the best shift, here (0.3 m, 0.1 m, 5°), is the motion the odometry got wrong.
Map matching (G-2397)Map matching (correlation-based): Scoring a guessed pose by placing a local map built from the scan on the global map there and computing their correlation, cut at zero; it is cheap but coarse, limited by the cell size. Explained in §6.1 A local map from the scan. compares a local map of the scan with the global map by their correlation, cut at zero, because the raw sum of products would reward a local map that marks everything.

Now the robot can score hundreds of guessed poses per scan quickly, and measure its own motion by matching one scan against the last. Still missing: one laser end point looks like any other, so a score says how well the scan fits the walls but not which object each beam hit; a landmark readingExplained in: Landmark Measurement Model, §1. Overview, such as the range and bearing to a known pole, says which object it saw.

RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-012-.title: Landmark Measurement Model
RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-012-.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Normal distributionNormal distribution: A symmetric, bell-shaped distribution: most values sit near the mean and they get rarer the further out we go; its mean and standard deviation set its centre and width. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is; Independent and mutually exclusive eventsExplained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Independent Events, §2. The definition; Maps and landmarksMap: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §2.1 What a map is for.
Compare with: Likelihood field modelLikelihood field model: A measurement model for range finders that scores each reading by how close its beam endpoint lands to an obstacle in the map (a Gaussian of that distance plus a small uniform part p_{\text{rand}}, so no reading scores 0); it is fast and smooth because it skips ray casting, but it ignores what lies along the beam. Explained in: Likelihood Fields and Scan Matching, §3. The likelihood field model.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A landmark reading is a range and a bearing to a known point, and the model scores a guessed pose with two Gaussians (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is around the range and bearing that pose predicts. One reading puts the robot on a ring, three readings pin it to one spot, and a reading can also be turned around to propose poses.



Figure 1: The 5 m by 4 m room with three coloured poles: pink at (4.4, 3.8), green at (0.4, 3.2), blue at (3.2, 0.4). The robot at A = (2, 2, 0) reads each one as a range and a bearing: pink 3.10 m at 40 degrees, green 1.95 m at 141 degrees, blue 2.05 m at −55 degrees
The likelihood field (G-2393)Likelihood field: A grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam. Explained in: Likelihood Fields and Scan Matching, §4.2 From distances to the likelihood field lets the robot score a laser scan about 250 times faster than the beam model. What still breaks: a scan gives hundreds of distances, all of which look alike: wall, wall, wall. This Note adds readings that say which object was seen. A camera that spots a pink pole gives far less data, but the data says exactly which object it saw, and the map says exactly where that object stands. Such a recognisable object at a known place is a landmark. Robots pull landmarks (G-2342)Landmark: An object the robot can detect reliably and tell apart from the others, such as a coloured pole or a door; its known position in the map lets readings of it fix the robot’s pose. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §6.1 Why extract features out of sensor dataExplained in: Maps and Landmarks, §6.2 Finding the poles in a scan, and each one is seen as a range (how far), a bearing (at what angle from the robot’s heading (G-2284))Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading and a signature (what it looks like, here its colour).
Figure 1 shows the test case of this Note: the same 5 m by 4 m room and pose A = (2, 2, 0) as the beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture, now with three coloured poles that the robot sees. To use these readings, the robot needs the same thing the beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture gave it for a laser: a measurement model (G-2374)Measurement model p(z \mid \mathbf{x}, m): The density of getting sensor readings z if the robot were at pose \mathbf{x} in map m (also sensor or observation model); read over poses it is a likelihood that tells a filter which poses fit the readings. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §2.2 Why we need a measurement model, the density of the readings p(z \mid \mathbf{x}, m) for any guessed pose \mathbf{x} in the map m. The question is: how well does a guessed pose, such as A or a pose B 1 m to its right, explain these three readings? This Note builds the model that answers it:

what range and bearing a pole should show from a guessed pose, and the two pitfalls in computing the angle (Section 3);
the density of a reading, and why it is a product of two Gaussians (Section 4);
why one reading puts the robot on a ring, and several readings pin it down (Section 5);
how to turn one reading around and draw poses that fit it (Section 6).

2. A landmark reading


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Each reading is a range, a bearing and a signature; the signature tells us which landmark of the map was seen.


First, what the robot at A gets from each pole of Figure 1. We write one landmark reading as a list of three entries, the range, bearing and signature (G-2343, G-2344, G-2345)Range (of a landmark reading): The distance from the robot to a sensed landmark, such as 2.236 m; together with the bearing it fixes where the landmark is relative to the robot. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §6.3 Range, bearing and signatureBearing: The angle from the robot’s heading to a sensed landmark, positive to the left, such as 86.6 degrees; together with the range it fixes where the landmark is relative to the robot. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §6.3 Range, bearing and signatureSignature (of a landmark): A label that says what kind of landmark was sensed, such as its colour or ID number; it tells the robot which landmark in the map a reading belongs to. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §6.3 Range, bearing and signature:

r is the range: the distance from the robot to the landmark, in m (3.10 m for the pink pole);
\varphi (phi) is the bearing: the angle from the robot’s heading to the landmark, counter-clockwise positive, as for the heading (G-2284)Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading itself, in degrees (40° for the pink pole);
s is the signature: what identifies the landmark, here its colour (pink);
z is the whole reading, the three entries together.

z = (r,\ \varphi,\ s)
The three readings of Figure 1:





























PoleRange rBearing \varphiSignature spink3.10 m40°pinkgreen1.95 m141°greenblue2.05 m−55°blue
A sensor that gives both numbers, such as a laser that picks poles out of its scan or a calibrated camera that also judges size, is a range-bearing sensor (Brown CS148 tutorial; Freiburg sensor-model slides, “Landmarks”). The signature solves a problem the laser scan never had to face: which landmark of the map is this? Knowing which map landmark a reading belongs to is known correspondence (G-2405)Known correspondence: Knowing which landmark of the map a reading belongs to, for example from a unique colour (its signature); with it the model can predict that one landmark’s range and bearing. Explained in §2. A landmark reading.. Here each colour appears once, so the colour gives the correspondence directly (Brown CS148 tutorial, §3). For the landmark a reading belongs to:

c is its index, the number of that landmark in the map’s list;
m_{c,x} is its x coordinate in the map, in m (4.4 m for the pink pole);
m_{c,y} is its y coordinate in the map, in m (3.8 m for the pink pole).

For the pink pole:
(m_{c,x},\ m_{c,y}) = (4.4,\ 3.8)
When colours repeat, the correspondence is unknown and must be worked out too. Here each pole is known, so for any guessed pose the robot can ask what that pole should read.
3. What a guessed pose predicts


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

From a guessed pose, position (x, y) and heading (G-2284)Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading \theta, a landmark should appear at the straight-line distance and at its direction minus the heading. Compute the direction with atan2, and wrap every angle difference into −180° to 180°.


3.1 Expected range and bearing
To score a guessed pose against the three readings of Figure 1, we first ask what the robot would read from there. The steps are those that turn a known pose and the map into a readingExplained in: Maps and Landmarks, §6.3 Range, bearing and signature, now done from a guessed pose. Figure 2 draws the pink pole seen from (2, 2), with the robot turned 15° so that the direction to the pole (green) and the bearing (pink) can be told apart; at pose A the heading is 0° and the two are equal. The pole lies 2.4 m further along x and 1.8 m further along y:

\Delta x is how far the pole lies beyond the robot along x, in m;
\Delta y is how far it lies beyond the robot along y, in m.

\Delta x = 4.4 - 2 = 2.4
\Delta y = 3.8 - 2 = 1.8

Figure 2: The pink pole seen from a robot at (2, 2): a right-angled triangle with sides 2.4 along x and 1.8 along y and long side 3.0 m. The direction to the pole is 36.87 degrees from the x-axis; the bearing is that direction minus the robot’s heading
Expected range. The straight-line distance is the long side of the triangle (Pythagoras), the Euclidean distance (G-715)Euclidean distance: The straight-line distance between two points. Explained in: Handling Missing Data: KNN Imputer, §4.1 The Euclidean distance. A hat marks a predicted value:

\hat r is the expected range, the distance the robot should read, in m.

\hat r = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2}
= \sqrt{5.76 + 3.24} = 3.0 \text{ m}
Expected bearing. The direction from the robot to the pole, measured from the world x-axis, is the angle whose tangent is \Delta y / \Delta x:
\text{direction} = \operatorname{atan2}(1.8,\ 2.4) = 36.87^\circ
The bearing is measured from the robot’s heading (G-2284)Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, not from the x-axis, so we subtract the heading (Figure 2):

\theta is the robot’s heading, in degrees (0° at pose A);
\hat\varphi is the expected bearing, in degrees.

\hat\varphi = 36.87^\circ - \theta
= 36.87^\circ - 0^\circ = 36.87^\circ
In general, for landmark c and any guessed pose:

x is the guessed position’s x coordinate, in m (2 m at A);
y is its y coordinate, in m (2 m at A);
m_{c,x} is landmark c‘s x coordinate in the map, in m (4.4 m for the pink pole);
m_{c,y} is its y coordinate in the map, in m (3.8 m for the pink pole).

Together, the expected range and bearing (G-2402)Expected range and bearing (\hat r, \hat\varphi): The range and bearing a landmark would show from a guessed pose: the straight-line distance to its place in the map, and its direction (by atan2) minus the robot’s heading; the model compares the real reading with them. Explained in §3.1 Expected range and bearing. of landmark c from pose (x, y, \theta) are (Thrun §6.6; Brown CS148 tutorial, Eq. 5–6):
\hat r = \sqrt{(m_{c,x} - x)^2 + (m_{c,y} - y)^2}
\hat\varphi = \operatorname{atan2}(m_{c,y} - y,\ m_{c,x} - x) - \theta
3.2 Why atan2 and not arctan
The expected bearing of Section 3.1 takes the direction from atan2, not from the plain arctangent of the ratio. The green pole of Figure 1, at (0.4, 3.2), shows why. From A, how far it lies beyond the robot along x, \Delta x, and along y, \Delta y:
\Delta x = 0.4 - 2 = -1.6
\Delta y = 3.2 - 2 = 1.2
The plain arctangent of the ratio:
\arctan(1.2 / {-1.6}) = \arctan(-0.75)
= -36.87^\circ
That direction points down and to the right, away from the pole (Figure 3). The ratio has lost the signs: a point at (1.6, −1.2) gives the same ratio −0.75. So the formula uses atan2 (G-2325)atan2: A function atan2(rise, run) that returns the direction of a line over the full circle from its rise and run given separately; needed because the plain inverse tangent of the ratio cannot tell opposite directions apart. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §4.2 Turn, drive, turn, which takes \Delta y and \Delta x separately, so it knows which quarter of the plane the point lies in, and returns the angle in the right quarter, between −180° and 180° (Brown CS148 tutorial, §3):
\operatorname{atan2}(1.2,\ -1.6) = 143.13^\circ

Figure 3: The green pole, at (−1.6, 1.2) as seen from the robot. atan2 gives 143.13 degrees, pointing up and left at the pole; arctan of the ratio 1.2 / −1.6 gives −36.87 degrees, pointing down and right, the opposite way
3.3 Why angle differences must be wrapped
Scoring a reading means comparing it with the prediction. For range, the difference is a plain subtraction. For bearings it is not. None of the three poles sits near the ±180° line, where the trouble shows, so take a made-up case: the bearing reads 175° and the prediction is −178°. The two directions are only 7° apart, across the ±180° line, but the plain difference is:
175 - (-178) = 353^\circ
Figure 4 draws both directions on a dial, with 0° pointing right and angles growing counter-clockwise. Follow the two arcs from the prediction to the reading: the plain difference goes the long way round, 353°; the short way, across the ±180° line, is 7°.

Figure 4: A dial with 0 degrees to the right, 90 at the top and ±180 to the left. The reading, 175 degrees, and the prediction, −178 degrees, point left on either side of the ±180 line. A red dashed arc from the prediction goes counter-clockwise all the way round to the reading: the plain difference 175 − (−178) = 353 degrees. A short green arc goes clockwise across the ±180 line: the wrapped difference 353 − 360 = −7 degrees
A bell-shaped error curve around the prediction, a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, would call that a wild miss. The fix is to add or subtract 360° until the difference lies between −180° and 180°:
353^\circ - 360^\circ = -7^\circ
Adding or subtracting full turns in this way is angle wrapping (G-2404)Angle wrapping: Adding or subtracting full turns until an angle or angle difference lies between −180° and 180°, so that 175° and −178° count as 7° apart, not 353°; needed whenever bearings or headings are compared. Explained in §3.3 Why angle differences must be wrapped., the wrap-around of headings (G-2284)Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading on a dial, where 350° and 10° are 20° apart. Every bearing difference and every heading in this Note is wrapped (Brown CS148 tutorial, §3, which uses the angle between two unit vectors to the same effect). With the prediction and a fair way to subtract angles, the robot can now score how far each reading lies from what pose A predicts.
4. The landmark measurement model


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The density of a reading is a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is of the range error times a Gaussian of the bearing error, because the two errors are taken as independent. Several landmarks multiply in the same way.


4.1 Two Gaussians, multiplied
The pink pole reads 3.10 m and 40°, but from pose A it should read 3.00 m and 36.87°: the real reading differs from the prediction by sensor noise. As for the measurement noise of a laserExplained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §4.1 Measurement noise: a Gaussian around the expected range, small errors follow a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is centred on 0. Our sensor has these standard deviations (G-1871)Standard deviation: How far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n - 1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default). Explained in: Understanding Your Data: Seven First Questions, §7.1 Count, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum, the typical size of each error:

\sigma_r is the standard deviation of the range error, 0.1 m;
\sigma_\varphi is the standard deviation of the bearing error, 5°, which is 0.0873 rad.

We treat the range error and the bearing error as independent: knowing that the range came out 10 cm long says nothing about the bearing (Brown CS148 tutorial, Eq. 13). For independent events (G-934)Independent events: Events where one happening does not change the probability of the other; for them the probability that both happen is the product of their probabilities. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Independent Events, §2. The definition the probabilities multiply, and so do the densities. So the density of one reading is the product of two Gaussians. For one reading and one guessed pose:

r is the measured range, in m (3.10 m for the pink pole);
\hat r is the expected range from the guessed pose, in m (3.00 m from A);
\varphi is the measured bearing (40° for the pink pole);
\hat\varphi is the expected bearing (36.87° from A);
\mathcal{N}(e;\ 0, \sigma^2) is the Gaussian density of an error e, with mean 0 and standard deviation \sigma;
\mathbf{x} (bold) is the pose, the three numbers (x, y, \theta); plain x is its first number (pose A is (2, 2, 0));
m is the map, here the places of the three poles;
p(z \mid \mathbf{x}, m) is the density of the reading z given the guessed pose \mathbf{x} and the map m, in per m per rad.

p(z \mid \mathbf{x}, m) = \mathcal{N}(r - \hat r;\ 0, \sigma_r^2)
\qquad \times\ \mathcal{N}(\varphi - \hat\varphi;\ 0, \sigma_\varphi^2)
with the bearing difference wrapped. A camera can confuse colours, so Thrun adds a third Gaussian for the signature; with known correspondence (G-2405)Known correspondence: Knowing which landmark of the map a reading belongs to, for example from a unique colour (its signature); with it the model can predict that one landmark’s range and bearing. Explained in §2. A landmark reading. that factor is the same for every pose and can be left out (Thrun §6.6; Brown CS148 tutorial, Eq. 16–17). The product of the two Gaussians is the landmark measurement model (G-2401)Landmark measurement model: The density of a landmark reading (range, bearing) given a pose and the map: a Gaussian of the range error times a Gaussian of the bearing error, with the errors taken as independent; it scores how well a guessed pose explains what the robot saw. Explained in §4.1 Two Gaussians, multiplied. with known correspondence (Thrun §6.6, Table 6.4; Freiburg sensor-model slides, “Probabilistic Model”).
Worked example: the pink pole at pose A. The errors:
r - \hat r = 3.10 - 3.00 = 0.10 \text{ m}
\varphi - \hat\varphi = 40^\circ - 36.87^\circ = 3.13^\circ
3.13^\circ = 0.05463 \text{ rad}
Figure 5 marks each error on its own Gaussian. Read the height of each black dot: the range error, one standard deviation, lands at 2.420 per m; the bearing error, less than one standard deviation, lands higher up its curve, at 3.758 per rad. The density of the reading is the product of the two heights, worked out below.

The range Gaussian. Its peak height:
\frac{1}{\sigma_r \sqrt{2\pi}} = \frac{1}{0.1 \times 2.5066}

\frac{1}{\sigma_\varphi \sqrt{2\pi}} = \frac{1}{0.08727 \times 2.5066}

\frac{0.05463}{0.08727} = 0.626

2.420 \times 3.758 = 9.09

Python: the model for one reading (Brown CS148 tutorial, Table 2).
def landmark_density(pose, m, r, phi):
    x, y, th = pose
    r_hat = np.hypot(m[0] - x, m[1] - y)
    phi_hat = np.arctan2(m[1] - y, m[0] - x) - th
    return gauss(r - r_hat, 0.1) * gauss(wrap(phi - phi_hat), np.radians(5))

5. Where can the robot be?


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

One range reading allows every position on a ring around the landmark. Two rings meet in at most two points, and a third ring, or the map, picks one.


5.1 One landmark: a ring
Section 4 scored two guessed poses, A and B. Now turn the question around: the readings of Figure 1 are fixed, and we ask which robot positions fit them, starting with one. Take the pink pole’s range, 3.10 m, alone. Every position 3.10 m from the pole predicts that range exactly, whatever its direction from the pole. So the positions that fit form a ring of radius 3.10 m around the pole, blurred by the 0.1 m noise (Freiburg sensor-model slides, “Distances only”).
Figure 6 draws the range Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is over every position of the room as a surface: a curved ridge of height 3.99 per m along the ring, falling to zero on either side. The true position A sits on the ridge, and so does every other point of it.

5.2 Two and three landmarks: rings meet
The green pole’s range, 1.95 m, gives a second ring. A position that fits both readings must lie on both rings. Two circles cross in at most two points, and here one of the two lies outside the room. Finding a position from distances to known points is trilateration (G-2406)Trilateration: Finding a position from measured distances to points at known places: each distance puts the robot on a circle, and the circles meet at the position; GPS works this way. The bearings add the heading (G-2284)Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading. Once the position is known, a bearing says which way the robot faces: the pole must appear at the measured angle from the heading. Rings and bearings say where the robot could be; Section 6 turns them into poses the robot can try.
6. Sampling poses from a landmark reading


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

To propose poses that fit one reading, pick a random angle around the landmark, step out by the measured range, and turn the robot so the landmark appears at the measured bearing.


6.1 Why turn a reading around
The scores of Section 4 can only judge guesses the robot already has; they cannot help when no guess lies near A. A particle filter (G-2492)Particle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in: Particle Filter, §4. The particle filter, step by step keeps a cloud of guessed poses and moves them with the motion model (G-2319)Motion model p(\mathbf x_t \mid u_t, \mathbf x_{t-1}): The probability distribution of a robot’s pose after a move, given its pose before and the control (command or odometry); it describes how uncertain motion is, so a filter can score possible end poses or draw them at random. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §2.2 The motion model and its density, the distribution of where a move ends. If the robot is carried somewhere else, or starts with no idea where it is, none of its guesses may lie near the truth, and weighting them by the measurement model (G-2374)Measurement model p(z \mid \mathbf{x}, m): The density of getting sensor readings z if the robot were at pose \mathbf{x} in map m (also sensor or observation model); read over poses it is a likelihood that tells a filter which poses fit the readings. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §2.2 Why we need a measurement model cannot fix that. A remedy is to add guesses drawn from the reading itself: poses where the robot could be, given what it just saw. Lenser and Veloso used exactly this on soccer-playing legged robots, adding poses drawn from the landmark readings whenever the filter was lost (“sensor resetting localization”, Lenser and Veloso 2000). Drawing poses that fit a reading is sampling poses from a measurement (G-2408)Sampling poses from a measurement: Drawing poses that fit one reading: for a landmark, a random angle around it, the measured range plus noise, and the heading that makes the landmark appear at the measured bearing; used to add good guesses to a particle filter that is lost. Explained in §6.1 Why turn a reading around. (Thrun §6.6.3). The particle filter loopExplained in: Particle Filter, §4.6 The algorithm runs the filter itself; drawing random values from a distribution is sampling (G-2326)Sampling (from a distribution): Drawing random values so that, over many draws, each value comes up as often as a given distribution says; it turns a motion model into a cloud of possible poses for particle filters. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §5.1 Why sample instead of scoring.
6.2 The recipe, and where the heading comes from
Section 5.1 says the robot lies on a ring around the pole, at any angle. So we pick that angle at random, and add noise to the reading so the samples spread as the sensor’s errors do (Thrun §6.6.3, Table 6.5). For one reading of the pink pole:

r is the measured range, 3.10 m;
\varphi is the measured bearing, 40°;
\sigma_r is the standard deviation of the range noise, 0.1 m;
\sigma_\varphi is the standard deviation of the bearing noise, 5°;
m_{c,x} is the pole’s x coordinate in the map, 4.4 m;
m_{c,y} is its y coordinate in the map, 3.8 m;
\gamma (gamma) is the direction from the pole to the robot, in degrees, drawn at random;
\tilde r is the range with noise added, in m;
\tilde\varphi is the bearing with noise added, in degrees;
x is the sampled robot’s x coordinate, in m;
y is its y coordinate, in m;
\theta is the direction the sampled robot faces, in degrees.

The recipe:


Draw an angle \gamma (gamma) around the pole, uniformly from 0° to 360°.


Draw a noisy range and bearing:
\tilde r = r + \text{noise of std. dev. } \sigma_r
\tilde\varphi = \varphi + \text{noise of std. dev. } \sigma_\varphi


Place the robot at distance \tilde r from the pole, in direction \gamma:
x = m_{c,x} + \tilde r \cos\gamma
y = m_{c,y} + \tilde r \sin\gamma


Set the heading (G-2284)Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading (wrapped):
\theta = \gamma + 180^\circ - \tilde\varphi


Step 4 needs a reason. The robot sits in direction \gamma from the pole, so seen from the robot the pole lies the opposite way, half a turn further:
\text{direction to the pole} = \gamma + 180^\circ
The bearing is that direction minus the heading (Section 3.1):
\tilde\varphi = \gamma + 180^\circ - \theta
Solving for the heading gives step 4. Thrun writes the same step in radians, where \pi rad is 180°:
\theta = \gamma - \pi - \tilde\varphi
Both give the same heading, since adding 180° and subtracting 180° differ by a full turn.
Figure 8 runs the recipe on the noise-free reading of A, range 3.0 m and bearing 36.87°, one step at a time. Watch the angle \gamma swing round the pole to 216.87°, the robot step out 3.0 m to (2, 2), and its heading turn from the pole until the pole sits 36.87° to its left: the heading ends at 0°, so the recipe gives back pose A. The animation then runs the same four steps with the real reading and noise, 200 times (Section 6.3).

Terms taught in this Note come first; linked terms are recaps, taught in the Note the link opens.

RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-013-.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Conditional probabilityExplained in: Joint, Marginal and Conditional Probability, §4. Conditional probability; Probability distributionsProbability distribution: A list (or curve) of every possible outcome of a random variable with its probability, adding up to 1; it says how likely each outcome is, so the chance of any event can be worked out from it. Explained in: Random Variables and Probability Distributions, §3. Probability distributions as tables; State, controls and measurementsExplained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §4. The state: what the robot keeps track of; Probabilistic motion modelsMotion model p(\mathbf x_t \mid u_t, \mathbf x_{t-1}): The probability distribution of a robot’s pose after a move, given its pose before and the control (command or odometry); it describes how uncertain motion is, so a filter can score possible end poses or draw them at random. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §2.2 The motion model and its density; Beam modelBeam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture.
Leads to: Bayes filterBayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm; Smoothing and the Viterbi algorithmExplained in: Grid Filters: Histogram Filter and Binary Bayes Filter, §5. Looking back: smoothing and the most likely path.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A robot never sees its own position. What it can keep is a belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in §4.2 The definition.: a probability for every place it might be, computed from the commands it gave and the readings it got.



Figure 1: A hallway of 10 cells, numbered 0 to 9 and joined into a loop, with doors in front of cells 1, 3 and 7; a robot stands in cell 1 and does not know it
With the landmark modelExplained in: Landmark Measurement Model, §4. The landmark measurement model, the robot has a motion model (G-2319)Motion model p(\mathbf x_t \mid u_t, \mathbf x_{t-1}): The probability distribution of a robot’s pose after a move, given its pose before and the control (command or odometry); it describes how uncertain motion is, so a filter can score possible end poses or draw them at random. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §2.2 The motion model and its density and sensor models, so it can score any guessed pose for one command or one reading. What still breaks: each score covers one moment, and nothing says what the robot should carry from one step to the next. This Note adds that memory, the belief.
Figure 1 shows the world of this Note: the same hallway of 10 cellsExplained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §1. Overview as before, with the same layout and numbers, because a belief over 10 cells is 10 numbers we can draw and check by hand. A robot stands in a hallway of 10 cells, each 1 m long. The hallway is a loop: one step to the right of cell 9 is cell 0. There are doors in front of cells 1, 3 and 7, and all three look the same.
The robot has two things to go on:

a door sensor that reads “door” or “wall”, and is sometimes wrong;
its commands, such as “move 2 cells to the right”, which its wheels carry out only roughly.

The robot stands in cell 1, but nothing tells it so. A reading of “door” fits three cells. A move of “2 cells” may really be 1 or 3. So the question of this Note is: what should the robot keep in memory about where it is, so that it can act sensibly?
We answer it in steps:

what the robot really knows: the list of its commands and readings (Section 2);
a first summary of that list: the set of cells it could be in, and why a set is not enough (Section 3);
a better summary: a probability for every cell, the belief (Section 4);
the two probability tables that tell the robot how commands and readings change the belief (Section 5);
one picture of how states, commands and readings depend on each other, the hidden Markov model (G-2439)Hidden Markov model (HMM): A Markov chain whose states cannot be seen, where each state produces an observation that can, such as hidden robot cells producing “door” or “wall” readings; it is the model behind robot state estimation, speech recognition and many trackers. Explained in §6.3 Hidden Markov model. (Section 6).

The state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §4.1 State: from one number to many is what the robot keeps track of, and the commands and readingsExplained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §5.1 Measurements and controls are the two streams of data it receives. In symbols:

t is the time step, counted 1, 2, 3;
x_t is the state, the robot’s cell at time t, a cell number from 0 to 9 (cell 1 at t = 1);
u_t is the command at time t, such as “move 2”;
z_t is the reading at time t, “door” or “wall”.

2. What the robot knows: its history


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The robot cannot know its true cell. It can only know the commands it gave and the readings it got; that list is its information state (G-2431)Information state (history): Everything a robot knows at time t: its starting knowledge plus every command and every reading so far, such as (stay, door, move 2, door); every decision must be based on it, because the true state is never seen. Explained in §2.2 The information state: everything the robot knows..


2.1 Why the true cell is out of reach
The robot stands in cell 1, but its sensor reads “door” in front of three different cells, and it is sometimes wrong. The wheels slip, so the command “move 2” does not say exactly how far the robot went. Nothing the robot has ever received names its cell. Figure 2 sorts the pieces into what the robot cannot see (the top row) and what it can (the framed rows).

Figure 2: Top row, hidden: the true cells x1 = 1, x2 = 3, x3 = 5. Framed rows, known: the commands stay, move 2, move 2 and the readings door, door, wall. The frame is the history the robot knows at t = 3
The robot’s run in Figure 2 is the running example of this Note:





























Time tCommand u_tReading z_tTrue cell x_t (hidden)1staydoor12move 2door33move 2wall5
2.2 The information state: everything the robot knows
The framed part of Figure 2 is everything the robot knows at time t: what it knew at the start, followed by every command and every reading so far. This list is the information state (G-2431)Information state (history): Everything a robot knows at time t: its starting knowledge plus every command and every reading so far, such as (stay, door, move 2, door); every decision must be based on it, because the true state is never seen. Explained in §2.2 The information state: everything the robot knows., also called the history information state (LaValle §11.1.2). At time 2 it is the list (stay, door, move 2, door). Each new step adds one command and one reading.
Why give the list a name? Because it is the only thing a robot’s decisions can be based on. A rule such as “if you think you are at the second door, open it” has to be a rule on what the robot knows, not on its true cell, which it never sees (LaValle §11.1.3).
The trouble with the list is its length. The list grows by two entries every step and never shrinks. A robot that reads its sensor 10 times a second has, after one hour:
10 \times 3600 = 36{,}000 \text{ readings}
Storing and searching that whole list at every step is not practical. So we look for a short summary of the history that keeps everything the robot needs and throws away the rest (LaValle §11.2). Sections 3 and 4 give two such summaries.
3. Summary 1: the set of cells the robot could be in


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

We can keep the set of cells that agree with every command and reading: a move turns each cell into all the cells it can reach, and a reading keeps only the cells that agree with it. With a sensor that can be wrong, the set stops shrinking.


3.1 The set, step by step
A first thing to keep in memory, shorter than the history: the cells the robot could be in. Suppose for a moment that the sensor is never wrong. The reading “door” then means “one of the door cells”. So after the first reading the robot can be in:
\lbrace1, 3, 7 \rbrace
Next, the command “move 2” moves the robot 1, 2 or 3 cells. Every cell of the set becomes all the cells it can reach, and we collect them together (the move stage of Figure 3). The symbol \cup (union) means “all cells in either set”:
\lbrace2,3,4\rbrace\cup \lbrace4,5,6\rbrace\cup \lbrace8,9,0\rbrace
= \lbrace0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 \rbrace
The second reading “door” keeps only the cells of this set that are doors. The symbol \cap (intersection) means “cells in both sets”:
\lbrace0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 \rbrace\cap \lbrace1, 3, 7 \rbrace
= \lbrace3 \rbrace
Figure 3 plays these steps, one set per row. Watch the reading cross out the wall cells, each door cell fan out to the three cells the move can reach, and the second reading cross out every cell but cell 3. Its last stages replay the second reading with a sensor that can be wrong (Section 3.2).

Figure 3: Animation: the hallway of 10 cells with doors (brown tabs) at cells 1, 3 and 7; blue cells are the cells the robot could be in. With a sensor that is never wrong: before any reading, all 10 cells; the reading door crosses out the wall cells and leaves {1, 3, 7}; the move of 2 cells (really 1, 2 or 3) fans cell 1 out to {2, 3, 4}, cell 3 to {4, 5, 6} and cell 7 to {8, 9, 0}, round the loop, and their union is {0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9}; the second reading door crosses out every wall cell and leaves only cell 3. With the real sensor, which reads door at a wall 20 percent of the time, door can be read in all 10 cells, so the second reading removes nothing, and the next move fills all 10 cells. The last frame shows the full hallway: the set never shrinks
The perfect-sensor stages of Figure 3 end on three sets. Only cell 3 can be reached from a door by one move and is itself a door, so the robot knows exactly where it is. This set of possible states (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §4.1 State: from one number to many is the nondeterministic information state (G-2432)Nondeterministic (set-valued) information state: The set of states that agree with every command and reading so far, such as cells {1, 3, 7} after reading “door”; a move replaces it by all reachable states, a reading keeps only the states that fit, but it says nothing about how likely each state is. Explained in §3.1 The set, step by step., also called the set-valued information state (G-2431)Information state (history): Everything a robot knows at time t: its starting knowledge plus every command and every reading so far, such as (stay, door, move 2, door); every decision must be based on it, because the true state is never seen. Explained in §2.2 The information state: everything the robot knows. (LaValle §11.2.2). The set is far shorter than the history: at most 10 cells, however long the robot runs.
3.2 Why a set is not enough
Now use the real sensor, which reads “door” at a wall 20 percent of the time. A reading of “door” is then possible in every cell. In symbols:

S is the set of cells the robot could be in before the reading, such as \lbrace0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 \rbrace after the move of Section 3.1;
\lbrace0, 1, \ldots, 9 \rbrace is the set of cells where “door” can be read, which is now all 10 cells.

So the intersection \cap removes nothing:
S \cap \lbrace0, 1, \ldots, 9 \rbrace= S
The set never shrinks, however many readings arrive (the last stages of Figure 3). Crossing places out only works for a perfect sensor, for the reason shown in why noisy sensors forbid crossing places outExplained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §3.3 Why noisy sensors forbid crossing places out: a wrong reading would cross out the true cell. The set also cannot say that cell 3 fits the readings much better than cell 9: both are simply “possible”. We need a summary that keeps a number for every cell, saying how strongly the readings point to it. Probabilities are that number.
4. Summary 2: a probability for every cell


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in §4.2 The definition. gives every cell the probability that the robot is there, given its whole history. A reading sharpens it; a move shifts it and blurs it.


4.1 The belief, as a picture
The second thing the robot can keep in memory: instead of “possible” or “impossible”, one probability for each of the 10 cells. Together they form a probability distribution (G-1571)Probability distribution: A list (or curve) of every possible outcome of a random variable with its probability, adding up to 1; it says how likely each outcome is, so the chance of any event can be worked out from it. Explained in: Random Variables and Probability Distributions, §3. Probability distributions as tables (a list of every outcome with its probability, adding to 1). Figure 4 plays the running example.

Figure 4: The belief over the 10 cells in five stages: uniform at 0.1; after reading door, three peaks (modes) of 0.19 at the doors; after moving 2 cells, the modes sit at cells 3, 5 and 9; because the move is uncertain, they spread to 0.16; after reading door again, one main mode of 0.31 at cell 3. An arrow marks the true cell
What to watch in each stage:


No idea yet. The robot has no reason to prefer any cell, so each gets the same share:
\frac{1}{10} = 0.1


Reads “door”. The three door cells grow and the seven wall cells shrink. The wall cells do not drop to zero, because the sensor reads “door” at a wall 20 percent of the time. Each door cell is now a peak of the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in §4.2 The definition., a mode (G-1251)Mode: The value that appears most often in the data, so it sits under the highest peak of a histogram or a distribution curve; it gives a centre for data that are not numbers, and a belief with several peaks has several modes. Explained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §5. Mode, so the belief has three modes: it is multimodal (G-1275)Multimodal: Having more than one mode, that is more than one peak (two peaks: bimodal), such as a robot’s belief peaking at three doors; it shows the data point to several separate values, so one mean or one best guess would hide them. Explained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §5. Mode.


Moves 2 cells. Every mode moves 2 cells to the right, with the robot.


The move is uncertain. The move may have been 1 or 3 cells, so each mode spreads onto its neighbours and gets lower (0.19 becomes 0.16).


Reads “door” again. Only the mode at cell 3 sits on a door, so it grows to 0.31 while the others shrink. The tallest bar is the true cell.


Why do the door cells get 0.19 in stage 2? The sensor reads “door” 0.6 of the time at a door and 0.2 at a wall, so each door cell keeps 3 shares to a wall cell’s 1, and with 3 doors and 7 walls a door cell gets 3 of the 16 shares, 0.1875, shown rounded to 0.19 (why noisy sensors forbid crossing places outExplained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §3.3 Why noisy sensors forbid crossing places out). The exact rule behind this share-counting is Bayes’ theorem, applied at every reading by the correction step (G-2448)Correction step (measurement update): The Bayes-filter step after a reading: multiply each state’s predicted belief by the measurement probability p(z_t \mid x_t) and rescale so the beliefs add to 1; it raises the states that explain the reading and sharpens the belief. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.3 The correction step.
4.2 The definition
The robot’s probability for each cell, given everything it knows, is its belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in §4.2 The definition.. Each symbol:

t is the time step, here 2;
\text{bel}(x_t) is the belief, the probability that the robot is in cell x_t at time t, a number from 0 to 1 (0.31 for cell 3 at t = 2);
x_t is the cell at time t, any cell number from 0 to 9; the belief has one value for every possible cell;
p(\ldots) is the probability of what stands left of the bar;
z_{1:t} means all readings from time 1 to t, here (z_1, z_2) = (\text{door}, \text{door}) at t = 2;
u_{1:t} means all commands from time 1 to t, here (\text{stay}, \text{move 2});
the bar \mid is read “given”, as in a conditional probability (G-444)Conditional probability: The probability of an event given that another event has happened: P(A \mid B); it updates a probability with what is now known, such as the chance of reading “door” once the robot is known to be at a door. The robot is always in exactly one cell. The definition conditions on every command and reading since the start, which looks like the long list we wanted to avoid. The history is there because the robot does not know its earlier cells either: if it knew its previous cell x_{t-1}, that one cell plus the latest command and reading would be enough, but it only has the history (PR §2.3.4). 4.5 The predicted belief: after the move, before the reading

Moving makes the robot less sure, sensing makes it more sure showed. A move adds doubt, because the robot cannot be sure how far it went. A reading removes doubt, because it rules places in or out. A Bayesian network (G-2531)Bayesian network: A graph of random variables drawn as circles, with an arrow into each variable from the variables its probability depends on directly; each circle holds one table of its probability given those variables, and multiplying the tables gives the probability of everything together, so one huge table splits into small ones. Explained in §6.1 A small piece of maths: Bayesian networks. draws each variable as a circle, with arrows into it from the variables its probability depends on directly. Each circle has one table, its probability given the circles with arrows into it, and the probability of all variables together is the product of these tables (CS188 §6.3).
