Explained in §5.1 How a command moves the robot: the state transition probability.A sequence of random states in which the next state depends only on the current one, not on earlier ones, such as a robot repeating “move 2”; it lets a whole sequence be described by one table of transition probabilities.Measurement probability (G-2435)Measurement probability: The probability of a sensor reading given the true state, p(z_t \mid x_t), such as 0.6 for reading “door” in front of a door; it tells the robot how well each state explains a reading. Explained in §5.2 What the sensor reads in each place: the measurement probability.The probability of a sensor reading given the true state, p(z_t \mid x_t), such as 0.6 for reading “door” in front of a door; it tells the robot how well each state explains a reading.Bayesian network (G-2531)Bayesian network: A graph of random variables drawn as circles, with an arrow into each variable from the variables its probability depends on directly; each circle holds one table of its probability given those variables, and multiplying the tables gives the probability of everything together, so one huge table splits into small ones. Explained in §6.1 A small piece of maths: Bayesian networks.A graph of random variables drawn as circles, with an arrow into each variable from the variables its probability depends on directly; each circle holds one table of its probability given those variables, and multiplying the tables gives the probability of everything together, so one huge table splits into small ones.Dynamic Bayes network (G-2441)Dynamic Bayes network: A Bayesian network that repeats the same variables at every time step, such as states, commands and readings of a robot; it shows which variable depends on which over time, so a whole run’s probability splits into small factors. Explained in §6.2 The robot as a dynamic Bayes network.A Bayesian network that repeats the same variables at every time step, such as states, commands and readings of a robot; it shows which variable depends on which over time, so a whole run’s probability splits into small factors.Motion model p(\mathbf x_t \mid u_t, \mathbf x_{t-1}) (G-2319)Motion model p(\mathbf x_t \mid u_t, \mathbf x_{t-1}): The probability distribution of a robot’s pose after a move, given its pose before and the control (command or odometry); it describes how uncertain motion is, so a filter can score possible end poses or draw them at random. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §2.2 The motion model and its densityThe probability distribution of a robot’s pose after a move, given its pose before and the control (command or odometry); it describes how uncertain motion is, so a filter can score possible end poses or draw them at random.State x_t (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §4.1 State: from one number to manyThe quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate.Probability distribution (G-1571)Probability distribution: A list (or curve) of every possible outcome of a random variable with its probability, adding up to 1; it says how likely each outcome is, so the chance of any event can be worked out from it. Explained in: Random Variables and Probability Distributions, §3. Probability distributions as tablesA list (or curve) of every possible outcome of a random variable with its probability, adding up to 1; it says how likely each outcome is, so the chance of any event can be worked out from it.Mode (G-1251)Mode: The value that appears most often in the data, so it sits under the highest peak of a histogram or a distribution curve; it gives a centre for data that are not numbers, and a belief with several peaks has several modes. Explained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §5. ModeThe value that appears most often in the data, so it sits under the highest peak of a histogram or a distribution curve; it gives a centre for data that are not numbers, and a belief with several peaks has several modes.Multimodal (G-1275)Multimodal: Having more than one mode, that is more than one peak (two peaks: bimodal), such as a robot’s belief peaking at three doors; it shows the data point to several separate values, so one mean or one best guess would hide them. Explained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §5. ModeHaving more than one mode, that is more than one peak (two peaks: bimodal), such as a robot’s belief peaking at three doors; it shows the data point to several separate values, so one mean or one best guess would hide them.Correction step (measurement update) (G-2448)Correction step (measurement update): The Bayes-filter step after a reading: multiply each state’s predicted belief by the measurement probability p(z_t \mid x_t) and rescale so the beliefs add to 1; it raises the states that explain the reading and sharpens the belief. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.3 The correction stepThe Bayes-filter step after a reading: multiply each state’s predicted belief by the measurement probability p(z_t \mid x_t) and rescale so the beliefs add to 1; it raises the states that explain the reading and sharpens the belief.Conditional probability (G-444)Conditional probability: The probability of an event given that another event has happened: P(A \mid B); it updates a probability with what is now known, such as the chance of reading “door” once the robot is known to be at a door. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Conditional Probability, §2. The definitionThe probability of an event given that another event has happened: P(A \mid B); it updates a probability with what is now known, such as the chance of reading “door” once the robot is known to be at a door.Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithmThe algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption.Histogram filter (discrete Bayes filter) (G-2461)Histogram filter (discrete Bayes filter): The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position. Explained in: Grid Filters: Histogram Filter and Binary Bayes Filter, §2.1 Why cellsThe Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position.Complete state (G-2315)Complete state: A state that, once known, makes earlier states, controls and measurements useless for predicting the future (position plus speed for a coasting robot, not position alone); it lets the robot keep only its latest estimate. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §4.3 Complete state and the Markov propertyA state that, once known, makes earlier states, controls and measurements useless for predicting the future (position plus speed for a coasting robot, not position alone); it lets the robot keep only its latest estimate.Markov property (G-2316)Markov property: The property of a sequence of states that the future depends on the past only through the present state; it lets a filter forget the history and work from the latest state alone. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §4.3 Complete state and the Markov propertyThe property of a sequence of states that the future depends on the past only through the present state; it lets a filter forget the history and work from the latest state alone.Beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixtureThe measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose.

RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-014-.title: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update
RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-014-.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Probability density function (PDF)Probability density function (PDF): A curve showing how likely each value is; areas under it are probabilities. Explained in: Probability Density Function and the CDF of a Continuous Variable, §4. Bars whose area is probability: the PDF; Bayes’ theoremBayes’ theorem: The rule that reverses a conditional probability: from P(B \mid A) it gives P(A \mid B), so a belief about A can be updated after seeing B; P(A \mid B) = P(B \mid A) P(A) / P(B). Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Bayes’ Theorem, §4. The formula and its proof; Probabilistic motion modelsMotion model p(\mathbf x_t \mid u_t, \mathbf x_{t-1}): The probability distribution of a robot’s pose after a move, given its pose before and the control (command or odometry); it describes how uncertain motion is, so a filter can score possible end poses or draw them at random. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §2.2 The motion model and its density; BeliefBelief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition.
Leads to: Binary Bayes filterBinary Bayes filter: The Bayes filter for a yes-or-no state that does not change, such as “door open” or “this map cell is occupied”, run in log odds: each reading adds the log of its Bayes factor. It is fast and does not round to 0 or 1. Explained in: Grid Filters: Histogram Filter and Binary Bayes Filter, §4. The binary Bayes filter; Histogram filterHistogram filter (discrete Bayes filter): The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position. Explained in: Grid Filters: Histogram Filter and Binary Bayes Filter, §2. The histogram filter; Particle filterParticle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in: Particle Filter, §4. The particle filter, step by step; Kalman filterKalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in §4.4 The algorithm. updates a robot’s belief one step at a time: a prediction step pushes the belief through the motion model after each command, and a correction step multiplies it by the measurement probability after each reading. The robot never needs to store its history.


So far the robot keeps a belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition: a probability for every possible state, given every command and every reading since it started. That list is what still breaks. The list grows by one command and one reading at every step: a robot that reads its sensor 10 times a second holds 36,000 readings after an hour, and by its definition the belief must be recomputed from all of them. This Note adds the Bayes filter, which keeps only the last belief, and answers the question: how can a robot keep its belief up to date at every step, using only the newest command and the newest reading?

Figure 1: Thrun’s door world: a door that is open (left) or closed (right); a robot in front of it with an arm that can push the door and a sensor that reads open or closed
We leave the hallway, where the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition was a probability for each of 10 cells, for Thrun’s door world (Figure 1): 2 states instead of 10 cells, so every sum can be done by hand (PR §2.4.2). The grid filtersExplained in: Grid Filters: Histogram Filter and Binary Bayes Filter, §1. Overview bring the filter back to the hallway. This Note covers:

one reading at a time, with Bayes’ theorem (G-269)Bayes’ theorem: The rule that reverses a conditional probability: from P(B \mid A) it gives P(A \mid B), so a belief about A can be updated after seeing B; P(A \mid B) = P(B \mid A) P(A) / P(B). Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Bayes’ Theorem, §4. The formula and its proof that remembers earlier readings (Section 3);
the filter itself, a prediction step (G-2447)Prediction step (motion update): The Bayes-filter step after a command: for each state, add up the probability of reaching it from every previous state, weighted by the belief in that state, \overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) = \sum p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1})\ \text{bel}(x_{t-1}); it moves the belief with the robot and usually widens it, because the motion is uncertain; a near-certain command, such as a push that opens a door, can make the belief sharper. Explained in §4.2 The prediction step. and a correction step, worked on the door (Section 4);
why the two steps give the exact belief, and which three assumptions that needs (Section 5);
the same two steps on a continuous position along the hallway, where sums become integrals (G-957)Integration: Finding the area under a curve by adding up infinitely many thin strips. Explained in: Probability Density Function and the CDF of a Continuous Variable, §3. Area under the curve is probability (Section 6);
why the belief is all the robot needs to keep (Section 7), and which later filters are this one in disguise (Section 8).

2. The door world


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

One state (the door, open or closed), two commands (push, do nothing), one noisy sensor. Its two probability tables are all the filter needs.


The robot does not know whether the door is open. The two tables that drive the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition describe the robot (PR §2.4.2); with them and its last belief, the filter never needs the list of past readings. At step t:

x_t is the state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §4.1 State: from one number to many, the door at time t: open or closed;
x_{t-1} is the door one step earlier;
x_0 is the door at the start, before any command;
u_t is the command: push or do nothing (do nothing at t = 1, push at t = 2);
z_t is the reading: “sense open” or “sense closed” (“sense open” at both steps);
\text{bel}(x_t) is the robot’s belief, its probability for each door state at time t, a number from 0 to 1 (0.5 for open at the start).

The measurement probability (G-2435)Measurement probability: The probability of a sensor reading given the true state, p(z_t \mid x_t), such as 0.6 for reading “door” in front of a door; it tells the robot how well each state explains a reading. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §5.2 What the sensor reads in each place: the measurement probability p(z_t \mid x_t): the sensor reads “open” or “closed”, and is sometimes wrong.




















True doorp(sense open)p(sense closed)open0.60.4closed0.20.8
The numbers are the same as for the door sensor of the hallway.
The state transition probability (G-2434)State transition probability: The probability of the next state given the command and the previous state, p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1}), such as 0.8 for “move 2” taking the robot from cell 1 to cell 3; it tells the robot how a command changes where it is. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §5.1 How a command moves the robot: the state transition probability p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1}): the robot can push the door or do nothing.



































CommandDoor beforep(open after)p(closed after)pushopen10pushclosed0.80.2do nothingopen10do nothingclosed01
A push on a closed door fails one time in five, because the door is heavy. Doing nothing changes nothing.
The start. The robot has no idea, so its first belief is:
\text{bel}(x_0 = \text{open}) = 0.5
\text{bel}(x_0 = \text{closed}) = 0.5
The run. At t = 1 the robot does nothing and senses “open”. At t = 2 it pushes and senses “open” again. We want its belief after each step.
3. One reading at a time: Bayes’ theorem with past readings


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Bayes’ theorem (G-269)Bayes’ theorem: The rule that reverses a conditional probability: from P(B \mid A) it gives P(A \mid B), so a belief about A can be updated after seeing B; P(A \mid B) = P(B \mid A) P(A) / P(B). Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Bayes’ Theorem, §4. The formula and its proof turns “how likely is this reading in each state” into “how likely is each state given the reading”. Applied again with the first answer as the new prior, it adds a second reading, provided the readings are independent once the state is known.


3.1 Why the robot needs Bayes’ theorem
First the readings alone: can the robot take in a new reading without going back to the old ones? For now, nobody touches the door; the robot only reads. Its table tells it p(z \mid x): how often the sensor reads “open” for each kind of door. The robot needs the other direction, p(x \mid z): given the reading, how likely is each kind of door? For one reading:

x is the door, open or closed;
z is the reading, here “sense open”;
p(x) is the prior (G-1565)Prior: The probability of an event before any evidence is seen. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Bayes’ Theorem, §3. The names of the four parts, the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition in each door before the reading, 0.5 for open and 0.5 for closed;
p(z \mid x) is the chance of the reading given the door, from the table (0.6 for an open door, 0.2 for a closed one);
p(z) is the overall chance of the reading, 0.4 for “sense open” (found below);
p(x \mid z) is the posterior (G-1536)Posterior: The probability of an event after the evidence is taken into account. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Bayes’ Theorem, §3. The names of the four parts, the belief in each door after the reading (0.75 for open, found below).

Bayes’ theorem (G-269)Bayes’ theorem: The rule that reverses a conditional probability: from P(B \mid A) it gives P(A \mid B), so a belief about A can be updated after seeing B; P(A \mid B) = P(B \mid A) P(A) / P(B). Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Bayes’ Theorem, §4. The formula and its proof turns one into the other:
p(x \mid z) = \frac{p(z \mid x)\ p(x)}{p(z)}
First reading, “sense open”. Multiply each prior by how well that door explains the reading:
\text{open: } 0.6 \times 0.5 = 0.3
\text{closed: } 0.2 \times 0.5 = 0.1
The two products are not yet probabilities, because they add to 0.4, not 1. Their sum is the evidence (G-718)Evidence: The overall chance of seeing what we observed, counted over every possible hypothesis, written P(E). Bayes’ theorem divides by it: posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Bayes’ Theorem, §3. The names of the four parts p(z), the overall chance of the reading, by the law of total probability (G-1053)Law of total probability: The rule for the overall probability of an event: add its probability under each case, weighted by how likely that case is, P(B) = \sum_i P(B \mid A_i) P(A_i), when the cases A_i are mutually exclusive and cover every possibility. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: A Bayes’ Theorem Problem, §1. Overview. Divide by it:
p(\text{open} \mid z_1) = 0.3 / 0.4 = 0.75
p(\text{closed} \mid z_1) = 0.1 / 0.4 = 0.25
Dividing by the sum is the same as multiplying by its inverse, written \eta (eta):
\eta = 1 / 0.4 = 2.5
This number is the normaliser (G-2382)Normalizer \eta: The factor that rescales a set of numbers, or a density, so that they add up (or integrate) to 1; it is always one over the current total: the sum of the products in the Bayes filter (1/0.4 = 2.5 after a reading in the door world), the area under the cut curve in the beam model (1/0.655 = 1.53). Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §4.1 Measurement noise: a Gaussian around the expected range: whatever factor makes the products add to 1, the same job it does for the cut Gaussian of the beam modelExplained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §4.1 Measurement noise: a Gaussian around the expected range. We never need p(z) from anywhere else, because it is always the sum of the products (PR §2.2).
3.2 A second reading: Bayes’ theorem with background knowledge
One reading leaves a 0.25 chance of a closed door. To be surer, the robot reads again and again gets “open”. Now the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition must depend on both readings. For the second reading:

x is the door, open or closed;
z is the new reading, here the second reading z_2, “sense open”;
C is the background knowledge, everything known before z, here the first reading z_1, “sense open”.

Bayes’ theorem still works if every term also carries the earlier readings C behind the bar:
p(x \mid z, C) = \frac{p(z \mid x, C)\ p(x \mid C)}{p(z \mid C)}
The formula is Bayes’ rule with background knowledge (G-2452)Bayes’ rule with background knowledge: Bayes’ theorem with an extra condition C in every term, p(x \mid z, C) = p(z \mid x, C)\ p(x \mid C) / p(z \mid C), such as earlier readings; it lets the posterior after one reading serve as the prior for the next. Explained in §3.2 A second reading: Bayes’ theorem with background knowledge. (PR §2.2). The rule holds for the same reason as the plain rule: the joint probability of x and z given C splits two ways by the multiplication rule (G-2212)Multiplication rule: The chance that both A and B happen is the chance of B times the chance of A given B: P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B) \times P(B). Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Conditional Probability, §5. The multiplication rule. The door’s numbers for an open door, all found below: 0.6 for a second “sense open” given the door and the first reading, 0.75 before the second reading, 0.9 after it, and 0.5 for a second “sense open” given the first:
0.6 \times 0.75 = 0.45 = 0.9 \times 0.5
p(z \mid x, C)\ p(x \mid C) = p(x, z \mid C)
= p(x \mid z, C)\ p(z \mid C)
0.9 = 0.45 / 0.5
p(x \mid z, C) = p(x, z \mid C) / p(z \mid C)
With z_2 in place of z and z_1 in place of C, two of the terms are known:

p(x \mid z_1) is the answer of Section 3.1: the old posterior becomes the new prior;
p(z_2 \mid x, z_1) asks how likely the second reading is, given the door and the first reading.

Here the robot makes an assumption: once the state of the door is known, the first reading tells nothing more about the second. Each reading is the door plus its own independent sensor noise. So:
p(z_2 \mid x, z_1) = p(z_2 \mid x)
The assumption is conditional independence (G-443)Conditional independence: Independence that holds once a third variable is known: given the class, knowing one feature tells nothing more about another. Naive Bayes assumes it so it can multiply one probability per feature. Explained in: Naive Bayes: The Mathematics, §5. Step 3: the naive assumption: independence that holds given the state. The assumption does not say that the two readings are independent on their own. They are not, as the robot’s own numbers show:
p(z_2 = \text{open}) = 0.6 \times 0.5 + 0.2 \times 0.5
= 0.4
p(z_2 = \text{open} \mid z_1 = \text{open})
= 0.6 \times 0.75 + 0.2 \times 0.25 = 0.5
A first “open” makes a second “open” more likely (0.5 instead of 0.4), because it makes an open door more likely. Only when the door is known does that link disappear.
Second reading, “sense open”. Same recipe, with 0.75 and 0.25 as the prior:
\text{open: } 0.6 \times 0.75 = 0.45
\text{closed: } 0.2 \times 0.25 = 0.05
\eta = 1 / (0.45 + 0.05) = 2
p(\text{open} \mid z_1, z_2) = 2 \times 0.45 = 0.9
p(\text{closed} \mid z_1, z_2) = 2 \times 0.05 = 0.1
Figure 2 plays both readings. For each one, watch the two bars shrink when multiplied by 0.6 and 0.2, then grow back when rescaled by \eta, one over their sum: the belief in an open door climbs from 0.5 to 0.75, then to 0.9.

Figure 2: Animation of the two readings. Each panel holds the belief in an open and a closed door (blue bars). For each reading, the bars of the belief before it are multiplied by p(z | x), the chance of “sense open” given the door: 0.6 for open, 0.2 for closed. The products turn grey: they add to 0.4 after the first reading and 0.5 after the second, not 1, so they are not yet probabilities. Then both are multiplied by η (eta), one over their sum (2.5, then 2), and grow back into blue bars that add to 1. The last frame shows the belief before any reading (0.5 for open), after the first sense open (0.75) and after the second (0.9)
The robot never went back to the first reading: it kept one number, 0.75, and reused it. That reuse is the whole idea of a filter. So far, though, nothing has changed the door between readings.
4. The Bayes filter: predict, then correct


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Each step has two parts. Prediction: after the command, add up every way of reaching each state. Correction: after the reading, multiply by the measurement probability and rescale.


4.1 Why a moving world needs a second step
Section 3 kept only the last answer, but it assumed nothing changes the door. Once the robot pushes, the door may change between readings, and a robot that drives changes its own position. The belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. The direct way to know the belief is to recompute it from the whole history at every step (Figure 3, the archive row). 4.2 The prediction step
After the command, before the reading, the robot wants its predicted belief (G-2436)Predicted belief: The belief after the latest command but before the latest reading, \overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t-1}, u_{1:t}); it separates the doubt a move adds from the knowledge a reading brings. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.5 The predicted belief: after the move, before the reading \overline{\text{bel}}(x_t). The robot does not know the previous state, so it considers every previous state, asks how likely the command takes it to x_t, and weights that by how much it believed in that previous state. At step t:

x_{t-1} is the door before the command, open or closed;
x_t is the door after the command, open or closed;
u_t is the command, push at t = 2;
\text{bel}(x_{t-1}) is the belief before the command, a number from 0 to 1 (0.75 for open after t = 1);
p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1}) is the state transition probability of Section 2, the chance that the command turns door x_{t-1} into door x_t (0.8 for a push that opens a closed door);
\sum_{x_{t-1}} adds over every possible previous state, here open and closed;
\overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) is the predicted belief, after the command and before the reading, a number from 0 to 1 (0.95 for open at t = 2).

Adding up every way of reaching x_t is the law of total probability (G-1053)Law of total probability: The rule for the overall probability of an event: add its probability under each case, weighted by how likely that case is, P(B) = \sum_i P(B \mid A_i) P(A_i), when the cases A_i are mutually exclusive and cover every possibility. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: A Bayes’ Theorem Problem, §1. Overview:
\overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) = \sum_{x_{t-1}} p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1})
\times\ \text{bel}(x_{t-1})

4.4 The algorithm
Together the two steps are the Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in §4.4 The algorithm. (PR §2.4.1). With the symbols listed in Section 4.2 and Section 4.3, for every possible state x_t:

Predict: \overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) = \sum_{x_{t-1}} p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1})\ \text{bel}(x_{t-1}).
Correct: \text{bel}(x_t) = \eta\ p(z_t \mid x_t)\ \overline{\text{bel}}(x_t).

Then return \text{bel}(x_t) and wait for the next command and reading.

Python: one step of the filter for a finite set of states.
import numpy as np
T_push = np.array([[1.0, 0.0],    # from open: to open, closed
                   [0.8, 0.2]])   # from closed
p_z = np.array([0.6, 0.2])        # p(sense open | open, closed)
bel = np.array([0.75, 0.25])      # belief after t = 1
bel_bar = bel @ T_push            # predict: [0.95, 0.05]
bel = p_z * bel_bar
bel = bel / bel.sum()             # correct: [0.983, 0.017]

5. Why the two steps give the exact belief


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Starting from the definition of the belief, five steps lead to the filter: Bayes’ rule, a Markov assumption for readings, the law of total probability (G-1053)Law of total probability: The rule for the overall probability of an event: add its probability under each case, weighted by how likely that case is, P(B) = \sum_i P(B \mid A_i) P(A_i), when the cases A_i are mutually exclusive and cover every possibility. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: A Bayes’ Theorem Problem, §1. Overview, a Markov assumption for motion, and the assumption that the newest command says nothing about the past.


The two steps threw the history away. Here we show that nothing was lost: they give exactly p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}), the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition as defined over the whole history, and we name every assumption on the way (PR §2.4.3). The state x_t, the command u_t, the reading z_t and the two probability tables are those of Section 2. The other symbols:

z_{1:t-1} is all readings before time t, only z_1 = “sense open” at t = 2;
u_{1:t} is all commands u_1, \ldots, u_t, (do nothing, push) at t = 2;
\text{bel}(x_t) is the belief, the probability of each state given all readings and commands, a number from 0 to 1 (0.983 for open at t = 2);
\overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) is the belief before the newest reading z_t, as in Section 4.2 (0.95 for open at t = 2);
\eta is the factor that rescales the beliefs so they add to 1 (1.724 at t = 2).

The steps use three rules:

the definition of the predicted belief (G-2436)Predicted belief: The belief after the latest command but before the latest reading, \overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t-1}, u_{1:t}); it separates the doubt a move adds from the knowledge a reading brings. Explained in §4.2 The prediction step., and its last factor is the belief one step earlier, so the robot only has to keep its last belief. The derivation used three assumptions:

readings depend only on the current state: at an open door a second “sense open” has chance 0.6 whatever was read before, as in Section 3.2 and the arrows of the dynamic Bayes network (G-2441)Dynamic Bayes network: A Bayesian network that repeats the same variables at every time step, such as states, commands and readings of a robot; it shows which variable depends on which over time, so a whole run’s probability splits into small factors. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §6.2 The robot as a dynamic Bayes network; this drops z_{1:t-1} and u_{1:t} from the reading’s probability in the first chain;
the next state depends only on the previous state and the newest command: a push opens a closed door with chance 0.8 whatever came before; this drops z_{1:t-1} and u_{1:t-1} from the motion term in the second chain;
the newest command does not tell us about the previous state: the push at t = 2 leaves the belief at t = 1, 0.75, as it was; this drops u_t from the previous state’s probability, the last move of the second chain. The integral cuts the old belief into thin slices. The factor \text{bel}(x_{t-1})\ dx_{t-1} is one slice’s probability, its density times its width; for slices 0.2 m wide:
\text{door slice: } 0.1875 \times 0.2 = 0.0375
\text{wall slice: } 0.0625 \times 0.2 = 0.0125
The motion model carries each slice’s probability 2 m on and spreads it into a piece. The slice from 1.0 to 1.2 m, centred at 1.1 m, sends its 0.0375 to around:
1.1 + 2 = 3.1 \text{ m}
Adding the pieces of all 50 slices, 15 at doors and 35 at walls, gives the predicted belief, whose area is still 1:
15 \times 0.0375 + 35 \times 0.0125
= 0.5625 + 0.4375 = 1

7. The belief is the probabilistic information state


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, the robot’s probability for each state, can be updated from the previous belief, the newest command and the newest reading alone. So it carries everything the history knew, and the robot can throw the history away.


Why may the robot throw its history away? Because Section 5 showed that the new belief needs only the old belief, the newest command u_t and the newest reading z_t: whatever the history knew, the belief already holds. The set of possible statesExplained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §3. Summary 1: the set of cells the robot could be in also had two update rules, one per event. 8. One equation, many filters


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Every filter in the rest of this chapter is the Bayes filter with a particular way of storing the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, the robot’s probability for each state.


The Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in §4.4 The algorithm. keeps only the last belief, but it says what to compute, not how to store that belief over a continuous pose (position and heading), where the prediction sums over infinitely many previous states. Each practical filter answers that differently (PR §2.5):

grid filtersExplained in: Grid Filters: Histogram Filter and Binary Bayes Filter, §2. The histogram filter: chop the space into cells and keep one probability per cell, as in the hallway; the sum stays a sum;
particle filter (G-2492)Particle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in: Particle Filter, §4. The particle filter, step by step: keep a cloud of sample states; dense clouds mean high belief;
Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system: assume every belief is a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, a single bell-shaped curve, and keep only its mean and variance;
extended Kalman filter (G-2520)Extended Kalman filter (EKF): The Kalman filter for nonlinear motion and sensor models: it moves the mean through the nonlinear functions and uses their Jacobians at the latest estimate in place of F and H, so it can track unimodal beliefs through nonlinear models. Explained in: Extended Kalman Filter, §4.1 The algorithm: the Kalman filter for motion and sensor models whose graphs are curves, not straight lines: nonlinear functions (G-2530)Nonlinear function: A function whose graph is not a straight line, so it is not a fixed multiple of the input plus a constant, such as the beacon distance h(x) = \sqrt{(6 - x)^2 + 4}; it bends a Gaussian into another shape, which is why the Kalman filter cannot use it as it is and the extended Kalman filter linearises it. Explained in: Extended Kalman Filter, §1. Overview.

Look at whether each keeps the three bumps: the cells and the cloud of samples do, while one Gaussian with the belief’s mean, 5.22 m, and standard deviation, 2.83 m, is a single wide hump over the whole hallway (why one Gaussian is not enoughExplained in: Particle Filter, §3.1 Why one Gaussian is not enough is worked out on another corridor).

The formula and its proof turns the measurement probability p(z \mid x), which we can measure, into p(x \mid z), the chance of each door given the reading, which the robot needs, so one reading moves the door belief from 0.5 to 0.75.
With background knowledge, the old posterior becomes the new prior, so a second reading moves it to 0.9 without revisiting the first; this needs the readings to be independent given the state, not independent outright.

What the density at a point meansThe height of a continuous distribution’s curve; compares how likely nearby values are.Motion model p(\mathbf x_t \mid u_t, \mathbf x_{t-1}) (G-2319)Motion model p(\mathbf x_t \mid u_t, \mathbf x_{t-1}): The probability distribution of a robot’s pose after a move, given its pose before and the control (command or odometry); it describes how uncertain motion is, so a filter can score possible end poses or draw them at random. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §2.2 The motion model and its densityThe probability distribution of a robot’s pose after a move, given its pose before and the control (command or odometry); it describes how uncertain motion is, so a filter can score possible end poses or draw them at random.Gaussian distribution (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution isAnother name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements.Standard deviation of a random variable (G-1870)Standard deviation of a random variable: The square root of a random variable’s variance, in the units of X; it says how far values typically fall from the expected value. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4.1 Variance term by termThe square root of a random variable’s variance, in the units of X; it says how far values typically fall from the expected value.Particle filter (G-2492)Particle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in: Particle Filter, §4. The particle filter, step by stepA Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors.Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian systemThe Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible.Extended Kalman filter (EKF) (G-2520)Extended Kalman filter (EKF): The Kalman filter for nonlinear motion and sensor models: it moves the mean through the nonlinear functions and uses their Jacobians at the latest estimate in place of F and H, so it can track unimodal beliefs through nonlinear models. Explained in: Extended Kalman Filter, §4.1 The algorithmThe Kalman filter for nonlinear motion and sensor models: it moves the mean through the nonlinear functions and uses their Jacobians at the latest estimate in place of F and H, so it can track unimodal beliefs through nonlinear models.Nonlinear function (G-2530)Nonlinear function: A function whose graph is not a straight line, so it is not a fixed multiple of the input plus a constant, such as the beacon distance h(x) = \sqrt{(6 - x)^2 + 4}; it bends a Gaussian into another shape, which is why the Kalman filter cannot use it as it is and the extended Kalman filter linearises it. RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-015-.title: Grid Filters: Histogram Filter and Binary Bayes Filter
RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-015-.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Binning and binarizationExplained in: Binning and Binarization: Equal Width, Equal Frequency and k-means Binning, §3. Discretization; Sigmoid functionSigmoid function: An S-shaped function that squashes any number into the range 0 to 1, \sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z}); it turns a score into a probability, as in logistic regression. Explained in: Logistic Regression: The Sigmoid Function, §4. The sigmoid function; MemoizationMemoization: Storing the result of a function call and returning the stored result when the same input comes again. Explained in: Memoization in Backpropagation, §3. Memoization on the Fibonacci numbers; Convolution operation and feature mapsConvolution operation: Sliding a small filter over an input and, at each position, multiplying cell by cell and adding up, so the output (a feature map) is large where the input contains the filter’s pattern, such as an edge. Explained in: The Convolution Operation, §6. The convolution operation; Hidden Markov modelHidden Markov model (HMM): A Markov chain whose states cannot be seen, where each state produces an observation that can, such as hidden robot cells producing “door” or “wall” readings; it is the model behind robot state estimation, speech recognition and many trackers. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §6.3 Hidden Markov model; Bayes filterBayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm.
Leads to: Particle filterParticle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in: Particle Filter, §4. The particle filter, step by step.
Compare with: Particle filterParticle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in: Particle Filter, §4. The particle filter, step by step.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Chop the robot’s space into cells and keep one probability per cell: the Bayes filter then becomes plain arithmetic on a list of numbers. The same list of numbers also answers two questions about the past: where the robot most likely was, and which whole path it most likely took.



Figure 1: A hallway of 10 cells, numbered 0 to 9 and joined into a loop, with doors in front of cells 1, 3 and 7; a robot stands in cell 1 and does not know it
The robot can now update its belief from the newest command and reading alone, with the Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm. What still breaks is its prediction step, a sum over every possible previous state. In the door worldExplained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §2. The door world that sum had 2 terms; a position along the hallway can be any number of metres, so the sum has infinitely many terms and cannot be done as written. This Note adds one number per cell, and answers: how does a computer run the Bayes filter, and what else can the same numbers tell us?
We go back to the hallway (Figure 1) on which the robot’s belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, its probability for every cell, was defined, with the same numbers:

10 cells of 1 m in a loop, with doors at cells 1, 3 and 7;
a door sensor that reads “door” with probability 0.6 at a door and 0.2 at a wall;
a command “move 2” that moves the robot 1, 2 or 3 cells with probability 0.1, 0.8 and 0.1.

The Note covers:

the histogram filter (G-2461)Histogram filter (discrete Bayes filter): The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position. Explained in §2.1 Why cells.: one probability per cell, updated by multiplying (sensing) and sliding (moving) (Section 2);
how to cut a real, continuous space into cells: fixed cells or cells that adapt to the belief (Section 3);
the binary Bayes filter for a yes-or-no state that does not change, run in log odds (G-1116)Log-odds: The natural log of the odds, \ln(p/(1-p)): it turns a probability between 0 and 1 into any number (0 at p = 0.5), so a model such as logistic regression can predict it with a straight line, and the sigmoid turns it back into a probability. Explained in: Gradient Boosting for Classification, §4. Stage 1: the log-odds of class 1, the logarithm of the yes-to-no odds (Section 4);
looking back: the smoothed belief at an earlier time, and the most likely whole path (Section 5).

2. The histogram filter


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Keep one probability per cell: sensing multiplies every cell by how well it explains the reading, then rescales. Moving slides the list along and blurs it with the motion probabilities.


2.1 Why cells
A continuous position, such as “3.42 m along the hallway”, can take infinitely many values, and a computer can only store a finite list. So we cut the hallway into cells, here 10 cells of 1 m, and keep one probability for each: the probability that the robot is somewhere in that cell. Cutting a range into cells is the same move as discretization (G-619)Discretization: Turning a continuous column into a discrete one by cutting its range into intervals (bins), such as ages 0–18, 18–60 and 60+; it turns endless values into a few groups that a model or a table can handle. Explained in: Binning and Binarization: Equal Width, Equal Frequency and k-means Binning, §1. Overview of a feature into bins, and the list of probabilities, drawn as bars, is a histogram (G-899)Histogram: A bar chart of how many values fall in each equal range (bin) of a numerical column; it shows the shape of a distribution at a glance: where values pile up, how far they spread and whether there are several peaks. Explained in: Univariate Analysis: Exploring One Column at a Time, §6. Histogram of the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition.
The Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm run on such a list of cells is the histogram filter (G-2461)Histogram filter (discrete Bayes filter): The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position. Explained in §2.1 Why cells. (PR §4.1). When the states are finite to begin with, as in the door world, the same algorithm is called the discrete Bayes filter (Labbe ch.2). The sum of the prediction step now has only 10 terms, so it can be done exactly.
2.2 Sense: multiply, then rescale
The robot has no idea where it is, so each cell starts at 0.1. It reads “door”. Figure 2 runs the four stages in turn: watch each bar shrink as it is multiplied by its cell’s chance of a “door” reading, the 10 products stack up to 0.32, and the division by 0.32 grow them back until they add to 1, with each door cell now three times as tall as a wall cell.

Figure 2: The hallway’s 10 cells, with the doors at cells 1, 3 and 7 shaded. The bars start at 0.1, the prior. Each bar is multiplied by p(door | cell), the chance of reading door in that cell (0.6 at a door, 0.2 at a wall), and shrinks to 0.06 or 0.02. The 10 products stack one by one into the sum column, which reaches 0.32. Dividing every product by 0.32 grows them to 0.1875 at the doors and 0.0625 at the walls. Last frame: the new belief, with the prior 0.1 as a dashed line
Multiply each cell by the probability of the reading in that cell:
\text{door cell: } 0.1 \times 0.6 = 0.06
\text{wall cell: } 0.1 \times 0.2 = 0.02
Add the 10 products, 3 door cells and 7 wall cells:
3 \times 0.06 + 7 \times 0.02 = 0.32
Rescale by dividing every product by 0.32, so the cells add to 1 again:
\text{door cell: } 0.06 / 0.32 = 0.1875
\text{wall cell: } 0.02 / 0.32 = 0.0625
Multiplying and rescaling is the correction step of the Bayes filter, done cell by cell (Labbe ch.2). The robot reads “door” three times as often at a door as at a wall, and after the update each door cell holds three times the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition of a wall cell.
2.3 Move: shift, then blur
Next the robot moves 2 cells. If the move were exact, every probability would simply travel 2 cells to the right, wrapping round the loop (Figure 3, middle). But the move is 1 cell with probability 0.1 and 3 cells with probability 0.1, so some belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition also lands one cell short or one cell too far (Figure 3, right).
Make interactive
Figure 3: Left: the belief after reading door, 0.1875 at cells 1, 3 and 7. Middle: shifted exactly 2 cells, 0.1875 at cells 3, 5 and 9. Right: shifted and blurred by the 0.1/0.8/0.1 move, 0.1625 at cells 3, 5 and 9 and 0.0875 at cell 4
Which old cells can end in cell 3? Cell 2 (by moving 1), cell 1 (by moving 2) and cell 0 (by moving 3). Each contributes its old belief times the probability of that move:
\text{new cell 3} = 0.1 \times 0.0625
+\ 0.8 \times 0.1875
+\ 0.1 \times 0.0625
= 0.1625
Adding up the weighted old cells is the prediction step of the Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm: the law of total probability (G-1053)Law of total probability: The rule for the overall probability of an event: add its probability under each case, weighted by how likely that case is, P(B) = \sum_i P(B \mid A_i) P(A_i), when the cases A_i are mutually exclusive and cover every possibility. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: A Bayes’ Theorem Problem, §1. Overview with three terms instead of ten, because only three old cells can reach each new one.
Every new cell is built the same way, with the same three weights, slid along the hallway. Figure 4 builds the whole predicted belief this way, one cell at a time.

Figure 4: Top: the old belief with the three cells that can reach the new cell highlighted and weighted 0.1, 0.8 and 0.1. Bottom: the new belief filled in cell by cell; new cell 3 = 0.1 x 0.0625 + 0.8 x 0.1875 + 0.1 x 0.0625 = 0.1625
The list of weights, here (0.1, 0.8, 0.1), is the motion kernel (G-2462)Motion kernel: The short list of move probabilities, such as (0.1, 0.8, 0.1) for one cell short, exact, one cell too far, slid along the belief in the prediction step; it spreads each cell’s belief over the cells the robot may have reached. Explained in §2.3 Move: shift, then blur.. Sliding a small list of weights along a longer list and adding the products at each position is a convolution (G-481)Convolution operation: Sliding a small filter over an input and, at each position, multiplying cell by cell and adding up, so the output (a feature map) is large where the input contains the filter’s pattern, such as an edge. Explained in: The Convolution Operation, §6. The convolution operation, the same operation a CNN filter performs on an image (Labbe ch.2). Convolution is valid here because the move’s error does not depend on where the robot is: the same kernel applies in every cell.
2.4 Moving without looking loses everything
What if the robot keeps moving and never reads its sensor? Figure 5 starts it sure that it is in cell 1 and repeats “move 2”.

Figure 5: After 1 move the highest cell holds 0.80, after 3 moves 0.56, after 10 moves 0.29, after 80 moves 0.11: the belief flattens towards 0.1 in every cell
Each move spreads the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition of every cell over three cells, so the highest cell’s belief shrinks:





















Moves without a reading0131080Highest cell1.000.800.560.290.11
The belief tends to 0.1 in every cell, where the robot started before it knew anything. A prediction can only lose information; only readings bring it back (Labbe ch.2).
2.5 Sense and move together
A real robot alternates: move, read, move, read. Figure 6 runs seven steps; t counts them from 1 to 7. The true robot starts in cell 1 and really moves 2 cells each time (cells 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 1, 3). Every reading is correct except at t = 5, where the sensor says “door” in front of the wall of cell 9.

Figure 6: Seven steps of the histogram filter: orange frames show the predicted belief after each move, blue frames the belief after each reading; the tallest bar follows the true cell except at t = 5, after the wrong reading, when it jumps to cell 3; at t = 6 and t = 7 it is back on the true cell
The tallest bar at each step:













































t1234567True cell1357913Tallest bar1, 3, 7 (tied)357313Its belief0.190.310.300.420.320.370.47
The wrong reading at t = 5 moves the tallest bar to cell 3, a door. But the true cell 9 keeps a belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition of 0.24, because one reading never sets a cell to zero. Two correct readings later the filter is back on the true cell with 0.47. A filter that kept only one best guess would have been lost at t = 5 (Labbe ch.2).
2.6 The formal version
With the cells numbered 0 to 9, at time step t:

k is the number of a cell after the move, 0 to 9;
i is the number of a cell before the move, 0 to 9;
p_{i,t-1} is the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition in cell i one step earlier, a number from 0 to 1 (0.1875 for cell 1 after the first reading);
p(x_k \mid u_t,\ x_i) is the chance that the command u_t takes the robot from cell i to cell k (0.8 for “move 2” from cell 1 to cell 3);
\bar p_{k,t} is the predicted belief in cell k, after the move and before the reading (0.1625 for cell 3 at t = 2);
p(z_t \mid x_k) is the chance of the reading z_t when the robot is in cell k (0.6 for “door” at a door, 0.2 at a wall);
\eta is the factor that rescales the cells so they add to 1, one over the sum of the products (the sum is 0.32 after the first reading, Section 2.2);
p_{k,t} is the belief in cell k at time t, a number from 0 to 1 (0.3095 for cell 3 at t = 2).

The histogram filter (G-2461)Histogram filter (discrete Bayes filter): The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position. Explained in §2.1 Why cells. is (PR §4.1.1):
\bar p_{k,t} = \sum_{i} p(x_k \mid u_t,\ x_i)\ p_{i,t-1}
p_{k,t} = \eta\ p(z_t \mid x_k)\ \bar p_{k,t}
The first line is the prediction step with the sum over the old cells i; the second is the correction step. Both lines visit every cell, so one step costs a fixed amount of work per cell.

Python: the hallway filter, using np.roll to shift a list round the loop.
import numpy as np
door = np.isin(np.arange(10), [1, 3, 7])
def sense(bel, z):           # z = True: reads "door"
    p = np.where(door, 0.6, 0.2)
    if not z:
        p = 1 - p
    return p * bel / (p * bel).sum()
def move(bel):               # 1, 2 or 3 cells
    return (0.1 * np.roll(bel, 1)
            + 0.8 * np.roll(bel, 2)
            + 0.1 * np.roll(bel, 3))
bel = sense(np.full(10, 0.1), True)   # 0.1875 at doors
bel = sense(move(bel), True)          # 0.3095 at cell 3

The notebook RO-015-grid-filters.ipynb runs every example in this Note. Ten cells of 1 m make the sum exact on the hallway, but they place the robot only to the nearest metre.
3. Cutting a real space into cells


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Fine cells give an accurate belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, the robot’s probability for each cell, but their number explodes with the size of the space and the number of state variables. A static decomposition fixes the cells in advance; an adaptive one makes cells small only where the belief needs them.


3.1 Why the number of cells explodes
Cells turned the sum over infinitely many positions into 10 terms, at a price: with cells of 1 m, the robot’s position is never known better than “somewhere in this metre”. Smaller cells give a sharper answer, but every cell costs memory and time, because both steps visit every cell. A real floor robot has a pose, its position and heading (see pose (G-2280))Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, so the grid has three directions. On a 30 m by 30 m floor (Fox 1999):

the position along the floor runs from 0 to 30 m in cells of 15 cm;
the position across the floor runs from 0 to 30 m in cells of 15 cm;
the heading, the direction the robot faces, runs from 0° to 360° in steps of 2°.

Counting the cells:
\frac{30}{0.15} = 200 \text{ cells along the floor}
\frac{30}{0.15} = 200 \text{ cells across the floor}
\frac{360}{2} = 180 \text{ headings}
200 \times 200 \times 180 = 7{,}200{,}000 \text{ cells}
Halving the cell size multiplies the count by 4 for the position alone, and each extra state variable, such as speed, multiplies it again by the number of its values (Labbe ch.2). Fox, Burgard and Thrun found that updating 7.2 million cells at every reading was too slow for the computers of 1999 (Fox 1999).
3.2 Static and adaptive decomposition
Most of those millions of cells hold a belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition close to zero: the robot is not inside a wall or at the far end of the building. Two ways of cutting the space follow from that (PR §4.1.4):

A static decomposition (G-2464)Static decomposition: Cutting the state space into cells fixed before the robot starts, usually a regular grid such as 15 cm cells and 2° headings; simple, but it spends as much work on empty regions as where the robot is. Explained in §3.2 Static and adaptive decomposition. fixes the cells before the robot starts, whatever the belief turns out to be. A regular grid of equal cells is the usual choice (Fox 1999). A fixed grid is simple, and every cell is updated the same way, but it spends as much work on empty regions as on the region where the robot is.
An adaptive decomposition (G-2465)Adaptive (dynamic) decomposition: Cutting the state space into cells that change with the belief: small cells where the belief is high, large cells where it is near zero, as in a quadtree; it gives fine detail with far fewer cells. Explained in §3.2 Static and adaptive decomposition., also called a dynamic decomposition, changes the cells as the belief changes: small cells where the belief is high, large cells where it is near zero. A common way is a quadtree, which splits a square into four only where more detail is needed (ShanghaiTech slides; Fox 1999, §6).


Figure 7: Left: an 8 m by 8 m floor cut into 64 fixed 1 m cells, with the belief concentrated in one spot. Right: the same floor cut adaptively into 19 cells: 4 m cells where the belief is near zero, down to 0.5 m cells at the peak
Figure 7 compares the two on an 8 m by 8 m floor. The fixed grid uses 64 cells of 1 m. The adaptive one uses 19 cells, yet its smallest cells (0.5 m) are finer than the fixed grid’s where the belief peaks. The price is bookkeeping: cells must be split and merged as the belief moves. The smallest grid of all has just 2 cells.
4. The binary Bayes filter


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

For a yes-or-no state that never changes, each reading multiplies the odds by a fixed factor. In log odds (G-1116)Log-odds: The natural log of the odds, \ln(p/(1-p)): it turns a probability between 0 and 1 into any number (0 at p = 0.5), so a model such as logistic regression can predict it with a straight line, and the sigmoid turns it back into a probability. Explained in: Gradient Boosting for Classification, §4. Stage 1: the log-odds of class 1, the logarithm of the odds, that becomes adding a fixed number, which is fast and does not round to 0 or 1.


4.1 A state that does not change
The smallest grid has 2 cells, open and closed. Go back to the door worldExplained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §2. The door world, but now nobody touches the door: it is open or closed, and it stays that way while the robot reads its sensor again and again. A state that the robot’s commands do not change is a static state (G-2467)Static state: A state that the robot’s commands do not change while it is being estimated, such as a door nobody touches; the prediction step then does nothing and only readings update the belief. Explained in §4.1 A state that does not change. (PR §4.2). With a static state the prediction step does nothing (the belief (G-2433), the robot’s probability for each door state, before a step equals the belief after it)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, so only the correction step is left.
The same situation appears in mapping: whether one small square of the floor is occupied by an obstacle is a yes-or-no question about something that does not move. A map built this way keeps one such filter per square (PR §4.2; Freiburg mapping slides).
4.2 Each reading multiplies the odds
The odds (G-1376)Odds: How often an event happens divided by how often it does not, e.g. 5 placed to 3 not placed is 5/3; unlike a probability, odds have no upper limit, so evidence updates them by one multiplication, and their log can be predicted with a straight line. Explained in: Gradient Boosting for Classification, §4. Stage 1: the log-odds of class 1 of the door being open compare the two possibilities. In symbols:

p(\text{open}) is the probability that the door is open, 0.5 at the start;
p(\text{closed}) is the probability that it is closed, 0.5 at the start.

The odds are their ratio:
\text{odds} = \frac{p(\text{open})}{p(\text{closed})}
Why does a reading multiply the odds? Bayes’ theorem (G-269)Bayes’ theorem: The rule that reverses a conditional probability: from P(B \mid A) it gives P(A \mid B), so a belief about A can be updated after seeing B; P(A \mid B) = P(B \mid A) P(A) / P(B). Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Bayes’ Theorem, §4. The formula and its proof gives each door state’s probability after a reading, with the same denominator for both: the overall chance of the reading. For one “sense open” from 0.5, the sensor reads it with chance 0.6 at an open door, 0.2 at a closed one and 0.4 overallExplained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §3.1 Why the robot needs Bayes’ theorem:
\text{open: } \frac{0.6 \times 0.5}{0.4} = 0.75
\text{closed: } \frac{0.2 \times 0.5}{0.4} = 0.25
\text{new odds} = \frac{0.75}{0.25}
= \frac{0.6 \times 0.5}{0.4} \div \frac{0.2 \times 0.5}{0.4}
= \frac{0.6 \times 0.5}{0.2 \times 0.5}
= \frac{0.6}{0.2} \times \frac{0.5}{0.5}
= 3 \times 1 = 3
The same steps for any reading:

z is the reading, “sense open” or “sense closed”;
p(z \mid \text{open}) is the chance of that reading when the door is open (0.6 for “sense open”);
p(z \mid \text{closed}) is the chance of that reading when the door is closed (0.2 for “sense open”);
p(z) is the overall chance of the reading, the same denominator in both lines (0.4 for “sense open”);
p(\text{open} \mid z) is the probability that the door is open after the reading (0.75 after one “sense open” from 0.5);
p(\text{closed} \mid z) is the probability that it is closed after the reading (0.25 after one “sense open” from 0.5).

p(\text{open} \mid z) = \frac{p(z \mid \text{open})\ p(\text{open})}{p(z)}
p(\text{closed} \mid z) = \frac{p(z \mid \text{closed})\ p(\text{closed})}{p(z)}
\text{new odds} = \frac{p(\text{open} \mid z)}{p(\text{closed} \mid z)}
= \frac{p(z \mid \text{open})\ p(\text{open})}{p(z)}
\div\ \frac{p(z \mid \text{closed})\ p(\text{closed})}{p(z)}
= \frac{p(z \mid \text{open})\ p(\text{open})}{p(z \mid \text{closed})\ p(\text{closed})}
= \frac{p(z \mid \text{open})}{p(z \mid \text{closed})} \times \frac{p(\text{open})}{p(\text{closed})}
The first fraction, the ratio of the two measurement probabilities, is the Bayes factor (G-2215)Bayes factor: A number that says how strongly the evidence favours yes over no: how many times more likely the evidence is if the answer is yes than if it is no, P(\text{evidence} \mid \text{yes}) / P(\text{evidence} \mid \text{no}). Multiplying the prior odds by it gives the posterior odds. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: A Bayes’ Theorem Problem, §6.1 The size of the update: the Bayes factor; the second is the old odds:
\text{new odds} = \text{old odds} \times \frac{p(z \mid \text{open})}{p(z \mid \text{closed})}
We never need p(z), whose inverse is the normaliser \eta of the correction step, which is why odds are convenient.
The factor is 3 for “sense open”, as above. For “sense closed” it is:
0.4 / 0.8 = 0.5
Starting from odds of 1 (that is, 0.5 against 0.5), two readings of “open” give:
1 \times 3 \times 3 = 9
Odds of 9 mean 9 parts open to 1 part closed:
p(\text{open}) = \frac{9}{9 + 1} = 0.9
the same 0.9 as in the Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm.
4.3 Log odds turn the products into sums
Taking the logarithm turns a product into a sum. The natural log of the odds (G-1376)Odds: How often an event happens divided by how often it does not, e.g. 5 placed to 3 not placed is 5/3; unlike a probability, odds have no upper limit, so evidence updates them by one multiplication, and their log can be predicted with a straight line. Explained in: Gradient Boosting for Classification, §4. Stage 1: the log-odds of class 1 is the log odds (G-1116)Log-odds: The natural log of the odds, \ln(p/(1-p)): it turns a probability between 0 and 1 into any number (0 at p = 0.5), so a model such as logistic regression can predict it with a straight line, and the sigmoid turns it back into a probability. Explained in: Gradient Boosting for Classification, §4. Stage 1: the log-odds of class 1. In symbols:

p is the probability that the door is open, a number from 0 to 1 (0.5 at the start);
1 - p is the probability that it is closed;
\ln is the natural logarithm;
l is the log odds, a number with no unit that can be any size (0 at the start).

Written out:
l = \ln \frac{p}{1 - p}
Figure 8 shows how probabilities map to log odds: 0.5 goes to 0, probabilities above 0.5 to positive numbers, below 0.5 to negative ones, and 0 and 1 are never reached.

Each reading now adds a fixed amount:
\text{sense open: } \ln 3 = +1.0986
\text{sense closed: } \ln 0.5 = -0.6931
Figure 9 runs five readings: open, open, closed, open, open.

Step by step, the log odds l after each reading:
\text{open: } l = 0 + 1.0986 = 1.0986
\text{open: } l = 1.0986 + 1.0986 = 2.1972
\text{closed: } l = 2.1972 - 0.6931 = 1.5041

To read a probability back out, undo the log, which is the sigmoid function (G-1798)Sigmoid function: An S-shaped function that squashes any number into the range 0 to 1, \sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z}); it turns a score into a probability, as in logistic regression. Explained in: Logistic Regression: The Sigmoid Function, §4. The sigmoid function; e, about 2.718, is the base of the natural log:
p = 1 - \frac{1}{1 + e^{l}}
l = 3.7013: \quad p = 0.976
The notebook checks that Bayes’ theorem applied five times gives the same 0.976.
This filter, a static binary state updated in log odds, is the binary Bayes filter (G-2466)Binary Bayes filter: The Bayes filter for a yes-or-no state that does not change, such as “door open” or “this map cell is occupied”, run in log odds: each reading adds the log of its Bayes factor. It is fast and does not round to 0 or 1. Explained in §4.3 Log odds turn the products into sums. (PR §4.2).
4.4 Why work in log odds
Two reasons:

Adding is cheaper than multiplying and rescaling. A map can hold millions of cells, each updated at every scan; one addition per cell is the cheapest update possible, and every cell can be updated at the same time (Freiburg mapping slides: the log odds (G-1116) update “only requires to compute sums”)Log-odds: The natural log of the odds, \ln(p/(1-p)): it turns a probability between 0 and 1 into any number (0 at p = 0.5), so a model such as logistic regression can predict it with a straight line, and the sigmoid turns it back into a probability. Explained in: Gradient Boosting for Classification, §4. Stage 1: the log-odds of class 1.
Probabilities near 0 or 1 round off. Run 40 readings of “open” in ordinary probabilities. The odds (G-1376)Odds: How often an event happens divided by how often it does not, e.g. 5 placed to 3 not placed is 5/3; unlike a probability, odds have no upper limit, so evidence updates them by one multiplication, and their log can be predicted with a straight line. Explained in: Gradient Boosting for Classification, §4. Stage 1: the log-odds of class 1 become 3 to the power 40, about 12 billion billion, and the computer stores p(\text{open}) as exactly 1.0. After that, a reading of “closed” changes nothing, because 1.0 times anything, divided by itself, is still 1.0. Later readings also say where the robot was earlier. The forward-backward algorithm combines readings from before and after a time step into the smoothed belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state.
