Explained in §6.2 The fix: a guess that never drops faster than the distance., also called a monotone heuristic (CMU 16-350, A*; Wikipedia, A* search algorithm). The rule is a triangle inequality: going from n to G directly is estimated no longer than going by way of n'. Figure 7 checks one move of each example.

= h^\ast(n_0)
The same steps in symbols, with c_1, c_2, c_3 the three moves:
h(n_0) \le c_1 + h(n_1)
\le c_1 + c_2 + h(n_2)
\le c_1 + c_2 + c_3 + h(G)
= h^\ast(n_0)
The last line uses h(G) = 0: the moves add up to the shortest route. The converse does not hold: run 1’s heuristic is admissible but not consistent.
6.3 Why consistency keeps g right
The consistent rule makes f never fall along a route. Take a move from the cell below the table’s corner, n, to the cell above it, n', with:

g(n), the cost so far at n, 1.707 m;
h(n), its heuristic, 1.414 m, so f(n) = 3.121 m;
c, the move, 0.5 m;
h(n'), the heuristic at n', 1.207 m.

f(n') = 1.707 + 0.5 + 1.207
= 3.414
\ge 1.707 + 1.414
= 3.121
= f(n)
The same steps in symbols:
f(n') = g(n) + c + h(n')
\ge g(n) + h(n)
= f(n)
The second line is the consistent rule with g(n) added to both sides. So the f values along any route never decrease, and A* takes cells off the open list in order of f. A cell reached first by a long way, as C by way of B, has a larger f than every cell on its short way in, so those cells come off first and lower its g before it is closed (CMU 16-350, A*; Wikipedia, A* search algorithm).
On the roadmap, run 1’s f falls from 3.653 at A to 2.487 at C by way of A: that fall is what let C close early.
A second fix keeps any admissible heuristic: reopen a closed cell when a shorter way into it turns up, at the price of expanding some cells more than once (CS188 §1.4). The octile heuristic is consistent, so on the grid A* expands each cell once and returns the shortest route. What it still costs is memory: it keeps every cell it has reached.
7. Saving memory: iterative deepening and IDA*


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A* stores every cell it has reached; a depth-first search stores only its current route. Iterative deepening repeats a depth-first search with a growing limit; IDA* puts the limit on f, the cost so far plus the heuristic, so it returns the shortest route while storing at most one route: on the door trip, 17 visits with at most 7 cells in memory.


When A* stopped on the door trip it held 23 cells: 9 on the closed list and 14 on the open list (notebook). The room is small, but a planner over position and heading, or over the joints of an arm, has far more states, and A*‘s lists grow with the number of states it reaches (CMU 16-350, heuristics).
The idea. Depth-first search (G-2552)Depth-first search (DFS): A search whose frontier is a stack, so it always extends the newest path and dives deep before backing up; it backs up to its last untried choice at dead ends and finds a route, but which one, and how long, depends on the order the moves are tried (22 moves where breadth-first search found 8). Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §6. Depth-first search: dive, then back up, the search that dives along one route and backs up at dead ends, stores only the route it is on: memory that grows with the length of a route, not with the number of cells (LaValle §2.2.2). But it returns whatever route it finds first. The fix is to give the dive a limit and repeat it with a larger limit until a route fits.
The standard term. Depth-first search with a limit on the number of moves, run with the limits 0, 1, 2 and so on until it reaches the goal, is iterative deepening (G-2581)Iterative deepening (DFID): Depth-first search with a limit on the number of moves, repeated with the limits 0, 1, 2 and so on until the goal is reached; it finds the fewest moves, like breadth-first search, while storing only one route, like depth-first search. Explained in §7. Saving memory: iterative deepening and IDA., also called depth-first iterative deepening (DFID) (LaValle §2.2.2; Korf 1985). Iterative deepening finds the route with the fewest moves, like breadth-first search, with the memory of depth-first search. At the limit of 6 moves it reaches G, after 24,879 visits in all, by a route of 6 moves and 3.828 m: the fewest moves, not the shortest length, because moves here have two lengths.
IDA*. Put the limit on the estimated total cost f = g + h, the cost so far plus the heuristic (Section 4.1), instead of on the number of moves. Round 1 dives from S and drops any branch whose f passes the limit, which starts at h(S) = 3.121 m. If no route fits, the next round’s limit is the smallest f that passed: no route can be shorter, since f never overestimates.
Depth-first search with a limit on f is IDA* (G-2582)IDA (iterative-deepening A):** Iterative deepening with the limit on f = g + h instead of on moves, each new limit being the smallest f that passed the last; it returns the shortest route with an admissible heuristic while storing only the current route. Explained in §7. Saving memory: iterative deepening and IDA., iterative-deepening A* (Korf 1985; LaValle §2.2.2). Figure 8 runs it: watch the blue route, the only thing in memory, grow and shrink.

8. Searching from the door: backward and bidirectional search


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A search can run from the goal back to the start, or from both ends until they meet. From the door, which stands against the wall, Dijkstra needs 31 cells instead of 54; from both ends, 38. Two searches that meet must still compare every cell both have reached, because the cell where they meet need not lie on the shortest route.


Every search so far started at S. But the door never moves while robots, and the same robot later, start from many places; and the door’s side of the room is narrow, against the top wall.
8.1 Backward search
The idea. Run the search from G, following each move backwards, until it reaches S. Our moves cost the same in both directions, so the backward search uses the same moves (LaValle §2.2.3). Its cost so far g at a cell is then the distance left from that cell to G, the true distance left h^\ast of Section 5.1.
Run to the end, one backward search gives every cell’s distance to the door at once: a perfect heuristic for later searches, and the route for any start (CMU 16-350, heuristics). Many robots sharing one destination can use one search from the destination instead of one A* each (Patel, Variants).
The standard term. Searching from the goal towards the start, with every move reversed, is backward search (G-2583)Backward search: A search that starts at the goal and follows every move backwards until it reaches the start; it is cheaper when the goal’s side branches less, and run to the end it gives every state’s cost to the goal. Explained in §8.1 Backward search. (LaValle §2.2.3). Figure 9 (top) runs Dijkstra backwards from G: it reaches S after 31 cells, against 54 forwards (notebook).
Only 30 free cells lie within 3.414 m of G, against 53 within 3.414 m of S, because the door stands against the wall and much of the circle round it lies outside the room. A backward search pays when the goal’s side branches less than the start’s (LaValle §2.2.3).

Figure 9: Backward and bidirectional search on the room grid, one expansion per frame in both panels. Bottom: bidirectional Dijkstra, one expansion from S (red and green) and one from G (blue) in turn; it stops after 38 cells, when a cell has come off both open lists (purple outline), and its route is 3.414 m. The forward search alone needs 54 cells
8.2 Bidirectional search
The idea. Grow two searches at once, one from S and one from G, a step of each in turn; a route exists as soon as a cell has been reached by both. Each search then has to cover only about half the distance.
The standard term. Running a forward search from the start and a backward search from the goal until they meet is bidirectional search (G-2584)Bidirectional search: A forward search from the start and a backward search from the goal run in turn until some state has been expanded by both; the route is the smallest sum of the two costs over all states both reached, since the meeting state can be off the shortest route. Explained in §8.2 Bidirectional search. (LaValle §2.2.3; MIT 6.006 L18 notes). Figure 9 (bottom) alternates one Dijkstra step from S and one from G: the red ring round S and the blue ring round G grow until a cell has come off both open lists, after 38 cells, 19 from each side.
The 38 are fewer than the 54 of the forward search, but more than the backward search alone: in our room, the door’s narrow side is the cheaper one to search from. In many larger problems bidirectional search cuts the exploration sharply (LaValle §2.2.3).
8.3 When to stop, and where the route is
The two searches stop when some cell, call it w, has come off both open lists (MIT 6.006 L18 notes). The route through w seems the obvious answer, but w need not lie on the shortest route. On the door trip the meeting cell happens to lie on a shortest route, so Figure 10 shows the trap on a shorter trip: from R, the cell two above S, to G.

When any of several goals will do, join each goal to one added vertex, the virtual goal, and run A* to it once, with the smallest of the guesses to the goals: for three charging docks this takes 12 cells instead of 30 for three separate runs, and ends at the dock nearest by route, 3.207 m away, which is not the dock nearest in a straight line. A goal that moves becomes many goals, one per cell and time: searching over (cell, time), the robot meets a walking person at 5.414 s.

9.1 The virtual goal
The idea. The three runs search the same room three times; one search can find the nearest dock instead. Add one new vertex V and join each dock to it by an edge of 0 m (CMU 16-350, A*). V is not a place in the room; reaching it stands for “docked”. Every route to V passes through one dock and costs exactly as much as the route to that dock, so the shortest route to V ends at the dock nearest by route (Patel, Heuristics).
The guess. A* to V needs a heuristic: a guess of the distance left to V, which is the distance to whichever dock is nearest. The guess is the smallest of the octile distances of Section 2 to the three docks (Patel, Heuristics). D1 is 4 columns and 5 rows from S, D2 is 6 columns and 1 row, so with:

h_{\text{G}}, h_{\text{D1}}, h_{\text{D2}}, the octile distances from a cell to G, D1 and D2, in m;

h_{\text{G}}(S) = 3.121 \text{ m}
h_{\text{D1}}(S) = 4 \times 0.707 + 1 \times 0.5
= 3.328 \text{ m}
h_{\text{D2}}(S) = 1 \times 0.707 + 5 \times 0.5
= 3.207 \text{ m}
h(S) = \min(3.121, 3.328, 3.207)
= 3.121 \text{ m}
The same in symbols:
h = \min(h_{\text{G}}, h_{\text{D1}}, h_{\text{D2}})
The guess never overestimates: the shortest route to V ends at some dock, its length is at least the octile distance to that dock, and that distance is at least the smallest of the three.
The standard term. A* run to an added vertex joined to every acceptable goal is multi-goal A* (G-2585)Multi-goal A:* A* run to an added vertex joined to every acceptable goal, so one search finds the cheapest of several goals, such as the nearest of three charging docks by route or the first reachable meeting point with a moving person. 9.2 A moving goal
Suppose instead the robot must meet a person who walks under the top wall, along a path the robot knows: the person starts in the cell x 5.0 to 5.5 m and moves one cell (0.5 m) to the left every second, so the person is in the first cell from 0 to 1 s, in the next from 1 to 2 s, and so on. A cell of that walk is a goal only while the person is in it, so the cell alone cannot say whether the robot has arrived in time. The search state (G-2562)Search state: What a search keeps for each vertex: the quantities that decide which moves are allowed and what they cost, and nothing more, such as (cell, charge left) for a robot with a battery; leaving one out breaks the Markov property and can hide routes. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §10. Choosing the search state: the Markov rule, everything the next moves depend on, must hold the time as well as the cell (LaValle §7.1.1). Each pair of a cell and a time at which the person is in that cell joins the virtual goal V: these are the possible intercept points (CMU 16-350, A*).
The moves. The robot drives at 0.5 m/s. From a state (cell, time) it can:

move straight, 0.5 m, which adds 1 s;
move diagonally, 0.707 m, which adds 1.414 s;
wait one second in its cell, which adds 1 s.

Time only moves forward, so no move leads back to an earlier time (LaValle §7.1.1). A route’s cost is its time, so the cheapest route to V is the earliest meeting.
The guess. The cost is now time, so the cost so far, the guess and their sum are in seconds. With:

10. Trading length for time: weighted A* and anytime A*


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Multiplying the heuristic by a weight \varepsilon above 1 makes A* rush towards the goal: fewer cells, and a route at most \varepsilon times the shortest. Anytime A* runs weighted A* with falling weights and always has a route ready: on the long trip, 9.243 m at once, then 8.414 m, then the shortest, 8.000 m.


A robot must often start moving before an exact search finishes, and a slightly longer route found at once is better than the best route found too late (CMU 16-350, anytime). The door trip is too easy to show the trade: every weight there returns the same 3.414 m. So we use the long trip of Section 3, where A* takes 43 cells to find 8.000 m.
10.1 Weighted A*
The idea. Between Dijkstra, which ignores the heuristic, and greedy search, which follows nothing else, lies a whole range: count the heuristic more than the distance driven. With:

g, h, the cost so far and the heuristic of Section 4.1, in m.

A* takes off the open list the cell with the smallest

10.2 Anytime A* and ARA*
The idea. Run weighted A* with a large \varepsilon to get a route at once, and then again with smaller and smaller \varepsilon, each run giving a better route, until \varepsilon = 1 gives the shortest. The robot can stop the planner whenever it must move and use the best route so far (CMU 16-350, anytime).
The standard terms. Three fresh weighted A* runs repeat much of the same work. 11. Skipping equal routes: jump point search


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

On a grid where every move of one kind costs the same, many routes tie, and A* puts cells of all of them on its open list. Jump point search scans along straight lines and diagonals and puts on the open list only the cells where a route may have to turn: on the door trip, 7 cells ever enter its open list, against 23 for A*, for the same 3.414 m route.


In Figure 1, Dijkstra and A* returned two different routes of the same 3.414 m. On a grid with no obstacles in the way, the number of such equal routes between two cells grows fast, and A* treats each one as a separate possibility, putting its cells on the open list and keeping their numbers.
The idea. Equal routes differ only in the order of the same moves, such as up then up-right against up-right then up (zerowidth JPS). So from a cell, keep going in one direction for as long as nothing could make a turn necessary, without putting the cells passed on the open list. Stop only at the goal, or next to an obstacle’s corner, where a cell beside the line has just opened up and a route may have to turn into it.
The standard terms. A neighbour that the cell before could normally reach by an equally short route of its own, but which an obstacle beside the line leaves reachable by a shortest route only by turning at the current cell, is a forced neighbour (G-2592)Forced neighbour: A neighbour that the cell before could normally reach by an equally short route of its own, but which an obstacle beside the line of travel leaves reachable by a shortest route only by turning at the current cell; it makes that cell a jump point. Explained in §11. Skipping equal routes: jump point search.: the search is forced to look at it there.
A cell where a scan stops, because it is the goal or has a forced neighbour, is a jump point (G-2593)Jump point: A cell where a scan of jump point search stops because it is the goal or has a forced neighbour, a place where a route may have to turn; only jump points go on the open list. Explained in §11. Skipping equal routes: jump point search., and A* that puts only jump points on its open list is jump point search (G-2594)Jump point search (JPS): A* for grids with equal move costs that scans along straight lines and diagonals and puts only jump points on the open list; it skips equal routes that differ only in the order of their moves, and returns the same shortest route with far fewer open-list operations. Explained in §11. Skipping equal routes: jump point search., JPS (Harabor and Grastien 2011; zerowidth JPS).
A diagonal scan checks a straight scan in both of its directions at every step, and stops where one of them finds a jump point (zerowidth JPS). Our grid forbids cutting corners, so we use the version for that rule (Harabor and Grastien 2012). Figure 14 runs it on the door trip.

Figure 14: Jump point search on the room grid from S to G, one scan per frame. From each cell it takes off the open list, it scans in straight lines and diagonals without putting the cells it passes on the open list (light orange: this scan; grey: earlier scans); a scan stops at a wall or obstacle (nothing found) or at a jump point (green: on the open list; red: taken off it): G, or a cell with a forced neighbour (purple outline), a cell past an obstacle’s corner where a route may have to turn. Scanning up from the cell up-right of S stops beside the table’s corner, where the cell to the right opens up. JPS takes 5 cells off the open list (A*: 9) and only 7 cells ever enter it (A*: 23); the route through the jump points is 3.414 m
Watch frame “cell 2 off the open list: scan up”: the scan from the cell up-right of S runs up the table’s left side and stops beside the table’s corner, where the cell to its right (purple outline) has just come free. The route turns there. JPS takes 5 cells off its open list, against A*‘s 9, and only 7 cells ever enter it, against A*‘s 23 (notebook); on the long trip it takes 6 cells off against A*‘s 43.
The scans still look at cells, but looking costs far less than putting a cell on the open list and taking it off again, so JPS is faster without giving up the shortest route, on grids where every straight move and every diagonal move costs the same (Harabor and Grastien 2011; zerowidth JPS). Its route is still a chain of grid moves at 0° or 45°.
12. Routes at any angle: Theta*


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A grid route can only turn by multiples of 45°, so it is longer than a straight line through free space. Theta* lets a cell take its parent’s parent as its own parent whenever the straight line between them is clear, which shortens the door route from 3.414 m to 3.193 m.


Every route so far, from Dijkstra’s to JPS’s, is made of moves along the grid: straight or at 45°. The 3.414 m route of Section 4 goes up-right, up, up, up, up-right, right, while a robot could drive one straight line from S to beside the door and then turn.
The idea. A* builds every route from parent links between neighbouring cells. If a cell’s parent can see the cell’s neighbour directly, along a straight line that crosses no blocked cell, the neighbour can link to that parent instead, and its route becomes one straight segment instead of a bend (Daniel et al. 2010).
The standard terms. Two cells can see each other when the straight segment between their centres crosses no blocked cell. Search whose routes may run at any angle between cell centres, not just along grid moves, is any-angle search (G-2596)Any-angle search: Search on a grid whose routes may run at any angle between cell centres instead of only along grid moves at 0° and 45°, so they are shorter and need fewer turns. Explained in §12. Routes at any angle: Theta., and Theta* (G-2597)Theta:* An any-angle search: A* in which a neighbour takes the expanded cell’s own parent as its parent whenever the straight segment between their centres crosses no blocked cell; it gives routes of straight segments at any angle (3.193 m against 3.414 m on the room grid), but not always the shortest. Explained in §12. Routes at any angle: Theta. is A* with the shortcut above (Daniel et al. 2010; Patel, Variants). Figure 15 runs it on the door trip; most cells end up linked straight to S.

Figure 15: Theta* on the door trip, on the part of the room it touches (x 1.0 to 4.5 m, y 0 to 4 m). Theta* is A* with one change: when a cell is taken off the open list, each neighbour first tries the cell’s own parent as its parent, and keeps it if the straight line between their centres crosses no blocked cell, so the two cells can see each other. Grey lines join each cell to its parent; most cells see S directly. One expansion per frame. When the cell left of G is expanded, S cannot see G (the red dashed line crosses a table cell), so G’s parent is that cell. Last frame: the Theta* route, 2.693 + 0.500 = 3.193 m (blue), against the grid route of A*, 3.414 m (grey, dashed)
The Theta* route is one straight segment from the centre of S to the centre of the cell left of G, 1.0 m across and 2.5 m up, then one 0.5 m move into G:
\text{segment} = \sqrt{1.0^2 + 2.5^2}
= \sqrt{7.25}
= 2.693 \text{ m}
\text{route} = 2.693 + 0.5
= 3.193 \text{ m}
The Theta* route is shorter than the grid route by
3.414 - 3.193 = 0.221 \text{ m}
S cannot see G itself, because that line crosses a table cell (frame “cell 9 off the open list”). Theta* does not promise the shortest route at any angle (Daniel et al. 2010): a taut string from S round the corner of the blocked cell at (3.0 m, 3.0 m) to G would be 2.965 m (notebook).

Explained in §7. RO/navigation/04-graph-search-and-config.title: Symbolic Task Planning: STRIPS and PDDL
RO/navigation/04-graph-search-and-config.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Breadth-first searchBreadth-first search (BFS): A search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ring; Choosing the search stateSearch state: What a search keeps for each vertex: the quantities that decide which moves are allowed and what they cost, and nothing more, such as (cell, charge left) for a robot with a battery; leaving one out breaks the Markov property and can hide routes. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §10. Choosing the search state: the Markov rule; Explicit and implicit graphsImplicit graph: A graph never built in full: the search starts from the start vertex and calls a function that returns a vertex’s neighbours when it is expanded, so only the vertices the search reaches are made; this is what makes state spaces of millions of states searchable. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §9. Explicit and implicit graphs; A* searchA search:* Dijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid). Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.5 The algorithm.
Leads to: Manipulation planning (transit and transfer)Manipulation planning: Planning the motions of a robot together with the objects it moves, as a sequence of transit and transfer motions joined at transition configurations, each planned in its own free space. Explained in: Manipulation Planning, §2.3 The plan: transit, transfer, transit.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Carrying the cup from the table to the door takes steps in a fixed order (go to the table, pick up the cup, go to the door, put it down), not one route. We write the world as true-or-false facts and each action as the facts it needs, makes true and makes false; the task then becomes a search over sets of facts, which the graph searches of the earlier Notes already know how to do.


The robot can already plan a route. On the room’s occupancy gridOccupancy grid: A grid map that stores in each cell a number between 0 and 1, such as the probability that the cell is occupied, instead of a hard 0 or 1; the standard grid map of robotics, since sensors are never sure. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §5.2 Bitmaps and occupancy grids of 0.5 m cells, breadth-first search (G-2550)Breadth-first search (BFS): A search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ring takes it from its start cell to the cell just inside the door in 8 moves of 0.5 m, 4.0 m in all. With diagonal moves, Dijkstra’s algorithm (G-2565)Dijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §3.2 The algorithm: settle the nearest, update its neighbours and A* (G-2577)A search:* Dijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid). Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.5 The algorithm find the shortest route, 3.414 m. The robot stands at (2 m, 1 m), on the corner of its start cell.
Now give the robot a task (Figure 1): a cup stands on the table; carry it to the door. Route search fails on this task in two ways:

its search state (G-2562)Search state: What a search keeps for each vertex: the quantities that decide which moves are allowed and what they cost, and nothing more, such as (cell, charge left) for a robot with a battery; leaving one out breaks the Markov property and can hide routes. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §10. Choosing the search state: the Markov rule, what the search keeps for each place it reaches, is one of the 76 free cells, so it records where the robot is and nothing about the cup or the robot’s hand;
the task needs steps in a fixed order: go to the table, pick up the cup, go to the door, put it down. The shortest route to the door, 3.414 m, leaves the cup behind.


Figure 1: The room of the chapter, 7 m by 4 m, with the table, the cabinet and the two poles. The robot stands at (2, 1) facing 30 degrees; a cup stands on the table near its left edge. Three places are marked with dashed green circles: start (the robot’s spot), table (beside the table, where the robot can reach the cup) and door (just inside the doorway). On the right, the eight facts of the task, with the three true at the start in black: robot-at start, cup-at table, hand-empty. The goal is cup-at door
So the robot needs two things: a way to write down where things are and what it holds, and a way to write down what each step changes. Choosing a sequence of steps from a description of the world in true-or-false statements is symbolic task planning (G-2600)Symbolic task planning: Choosing a sequence of actions that reaches a goal, from a description of the world in true-or-false facts such as “the cup is on the table”; it decides the order of steps (go to the table, pick up, go to the door, put down) that a route search alone cannot. Explained in §1. Overview. (P&M §6.1; LaValle §2.4). “Symbolic” because the planner reasons with names, such as “the cup is on the table”, not with coordinates in metres.
The planner works with three places, marked in Figure 1:

start, where the robot stands now: the start cell (x 2.0 to 2.5 m, y 1.0 to 1.5 m);
table, the cell beside the table’s left edge (x 2.5 to 3.0 m, y 1.5 to 2.0 m), where the robot can reach the cup;
door, the goal cell of route search, just inside the doorway (x 3.5 to 4.0 m, y 3.5 to 4.0 m).

Going from one place to another is one step for the planner; the route search of the earlier Notes drives it (Section 5.3). In this Note we build the planner for the cup task:

facts and states, and why we never list every state (Section 2);
STRIPS actions, with their precondition, add list and delete list, and the frame problem they avoid (Section 3);
PDDL, the standard way to write a task down for any planner (Section 4);
forward search, which finds the plan on a graph of states, first breadth-first and then with A* (Section 5).

2. Describing the task with facts


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The first gap of route search is that a cell says nothing about the cup. We fix it with eight true-or-false facts about the robot, the cup and the hand; a state is the set of facts true now, and the start state holds robot-at start, cup-at table and hand-empty.


2.1 Facts and states
A grid cell says nothing about the cup, so we list the statements about the task that can be true or false. Such a statement is a fact (G-2601)Fact (task planning): A statement about the task that is either true or false, such as robot-at table or holding-cup; facts are what a planner’s states, actions and goals are made of. Explained in §2.1 Facts and states. (P&M §6.1; LaValle §2.4.1). The cup task needs eight facts:

robot-at start, robot-at table, robot-at door: where the robot is;
cup-at start, cup-at table, cup-at door: where the cup is lying;
holding-cup: the robot holds the cup;
hand-empty: the robot holds nothing.

The list on the right of Figure 1 marks the facts that are true at the start. The set of facts that are true at one moment is a state (G-2602)State (task planning): The set of facts that are true at one moment, every other fact being false, such as {robot-at start, cup-at table, hand-empty}; it records the objects and the robot’s hand, which a grid cell cannot. Explained in §2.1 Facts and states. of the task; every fact not in the set is false. The start state, which we name S0, holds three facts:

robot-at start;
cup-at table;
hand-empty.

hand-empty looks redundant, since holding-cup being false says the same. hand-empty is needed because a STRIPS precondition lists only facts that must be true, never facts that must be false (FAU AI-1 notes §8.4), so “the hand is empty” must be a fact of its own; the Blocks World domain, a standard planning example, uses arm-empty the same way (UMBC PDDL notes).
The task asks for one fact: cup-at door. The set of facts that must all be true at the end is the goal of the task (P&M §6.2). The goal says nothing about where the robot ends up, so every state that holds cup-at door meets it: with the robot at the start, at the table or at the door (LaValle §2.4.1: a goal stands for a set of states).
A sequence of actions that turns the start state into a state that meets the goal is a plan (P&M §6.2). For the cup task a person sees one at once:

move from the start to the table;
pick up the cup;
move from the table to the door;
put the cup down.

A computer does not see the plan. The computer must be able to tell, for any state, which actions it can take and where they lead. The next question is how many states it might have to consider.
2.2 Why we never list every state
A computer could list every state with the result of every action in it. Each fact is true or false on its own, so every new fact doubles the number of possible sets of facts. Figure 2 grows the true-or-false choices for the three robot-at facts, one fact per frame. Watch each level split every set in two: 1 set, then 2, 4 and 8. In the frame “only 3 of the 8 sets can happen”, only {start}, {table} and {door} stay, because the robot is always in exactly one place.

Figure 2: A tree of true-or-false choices, one fact per frame. Frame ‘no fact decided yet’: 1 set. Frames for robot-at start, robot-at table and robot-at door: each set splits into a true branch (green) and a false branch (red), giving 2, 4 and 8 sets; the 8 leaves list the places where robot-at is true, from {start, table, door} to {}. Frame ‘only 3 of the 8 sets can happen’: {start}, {table} and {door} turn blue, the other 5 are crossed out. Last frame: the count table on the right reaches 8 facts and 256 sets
With all eight facts, eight twos are multiplied:
2 \times 2 = 4
2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8
2^8 = 256
The same in symbols:

n is the number of facts, 8 for the cup task;
N is the number of possible sets of facts.

N = 2^n
= 2^8 = 256
Most of the 256 sets can never happen, such as a robot at the start and at the door at once. From the start state only 12 can (notebook): the robot in one of 3 places, and the cup in one of 4 spots (on the table, in the hand, at the start, at the door):
3 \times 4 = 12
Even so, a table that lists every state with the result of every action in it, such as “in S0, moving to the table gives S1”, is a poor way to describe a task, for three reasons (P&M §6.1.1):

Too many states. A fourth place adds two facts, one robot-at and one cup-at, so the 8 facts become 10 and the number of possible sets grows from 256 to 1024.
One change rewrites everything. Adding a battery level to the task changes every state in the table.
The pattern is hidden. Moving from the start to the table changes only where the robot is, in every state where the move is possible, but a table of states cannot say so.

Reason 1 in numbers, with 10 facts:
2^{10} = 1024
The third reason is the way out: describe each action once, by the few facts it changes, and let the computer build the states when it needs them.
3. STRIPS actions


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The second need of the Overview, a way to write down what each step changes, is met by describing each action once by three lists of facts: its precondition (what must be true to do it), its add list (what it makes true) and its delete list (what it makes false). Every fact on neither list keeps its value; in the state S1, pick-up table removes cup-at table and hand-empty, adds holding-cup and leaves the other five facts alone.


3.1 Precondition, add list and delete list
Section 2.2 left us needing a description of each action by the few facts it changes. Take picking up the cup at the table:

before it, three facts must be true: the robot is at the table, the cup is on the table, the hand is empty;
after it, one fact has become true: the robot holds the cup;
and two facts have become false: the cup is no longer on the table, and the hand is no longer empty.

These three lists are how the STRIPS planner describes an action (P&M §6.1.2; LaValle §2.4.1). STRIPS, the STanford Research Institute Problem Solver, was the planner of Shakey, one of the first robots built with artificial intelligence (P&M §6.1.2). The three lists are:

the precondition (G-2606)Precondition: The facts that must be true for an action to be done, such as robot-at table, cup-at table and hand-empty for picking up the cup; the planner tries an action only in states that hold all of them. Explained in §3.1 Precondition, add list and delete list.: the facts that must be true for the action to be done;
the add list (G-2607)Add list: The facts an action makes true, such as holding-cup for picking up the cup; applying the action puts them into the state. Explained in §3.1 Precondition, add list and delete list.: the facts the action makes true;
the delete list (G-2608)Delete list: The facts an action makes false, such as cup-at table and hand-empty for picking up the cup; applying the action takes them out of the state. Explained in §3.1 Precondition, add list and delete list.: the facts the action makes false.

An action described by these three lists is a STRIPS action (G-2605)STRIPS action: An action described by three lists of facts, its precondition, add list and delete list, as in the STRIPS planner of the Shakey robot; one such description replaces a table of the action’s result in every state. Explained in §3.1 Precondition, add list and delete list.. The four actions of the plan of Section 2.1:



































ActionPreconditionAdd listDelete listmove start tablerobot-at startrobot-at tablerobot-at startpick-up tablerobot-at table, cup-at table, hand-emptyholding-cupcup-at table, hand-emptymove table doorrobot-at tablerobot-at doorrobot-at tableput-down doorrobot-at door, holding-cupcup-at door, hand-emptyholding-cup
A move deletes the old place because the robot cannot be in two places at once. The other actions of the task are the same three kinds at the other places (notebook):

a move from each of the 3 places to each of the other 2;
a pick-up at each of the 3 places;
a put-down at each of the 3 places.

3 \times 2 = 6 \text{ moves}
6 + 3 + 3 = 12 \text{ actions}
The 12 actions describe the whole task. What they are for is applying them to a state, which Section 3.2 does.
3.2 Applying an action
With the three lists, the computer can now check the plan of Section 2.1 by itself, one action at a time. An action can be done in a state only when every fact of its precondition is true there; the action is then applicable in that state (P&M §6.2). Doing it takes the delete list out of the state and puts the add list in (P&M §6.1.2; LaValle §2.4.1). Our example is pick-up table in the state S1, the state after move start table:

s is the state before the action, a set of facts; here S1, which holds robot-at table, cup-at table and hand-empty;
\text{pre} is the action’s precondition: robot-at table, cup-at table, hand-empty;
\text{del} is its delete list: cup-at table, hand-empty;
\text{add} is its add list: holding-cup;
s' is the state after the action;
\subseteq means “every fact on the left is also on the right”: the set {robot-at table} \subseteq S1 is true, while {holding-cup} \subseteq S1 is false;
\setminus means “take out”: S1 \setminus del keeps the facts of S1 that are not in del;
\cup is the union (G-2045)Union (A ∪ B): The set of elements in A or B (or both), such as the points inside either of two convex pieces of an obstacle; for events, the event that A or B (or both) happens. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Mutually Exclusive Events, §5. The addition rule: where mutual exclusivity pays off of two sets: every fact that is in either one.

The test for applying the action, and the next state:
\text{pre} \subseteq s
s' = (s \setminus \text{del}) \cup \text{add}
On S1, the three facts of the precondition are all in S1, so pick-up table is applicable. Taking out the delete list leaves one fact:
s \setminus \text{del} = \lbrace\text{robot-at table} \rbrace
Putting in the add list gives the next state. We call it S3, because Section 5.1 numbers the states in the order its search makes them:
s' = \lbrace\text{robot-at table}, \text{holding-cup} \rbrace
The order of the two steps does not matter here, because no fact is on both lists of an action.
Figure 3 applies the whole plan this way, one action at a time. Watch the fact list on the right. In each frame named “is its precondition true?”, the needed facts turn blue. In the next frame, named “delete list removed, add list added”, the deleted facts turn red and the added ones green, while the room on the left shows the robot and the cup where the facts now say they are. The last frame, “goal reached”, holds cup-at door, so the plan meets the goal.

Figure 3: The four-action plan applied, one action per stage. Left: the room, with the robot driving each move along a shortest route of grid cells (orange trail) and the cup (orange dot) on the table, then in the robot’s hand, then at the door. Right: the eight facts, black when true and grey when false, with a card giving the action’s precondition, add list and delete list. In the stage ‘is its precondition true?’ the precondition’s facts are blue with a tick; in the stage ‘delete list removed, add list added’ the deleted facts are red and the added ones green. The last frame shows robot-at door, cup-at door and hand-empty true: goal reached after 4 actions
Checking a plan we were given takes four applications of the rule. Two questions are still open: why describe actions by their changes at all (Section 3.3), and how a computer finds a plan that nobody gave it (Section 5).
3.3 Why lists of changes: the frame problem
Section 3.2 changed only 3 of the 8 facts with pick-up table; the other 5 stayed as they were. Writing down what every fact is after the action needs a line for each of the 8 facts, and 5 of those 8 lines only say “stays the same”. Figure 4 puts the two descriptions of pick-up table side by side: on the left, the full list, with five grey lines that say “stays”; on the right, the STRIPS lists, with only the three coloured changes.

Figure 4: The action pick-up table, done in the state S1, described two ways. Left, ‘every fact, after the action’: eight lines; robot-at start, robot-at table, robot-at door, cup-at start and cup-at door are grey and say ‘stays false’ or ‘stays true’; cup-at table and hand-empty are red, ‘becomes false’; holding-cup is green, ‘becomes true’. Right, ‘STRIPS: only the changes’: precondition robot-at table, cup-at table, hand-empty; add holding-cup; delete cup-at table, hand-empty; every other fact keeps its value. Below: over all 12 actions, 12 times 8 = 96 lines on the left, 66 of them ‘stays the same’; STRIPS writes 30 list entries and leaves the 66 out
Over all 12 actions of the task:

A is the number of actions, 12;
n is the number of facts, 8;
c is the number of changes, counted over all actions: 2 for each move (one fact added, one deleted), 3 for each pick-up and each put-down;
L is the number of lines needed to say every fact after every action;
F is the number of those lines that only say “stays the same”.

The changes first, counted from the action lists:
c = 6 \times 2 + 3 \times 3 + 3 \times 3
= 12 + 9 + 9 = 30
Then the lines, our numbers first, each followed by the same step in symbols:
L = 12 \times 8 = 96
L = A\thinspace n
F = 96 - 30 = 66
F = A\thinspace n - c
So 66 of the 96 lines say only that nothing else changes. Written in logic, each of these “stays the same” statements must be spelled out, one for each action and each fact it leaves alone, and their number grows with every new fact and every new action (P&M §6.1.3 calls them frame rules). Having to state everything an action does not change is the frame problem (G-2610)Frame problem: The difficulty that a logical description of an action must also state everything the action leaves unchanged, one statement per action and fact (66 of 96 lines in the cup task); STRIPS avoids it with the rule that a fact on neither list keeps its value. Explained in §3.3 Why lists of changes: the frame problem. (FAU AI-1 notes §8.1). An everyday comparison: a recipe says “add the salt”; it never adds “the flour, the oven and the rest of the kitchen stay as they are”.
STRIPS avoids the 66 lines with one rule: a fact that is on neither list keeps its value (P&M §6.1.2). So STRIPS writes the 30 changes and nothing else, which is why a state can be updated by taking out the delete list and putting in the add list, as in Section 3.2.
The price is that every STRIPS action has fixed lists. A move to the table and a move to the door change different facts, so each pair of places needs its own move action (P&M §6.1.2). With 3 places that is 6 moves; Section 4 shows how the count grows, and how a planning language writes all of them at once.
4. PDDL: the task in two files


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

To hand the cup task to a planner, we write it in PDDL, the standard language that planners read. STRIPS needs one move action per pair of places, 6 for our 3 places and 90 for 10; PDDL writes one move with the parameters ?from and ?to, and splits the task into a domain file (the predicates and actions, written once) and a problem file (the places, the start state and the goal, one per task).


4.1 One action with parameters
Section 3.3 ended with one STRIPS move action per pair of places. A move leaves one of the places for one of the others:

k is the number of places, 3 for the cup task;
M is the number of STRIPS move actions.

M = 3 \times 2 = 6
M = k\thinspace(k - 1)
A building with 10 places would need:
M = 10 \times 9 = 90
All 90 say the same thing: be at one place, end at another. So we write the move once, with blanks for the two places, and let the planner fill them in. Such a blank is a parameter (G-2614)Parameter (PDDL action): A blank in an action, written with a question mark such as ?from and ?to in move ?from ?to, that the planner fills with objects; one action with parameters replaces many STRIPS actions (6 moves for 3 places, 90 for 10). Explained in §4.1 One action with parameters. of the action, written with a question mark: move ?from ?to (UMBC PDDL notes; LaValle §2.4.1). Facts get blanks too: robot-at ?p stands for the three facts robot-at start, robot-at table and robot-at door. A fact pattern with blanks is a predicate (G-2613)Predicate (PDDL): A fact pattern with blanks, such as robot-at ?p, which stands for one fact per object (robot-at start, robot-at table, robot-at door); it lets a domain name a whole family of facts at once. Explained in §4.1 One action with parameters. (LaValle §2.4.1).
The language that writes tasks this way is the Planning Domain Definition Language (G-2612)PDDL (Planning Domain Definition Language): The standard language for writing a planning task, defined in 1998 for the International Planning Competition: actions with parameters, preconditions and effects, in a domain file and a problem file; a task written in it can be handed to any planner that reads PDDL. Explained in §4.1 One action with parameters., PDDL, defined in 1998 for the International Planning Competition and read by many planners today (planning.wiki; UMBC PDDL notes). A common language means a robot’s task can be handed to any planner, and a better planner can replace the old one without rewriting the task. PDDL keeps the STRIPS idea: an action’s effect lists the facts it makes true, and the facts it makes false inside (not ...). A PDDL task comes in two files, one for what never changes and one for the task itself, which Sections 4.2 and 4.3 write for the cup task.
4.2 The domain file
The parts of the cup task that never change go in the domain file (G-2615)Domain file (PDDL): The PDDL file that holds the parts of a task family that never change: its predicates and its actions; it is written once and reused for every problem in that family. Explained in §4.2 The domain file.: the predicates and the three actions (UMBC PDDL notes). Our domain file, data/cup-domain.pddl:
(define (domain cup-room)
  (:requirements :strips)
  (:predicates (robot-at ?p) (cup-at ?p) (holding-cup) (hand-empty))
 
  (:action move
    :parameters (?from ?to)
    :precondition (robot-at ?from)
    :effect (and (robot-at ?to) (not (robot-at ?from))))
 
  (:action pick-up
    :parameters (?p)
    :precondition (and (robot-at ?p) (cup-at ?p) (hand-empty))
    :effect (and (holding-cup) (not (cup-at ?p)) (not (hand-empty))))
 
  (:action put-down
    :parameters (?p)
    :precondition (and (robot-at ?p) (holding-cup))
    :effect (and (cup-at ?p) (hand-empty) (not (holding-cup)))))
Reading it line by line:

:requirements :strips says that the file uses only the STRIPS features of PDDL: preconditions, add lists and delete lists;
:predicates lists the four predicates;
each :action has its :parameters, its :precondition, and an :effect that holds the add list (the plain facts) and the delete list (the facts inside not).

The move action with ?from = start and ?to = table is the STRIPS action move start table of Section 3.1, with the same three lists. The many round brackets are the notation of the Lisp programming language, which PDDL keeps (UMBC PDDL notes). The domain file says what the robot can do, but not where it starts or what it must achieve.
4.3 The problem file
What changes from task to task goes in the problem file (G-2616)Problem file (PDDL): The PDDL file that holds one task: its objects, its start state and its goal; a new task needs only a new problem file for the same domain file. Explained in §4.3 The problem file.: the objects (here the three places), the start state and the goal (UMBC PDDL notes). Our problem file, data/cup-problem.pddl:
(define (problem cup-to-door)
  (:domain cup-room)
  (:objects start table door)
  (:init (robot-at start) (cup-at table) (hand-empty))
  (:goal (cup-at door)))
:init is the start state S0 of Section 2.1, and :goal the goal. Figure 5 shows how the files are used: the planner reads both and returns a plan. A new task, such as bringing the cup back from the door to the table, needs only a new problem file with a new :init and :goal (in data/cup-problem-back.pddl); the domain file stays as it is.

Figure 5: The domain file (written once: the predicates robot-at ?p, cup-at ?p, holding-cup, hand-empty and the actions move ?from ?to, pick-up ?p, put-down ?p) and the problem file (one per task: the objects start, table, door, the start state and the goal cup-at door) both go into the planner, which runs forward search and returns the plan: 1 move start table, 2 pick-up table, 3 move table door, 4 put-down door. A note under the problem file: a new task needs only a new problem file
As a check, the notebook reads the two files the way a PDDL planner does: it fills each action’s parameters with the three places and runs breadth-first search (Section 5.1). The search returns the four actions of Section 2.1, and for the cup-back problem file it returns move start door, pick-up door, move door table, put-down table. The files say what the task is; how the planner finds the plan is the subject of Section 5.
5. Forward search: finding the plan


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The last part of the problem is finding the plan without being told it. Forward search starts from the start state, applies every applicable action to make the next states, and searches the resulting graph of states for one that meets the goal; breadth-first search finds the 4-action plan after taking 8 states from the frontier, and A* with a count of the actions still needed takes only 5.


5.1 The state graph, built while searching
The rule of Section 3.2 turns one state into the next. Applied to every applicable action of every state, it links the states into a graph (G-2540)Graph: A set of vertices (points) joined by edges (lines), such as the room’s 76 free cells joined by 114 moves; it keeps only which places connect directly, so one search method works for maps, puzzles and any problem of states and moves. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edges, points joined by links: each state is a vertex (G-2541)Vertex (graph): One point of a graph, such as one free cell of the room or one waypoint; the places a search moves between. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edges of the graph, and each action is an edge (G-2542)Edge (graph): A link between two vertices of a graph, such as one 0.5 m move between two free cells that share a side; it says the search can go directly from one vertex to the other. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edges, a link from one state to the state it leads to (P&M §6.2). The graph is never stored in full; the planner makes a state’s neighbours from the action lists only when it reaches that state, as for the implicit graph (G-2561)Implicit graph: A graph never built in full: the search starts from the start vertex and calls a function that returns a vertex’s neighbours when it is expanded, so only the vertices the search reaches are made; this is what makes state spaces of millions of states searchable. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §9. Explicit and implicit graphs of route search, a graph whose neighbours are made on demand.
A planner that starts at the start state and moves forward, action by action, until it reaches a state that meets the goal is doing forward search (G-2617)Forward search (progression): Planning by starting at the start state, applying every applicable action to make the next states, and searching the resulting graph of states until one meets the goal; any graph search, such as breadth-first search or A*, can run it. Explained in §5.1 The state graph, built while searching., also called progression (P&M §6.2; LaValle §2.4). Any graph search of the earlier Notes can run it. We start with breadth-first search (G-2550)Breadth-first search (BFS): A search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ring, which keeps a frontier (G-2547)Frontier (open list): The vertices a search has reached but not yet expanded, waiting to be taken off one at a time; which one comes off next is what makes one search differ from another. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §4. Searching with a frontier and a visited list, the states made but not yet taken, and takes them in the order they were made.
From S0, two actions are applicable: move start table and move start door. pick-up start is not, because the cup is not at the start. So S0 has two neighbours, and the search grows from there. Figure 6 runs breadth-first search on the cup task, one state taken per frame. Columns are where the robot is and rows where the cup is; every line is a move along a row or a pick-up or put-down down a column, and each line stands for two actions, one each way. The states are numbered in the order the search makes them. Watch the frontier list at the bottom:

frame “take S0” makes S1 and S2;
frame “take S2: makes nothing new”: with the robot at the door and the cup on the table, both moves lead back to states already made;
S3 is the state of Section 3.2, the cup in the hand at the table;
frame “take S7” stops, because S7 holds cup-at door.


Figure 6: Breadth-first forward search on the cup task’s states, one state taken per frame. Each box is a state with its true facts; columns: robot at start, table, door; rows: cup on the table, in the hand, at the door, at the start. Blue: the state taken now; orange: states in the frontier; grey: states taken before. The first frame takes S0 and makes S1 (move start table) and S2 (move start door). ‘take S2: makes nothing new’. The search goes on to S3 (pick-up table), S4 and S5 (the two moves holding the cup), S6 (put-down start), S7 (put-down door), S8 and S9. Frame ‘take S7’ stops at the goal. Last frame: the plan read back from S7 in green, S0, S1, S3, S5, S7; S10 and S11, the other two states with the cup at the door, were never made; 8 states taken, 10 made, 12 reachable
The last frame reads the plan back from S7, following each state to the state it was made from:

move start table (S0 to S1);
pick-up table (S1 to S3);
move table door (S3 to S5);
put-down door (S5 to S7).

The search took 8 states from the frontier and made 10 of the 12 states the task can reach, the states that some sequence of actions leads to from the start (notebook). The other 244 of the 256 possible sets were never touched. Breadth-first search also returns a plan with the fewest actions, because it looks at all states one action away before any state two actions away. The plan is the one of Section 2.1, now found by the computer.
Eight states is cheap here, but the count grows with the number of facts. With n facts there can be up to 2^n states (Section 2.2), so a task with a few more places, cups and doors has far more states for breadth-first search to take, and the search needs a guide.
5.2 A heuristic cuts the search
Section 5.1 took 8 states to find a 4-action plan. A* (G-2577)A search:* Dijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid). Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.5 The algorithm takes fewer when it has a heuristic (G-2570)Heuristic h: A cheap guess of the cost still to go from a state to the goal, such as 3.121 m from the start cell to the door; a search uses it to prefer states that look nearer the goal. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §2. A guess of the distance left: the heuristic, a guess of the cost still to go, that never overestimates that cost: an admissible heuristic (G-2578)Admissible heuristic: A heuristic that is never more than the true cost left from any state, h \le h^\ast; it makes f a lower bound on every route through a state, so the first route A* takes off the open list is the shortest. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §5.1 A guess that never overestimates. With every action costing 1, a good guess is the fewest actions still needed, counted like the coffee-delivery example of P&M §6.2:

if the cup is at the door: 0;
if the robot holds the cup: 1 for the put-down, plus 1 for a move if the robot is not at the door;
if the cup lies elsewhere: 3 for pick-up, move and put-down, plus 1 for a move to the cup if the robot is not there.

Each action counted must happen at least once, so the count never overestimates. For the start state S0:

g is the cost so far (G-2574)Cost so far g (g-value): The length of the best route found so far from the start to a state; A* lowers it whenever a shorter way into the state turns up. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.1 g, h and f on the first step, here the number of actions taken, 0 in S0;
h is the heuristic, the fewest actions still needed;
f is their sum (G-2575)Estimated total cost f (f-value): The cost so far plus the heuristic, f = g + h: the length of the best route through a state if the guess were exact; A* expands the open state with the smallest f. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.1 g, h and f on the first step, the cost A* expects for a plan through the state.

h = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4
f = g + h = 0 + 4 = 4
The four 1s are the move to the table, the pick-up, the move to the door and the put-down. Figure 7 runs A* on the same state graph, with the same state names as Figure 6, and writes g + h = f in the corner of each box. A* always takes the frontier state with the smallest f. Watch the frontier list: S2 (f = 5, the robot drove to the door without the cup) and S4 (f = 5, the robot carried the cup back to the start) wait in the frontier, while every state with f = 4 lies on the plan.

Figure 7: A* forward search on the same states as Figure 6, one state taken per frame, with g + h = f in the corner of each box (g: actions so far, h: fewest actions still needed). The first frame shows S0 with 0 + 4 = 4. ‘take S1 (f = 4): makes S3’ (2 + 2 = 4). ‘take S5 (f = 4): makes S7’ (4 + 0 = 4). Last frame: A* takes 5 states, breadth-first search 8; the same 4-action plan in green; S2 (1 + 4 = 5) and S4 (3 + 2 = 5) were made but never taken
A* takes 5 states, S0, S1, S3, S5 and S7, against 8 for breadth-first search, and returns the same 4-action plan (notebook). Our heuristic was written by hand for this one task. Planners built for any task guide forward search with a heuristic too: the default planner of the free planning.domains service is a forward search guided by a heuristic (UMBC PDDL notes). The plan is found; each of its moves still has to be driven.
5.3 From the plan back to routes
The plan of Section 5.2 says “move start table”, not how to drive there. Each move is handed to the route search of the earlier Notes, on the 8-connected grid (G-2564)8-connected grid: A grid made into a graph by joining each cell to all 8 cells around it: 4 straight moves of one cell side and 4 diagonal moves of 1.414 cell sides (0.707 m for 0.5 m cells), usually without cutting the corner of a blocked cell; it gives shorter, less jagged routes than a 4-connected grid. Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §2.1 Diagonal moves: the 8-connected grid, the 0.5 m grid with diagonal moves, from the cell of one place to the cell of the next (P&M §6.1 leaves the actions to a lower-level controller in the same way). The last frame of Figure 3 shows the two routes:

move start table: one diagonal step, 0.707 m;
move table door: 2.707 m.

0.707 + 2.707 = 3.414 \text{ m}
Fetching the cup costs no extra distance, because the table place lies on a shortest route from the start to the door: the plan’s two routes add up to the 3.414 m of the direct route of the Overview (notebook). The task now has its answer: four actions in a fixed order, found by forward search, each move driven by route search.
