8. Key terms
Terms taught in this Note come first; linked terms are recaps, taught in the Note the link opens.





























































































































TermMeaningSymbolic task planning (G-2600)Symbolic task planning: Choosing a sequence of actions that reaches a goal, from a description of the world in true-or-false facts such as “the cup is on the table”; it decides the order of steps (go to the table, pick up, go to the door, put down) that a route search alone cannot. Explained in §1. Overview.Choosing a sequence of actions that reaches a goal, from a description of the world in true-or-false facts such as “the cup is on the table”; it decides the order of steps (go to the table, pick up, go to the door, put down) that a route search alone cannot.Fact (task planning) (G-2601)Fact (task planning): A statement about the task that is either true or false, such as robot-at table or holding-cup; facts are what a planner’s states, actions and goals are made of. Explained in §2.1 Facts and states.A statement about the task that is either true or false, such as robot-at table or holding-cup; facts are what a planner’s states, actions and goals are made of.State (task planning) (G-2602)State (task planning): The set of facts that are true at one moment, every other fact being false, such as {robot-at start, cup-at table, hand-empty}; it records the objects and the robot’s hand, which a grid cell cannot. Explained in §2.1 Facts and states.The set of facts that are true at one moment, every other fact being false, such as {robot-at start, cup-at table, hand-empty}; it records the objects and the robot’s hand, which a grid cell cannot.Precondition (G-2606)Precondition: The facts that must be true for an action to be done, such as robot-at table, cup-at table and hand-empty for picking up the cup; the planner tries an action only in states that hold all of them. Explained in §3.1 Precondition, add list and delete list.The facts that must be true for an action to be done, such as robot-at table, cup-at table and hand-empty for picking up the cup; the planner tries an action only in states that hold all of them.Add list (G-2607)Add list: The facts an action makes true, such as holding-cup for picking up the cup; applying the action puts them into the state. Explained in §3.1 Precondition, add list and delete list.The facts an action makes true, such as holding-cup for picking up the cup; applying the action puts them into the state.Delete list (G-2608)Delete list: The facts an action makes false, such as cup-at table and hand-empty for picking up the cup; applying the action takes them out of the state. Explained in §3.1 Precondition, add list and delete list.The facts an action makes false, such as cup-at table and hand-empty for picking up the cup; applying the action takes them out of the state.STRIPS action (G-2605)STRIPS action: An action described by three lists of facts, its precondition, add list and delete list, as in the STRIPS planner of the Shakey robot; one such description replaces a table of the action’s result in every state. Explained in §3.1 Precondition, add list and delete list.An action described by three lists of facts, its precondition, add list and delete list, as in the STRIPS planner of the Shakey robot; one such description replaces a table of the action’s result in every state.Frame problem (G-2610)Frame problem: The difficulty that a logical description of an action must also state everything the action leaves unchanged, one statement per action and fact (66 of 96 lines in the cup task); STRIPS avoids it with the rule that a fact on neither list keeps its value. Explained in §3.3 Why lists of changes: the frame problem.The difficulty that a logical description of an action must also state everything the action leaves unchanged, one statement per action and fact (66 of 96 lines in the cup task); STRIPS avoids it with the rule that a fact on neither list keeps its value.Parameter (PDDL action) (G-2614)Parameter (PDDL action): A blank in an action, written with a question mark such as ?from and ?to in move ?from ?to, that the planner fills with objects; one action with parameters replaces many STRIPS actions (6 moves for 3 places, 90 for 10). Explained in §4.1 One action with parameters.A blank in an action, written with a question mark such as ?from and ?to in move ?from ?to, that the planner fills with objects; one action with parameters replaces many STRIPS actions (6 moves for 3 places, 90 for 10).Predicate (PDDL) (G-2613)Predicate (PDDL): A fact pattern with blanks, such as robot-at ?p, which stands for one fact per object (robot-at start, robot-at table, robot-at door); it lets a domain name a whole family of facts at once. Explained in §4.1 One action with parameters.A fact pattern with blanks, such as robot-at ?p, which stands for one fact per object (robot-at start, robot-at table, robot-at door); it lets a domain name a whole family of facts at once.PDDL (Planning Domain Definition Language) (G-2612)PDDL (Planning Domain Definition Language): The standard language for writing a planning task, defined in 1998 for the International Planning Competition: actions with parameters, preconditions and effects, in a domain file and a problem file; a task written in it can be handed to any planner that reads PDDL. Explained in §4.1 One action with parameters.The standard language for writing a planning task, defined in 1998 for the International Planning Competition: actions with parameters, preconditions and effects, in a domain file and a problem file; a task written in it can be handed to any planner that reads PDDL.Domain file (PDDL) (G-2615)Domain file (PDDL): The PDDL file that holds the parts of a task family that never change: its predicates and its actions; it is written once and reused for every problem in that family. Explained in §4.2 The domain file.The PDDL file that holds the parts of a task family that never change: its predicates and its actions; it is written once and reused for every problem in that family.Problem file (PDDL) (G-2616)Problem file (PDDL): The PDDL file that holds one task: its objects, its start state and its goal; a new task needs only a new problem file for the same domain file. Explained in §4.3 The problem file.The PDDL file that holds one task: its objects, its start state and its goal; a new task needs only a new problem file for the same domain file.Forward search (progression) (G-2617)Forward search (progression): Planning by starting at the start state, applying every applicable action to make the next states, and searching the resulting graph of states until one meets the goal; any graph search, such as breadth-first search or A*, can run it. Explained in §5.1 The state graph, built while searching.Planning by starting at the start state, applying every applicable action to make the next states, and searching the resulting graph of states until one meets the goal; any graph search, such as breadth-first search or A*, can run it.Breadth-first search (BFS) (G-2550)Breadth-first search (BFS): A search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ringA search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same.Dijkstra’s algorithm (G-2565)Dijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §3.2 The algorithm: settle the nearest, update its neighboursA search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals).A* search (G-2577)A search:* Dijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid). Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.5 The algorithmDijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid).Search state (G-2562)Search state: What a search keeps for each vertex: the quantities that decide which moves are allowed and what they cost, and nothing more, such as (cell, charge left) for a robot with a battery; leaving one out breaks the Markov property and can hide routes. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §10. Choosing the search state: the Markov ruleWhat a search keeps for each vertex: the quantities that decide which moves are allowed and what they cost, and nothing more, such as (cell, charge left) for a robot with a battery; leaving one out breaks the Markov property and can hide routes.Union (A ∪ B) (G-2045)Union (A ∪ B): The set of elements in A or B (or both), such as the points inside either of two convex pieces of an obstacle; for events, the event that A or B (or both) happens. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Mutually Exclusive Events, §5. The addition rule: where mutual exclusivity pays offThe set of elements in A or B (or both), such as the points inside either of two convex pieces of an obstacle; for events, the event that A or B (or both) happens.Graph (G-2540)Graph: A set of vertices (points) joined by edges (lines), such as the room’s 76 free cells joined by 114 moves; it keeps only which places connect directly, so one search method works for maps, puzzles and any problem of states and moves. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edgesA set of vertices (points) joined by edges (lines), such as the room’s 76 free cells joined by 114 moves; it keeps only which places connect directly, so one search method works for maps, puzzles and any problem of states and moves.Vertex (graph) (G-2541)Vertex (graph): One point of a graph, such as one free cell of the room or one waypoint; the places a search moves between. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edgesOne point of a graph, such as one free cell of the room or one waypoint; the places a search moves between.Edge (graph) (G-2542)Edge (graph): A link between two vertices of a graph, such as one 0.5 m move between two free cells that share a side; it says the search can go directly from one vertex to the other. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edgesA link between two vertices of a graph, such as one 0.5 m move between two free cells that share a side; it says the search can go directly from one vertex to the other.Implicit graph (G-2561)Implicit graph: A graph never built in full: the search starts from the start vertex and calls a function that returns a vertex’s neighbours when it is expanded, so only the vertices the search reaches are made; this is what makes state spaces of millions of states searchable. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §9. Explicit and implicit graphsA graph never built in full: the search starts from the start vertex and calls a function that returns a vertex’s neighbours when it is expanded, so only the vertices the search reaches are made; this is what makes state spaces of millions of states searchable.Frontier (open list) (G-2547)Frontier (open list): The vertices a search has reached but not yet expanded, waiting to be taken off one at a time; which one comes off next is what makes one search differ from another. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §4. Searching with a frontier and a visited listThe vertices a search has reached but not yet expanded, waiting to be taken off one at a time; which one comes off next is what makes one search differ from another.Heuristic h (G-2570)Heuristic h: A cheap guess of the cost still to go from a state to the goal, such as 3.121 m from the start cell to the door; a search uses it to prefer states that look nearer the goal. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §2. A guess of the distance left: the heuristicA cheap guess of the cost still to go from a state to the goal, such as 3.121 m from the start cell to the door; a search uses it to prefer states that look nearer the goal.Admissible heuristic (G-2578)Admissible heuristic: A heuristic that is never more than the true cost left from any state, h \le h^\ast; it makes f a lower bound on every route through a state, so the first route A* takes off the open list is the shortest. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §5.1 A guess that never overestimatesA heuristic that is never more than the true cost left from any state, h \le h^\ast; it makes f a lower bound on every route through a state, so the first route A* takes off the open list is the shortest.Cost so far g (g-value) (G-2574)Cost so far g (g-value): The length of the best route found so far from the start to a state; A* lowers it whenever a shorter way into the state turns up. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.1 g, h and f on the first stepThe length of the best route found so far from the start to a state; A* lowers it whenever a shorter way into the state turns up.Estimated total cost f (f-value) (G-2575)Estimated total cost f (f-value): The cost so far plus the heuristic, f = g + h: the length of the best route through a state if the guess were exact; A* expands the open state with the smallest f. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.1 g, h and f on the first stepThe cost so far plus the heuristic, f = g + h: the length of the best route through a state if the guess were exact; A* expands the open state with the smallest f.8-connected grid (G-2564)8-connected grid: A grid made into a graph by joining each cell to all 8 cells around it: 4 straight moves of one cell side and 4 diagonal moves of 1.414 cell sides (0.707 m for 0.5 m cells), usually without cutting the corner of a blocked cell; it gives shorter, less jagged routes than a 4-connected grid. Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §2.1 Diagonal moves: the 8-connected gridA grid made into a graph by joining each cell to all 8 cells around it: 4 straight moves of one cell side and 4 diagonal moves of 1.414 cell sides (0.707 m for 0.5 m cells), usually without cutting the corner of a blocked cell; it gives shorter, less jagged routes than a 4-connected grid.

RO/navigation/04-graph-search-and-config.title: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom
RO/navigation/04-graph-search-and-config.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: PosePose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading; Why exact planning is hardExplained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §8. Why exact planning is hard: NP-hard and PSPACE-hard.
Leads to: Obstacle region and free spaceFree space: All configurations at which the robot touches no obstacle, C_{\text{free}}, the C-space without the obstacle region; a planner looks for a path that stays inside it. Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle; Complete, resolution-complete and probabilistically completeExplained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §5. Can a planner miss a route? Completeness; Manipulation planning (transit and transfer)Manipulation planning: Planning the motions of a robot together with the objects it moves, as a sequence of transit and transfer motions joined at transition configurations, each planned in its own free space. Explained in: Manipulation Planning, §2.3 The plan: transit, transfer, transit; Kinodynamic planning and phase spaceKinodynamic planning: Planning a motion that avoids obstacles and also obeys limits on how the state can change, \dot{x} = f(x, u) with bounded inputs, such as a top speed and an acceleration limit; its plans can be driven as they are, without stops the robot cannot make. Explained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §2.3 Kinodynamic planning.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The routes of the earlier Notes move a point from cell to cell, but the robot is a body with a size and a heading, and placing it takes three numbers, (x, y, θ). The numbers that place every point of a robot are its configuration; all configurations together form the configuration space, and planning a motion means finding a path through that space.


The robot can now plan a task. The task plannerExplained in: Symbolic Task Planning: STRIPS and PDDL, §5. Forward search: finding the plan of the cup task returns four actions, and each move is a route on the 0.5 m grid, such as the shortest route from the start cell to the cell just inside the door, 3.414 m long (routes of the planExplained in: Symbolic Task Planning: STRIPS and PDDL, §5.3 From the plan back to routes).
What still breaks is the robot itself (Figure 1). The route moves a point from cell centre to cell centre. The real robot is a body: seen from above, a disk of radius 0.25 m centred on the middle of its axle, big enough to hold the 0.2 m axle and the wheels. At the start it stands at (2 m, 1 m) and faces 30°. Two problems follow:

the two numbers (x, y) say where the centre is, but not which way the robot faces, and a robot facing the table drives off differently from one facing the door;
the heading wraps round: 350° and 10° are only 20° apart, so a planner that treats the heading as an ordinary number thinks the two are 340° apart.


Figure 1: The room with the table, the cabinet and the two poles. Orange: a route of the graph-search Notes, a point moved from cell centre to cell centre towards the door. Red: the robot, a disk of radius 0.25 m centred at (2, 1), with an arrow for its heading of 30 degrees measured from the x-axis
In this Note we answer three questions:

Which numbers place the whole robot, and how many are needed (Section 2 and Section 3)?
What shape do all those numbers form, and how do we write them down without a jump at 360° (Section 4 and Section 5)?
What is the planning problem in that space (Section 6)?

A second robot joins the floor robot in this Note: an arm with two joints on the robot’s top plate, the kind of arm that picks up the cup. Each of its two joints turns all the way round, so it shows a shape that the floor robot’s single angle cannot (the 2R arm of MR §2.3.1, R for a revolute joint). Two facts from earlier work are used throughout. A robot arm is a chain of rigid links joined by joints, and a revolute joint lets one link turn about the other. And once the position and heading of a rigid body are known, the position of each of its points follows by a rotation by the heading and a shift by the position.
2. Configuration and configuration space


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The first question is which numbers place the whole robot. For the floor robot, the centre (x, y) and the heading θ fix every point of its body, so (2, 1, 0.524) is its configuration; all configurations together form the configuration space, a box whose top face and bottom face are the same headings.


2.1 The configuration: numbers that place every point
The route gives two numbers, the (x, y) of a point. The robot’s body is rigid: every point of it keeps its distance from every other point. So once we know where the centre is and which way the robot faces, every other point of the body is fixed: rotate the point by the heading, then shift it by the centre’s position.
Take the front point of the body, 0.25 m ahead of the centre:

x, y are the centre’s position, 2 m and 1 m;
\theta is the heading, 30°, which is 0.524 rad;
a is how far the point lies ahead of the centre, in the robot’s own frame, 0.25 m;
x_f, y_f are the front point’s position in the room, in m.

The point lies a along the heading, and a length along the heading splits into a run along x and a rise along y, the same split as the robot’s speed in cosine and sine partsExplained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §5.1 Why the speed splits into cosine and sine parts:
x_f = x + a\cos\theta
= 2 + 0.25 \times 0.8660
= 2 + 0.2165 = 2.2165 \text{ m}
y_f = y + a\sin\theta
= 1 + 0.25 \times 0.5 = 1.125 \text{ m}
Any other point of the body works the same way, so three numbers fix all of them. A list of numbers that fixes the position of every point of a robot is its configuration (G-2286)Configuration: The list of numbers that fixes the position of every point of a robot, such as q = (x, y, \theta) = (2, 1, 0.524) for a floor robot or the joint angles (\theta_1, \theta_2) of a 2R arm; with it a planner treats the whole robot as one point. Explained in §2.1 The configuration: numbers that place every point. (MR Definition 2.1). We write it as one vector (G-2081)Vector: A list of numbers: a 1D tensor. Explained in: Tensors, §2. What a tensor is, a list of numbers, named q:
q = (x,\ y,\ \theta)
q = (2,\ 1,\ 0.524)
For the floor robot the configuration is its pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, the position and heading of RO-001, because the body is rigid. For the arm, the two joint angles fix every point: with joint 1 turned to \theta_1 = 30° and joint 2 to \theta_2 = 60°, its configuration is
q = (\theta_1,\ \theta_2) = (30^\circ,\ 60^\circ)
and, with links 0.3 m and 0.2 m long, the hand sits at (0.260 m, 0.350 m) from the shoulder (notebook; the arm is drawn in Section 3.2). One configuration is one placement of the robot; a planner needs all of them at once.
2.2 The configuration space of the floor robot
A planner has to consider every placement of the robot, not just the present one. All configurations of a robot together form its configuration space (G-2287)Configuration space (C-space): The set of all configurations of a robot, one point per placement of the whole robot, such as a box of (x, y, \theta) whose top and bottom faces are the same headings for a floor robot; motion planning looks for paths through it. Explained in §2.2 The configuration space of the floor robot., or C-space for short (MR Definition 2.1). Each point of the C-space is one placement of the whole robot.
Figure 2 draws the floor robot’s C-space as a box: the room’s floor across, x from 0 to 7 m and y from 0 to 4 m, and the heading θ upward, from 0 to 2π. The robot at (2, 1, 0.524) is one point of the box. The same robot turned round on the spot, facing 180° (3.142 rad), is the point straight above it: a different configuration, although the centre has not moved.
Make interactive
Figure 2: The configuration space of the floor robot as a box: x from 0 to 7 m and y from 0 to 4 m across, the heading theta from 0 to 2 pi upward. The robot at (2, 1, 0.524) is a red point near the floor of the box; the same spot facing the other way, (2, 1, 3.142), is a blue point straight above it. The top face (theta = 2 pi) and the bottom face (theta = 0) are shaded: they are the same headings
The box has one feature a room does not. Turning by a full 2π brings the robot back to the same heading, so the top face, θ = 2π, holds the same configurations as the bottom face, θ = 0. A point that climbs out through the top comes back in through the bottom. The glued faces are the wrap-around of headings, the angle wrapping (G-2404)Angle wrapping: Adding or subtracting full turns until an angle or angle difference lies between −180° and 180°, so that 175° and −178° count as 7° apart, not 353°; needed whenever bearings or headings are compared. Explained in: Landmark Measurement Model, §3.3 Why angle differences must be wrapped of RO-012, seen in the C-space.
Figure 3 plays it. The robot drives once round the circle of radius 0.5 mExplained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §5.3 Why we predict the path step by step of RO-001, at 0.5 m/s while turning at 1 rad/s. Watch the right panel: the point climbs as the heading turns, leaves through the top face in the frame “t = 5.74 s”, is back at the bottom face in the frame “θ passed 2π”, and in the last frame stands where it started. The time at which the heading reaches 2π:

\theta_0 is the start heading, 0.5236 rad;
\omega is the angular velocity, 1 rad/s;
t is the time, in s.

Our numbers first, each followed by the same step in symbols:
0.5236 + 1 \times t = 6.2832
\theta_0 + \omega\thinspace t = 2\pi
t = (6.2832 - 0.5236) / 1 = 5.7596 \text{ s}
t = (2\pi - \theta_0) / \omega

Figure 3: The robot drives RO-001’s circle of radius 0.5 m for one full turn, 6.28 s. Left: the room seen from above, the robot as a red disk of radius 0.25 m with its heading arrow and its orange trail. Right: the configuration space box; the red point climbs a curve as the heading grows. In the frame ‘t = 5.74 s’ the point is about to leave the top face; in the frame ‘θ passed 2π’ it is back at the bottom face, and a grey dashed line joins the exit and the entry, which are the same configuration. Last frame: after one full turn the robot is back at (2, 1, 0.524), the point where it started
So the C-space of the floor robot is a box with its top and bottom glued together. The box needs three numbers per point. Section 3 asks whether three is the right count, and how to count for any robot.
3. Degrees of freedom


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

How many numbers are needed, the rest of the first question, is a robot’s degrees of freedom, the smallest number of numbers that places it: 3 for the floor robot and 2 for the arm. We count them as freedoms minus independent constraints, point by point for one body (2, 1 and 0 freedoms for three of its points), and with Grübler’s formula for links joined by joints.


3.1 Counting point by point
Section 2 placed the floor robot with three numbers. A body has endless points, each with two numbers of its own in the plane, so why exactly three? We count point by point (MR §2.1), on three points of the robot’s body:

A, the centre, at (2, 1);
B, 0.25 m ahead of A, at (2.2165, 1.125), the front point of Section 2.1;
C, 0.25 m to the left of A, at (1.875, 1.217), and 0.354 m from B.

Figure 4 places them one at a time. Watch the table on the right fill in, one row per point:

frame “A, the centre”: A can be anywhere in the plane: 2 numbers, no rule, so 2 freedoms;
frame “B stays 0.25 m from A”: B has 2 numbers, but one rule, its fixed distance to A, keeps it on the orange circle round A. Only its place on the circle is free, 1 freedom, and sliding B round the circle turns the body;
frame “C stays 0.25 m from A and 0.354 m from B”: two rules keep C on two circles, which meet in only 2 points, and one of them is the body flipped upside down, which a floor robot cannot do. So C is fixed: 0 freedoms.


Figure 4: Close-up of the robot’s body, a grey disk of radius 0.25 m at (2, 1), with a table of ‘numbers − rules = freedoms’. Frame ‘A, the centre’: A (blue) at the centre, row A: 2 − 0 = 2. Frames ‘B stays 0.25 m from A’: B (orange) slides round the orange dashed circle of radius 0.25 m about A, and the red line from A to B turns with it, its direction being the heading θ; row B: 2 − 1 = 1. Frame ‘C stays 0.25 m from A and 0.354 m from B’: the purple dashed circle about B meets the circle about A at C and at a grey cross marked ‘upside down’; row C: 2 − 2 = 0. Last frame: total 2 + 1 + 0 = 3, the three numbers (x, y, θ); the same count in space, 3 + 2 + 1 = 6
Any further point is fixed by its distances to A, B and C, so it adds nothing. The total:
2 + 1 + 0 = 3
A’s two numbers are x and y, and B’s place on its circle is the heading \theta. The smallest number of real numbers needed to place a robot is its degrees of freedom (G-2310)Degrees of freedom (of a robot): The smallest number of real numbers that places a robot, which is also the number of dimensions of its C-space: the freedoms of its points minus the independent constraints on them, such as 3 for a floor robot (x, y, \theta) and 2 for a 2R arm; it tells a planner how many numbers it must search over. Explained in §3.1 Counting point by point., DOF for short; it is also the number of dimensions of its C-space, 3 for the box of Figure 2 (MR Definition 2.1).
The general rule (MR eq. 2.1):

F is the sum of the freedoms of the points, before any rule;
c is the number of independent constraints, rules that fix how the points may lie relative to each other;
DOF is the degrees of freedom.

\text{DOF} = F - c
For the three points of the body in the plane, and then the same body in space, where each point has 3 numbers:
F = 3 \times 2 = 6
\text{DOF} = 6 - 3 = 3
F = 3 \times 3 = 9
\text{DOF} = 9 - 3 = 6
Point by point, as in the last frame of Figure 4, the body in space gives the same 6: A has 3 freedoms, B 2 and C 1.
3 + 2 + 1 = 6
A body that moves in space, such as a flying drone, has 6 degrees of freedom: 3 numbers for its position and 3 angles (MR §2.1).
“Independent” matters. A fourth point D of the body in the plane has 3 distance rules, to A, B and C, but once two of them hold the third holds too, so only 2 are independent, and D’s 2 numbers minus its 2 independent rules leave it no freedom (MR §2.1). A rule that follows from the others removes nothing.
The wheels’ rule of RO-001, that the robot cannot slide sideways, is not a constraint of this kind. The rule limits which way the robot can move at each momentExplained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §6.2 Can the robot still get everywhere?, not where it can be, so the floor robot keeps all 3 degrees of freedom (MR §2.4). Counting point by point works for one body; a robot of several links needs a quicker count.
3.2 Degrees of freedom of a robot made of links
The arm of the Overview is our example of a robot made of several links: link 1 turns on the robot’s top plate at joint 1, and link 2 turns on link 1 at joint 2 (Figure 5, left). Both are revolute joints.

Each link moving freely in the plane would have 3 freedoms, like the robot’s body in Section 3.1.
A revolute joint lets one link only turn about the other: it leaves 1 of the 3 freedoms and so removes 2 (MR §2.2.1).


Figure 5: Left: the 2R arm on the robot. The robot’s top plate is the ground (link 0); link 1 (blue) turns about joint 1 at angle theta1, link 2 (orange) turns about joint 2 at angle theta2, ending at the hand; joints are open circles. N = 3 links with the ground, J = 2 revolute joints: 3 (3 − 1 − 2) + 2 = 2. Right: a closed loop, three links (blue, orange, purple) and the ground joined end to end by 4 revolute joints. N = 4, J = 4: 3 (4 − 1 − 4) + 4 = 1
For the arm, the count goes:

m is the number of freedoms of one body, 3 in the plane;
N is the number of links, counting the ground (here the top plate) as a link: 3; the ground does not move, so only the other 2 links have freedoms to lose;
J is the number of joints, 2;
f_i is the number of freedoms joint i leaves, 1 for a revolute joint;
\sum means add upExplained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §3. Mean, here over the joints i from 1 to J.

Our numbers first, each followed by the same step in symbols:
\text{DOF} = 3 \times 2 - (3 - 1) - (3 - 1)
\text{DOF} = m\thinspace(N - 1) - \sum_{i=1}^{J}(m - f_i)
= 3 \times 2 - 3 \times 2 + 1 + 1
= m\thinspace(N - 1) - m\thinspace J + \sum_{i=1}^{J} f_i
= 3\thinspace(3 - 1 - 2) + 2 = 2
= m\thinspace(N - 1 - J) + \sum_{i=1}^{J} f_i
The last line is Grübler’s formula (G-2620)Grübler’s formula: The count of a mechanism’s degrees of freedom from its links and joints, m(N - 1 - J) + \sum f_i (m = 3 in the plane, N links with the ground, J joints, f_i freedoms of joint i), such as 2 for a 2R arm; it holds when the joints’ constraints are independent. Explained in §3.2 Degrees of freedom of a robot made of links. (MR eq. 2.4). The arm has 2 degrees of freedom, its two joint angles (\theta_1, \theta_2).
Two checks:

The floor robot is one body and no joint, N = 2 (the floor and the body) and J = 0: the formula gives 3 (first line below), as in Section 3.1.
The closed loop of Figure 5, right, has 3 moving links joined end to end, with both ends pinned to the ground, so 4 joints, and the formula gives 1 (second line below). Pinning the end of the third link to the ground removes 2 more freedoms (MR §2.2.2).

3\thinspace(2 - 1 - 0) + 0 = 3
3\thinspace(4 - 1 - 4) + 4 = 1
The formula holds only when the joints’ constraints are independent; when some of them follow from the others, the true count is higher than the formula says (MR §2.2.2). The robot carrying the arm has the 3 degrees of freedom of its body plus the 2 of the arm, 5 in all.
The counts say how many numbers place each robot: 3 for the floor robot, 2 for the arm. They do not say what shape those numbers form, and both of the arm’s angles wrap round, which Section 4 takes up.
4. The shape of a configuration space


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The second question is what shape all those numbers form: a heading lives on a circle, not on a line, and the arm’s two angles live on a torus, the surface of a doughnut. Two spaces have the same shape when one can be bent or stretched into the other without cutting or gluing.


4.1 Same shape: bending allowed, cutting and gluing not
Section 3 counted the numbers, but the count is not the whole story. The heading is one number, like the position of a cart on a rail. Yet on a rail, 3.5 m and 0.1 m are 3.4 m apart, while the headings 350° and 10° are 20° apart. The difference is the shape: a heading’s values close up into a circle, while a rail’s values run along a line with nothing joining the ends.
Figure 6 makes “same shape” precise. Watch the circle of headings in the frames “stretch and bend the circle”: it becomes an ellipse and a squashed loop, but it stays one closed loop, so it is still the same shape. In the frames “cut at θ = 0 and open it out”, the circle has to be cut before it can be laid straight, and the cut makes two ends that the circle did not have.

Figure 6: The circle of headings, with θ = π marked green and θ = 0 = 2π marked orange. Frames ‘stretch and bend the circle’: it becomes an ellipse and then a squashed loop, still closed: no cut, no glue, the same shape. Frames ‘cut at θ = 0 and open it out’: the circle opens at θ = 0 into an arc and then a straight segment, with red ends marked θ = 0 and θ = 2π. Last frame: a segment from 0 to 2π, not the same shape as the circle: two ends the circle did not have
Two spaces are topologically equivalent (G-2622)Topologically equivalent: Said of two spaces when one can be deformed into the other by bending and stretching, without cutting or gluing, such as a circle and an ellipse, or a coffee mug and a doughnut; equivalent spaces have the same shape for planning. Explained in §4.1 Same shape: bending allowed, cutting and gluing not. when one can be deformed into the other by bending and stretching, without cutting or gluing (MR §2.3.1). A coffee mug and the surface of a doughnut are equivalent this way: the handle’s hole is the doughnut’s hole. Three shapes of one dimension appear in robots (MR §2.3.1):

the circle, written S^1: a heading, or a revolute joint that turns all the way round;
the line, written \mathbb{R}, all real numbers: a sliding joint with no end stops;
the closed interval, written [a, b], the numbers from a to b with both ends included: a sliding joint with end stops, such as one that slides from 0 to 0.5 m.

None of the three is equivalent to another: the circle has no end, the line has no end but does not close up, and the interval has two ends. Our robots have more than one number, so their spaces are built from these shapes.
4.2 Building bigger spaces: the Cartesian product
The floor robot has three numbers: x and y each run along a line, and θ runs round a circle. What shape do the three make together? Every choice of (x, y) can be combined with every heading, so the space holds every pair of a point of the plane with a point of the circle. Taking every pair of one point from each of two spaces makes a new space, their Cartesian product (G-2625)Cartesian product (of spaces): The space X \times Y of every pair made of one point of X and one point of Y, with as many dimensions as both together, such as \mathbb{R}^2 \times S^1 for a floor robot’s position and heading; it builds a robot’s C-space from the spaces of its parts. Explained in §4.2 Building bigger spaces: the Cartesian product., written with ×; its number of dimensions is the sum of theirs (MR §2.3.1; LaValle §4.1.2). In symbols:

\mathbb{R}^2 is the plane, all pairs of real numbersExplained in: Vectors and Feature Vectors, §2.4 From 2D to n dimensions such as (2, 1), itself the product \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R};
S^1 is the circle of headings;
\mathbb{R}^2 \times S^1 is every pair of a point (x, y) with a heading θ, such as (2, 1, 0.524).

4.3 Manifolds: every small patch looks flat
Section 4.2 built curved and wrapped spaces, but a robot moves in small steps. What does a C-space look like close to one configuration? Figure 8 zooms in on one point of three shapes. A small piece of the circle looks like a piece of a straight line, and a small patch of the torus looks like a piece of a flat plane. At the joint of a T, three pieces of line meet, which no single line looks like.

A space in which the neighbourhood of every point looks like a piece of flat space of the same number of dimensions, a line for one dimension, a plane for two, is a manifold (G-2626)Manifold: A space in which a small neighbourhood of every point looks like a piece of flat space of the same dimension (a line, a plane), such as a circle or a torus but not a T-junction; near any configuration a robot can then move a little in each of its directions. Explained in §4.3 Manifolds: every small patch looks flat. (LaValle §4.1.2). Near any point of a manifold, “the set of directions that one can move appears the same” as in flat space (LaValle §4.1.2), so a robot at any configuration can move a little in each of its directions, 3 for the floor robot. The C-spaces of this Note are all manifolds: the circle, and the cylinder, the torus and the floor robot’s \mathbb{R}^2 \times S^1, which are built as Cartesian products of manifolds (LaValle §4.1.2).
A manifold is flat only up close. Its overall shape, the circle closing up or the torus wrapping round in two directions, still matters as soon as we write a configuration down as numbers, which is the subject of Section 5.
5. Writing a configuration as numbers


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The rest of the second question is how to write a configuration down without a jump at 360°. The fewest numbers, θ for a heading and (θ1, θ2) for the arm, jump at 2π, because the circle and the torus must be cut open to lay them flat; more numbers with a rule, such as (cos θ, sin θ) with cos² θ + sin² θ = 1, never jump.


5.1 Cutting the torus into a square
The arm’s configurations form a torus, but a program stores two numbers, \theta_1 and \theta_2, each from 0 to 2π. Those pairs fill a square. Figure 9 shows how the square and the torus are related. Watch the frame “roll it until the orange edges meet”: the square rolls into a tube, because \theta_2 = 0 and \theta_2 = 2π are the same angle of joint 2. In the frames “stretch and bend the tube”, the tube bends round until its blue ends, \theta_1 = 0 and \theta_1 = 2π, meet. Run backwards, the film cuts the torus twice to lay it flat as the square (MR §2.3.1).

Figure 9: Frame ‘the square of joint angles’: a flat square, θ1 along and θ2 across, each from 0 to 2π; its edges θ2 = 0 and θ2 = 2π are orange, its edges θ1 = 0 and θ1 = 2π blue; the red point is the arm at (30°, 60°). Frames ‘roll it until the orange edges meet’: the square curls into a tube with the orange edges joined. Frames ‘stretch and bend the tube until the blue ends meet’: the tube bends into a ring. Last frame: a torus, seen from below, with no edge left, and the red point on it
The cut has a price. Figure 10 moves the arm smoothly, \theta_1 from 300° on past 360° to 60°, while \theta_2 goes from 60° to 120°. Watch the middle panel: in the frame “θ1 passes 360°”, the point in the square jumps from the right edge to the left edge, while on the torus, right, it moves on without a jump. The last frame shows the square’s path cut in two and the torus path in one piece.

The jump belongs to the numbers, not to the arm: the arm moved smoothly, and the torus shows it (MR §2.3.1). Writing a space with exactly as many numbers as it has dimensions, such as (\theta_1, \theta_2) for the torus or latitude and longitude for the Earth’s surface, is an explicit parametrization (G-2627)Explicit parametrization: Writing an n-dimensional space with exactly n numbers, such as a heading \theta from 0 to 2\pi or latitude and longitude on a sphere; it uses the fewest numbers but jumps or breaks somewhere on a space that is not flat. Explained in §5.1 Cutting the torus into a square. of it (MR §2.3.2). An explicit parametrization uses the fewest numbers, but for the torus and the sphere it breaks somewhere: a jump at 2π, or a pole (MR §2.3.1, §2.3.2). Section 5.2 removes the jump with more numbers.
5.2 More numbers, no jump: the implicit representation
The jump of Section 5.1 in numbers, for the heading, which turns 2° from 359° to 1°:

\theta is the explicit coordinate, in rad, from 0 to 2π.

\theta(359^\circ) = 6.26573
\theta(1^\circ) = 0.01745
0.01745 - 6.26573 = -6.24828 \text{ rad}
A turn of 0.0349 rad shows up as a change of −6.24828 rad. The fix is to write the heading as the point where its direction meets a circle of radius 1. Two numbers with one rule:

\cos\theta and \sin\theta are the two numbers, the point’s distance across and up from the circle’s centre;
the rule is that the point lies on the circle of radius 1.

\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1
By the rule of Section 3.1, 2 numbers minus 1 independent rule leave 1 degree of freedom, as a heading should. At the same two headings (notebook):
(\cos 359^\circ, \sin 359^\circ) = (0.9998, -0.0175)
(\cos 1^\circ, \sin 1^\circ) = (0.9998, 0.0175)
The point moves 0.035, the size of the 2° turn, and nothing jumps. The same pair settles the second problem of the Overview, the headings 350° and 10°. As explicit numbers they lie far apart:
\theta(350^\circ) - \theta(10^\circ)
= 6.10865 - 0.17453 = 5.93412 \text{ rad}
As implicit pairs they lie close together:
(\cos 350^\circ, \sin 350^\circ) = (0.98481, -0.17365)
(\cos 10^\circ, \sin 10^\circ) = (0.98481, 0.17365)
0.17365 - (-0.17365) = 0.34730
The two points differ only in their second number, \sin\theta, by 0.3473, about the 0.349 rad of a 20° turn, so a planner that compares the pairs sees two nearby headings. Figure 11 turns the heading from 330° to 30°. Watch the two plots on the right: in the frame “heading 360° = 0°” the explicit θ drops from 2π to 0, while cos θ and sin θ move on smoothly; the last frame shows one jump in θ and none in the other two.

The sphere looks the same everywhere, at the pole as on the equator, so the trouble is in the numbers, not in the space (MR §2.3.2). The implicit representation, three numbers for the point’s position in space with one rule, that its distance from the centre is 1, has no such bad point (MR §2.3.2). Robots meet the sphere as the C-space of a pendulum that can swing in every direction (MR §2.3.1), and planners meet the heading’s jump whenever they measure how far apart two configurations are, which needs the distance between two headingsExplained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §7.2 The distance between two headings measured the short way round.
Every configuration can now be written down as numbers, with or without jumps. What is left is the question the C-space was built for: how to plan a motion through it.
6. The basic motion planning problem


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The third question is the planning problem itself: find a path in the C-space from the start configuration to the goal configuration along which the robot touches no obstacle. The question is the basic motion planning problem, also called the piano mover’s problem.


We can now restate the opening problem. The robot’s body is a disk with a heading, and every placement of it is one point of the box of Figure 2. The robot starts at the configuration (2, 1, 0.524) and should end in the doorway, with its centre at the doorway’s centre, (3.6, 4.0). The grid routes stopped at the centre of the cell under the door, (3.75, 3.75), because a grid route can only stop at a cell centre; a configuration can be any point, so from here on the goal is the doorway’s centre.
Figure 13 plays the simplest motion that does it, in the room and in the C-space at once:

turn on the spot from 30° to 61.9°, to face the doorway’s centre;
drive 3.4 m straight to (3.6, 4.0).

The turn and the drive come from how far the doorway’s centre lies along x and along y:

\Delta x is the run of the drive, in m;
\Delta y is its rise, in m;
atan2 (G-2325)atan2: A function atan2(rise, run) that returns the direction of a line over the full circle from its rise and run given separately; needed because the plain inverse tangent of the ratio cannot tell opposite directions apart. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §4.2 Turn, drive, turn turns the rise and the run into the direction of the drive.

\Delta x = 3.6 - 2.0 = 1.6 \text{ m}
\Delta y = 4.0 - 1.0 = 3.0 \text{ m}
\text{length} = \sqrt{1.6^2 + 3.0^2} = 3.4 \text{ m}
\text{heading} = \text{atan2}(3.0,\ 1.6) = 61.9^\circ
The robot ends facing along its drive, so the goal configuration is (3.6, 4.0, 1.081), with 61.9° written as 1.081 rad. Watch the right panel of Figure 13. In the frames “turn on the spot”, only θ changes, so the point moves straight up. In the frames “drive straight”, θ stays the same, so the point moves level. The last frame shows the whole motion as one connected path from the grey start point to the green goal point. Along it, the robot’s centre keeps at least 0.382 m from every obstacle and wall, passing closest to the table’s corner, so the 0.25 m body clears the table by 0.132 m (notebook; obstacles in C-spaceExplained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2.4 The room in C-space, and the drive to the door shows the same drive in its C-space):
0.382 - 0.25 = 0.132 \text{ m}

The planner must find a path with
\tau(0) = q_{\text{start}}
\tau(1) = q_{\text{goal}}
\tau(s) \in C_{\text{free}} \text{ for every } s
or report correctly that no such path exists (LaValle §4.3.1, Formulation 4.1; MR §10.1). The task of finding such a path is the basic motion planning problem (G-2630)Basic motion planning problem (piano mover’s problem): Given a robot, its obstacles, a start configuration and a goal configuration, find a continuous path in C-space between them through configurations where the robot touches no obstacle, or report that none exists; it states every collision-free motion task as one search through C-space. Explained in §6. The basic motion planning problem.. The problem is also called the piano mover’s problem (MR §10.1; LaValle §4.3.1): moving a piano through a tight doorway is pure geometry, and the piano often has to turn on the way, so its heading is part of the path just as the robot’s θ is. Solving it exactly is very hard in general: it is PSPACE-hard (G-2559)PSPACE-hard: Said of a problem at least as hard as every problem solvable with memory growing like a power of the input size (PSPACE, which contains NP); the general motion planning problem and Sokoban are PSPACE-hard, which is why practical planners give up exactness. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §8. Why exact planning is hard: NP-hard and PSPACE-hard, at least as hard as every problem that a computer can solve with memory growing like a power of the input size, because the number of C-space dimensions grows with the robot (LaValle §4.3.1).
The opening question has its answer: the robot’s motion to the door is a path through a three-dimensional C-space, from (2, 1, 0.524) to (3.6, 4.0, 1.081), and the route of the earlier Notes was its shadow on the floor. What is still unknown is which part of the box is free.

The degrees of freedom (G-2310)Degrees of freedom (of a robot): The smallest number of real numbers that places a robot, which is also the number of dimensions of its C-space: the freedoms of its points minus the independent constraints on them, such as 3 for a floor robot (x, y, \theta) and 2 for a 2R arm; it tells a planner how many numbers it must search over. Explained in §3.1 Counting point by point. are freedoms minus independent constraints, 3 for the robot’s body in the plane (2, 1 and 0 for three of its points), because each fixed distance removes one freedom; the wheels’ sideways rule removes none, because it limits velocities, not configurations.
Grübler’s formula (G-2620)Grübler’s formula: The count of a mechanism’s degrees of freedom from its links and joints, m(N - 1 - J) + \sum f_i (m = 3 in the plane, N links with the ground, J joints, f_i freedoms of joint i), such as 2 for a 2R arm; it holds when the joints’ constraints are independent. Explained in §3.2 Degrees of freedom of a robot made of links. gives 2 for the arm and 1 for a closed loop of three links, because each revolute joint removes 2 of a link’s 3 freedoms; it holds only when the joints’ constraints are independent.
Spaces are topologically equivalent (G-2622)Topologically equivalent: Said of two spaces when one can be deformed into the other by bending and stretching, without cutting or gluing, such as a circle and an ellipse, or a coffee mug and a doughnut; equivalent spaces have the same shape for planning. Explained in §4.1 Same shape: bending allowed, cutting and gluing not. when bending and stretching, without cutting or gluing, turns one into the other, so the circle of headings is not the same shape as a line or an interval.
The Cartesian product (G-2625)Cartesian product (of spaces): The space X \times Y of every pair made of one point of X and one point of Y, with as many dimensions as both together, such as \mathbb{R}^2 \times S^1 for a floor robot’s position and heading; it builds a robot’s C-space from the spaces of its parts. Explained in §4.2 Building bigger spaces: the Cartesian product. builds C-spaces from simple ones, so two joint circles make a torus (G-2624)Torus T^2: The surface of a doughnut, the Cartesian product of two circles S^1 \times S^1; it is the C-space of a 2R arm, one point per pair of joint angles. Explained in §4.2 Building bigger spaces: the Cartesian product., not a sphere, and the robot carrying the arm has a five-dimensional C-space.
Every C-space here is a manifold (G-2626)Manifold: A space in which a small neighbourhood of every point looks like a piece of flat space of the same dimension (a line, a plane), such as a circle or a torus but not a T-junction; near any configuration a robot can then move a little in each of its directions. Explained in §4.3 Manifolds: every small patch looks flat., flat near every point, so a robot can move a little in each of its directions from any configuration.
An explicit parametrization (G-2627)Explicit parametrization: Writing an n-dimensional space with exactly n numbers, such as a heading \theta from 0 to 2\pi or latitude and longitude on a sphere; it uses the fewest numbers but jumps or breaks somewhere on a space that is not flat. Explained in §5.1 Cutting the torus into a square. uses the fewest numbers and jumps by 2π (−6.24828 rad for a 2° turn) or misbehaves at a pole, because a circle, a torus or a sphere cannot be laid flat without cutting; an implicit representation (G-2628)Implicit representation: Writing a space with more numbers than its dimension, tied by rules, such as a heading as (\cos\theta, \sin\theta) with \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1; it costs extra numbers but has no jumps and no bad points such as a pole. Explained in §5.2 More numbers, no jump: the implicit representation. such as (cos θ, sin θ) uses more numbers with a rule and never jumps.
The basic motion planning problem (G-2630)Basic motion planning problem (piano mover’s problem): Given a robot, its obstacles, a start configuration and a goal configuration, find a continuous path in C-space between them through configurations where the robot touches no obstacle, or report that none exists; it states every collision-free motion task as one search through C-space. Explained in §6. The basic motion planning problem., or piano mover’s problem, asks for a path \tau from the start to the goal through free configurations, because a motion of the whole robot is exactly such a curve.

The robot can now describe every placement of its body as one point of its C-space, and state its motion to the door as a path through that space. Still missing: which configurations are free. The table and the cabinet are shapes in the room, not in the C-space; obstacles in C-spaceExplained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2. The obstacle region and free space grows them by the robot’s 0.25 m body to find the free space.

RO/navigation/04-graph-search-and-config.title: Obstacles in C-space
RO/navigation/04-graph-search-and-config.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Vector magnitude, distance and scalar operationsExplained in: Magnitude, Distance and Scalar Operations on Vectors, §2. Magnitude: the distance from the origin; Maps and landmarksMap: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §2.1 What a map is for; Configuration spaceConfiguration space (C-space): The set of all configurations of a robot, one point per placement of the whole robot, such as a box of (x, y, \theta) whose top and bottom faces are the same headings for a floor robot; motion planning looks for paths through it. Explained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §2.2 The configuration space of the floor robot.
Leads to: Collision detectionCollision detection: Deciding, yes or no, whether two bodies overlap, such as the robot’s disk and the table; planners call it thousands of times instead of building the obstacle region. Explained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §2.2 Broad phase and narrow phase; Distance queries and GJKExplained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §5.2 The Minkowski difference and GJK; Bug algorithmsBug algorithm: A strategy for a robot with no map that knows only the goal’s direction and what it touches: head for the goal, and follow the edge of any obstacle met until a rule says to leave (Bug 1: at the nearest point after a full loop; Bug 2: back on the straight start–goal line, nearer the goal). Explained in: Moving Through Unknown Maps: D* Replanning and Bug Algorithms, §6. No map at all: bug algorithms; Preimage planningPreimage planning: Planning a sequence of motion commands backwards from the goal, each command chosen to end inside the preimage of the next, so the sequence succeeds despite errors in motion and sensing. Explained in: Manipulation Planning, §4.2 The preimage of the holder; Inevitable collision statesExplained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §3.2 The region of inevitable collision.
Compare with: Breadth-first searchBreadth-first search (BFS): A search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ring.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A placement of the robot is free only if its whole body misses every obstacle, not just its centre. Drawing each obstacle in C-space as the set of placements that touch it (for a round robot, the obstacle grown by the robot’s radius) turns “is the robot clear?” into “is this point outside the grown obstacles?“.


Make interactive
Figure 1: Left: the room with the robot’s disk footprint, 0.25 m in radius, at the start (2, 1) and at a second placement whose centre is (3.5, 3.2); the doorway in the top wall is 1.2 m wide. Right: a zoom on the table’s corner (3.5, 3.0): the centre is 0.2 m above the corner, outside the table, but the disk reaches 0.25 m and overlaps the table by 0.05 m (red)
So far the robot can plan a route on the room’s grid: breadth-first searchBreadth-first search (BFS): A search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ring reaches the cell under the door in 8 moves, and A*Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4. A: cost so far plus the guess finds a 3.414 m route with diagonal moves. The grid routes move a point. The configuration space (G-2287)Configuration space (C-space): The set of all configurations of a robot, one point per placement of the whole robot, such as a box of (x, y, \theta) whose top and bottom faces are the same headings for a floor robot; motion planning looks for paths through it. Explained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §2.2 The configuration space of the floor robot, C-space for short, makes the whole robot a point too: each placement (x, y, \theta), position and heading, is one point, and the basic motion planning problemBasic motion planning problem (piano mover’s problem): Given a robot, its obstacles, a start configuration and a goal configuration, find a continuous path in C-space between them through configurations where the robot touches no obstacle, or report that none exists; it states every collision-free motion task as one search through C-space. Explained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §6. The basic motion planning problem is to find a path of free points from the start, (2 m, 1 m) facing 30°, to the doorway centre, (3.6 m, 4.0 m).
What still breaks is the word “free”. The map of the room marks where the obstacles are, but the robot is not a point. Its footprint, the floor it covers, is a disk of radius 0.25 m centred on the middle of its axle (Figure 1):

with its centre at (3.5, 3.2), the robot stands 0.2 m above the table’s corner (3.5, 3.0); the centre is outside the table, yet the disk reaches 0.25 m and overlaps the table by 0.05 m;
the doorway is 1.2 m wide, but a robot 0.5 m wide cannot put its centre close to either side of it;
if the robot carries a board 1.4 m long, which way it faces decides whether the board fits through the 1.2 m doorway at all.

The opening question of this Note: which placements (x, y, \theta) are free, so that a planner can search C-space for a route to the door? We answer it in steps:

the placements that touch an obstacle, drawn in C-space, and the free placements that remain, for the round robot (Section 2);
a rule that works for any shape, such as the board, and what turning does to it (Section 3);
whether a path can exist at all: the separate pieces of free space (Section 4).

2. The obstacle region and free space


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The obstacle region (G-2650)Obstacle region (C-obstacle): The set of all configurations at which the robot’s body touches or overlaps an obstacle, C_{\text{obs}}; drawing it in C-space lets a planner test a placement as one point, such as the disk robot’s centre (3.5, 3.2), which lies in it 0.2 m from the table. Explained in §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle. is every placement at which the robot touches an obstacle; free space (G-2651)Free space: All configurations at which the robot touches no obstacle, C_{\text{free}}, the C-space without the obstacle region; a planner looks for a path that stays inside it. Explained in §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle. is all the others. For the disk robot, a placement touches an obstacle exactly when its centre is within 0.25 m of it, so the obstacle region is every obstacle grown by 0.25 m.


2.1 Why the centre alone cannot say what is free
The first part of the opening problem is the placement with its centre at (3.5, 3.2). Its centre is outside the table, so a planner that tests only the centre calls it free. Figure 1 shows that it is not: the disk reaches below the centre to y = 2.95, and the table’s corner is at y = 3.0. With:

the centre’s height, 3.2 m;
the robot’s radius, 0.25 m;
the corner’s height, 3.0 m.

The lowest point of the disk, straight below the centre:
3.2 - 0.25 = 2.95 \text{ m}
The disk’s lowest point lies below the corner, by:
3.0 - 2.95 = 0.05 \text{ m}
So whether a placement is free depends on every floor point the robot covers, not on one point. Testing the whole disk against every obstacle for every placement a planner tries is the slow way; the rest of this section moves the test to the centre, where a planner can make it in one step.
2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle
To move the test to the centre, picture the robot sliding round the table while it keeps touching it, like a coin pushed round the edge of a book. Its centre traces a closed curve round the table (Figure 2). Every centre inside that curve puts the disk on the table; every centre outside leaves a gap. So the curve splits the placements in two, and we can draw the split once, in C-space, instead of testing the disk again and again.
Figure 2 plays the slide, counter-clockwise from under the table’s bottom edge. Watch the stages named in its titles. “Along an edge”: the centre runs parallel to the edge, 0.25 m out. “At a corner”: the centre swings round the corner on an arc of radius 0.25 m. The last stage, “the centre (3.5, 3.2) lies inside the grown table”, fills the curve and marks the placement of Figure 1, which falls inside.

Figure 2: Animation: the robot’s 0.25 m disk footprint slides counter-clockwise round the table, always touching it; a black line joins its centre to the touching point. Along an edge the centre runs parallel to the edge, 0.25 m out; at a corner it swings round on an arc of radius 0.25 m. The orange trace of the centre closes into the boundary of the grown table, which the last frames fill (orange) and in which they mark the centre (3.5, 3.2), 0.2 m from the corner, in collision
The standard terms (LaValle §4.3.1; Hauser ch.9):

The set of floor points the robot covers when it is placed at a configuration (a placement) is its footprint at that configuration (G-2286)Configuration: The list of numbers that fixes the position of every point of a robot, such as q = (x, y, \theta) = (2, 1, 0.524) for a floor robot or the joint angles (\theta_1, \theta_2) of a 2R arm; with it a planner treats the whole robot as one point. Explained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §2.1 The configuration: numbers that place every point.
The set of all configurations at which the footprint touches or overlaps an obstacle is the obstacle region (G-2650)Obstacle region (C-obstacle): The set of all configurations at which the robot’s body touches or overlaps an obstacle, C_{\text{obs}}; drawing it in C-space lets a planner test a placement as one point, such as the disk robot’s centre (3.5, 3.2), which lies in it 0.2 m from the table. Explained in §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle., also called the C-obstacle, or C-space obstacle.
Everything else in C-space is free space (G-2651)Free space: All configurations at which the robot touches no obstacle, C_{\text{free}}, the C-space without the obstacle region; a planner looks for a path that stays inside it. Explained in §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle.: the configurations at which the robot touches nothing.

The obstacle region of the table, the filled shape in the last frame of Figure 2, is the table’s C-obstacle. The configuration whose centre is (3.5, 3.2) lies in it; the start, (2, 1), does not.
The formal version needs set notation, which we read on small instances:

q is a configuration, such as the start, q = (2 \text{ m}, 1 \text{ m}, 30^\circ);
C is the C-space, the set of all configurations;
A(q) is the robot’s footprint at q, a set of floor points: at the start, every point within 0.25 m of (2, 1);
O is the obstacles, the set of floor points covered by the table, the cabinet, the poles and the walls;
\cap gives the intersection (G-967)Intersection (A ∩ B): The set of elements that are in both A and B, such as the points inside both of two half-planes; for events, the event that both A and B happen. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Conditional Probability, §2. The definition, the points in both sets, and \emptyset is the empty set, so A(q) \cap O \ne \emptyset reads “the robot and the obstacles share at least one point”;
\setminus removes one set from another: C \setminus C_{\text{obs}} is C without the obstacle region;
\in reads “is in”: q \in C says that q is one of the configurations in C;
in the braces, the bar reads “such that”.

C_{\text{obs}} = \lbrace q \in C \mid A(q) \cap O \ne \emptyset \rbrace
C_{\text{free}} = C \setminus C_{\text{obs}}
(LaValle §4.3.1, eq. 4.34; Hauser ch.9). A planner now asks one question per configuration: is q in C_{\text{obs}}? For the disk, the slide of Figure 2 already gave the answer’s shape; the next step gives its rule.
2.3 Growing the obstacles by the robot’s radius


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

For a disk robot, the obstacle region of each obstacle is a grown obstacle (G-2652)Grown obstacle (inflated obstacle): An obstacle with every point within the robot’s radius added, its edges pushed out and its corners rounded; for a disk robot it is exactly the obstacle region, so the robot can be treated as a point (the table, 3.625 m², grows to 5.747 m² for a 0.25 m radius). Explained in §2.3 Growing the obstacles by the robot’s radius.: the obstacle with its edges pushed out by the radius, 0.25 m, and its corners rounded with arcs of radius 0.25 m. The grown table covers 5.747 m² against the table’s 3.625 m².


Figure 2 found the table’s obstacle region by sliding the disk round it. A planner needs a rule it can compute for every obstacle of the room, and the disk gives a simple one.
Why the rule holds. The disk covers every floor point within 0.25 m of its centre. The disk touches an obstacle exactly when some obstacle point lies within 0.25 m of the centre: when the centre’s Euclidean distance (G-715)Euclidean distance: The straight-line distance between two points. Explained in: Handling Missing Data: KNN Imputer, §4.1 The Euclidean distance, the straight-line distance, to the nearest obstacle point is at most 0.25 m. So for the disk (Hauser ch.9, “Planar translating disks”):

r is the robot’s radius, 0.25 m;
\text{dist}(q, O) is the distance from the centre of configuration q to the nearest point of the obstacles O, in m: 0.2 m for the centre (3.5, 3.2).

C_{\text{obs}} = \lbrace q \mid \text{dist}(q, O) \le r \rbrace
The configuration of Figure 1 passes the test:
\text{dist} = 0.2 \le 0.25
so it is in the obstacle region, as the disk’s 0.05 m overlap showed. An obstacle grown this way, every point within r of it added, is a grown obstacle (G-2652)Grown obstacle (inflated obstacle): An obstacle with every point within the robot’s radius added, its edges pushed out and its corners rounded; for a disk robot it is exactly the obstacle region, so the robot can be treated as a point (the table, 3.625 m², grows to 5.747 m² for a 0.25 m radius). Explained in §2.3 Growing the obstacles by the robot’s radius., also called an inflated obstacle. The robot has become a point, and the obstacles have grown by its size.
Why lines and arcs. Along an edge, the nearest obstacle point is on that edge, so the centres at distance 0.25 m form a line parallel to the edge. Round a corner, the nearest point is the corner itself, so they form an arc of a circle of radius 0.25 m about the corner (Hauser ch.9). Each arc spans the angle by which the table’s outline turns at that corner. At the corner (3.5, 3.0) the two edges meet at a right angle, so its arc is a quarter circle. A centre straight above that corner, like the one of Figure 1, has the corner as its nearest table point, 0.2 m away.
A check: the grown table’s area. The growth adds a strip along every edge and a wedge of a circle at every corner. The table’s numbers (notebook):

the table’s area, 3.625 m²;
the table’s perimeter, the four edges added, 7.704 m;
the turns of its outline at its four corners: 104.0°, 71.6°, 94.4° and 90.0°.

Walking round a convex outline, we turn at each corner and finish facing the way we started, so the turns add up to one full turn:
104.0 + 71.6 + 94.4 + 90.0 = 360^\circ
The four corner wedges therefore make one whole circle of radius 0.25 m. The strips are each edge’s length times 0.25 m. Adding the parts:
\text{grown area} = 3.625 + 7.704 \times 0.25
+ \pi \times 0.25^2
= 3.625 + 1.926 + 0.196
= 5.747 \text{ m}^2
The same steps in symbols:

s is the obstacle’s area, in m²;
p is its perimeter, in m;
r is the robot’s radius, in m.

\text{grown area} = s + p\thinspace r + \pi r^2
The library that grows shapes in the notebook (shapely) measures the same 5.747 m². So the table’s obstacle region is 2.122 m² larger than the table:
5.747 - 3.625 = 2.122 \text{ m}^2
Every one of those extra square metres is floor that looks free on the map but where the robot’s centre cannot go. The table is one obstacle; the room has four more kinds.
2.4 The room in C-space, and the drive to the door


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Grow every obstacle of the room by 0.25 m, walls included, and what stays white is the free space of the disk robot. The doorway leaves 0.7 m for the centre, and the straight 3.4 m drive from the start to the doorway centre clears the grown table by 0.132 m.


The second part of the opening problem is the doorway. Growing every obstacle answers it and the first part at once. Figure 3 grows the whole room (Hauser ch.9):

the walls move 0.25 m into the room, because the centre must stay 0.25 m from each wall;
each pole, 0.1 m in radius, becomes a disk 0.35 m in radius;
the cabinet’s L grows along its outline;
the door jambs, the wall ends at (3.0, 4.0) and (4.2, 4.0), grow into quarter-disks of radius 0.25 m.
