3. The Minkowski sum: obstacles for any robot shape


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

For a robot of any shape that moves without turning, the obstacle region (the placements that touch an obstacle) is the Minkowski sum (G-2653)Minkowski sum: The set of all sums of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \oplus B, like sweeping one shape over the other; the obstacle region of a robot that keeps its heading is the obstacle’s Minkowski sum with the robot reflected through its centre. Explained in §3.2 Minkowski sum and difference. of the obstacle and the robot’s shape reflected through its centre: every obstacle point minus every robot point. For two convex polygons it is a convex polygon with at most as many corners as both together.


3.1 Why a board breaks the disk rule
The third part of the opening problem: the robot carries a board 1.4 m long and 0.3 m wide, centred over the middle of its axle and lying along its heading. The board is what now touches the obstacles, so its outline is the footprint; the 0.25 m disk lies inside it. The board is a new example for one reason: it is not round, so the direction the robot faces matters.
Facing along the wall, at heading 0°, the board lies across the doorway with its full 1.4 m:
1.2 - 1.4 = -0.2 \text{ m}
The board is 0.2 m too long to fit. Facing the door, at 90°, only its 0.3 m width crosses:
1.2 - 0.3 = 0.9 \text{ m}
So “grow every obstacle by one radius” cannot work: the board reaches 0.7 m ahead of its centre but only 0.15 m to the side. We need a rule that builds the obstacle region from any shape, then we can turn the shape.
3.2 Minkowski sum and difference
The rule starts from one placement on the edge of the board’s obstacle region.
Where the board touches. Fix the heading at 0° and slide the board towards the table until its front end touches the table’s bottom-left corner (the first frame of Figure 5). The configuration gives the position of one chosen point of the robot, the middle of its axle, which is also the board’s centre. Each point of the board sits at a fixed offset from that centre: the middle of the front end is 0.7 m ahead. The touching point is that offset added to the centre, and it equals the corner. With the numbers, the centre q is:
q + (0.7,\ 0) = (3.0,\ 1.0)
q = (3.0,\ 1.0) - (0.7,\ 0)
q = (2.3,\ 1.0)
The same steps in symbols, with:

q is the position of the centre, (2.3, 1.0) here;
a is the offset of a point of the robot from the centre, (0.7, 0) for the middle of the front end;
o is the obstacle point it touches, the corner (3.0, 1.0);
A is the robot’s shape as a set of offsets, the board at heading 0°;
O is the obstacle as a set of points, the table.

q + a = o
q = o - a
Touching means some robot point lands on some obstacle point, so the centre is the obstacle point minus the robot point’s offset. Collecting every such centre over every obstacle point and every robot offset gives the obstacle region of the robot moving without turning:
C_{\text{obs}} = \lbrace o - a \mid o \in O,\ a \in A \rbrace
= O \ominus A
(LaValle §4.3.2, eq. 4.37; Hauser ch.9; KAIST C-space slides). Taking every difference of points of two sets is the Minkowski difference (G-2654)Minkowski difference: The set of all differences of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \ominus B, which equals A \oplus (-B); obstacle minus robot gives the obstacle region, and two convex bodies overlap exactly when their difference contains the origin. Explained in §3.2 Minkowski sum and difference., written \ominus. Taking every sum instead is the Minkowski sum (G-2653)Minkowski sum: The set of all sums of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \oplus B, like sweeping one shape over the other; the obstacle region of a robot that keeps its heading is the obstacle’s Minkowski sum with the robot reflected through its centre. Explained in §3.2 Minkowski sum and difference., written \oplus, “add every point of one shape to every point of the other”. Subtracting a is adding -a, the offset turned through 180° about the centre. So with -A, the robot reflected through its centre:
O \ominus A = O \oplus (-A)
(LaValle §4.3.2). The board and the disk are both symmetric about their centre: each offset a has a partner -a on the far side (the front end’s middle (0.7, 0) and the back end’s middle (−0.7, 0)). So for them the reflected shape is the shape itself, and the obstacle region is the obstacle plus the robot. For the disk, adding a 0.25 m disk to every table point gives every point within 0.25 m of the table: the grown table of Section 2.3 is a Minkowski sum.
Building it. “Add every point of one shape to every point of the other” is a picture of sweeping one shape over the other (Hauser ch.9, “Minkowski sums and differences”): place a copy of the reflected board, centred, on every point of the table, and the copies cover the obstacle region. Figure 5 builds it in that order. Watch the stages named in its titles: the board touching the corner; a reflected board centred on each table corner in turn; copies along the edges; copies everywhere, which sweep out a region; and, in the last frame, its outline.

Figure 5: Animation: the board’s obstacle region at heading 0 as a Minkowski sum. First the board (1.4 m by 0.3 m, brown) with its front end on the table’s corner (3.0, 1.0): its centre q is at (2.3, 1.0). Then copies of the reflected board are centred on the table’s four corners, then along its edges, then inside it; together they sweep out a region. The last frames outline it (orange): a convex polygon with 7 corners, on whose left edge the centre (2.3, 1.0) lies
The last frame of Figure 5 has 7 corners. Every corner of the outline is a table corner plus a board corner, and every edge of the outline is a table edge or a board edge moved into place (LaValle §4.3.2, “A polygonal C-space obstacle”; KAIST C-space slides). So for two convex (G-479)Convex set: A set that contains the whole segment between any two of its points. Explained in: Convex Sets, Convex Functions and Convex Optimisation, §2.1 Walking along the segment polygons, sets that contain the segment between any two of their points, the Minkowski sum is convex and has at most as many corners as both together (Hauser ch.9; KAIST C-space slides):
4 + 4 = 8 \text{ corners at most}
At heading 0° the table’s bottom edge and the board’s long edges are all horizontal, so two edges line up into one and 7 corners remain; at 30° there are 8 (notebook). A recipe a computer can follow (Hauser ch.9): add each of the 4 board corners (reflected) to each of the 4 table corners, 16 points, and take their convex hull (G-477)Convex hull: The smallest region with straight edges that contains a set of points; every weighted average of the points lies inside it. Explained in: Self-Attention, Geometrically, §7.1 The output sits between the value vectors, the smallest region with straight edges that contains them. The cabinet, a union of two rectangles, gets one Minkowski sum per rectangle, joined (LaValle §4.3.2). So one rule now covers any shape that keeps its heading; the board, though, turns with the robot.
3.3 Turning: a different slice for every heading


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Each heading gives its own obstacle region in the plane, a slice of C-space; stacked by heading they make the obstacle region in (x, y, \theta). For the board the slices change shape: the doorway is closed to the centre at 0° and open over 0.90 m at 90°.


The board’s obstacle region of Figure 5 was for heading 0° only. Turn the robot to 30° and the board points a different way, so the reflected board in the Minkowski sum turns too, and the obstacle region changes shape. The obstacle region for all configurations (x, y, \theta) is three-dimensional; holding the heading fixed cuts it into a flat slice: the set of positions (x, y) that are free, or not, at that one heading (KAIST C-space slides; Hauser ch.9, “C-obstacles for rotational motion”).
Figure 6 plays the slices of the whole room for the robot with the board, one heading per frame, from 0° to 180° in steps of 10°. The small panel shows which way the board points. Watch the orange obstacle region swell along the board’s direction as it turns, and watch the green bar in the doorway: the doorway’s free stretch for the centre.

4. Connected components of free space


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Free space, the placements that touch nothing, can fall into separate pieces, its connected components (G-2656)Connected component (of free space): A piece of free space within which the robot can move from any configuration to any other without touching an obstacle; a path between two configurations exists only if both lie in the same component. Explained in §4.1 One piece or several., and a path between two configurations exists only if both lie in the same piece. For the disk the room’s free space is one piece; for the board single slices split into 2 to 4 pieces, but turning joins them all into one.


4.1 One piece or several
The opening question asks for free placements so that a planner can search for a route. Before any search, one question settles whether a route can exist: can the robot get from the start to the door without leaving free space?
Free space can fall into pieces that free paths cannot join. Within one piece, the robot can move from any configuration to any other without touching an obstacle; between two pieces, every path crosses the obstacle region. Each such piece is a connected component (G-2656)Connected component (of free space): A piece of free space within which the robot can move from any configuration to any other without touching an obstacle; a path between two configurations exists only if both lie in the same component. Explained in §4.1 One piece or several. of free space, and a path between two configurations exists only if both lie in the same component (MR 10.2).
The disk robot. In Figure 3 the white free space is one piece: every gap between grown obstacles stays open. The narrowest is between the green pole and the bottom wall:

the pole’s centre is 0.8 m above the wall;
the pole’s radius is 0.1 m;
the robot is 0.5 m wide.

The gap under the pole, and what is left of it once the robot is in it:
0.8 - 0.1 = 0.7 \text{ m}
0.7 - 0.5 = 0.2 \text{ m}
The notebook counts the pieces of the free space on a grid of 0.01 m and finds one. So the start and the door are in the same component, which is why the drive of Figure 4 could exist.
4.2 Turning joins the pieces
The board, one heading at a time. The disk’s free space is one piece; the board’s is not, at a fixed heading. Figure 8 colours the free pieces of two slices, one colour per piece. At heading 0° the free space has 2 pieces: a large one and a small one of 0.39 m² right of the table, above the green pole. At heading 90° there are 3:

a large piece that holds both the start (2, 1) and the doorway centre (3.6, 4.0);
a piece round the green pole, which holds the point (6.6, 1.3);
a sliver of 0.004 m² between the table and the cabinet.

At 60° there are 4 (notebook).

A robot at (6.6, 1.3) facing the door, if it kept that heading, could never reach the door: its piece of the 90° slice does not include the doorway. The robot can turn, though, and a turn moves it up or down through the stack of Figure 7 into another slice, where the pieces lie differently. So for the board too a path exists from the start to the door. The robot can turn on the spot at the start from 30° to 90°, which stays free at every heading in between (notebook), and the large piece of the 90° slice then holds both ends. A path in C-space may also move sideways, which a differential-drive robot cannot do directly (no sideways motionExplained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §6.1 The rule: no sideways motion); turning such a path into wheel commands is a later topic.
4.3 Why planners do not build the obstacle region
The obstacle regions of this Note were cheap to build: a disk and a board against a few convex shapes in a 3D C-space. Real robots break all three conditions:

the robot and the obstacles are not convex; a Minkowski sum of two non-convex shapes is the union of the sums of their convex pieces and can have many more corners (Hauser ch.9);
in 3D, two objects of 444 and 1,134 triangles give a Minkowski sum made of 66,667 pieces (KAIST C-space slides 15 and 16);
an arm with six joints has a six-dimensional C-space, in which no picture or stack of slices can hold the obstacle region.

So building the obstacle region exactly is impractical (MR 10.2; KAIST C-space slides). Most planners never build it. Instead, a planner asks a subroutine one question at a time: is this configuration free, and is this short path segment free (MR 10.2; Hauser ch.10, “Implicit C-obstacle representation”)? Answering those questions fast, for thousands of configurations, is collision checkingExplained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §2. Collision detection: broad phase and narrow phase.

Two convex polygons give a convex sum with at most as many corners as both together, so the sum is quick to build from the corner sums and their convex hull.
For a robot that is not round, each heading has its own slice of C-space, so the board must face the door: the doorway is shut to its centre at 0° and open over 0.90 m at 90°.

The robot can now tell, for any configuration, whether its body is clear of the room, and the disk robot has a free straight drive to the door. Still missing: building the obstacle region exactly costs too much for real robots, so planners test one configuration or one segment at a time, and they need those tests to be fast and their distances to treat headings correctly. Explained in §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle.The set of all configurations at which the robot’s body touches or overlaps an obstacle, C_{\text{obs}}; drawing it in C-space lets a planner test a placement as one point, such as the disk robot’s centre (3.5, 3.2), which lies in it 0.2 m from the table.Free space (G-2651)Free space: All configurations at which the robot touches no obstacle, C_{\text{free}}, the C-space without the obstacle region; a planner looks for a path that stays inside it. Explained in §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle.All configurations at which the robot touches no obstacle, C_{\text{free}}, the C-space without the obstacle region; a planner looks for a path that stays inside it.Grown obstacle (inflated obstacle) (G-2652)Grown obstacle (inflated obstacle): An obstacle with every point within the robot’s radius added, its edges pushed out and its corners rounded; for a disk robot it is exactly the obstacle region, so the robot can be treated as a point (the table, 3.625 m², grows to 5.747 m² for a 0.25 m radius). Explained in §2.3 Growing the obstacles by the robot’s radius.An obstacle with every point within the robot’s radius added, its edges pushed out and its corners rounded; for a disk robot it is exactly the obstacle region, so the robot can be treated as a point (the table, 3.625 m², grows to 5.747 m² for a 0.25 m radius).Minkowski sum (G-2653)Minkowski sum: The set of all sums of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \oplus B, like sweeping one shape over the other; the obstacle region of a robot that keeps its heading is the obstacle’s Minkowski sum with the robot reflected through its centre. Explained in §3.2 Minkowski sum and difference.The set of all sums of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \oplus B, like sweeping one shape over the other; the obstacle region of a robot that keeps its heading is the obstacle’s Minkowski sum with the robot reflected through its centre.Minkowski difference (G-2654)Minkowski difference: The set of all differences of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \ominus B, which equals A \oplus (-B); obstacle minus robot gives the obstacle region, and two convex bodies overlap exactly when their difference contains the origin. Explained in §3.2 Minkowski sum and difference.The set of all differences of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \ominus B, which equals A \oplus (-B); obstacle minus robot gives the obstacle region, and two convex bodies overlap exactly when their difference contains the origin.Connected component (of free space) (G-2656)Connected component (of free space): A piece of free space within which the robot can move from any configuration to any other without touching an obstacle; a path between two configurations exists only if both lie in the same component. Explained in §4.1 One piece or several.A piece of free space within which the robot can move from any configuration to any other without touching an obstacle; a path between two configurations exists only if both lie in the same component.Configuration space (C-space) (G-2287)Configuration space (C-space): The set of all configurations of a robot, one point per placement of the whole robot, such as a box of (x, y, \theta) whose top and bottom faces are the same headings for a floor robot; motion planning looks for paths through it. Explained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §2.2 The configuration space of the floor robotThe set of all configurations of a robot, one point per placement of the whole robot, such as a box of (x, y, \theta) whose top and bottom faces are the same headings for a floor robot; motion planning looks for paths through it.Configuration (G-2286)Configuration: The list of numbers that fixes the position of every point of a robot, such as q = (x, y, \theta) = (2, 1, 0.524) for a floor robot or the joint angles (\theta_1, \theta_2) of a 2R arm; with it a planner treats the whole robot as one point. Explained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §2.1 The configuration: numbers that place every pointThe list of numbers that fixes the position of every point of a robot, such as q = (x, y, \theta) = (2, 1, 0.524) for a floor robot or the joint angles (\theta_1, \theta_2) of a 2R arm; with it a planner treats the whole robot as one point.Intersection (A ∩ B) (G-967)Intersection (A ∩ B): The set of elements that are in both A and B, such as the points inside both of two half-planes; for events, the event that both A and B happen. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Conditional Probability, §2. The definitionThe set of elements that are in both A and B, such as the points inside both of two half-planes; for events, the event that both A and B happen.Euclidean distance (G-715)Euclidean distance: The straight-line distance between two points. Explained in: Handling Missing Data: KNN Imputer, §4.1 The Euclidean distanceThe straight-line distance between two points.atan2 (G-2325)atan2: A function atan2(rise, run) that returns the direction of a line over the full circle from its rise and run given separately; needed because the plain inverse tangent of the ratio cannot tell opposite directions apart. Explained in: Convex Sets, Convex Functions and Convex Optimisation, §2.1 Walking along the segmentA set that contains the whole segment between any two of its points.Convex hull (G-477)Convex hull: The smallest region with straight edges that contains a set of points; every weighted average of the points lies inside it. RO/navigation/04-graph-search-and-config.title: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space
RO/navigation/04-graph-search-and-config.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Vector magnitude, distance and scalar operationsExplained in: Magnitude, Distance and Scalar Operations on Vectors, §2. Magnitude: the distance from the origin; Dot productDot product: Multiplying two vectors entry by entry and adding the products, u^{\mathsf T}x, which gives one number. It is large when the vectors point the same way, so it measures similarity and gives projections. Explained in: Dot Product and Cosine Similarity, §3. Computing the dot product; Uniform distributionUniform distribution: A distribution in which every outcome in a range is equally likely. Explained in: Uniform and Log-normal Distributions, §2. The uniform distribution; K-nearest neighboursK-nearest neighbours (KNN): Predicting from the answers of the k closest stored points. Explained in: K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN), §2. How KNN predicts; Minkowski sumMinkowski sum: The set of all sums of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \oplus B, like sweeping one shape over the other; the obstacle region of a robot that keeps its heading is the obstacle’s Minkowski sum with the robot reflected through its centre. Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §3.2 Minkowski sum and difference; Obstacle region and free spaceFree space: All configurations at which the robot touches no obstacle, C_{\text{free}}, the C-space without the obstacle region; a planner looks for a path that stays inside it. Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle.
Leads to: Potential fieldsPotential field (artificial potential field): A height over the robot’s C-space that is lowest at the goal and rises near obstacles, built as an attractive bowl plus a repulsive hill round each obstacle; the robot reaches the goal by stepping downhill from wherever it is, with no grid and no search, but can stop in a local minimum. Explained in: Potential Fields, §2. The pull of the door: the attractive potential; Rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT)Rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT): A sampling-based planner that grows a tree from the start: each round it draws a random configuration, steps the tree’s nearest node at most a fixed distance towards it and keeps the new node if the step is free, until the tree reaches the goal; it explores fast but its routes zig-zag. Explained in: Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees (RRT), §2.1 One step: sample, nearest node, steer, check; Lazy collision checkingLazy collision checking: Delaying an edge’s collision check until a candidate route uses it, deleting edges found to collide and searching again; it saves the checks of the many edges no route uses. Explained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §8. Lazy collision checking; Probabilistic roadmap (PRM)Probabilistic roadmap (PRM): A graph of random free configurations (milestones) joined by straight edges that pass a collision check, built once and then searched with A*; it describes the free space without building the obstacle region, so it scales to robots with many joints. Explained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §2.2 Phase 1 and phase 2: milestones and edges; State lattice and control setExplained in: State Lattices and Motion Primitives, §3.2 The control set; Landmark heuristics (ALT)Landmark (route planning): A vertex chosen in advance whose fastest travel times to and from every other vertex are computed once and stored; by the triangle inequality the stored times give a lower bound on the time between any two vertices. Not the sensed landmark of localisation. Explained in: Route Planning on Road and Route Graphs, §6.1 The triangle inequality on travel times.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A planner that never builds the obstacle region asks three questions thousands of times: is this configuration free, is this straight segment free, and which stored configuration is nearest? Cheap box tests first, a tree of boxes, well-ordered checks along a segment and a distance that knows headings wrap answer them fast and correctly.


Make interactive
Figure 1: Left: the room with three test points. The robot’s disk centred at (3.5, 3.2) (red) overlaps the table. The segment from a = (2, 2) to b = (4, 3.6) has free ends and a free middle (green), yet the point (3.5, 3.2) on it is in collision. Right: a heading dial with a query at 350 degrees and stored headings at 15 and 320 degrees; round the circle 15 is 25 degrees from 350, while plain subtraction says 335
So far the robot knows which of its placements are free. The obstacle region (G-2650)Obstacle region (C-obstacle): The set of all configurations at which the robot’s body touches or overlaps an obstacle, C_{\text{obs}}; drawing it in C-space lets a planner test a placement as one point, such as the disk robot’s centre (3.5, 3.2), which lies in it 0.2 m from the table. Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle, the set of configurations at which the robot’s body touches an obstacle, is the room’s obstacles grown by the robot’s 0.25 m radius. In it, the robot’s disk with its centre at (3.5, 3.2) touches the table, and the straight drive from the start (2, 1) to the doorway centre (3.6, 4.0) is free. But building that region exactlyExplained in: Obstacles in C-space, §4.3 Why planners do not build the obstacle region is impractical for real robots, so planners ask one question at a time instead (MR 10.2; Hauser ch.10). Three questions come back thousands of times, and on our room each has a trap (Figure 1):

Is this configuration free? Testing the robot exactly against every obstacle for every configuration is slow: with 10,000 bodies there are 49,995,000 pairs to test (Müller SAP slides).
Is this straight segment free? A segment holds infinitely many configurations. The segment from (2, 2) to (4, 3.6) is free at both ends and in the middle, yet the robot at (3.5, 3.2), three quarters of the way along, hits the table.
Which stored configuration is nearest? Headings wrap round: a stored heading of 15° is 25° from a query at 350°, but plain subtraction says 335°, so a plain search returns the wrong neighbour.

This Note builds the tools that answer them, on the same room and the same 0.25 m disk:

cheap box tests before exact ones (Section 2), a tree of boxes (Section 3) and links of one robot that may hit each other (Section 4);
how far a robot is from an obstacle (Section 5) and how to check a whole segment (Section 6);
a distance for configurations with headings (Section 7), a nearest-neighbour search that knows headings wrap (Section 8), and random configurations that favour no direction (Section 9).

2. Collision detection: broad phase and narrow phase


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Collision detection (G-2665)Collision detection: Deciding, yes or no, whether two bodies overlap, such as the robot’s disk and the table; planners call it thousands of times instead of building the obstacle region. Explained in §2.1 The yes-or-no question and what it costs. answers “do these two bodies overlap?” in two steps: the broad phase (G-2666)Broad phase: The first, cheap step of collision detection: wrap each body in a simple shape such as a box and keep only the pairs whose shapes overlap, so the costly exact test runs on few pairs. Explained in §2.2 Broad phase and narrow phase. throws out pairs whose simple boxes do not overlap, and the narrow phase (G-2667)Narrow phase: The second step of collision detection: the exact overlap test on the pairs the broad phase kept, such as the distance from the robot’s centre to the table compared with its 0.25 m radius. Explained in §2.2 Broad phase and narrow phase. tests the few pairs left exactly. Sweep and prune finds the overlapping boxes by sorting them along one axis.


2.1 The yes-or-no question and what it costs
The first question of the opening problem: is the configuration with centre (3.5, 3.2) free? Answering it means collision detection (G-2665)Collision detection: Deciding, yes or no, whether two bodies overlap, such as the robot’s disk and the table; planners call it thousands of times instead of building the obstacle region. Explained in §2.1 The yes-or-no question and what it costs.: deciding, yes or no, whether two bodies overlap (Hauser ch.7, “Proximity queries”). Besides the walls, the robot can overlap four pieces of furniture in our room (the table, the cabinet and the two poles), so one configuration needs four exact tests for them, and a planner runs thousands of configurations. The exact test is the costly part: for the disk against the table it means the distance from the centre to a polygon; for detailed bodies, made of thousands of triangles like triangle meshes (G-2338)Triangle mesh: A set of triangles, each given by three corner points in space, that together cover an object’s surface (a table as 12 triangles on 8 corners); fast to draw in 3D, but it does not say what is inside. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §5.1 Triangle meshes, many more steps.
With n bodies there are this many pairs, because each body pairs with every other body and each pair is counted twice:

n is the number of bodies: 5 in our room (the robot and the four pieces of furniture).

\text{pairs} = \frac{n(n - 1)}{2}
= \frac{5 \times 4}{2} = 10
For a scene of 10,000 bodies, the same count gives 49,995,000 pairs (Müller SAP slides). Most of those pairs are far apart and could be ruled out at a glance. The question is how to glance cheaply.
2.2 Broad phase and narrow phase


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Wrap each body in its smallest box with sides along x and y. Two bodies can only touch if their boxes overlap, and two boxes are compared with four number comparisons.


A box round a body is a quick stand-in for it: if two boxes do not overlap, the bodies inside cannot overlap either. Comparing two boxes takes four comparisons of numbers, far fewer steps than an exact test. So collision detection runs in two phases (Müller SAP slides; LaValle §5.3.1):

the broad phase (G-2666)Broad phase: The first, cheap step of collision detection: wrap each body in a simple shape such as a box and keep only the pairs whose shapes overlap, so the costly exact test runs on few pairs. Explained in §2.2 Broad phase and narrow phase.: wrap every body in a simple shape and keep only the pairs whose shapes overlap;
the narrow phase (G-2667)Narrow phase: The second step of collision detection: the exact overlap test on the pairs the broad phase kept, such as the distance from the robot’s centre to the table compared with its 0.25 m radius. Explained in §2.2 Broad phase and narrow phase.: test the kept pairs exactly.

A simple shape that encloses a body for such a quick test is a bounding volume (G-2668)Bounding volume: A simple shape that encloses a body, such as a sphere or a box; if two bounding volumes do not overlap, neither do the bodies, so it gives a quick test before an exact one. Explained in §2.2 Broad phase and narrow phase.: a sphere, a box, or a box turned with the body (Hauser ch.7). The commonest is the smallest box with sides along the x and y axes that holds the body, which we call the body’s box. Two such boxes overlap exactly when their x-intervals overlap and their y-intervals overlap (Hauser ch.7).
On our room, with the robot’s centre at (3.5, 3.2) (notebook):















































Bodyx fromx toy fromy torobot3.253.752.953.45table3.05.51.03.0cabinet5.67.02.44.0pink pole0.91.12.93.1green pole5.96.10.70.9
Only the table’s box overlaps the robot’s: their x-intervals share 3.25 to 3.75, and their y-intervals share 2.95 to 3.0. So the broad phase leaves one pair, and the narrow phase tests it exactly: the centre is 0.2 m from the table, less than the 0.25 m radius, so the robot and the table overlap (the centre lies in the grown tableExplained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2.3 Growing the obstacles by the robot’s radius). One exact test instead of four. The walls are left out of this comparison for now: a wall’s long, thin box lies along a whole side of the room, which Section 3 handles.
2.3 Sweep and prune
Testing the robot’s box against every other box is still a test per pair, 10 for our 5 bodies. Sweep and prune (G-2670)Sweep and prune: A broad phase that sorts the boxes by their left edge and sweeps along x, comparing each box only with the boxes it overlaps along x; it cuts the pairs tested, though long boxes that span the axis defeat it. Explained in §2.3 Sweep and prune. cuts that number by sorting (Müller SAP slides):

sort the boxes by their left edge;
sweep a vertical line from left to right: a box joins the list of active boxes when the line reaches its left edge and leaves at its right edge;
a box that joins is compared only with the boxes already active, the ones it overlaps along x;
for those pairs, a full box test checks y as well; a pair that passes goes to the narrow phase.

Figure 2 runs the sweep on our five boxes. Watch the stage “x = 3.25 m: the robot joins”: the table is active, so the robot is compared with it, and the box test flags the pair. At “x = 5.9 m: the green pole joins”, the cabinet is active, but their y-intervals, 0.7 to 0.9 and 2.4 to 4.0, do not overlap. The last frame, “narrow phase on the one flagged pair”, runs the exact test.

Figure 2: Animation: sweep and prune on the room’s five bodies, the robot with its centre at (3.5, 3.2) (red dashed disk) and the table, cabinet and two poles, each inside its dashed box with sides along x and y; walls left out. The boxes are sorted by left edge: pink pole 0.9 m, table 3.0, robot 3.25, cabinet 5.6, green pole 5.9. An orange sweep line moves right; a box joins the active list (thick outline) at its left edge and leaves at its right edge. When the robot joins, the table is active: the boxes overlap along x and along y, so the pair is flagged. When the green pole joins, the cabinet is active: they overlap along x but not along y. The last frame: 2 box tests instead of 10 pairs; the narrow phase finds the robot 0.2 m from the table, less than 0.25 m: a collision
Sorting puts the boxes that might overlap next to each other, so each box looks only at its neighbours along x. The sort takes far fewer steps than testing all pairs (Müller SAP slides). With:

n the number of bodies, each in its box, now 10,000;
\log_2 n the number of times n can be halved before reaching 1, 13.3 for 10,000.

\text{sort steps} \approx n \log_2 n
\log_2 10{,}000 = 13.3
10{,}000 \times 13.3 = 133{,}000
The sort’s 133,000 steps are far below the 49,995,000 pairs, though how many pairs the sweep then compares depends on how the boxes lie (Müller SAP slides). Sweep and prune looks along one axis only, and a long wall’s box overlaps almost every other box along that axis.
3. Bounding-volume hierarchies


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A bounding-volume hierarchy (G-2671)Bounding-volume hierarchy (BVH): A tree of nested bounding volumes, each holding its two children’s down to one per body; a query skips every body inside a box that misses, so it needs about \log_2 n box tests for n bodies (9 among the room’s 25). Explained in §3.1 Why a tree of boxes. is a tree of boxes: each box holds two smaller ones, down to one box per body. A query opens a box only if it overlaps the robot’s box, so for n bodies it reaches the few near the robot after about \log_2 n levels: 9 box tests among the room’s 25 bodies.


3.1 Why a tree of boxes
The walls were left out of the sweep. Put them in, and each wall’s box stretches along a whole side of the room, overlapping almost every box along x, so sorting along one axis separates little (Müller BVH slides). With many bodies spread in two or three dimensions the problem grows: for 100 × 100 objects in a plane, sweep and prune still tests about 100 objects for each one (Müller BVH slides).
The fix is to group nearby bodies, and groups of groups, each group in one box. A query starts at the box that holds everything; if the robot’s box misses a group’s box, every body inside is ruled out at once. A tree of nested bounding volumes, each holding the boxes of its two children down to one box per body, is a bounding-volume hierarchy (G-2671)Bounding-volume hierarchy (BVH): A tree of nested bounding volumes, each holding its two children’s down to one per body; a query skips every body inside a box that misses, so it needs about \log_2 n box tests for n bodies (9 among the room’s 25). Explained in §3.1 Why a tree of boxes., BVH for short (Hauser ch.7; Müller BVH slides).
So that each wall takes up only a small box, we store it as panels about 1 m long, as a triangle mesh (G-2338)Triangle mesh: A set of triangles, each given by three corner points in space, that together cover an object’s surface (a table as 12 triangles on 8 corners); fast to draw in 3D, but it does not say what is inside. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §5.1 Triangle meshes stores a surface in small pieces: 7 panels along the bottom, 4 up each side and 3 on each side of the doorway, 21 in all. With the 4 pieces of furniture, the room has 25 bodies.
3.2 Building and searching the tree
The tree is built from the top down (Müller BVH slides; Hauser ch.7):

one box round all 25 bodies is the root;
sort the bodies of a box by the centres of their boxes along x and split them into two halves of equal count (13 and 12 here); each half gets its own box;
repeat inside each half, sorting along y, then x again, and so on, until each box holds one body.

A query for the robot’s box descends from the root (Hauser ch.7, “BVH queries”):

test the box of the current node against the robot’s box;
if they miss, skip the node and everything inside it;
if they overlap and the node holds one body, pass that body to the narrow phase; otherwise test both children.

Figure 3 builds the tree level by level, then runs the query for the robot at (3.5, 3.2). Watch the room on the left and the tree on the right: a red box is a miss, and every body under it is skipped without a test. The stage “query, test 4” is the first miss: the box of the room’s lower-left walls, which the robot’s box does not reach. The last frame shows the 9 tests that leave one body, the table.

Figure 3: Animation: a bounding-volume hierarchy over the room’s 25 bodies (4 pieces of furniture and 21 wall panels about 1 m long). Build: one box round everything, then each box split into two halves of equal count, sorting along x, then y, then x, coloured by level, on the room (left) and as a tree (right). Query for the robot with its centre at (3.5, 3.2), its box dotted red: each tested box turns green if it overlaps the robot’s box and red if it misses; a red box’s whole subtree is skipped. 9 box tests reach the table, the only body left for the narrow phase, 0.2 m from the robot’s centre: a collision. Brute force would test 25 boxes
The query needed 9 box tests instead of 25 (notebook). From the start (2, 1), where nothing is close, it needs 11, and over 2,000 random centres in the room it averages 12.0. The tree has 5 levels below the root, because halving 25 bodies 4 times still leaves boxes with two bodies, and 5 times leaves one:
2^4 = 16 < 25 \le 32 = 2^5
In general, for a balanced tree:

n is the number of bodies, such as 32;
L is the number of levels below the root, 5 for 32 bodies.

n = 2^L
L = \log_2 n
so a query that goes down one branch makes about \log_2 n box tests (Müller BVH slides). With 10,000 objects in a plane that is about 13 tests per object, against about 100 for sweep and prune and 10,000 for brute force (13.3 from Section 2.3); with 1,000,000 objects in 3D, about 20 against about 10,000 and 1,000,000 (Müller BVH slides):
\log_2 1{,}000{,}000 = 19.9
The count grows when the robot is close to many bodies at once, since then several branches must be opened (Hauser ch.7, “Performance”). A BVH is built once for bodies that do not move and reused for every query, which is why planners use it for the room’s furniture and walls. The robot itself, though, may be more than one body.
4. Self-collision


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A robot made of several links can hit itself. A self-collision (G-2672)Self-collision: Two links of the same robot overlapping, such as an arm’s third link folding back across its first; a configuration with a self-collision is not free, so planners test the robot’s own link pairs too. Explained in §4. Self-collision. check tests the pairs of links that can meet; links joined by a joint touch all the time and are left out.


The first question, is this configuration free, has one more part for robots with several links. Our disk robot is one rigid body, so it cannot hit itself. An arm can: its links move relative to each other, and a far link can fold back onto a near one. We switch to a new example for this one section: a planar arm with three links, 1.0 m, 0.8 m and 0.6 m long, drawn as line segments, like the 2R armExplained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §3.2 Degrees of freedom of a robot made of links, the arm with two joints on the robot’s top plate, with a third link added. Its configuration is three joint angles, each measured from the direction of the link before it.
Figure 4 shows two configurations. At joint angles (0°, 90°, 90°) the arm folds into a hook and link 3 stays clear of link 1. At (0°, 150°, 150°) link 3 folds back across link 1, crossing it at (0.54, 0): a self-collision (G-2672)Self-collision: Two links of the same robot overlapping, such as an arm’s third link folding back across its first; a configuration with a self-collision is not free, so planners test the robot’s own link pairs too. Explained in §4. Self-collision., the robot’s own links overlapping (LaValle §4.3.1, “Obstacle region for multiple bodies”).
Make interactive
Figure 4: A planar arm with three links (1.0 m blue, 0.8 m orange, 0.6 m purple) on a base at the origin. Left: joint angles (0, 90, 90) degrees; links 1 and 3 do not meet. Right: joint angles (0, 150, 150) degrees; link 3 folds back across link 1 and crosses it at (0.54, 0), marked red: a self-collision
Which pairs to test. The pairs to test are the pairs of links that must not overlap (LaValle §4.3.1). Links next to each other share a joint, so they touch all the time and are left out (LaValle §4.3.1). For a chain of m links, the count of pairs is the one we used for bodies:
\text{all pairs} = \frac{m(m - 1)}{2}
\text{pairs joined by a joint} = m - 1
For our arm, with 3 links:
\frac{3 \times 2}{2} - 2 = 1 \text{ pair: links 1 and 3}
For an arm with 7 links:
\frac{7 \times 6}{2} - 6 = 15 \text{ pairs}
Some of the remaining pairs can never meet whatever the joint angles, and some always overlap; testing them wastes time. So robot software such as MoveIt’s Setup Assistant samples 10,000 random configurations by default and turns off checking for the pairs that are never in collision, always in collision, in collision in the robot’s default pose, or joined by a joint (MoveIt docs). For our arm, links 1 and 3 cross in 735 of 10,000 random configurations, 7.35 percent (notebook), so the pair stays on the list.
The self-collision pairs join the broad phase and the narrow phase like any other pair: a configuration is free only if no link hits an obstacle and no pair on the list overlaps (LaValle §4.3.1, eq. 4.36). Every check so far answers yes or no; a planner often needs to know by how much.
5. Distance queries


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A distance query (G-2674)Distance query: A geometric query that returns the shortest distance between two bodies, 0 if they overlap; it tells a planner how much room the robot has, not only whether it is free. Explained in §5.1 How far, not only whether. returns how far apart two bodies are, not only whether they touch. 5.1 How far, not only whether
The second question, whole segments, needs more than yes or no. At the start (2, 1) the robot is free, but how much room does it have? A planner uses the answer to move fast where there is room and carefully near obstacles, and Section 6 uses it to clear whole segments at once. The distance from the robot’s body to the nearest obstacle is its clearance, the room it has to move.

The dot products of the table’s four corners (3, 1), (5, 1), (5.5, 2.5) and (3.5, 3) with -v are:
-3.0,\ -5.0,\ -5.5,\ -3.5
The largest is −3.0, so the table’s farthest point in the direction -v is the corner (3.0, 1.0). The robot’s farthest point in the direction v is its rim point straight ahead of the centre:
(2 + 0.25,\ 1) = (2.25,\ 1)
The farthest point of the difference in the direction v is the robot’s farthest point in v minus the table’s farthest point in -v (dyn4j GJK), because the dot product of a difference with v is the robot point’s dot product minus the table point’s, which is largest when the first is largest and the second smallest:

The point (−0.75, 0) is already the nearest point of the difference to the origin. A bounding-volume hierarchy speeds up distance queries as it speeds up yes-or-no checks, as in the collision libraries PQP and FCL (Hauser ch.7). With distances in hand, the second question of the opening problem, whole segments, can be answered.
6. Checking a path segment


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A segment cannot be checked point by point, so we check points at most a step apart: too large a step misses thin collisions, and checking in halving order (ends, middle, quarter points, …) finds a collision sooner. With clearances, a piece of segment is free once the free circles at its two ends meet.


6.1 A segment holds infinitely many configurations
The second question of the opening problem: is the straight segment from a = (2, 2) to b = (4, 3.6) free? Both ends are free and so is its middle, (3, 2.8). A planner cannot test every point, because a segment holds infinitely many configurations (LaValle §5.3.4), so it tests some points and hopes the rest are free. Checking a segment by testing points along it is edge resolution (G-2679)Edge resolution (segment checking): Checking a straight path segment in C-space for collisions by testing points along it, spaced at most a chosen step apart; too long a step can miss a thin collision, too short a step wastes time. Explained in §6.1 A segment holds infinitely many configurations., also called dynamic collision checking (Hauser ch.10).
The segment is 2.561 m long. The notebook finds its colliding stretch: from 0.620 to 0.777 of the way along, 0.403 m round the table’s corner, (3.5, 3.2) among it.
6.2 Step size and order
Step size. Split the segment into k equal steps no longer than a chosen step \varepsilon (Hauser ch.10, “Dynamic collision checking”):

d(a, b) is the segment’s length, 2.561 m;
\varepsilon is the longest step allowed, in m;
\lceil \cdot \rceil rounds up to a whole number;
k is the number of steps; the checks are its k + 1 end points.

k = \left\lceil \frac{d(a, b)}{\varepsilon} \right\rceil
With \varepsilon = 0.6 m:
k = \lceil 2.561 / 0.6 \rceil = \lceil 4.27 \rceil = 5
\text{step} = 2.561 / 5 = 0.512 \text{ m}
The checks sit at 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1 of the way. The colliding stretch runs from 0.620 to 0.777, between the checks at 0.6 and 0.8, so all six checks are free and the segment wrongly passes. A step shorter than the thinnest obstacle a collision can hide in is needed; too short a step wastes time (Hauser ch.10; LaValle §5.3.4). With \varepsilon = 0.1 m we halve the segment until each piece is shorter than 0.1 m, so that the halving order below can use the same points:
2.561 \to 1.281 \to 0.640 \to 0.320
\to 0.160 \to 0.080 \text{ m}
Five halvings give 32 steps of 0.080 m, so 33 points.
Order. Checking those 33 points from a towards b, the first collision is check 21, at 0.625 of the way. Checking them in halving order instead (both ends, then the middle point, then the two quarter points, then the eighths, and so on), the fifth check, three quarters of the way, is the point (3.5, 3.2), and it hits (LaValle §5.3.4). When both ends are free, the point most likely to be in collision is the one farthest from both, the middle (Hauser ch.10); the halving order keeps checking the points farthest from those already checked, so its early checks spread over the whole segment and a collision anywhere is found soon (LaValle §5.3.4). If the segment is free, every point must be checked in either order, so the order costs nothing then (LaValle §5.3.4).

6.3 Checking with clearance
A step of 0.1 m is a guess: a thinner obstacle could still hide between two checks. Clearances remove the guess (Hauser ch.10). Around a configuration with clearance c, the robot can move up to c in any direction without touching anything, so the circle of radius c round it is free. If the free circles at the two ends of a piece of segment reach each other, the piece is covered and free. With:

a and b the two ends of a piece of segment;
d(a, b) its length, in m;
c(a) and c(b) the clearances at its ends, in m.

d(a, b) \le c(a) + c(b)
If the length passes this test, the piece is free. Otherwise, check its middle and repeat on both halves (Hauser ch.10, “Visible-Exact1”; KAIST proximity slides). 7.2 The distance between two headings
Headings break the plain distance. The query at 350° and the stored 15° of Figure 1:
|350 - 15| = 335^\circ
but turning the other way, across 0°, is 25°. Worse, 0° and 360° are the same heading, yet:
|0 - 360| = 360^\circ
so plain subtraction breaks rule 2: two equal headings at a distance of 360°. d = \min(|\theta_1 - \theta_2|,\ 360 - |\theta_1 - \theta_2|)

7.3 Metres and radians in one distance
A configuration of the floor robot has a position in metres and a heading in radians, and a distance must combine them. One radian of turn moves the rim of the 0.25 m footprint 0.25 m (the arc rule of radians (G-2285))Radian: The unit of angle at which the arc of a circle is as long as its radius; a full turn is 2\pi rad, and with radians an arc is simply radius times angle. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.3 Why angles are measured in radians, so we count 0.25 m for each radian of angular distance (LaValle §5.3.4, eq. 5.30; KAIST C-space slides). A longer robot, such as one carrying a 1.4 m board, would need a larger weight: a small turn moves its far end a lot (LaValle §5.3.4). With:

q_1 = (x_1, y_1, \theta_1) and q_2 = (x_2, y_2, \theta_2) two configurations;
\Delta\theta the angular distance between \theta_1 and \theta_2, in rad;
w the weight, 0.25 m per rad;
d(q_1, q_2) their distance, in m.

d(q_1, q_2) = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2 + (w\thinspace\Delta\theta)^2}
where \Delta x and \Delta y are the differences in x and y (KAIST C-space slides). The weighted distance is a metric: it is the Euclidean distance on positions and on scaled headings measured the short way (LaValle §5.1.1, “Cartesian products of metric spaces”). For the query at x = 3.55 m, 350°, and the stored configuration E at x = 3.60 m, 15° (y equal), the heading part is 25°, which is 0.436 rad:
0.25 \times 0.436 = 0.109 \text{ m}
d = \sqrt{0.05^2 + 0.109^2} = 0.120 \text{ m}
With plain subtraction, 335° would make the heading part 1.462 m and E look far. A distance that wraps is half of the answer; the search must wrap too.
8. Nearest neighbours when headings wrap


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A k-d tree search skips a cell when the cell is farther than the best point found so far. If headings are treated as numbers from 0 to 360, a cell just across 0° looks a long way off and is skipped; measuring the cell’s distance the short way round fixes the search.


The opening problem’s third trap, in a search tree. A k-d tree stores points in cells split one coordinate at a time, so a nearest-neighbour search can skip every cell that lies farther away than the best point found so far (Hauser ch.10, “k-d trees”; LaValle §5.5.2). Figure 9 stores 8 configurations in one, with two coordinates so that it fits a page, x and heading; y would work like x. The tree splits on x, then heading, then x. The query is at x = 3.55 m, heading 350°. Distances use the weight of Section 7.3, 0.25 m per radian, and the heading axis is drawn in those metres, so a circle of equal distance is round.
Plain search. The search goes first into the cell that holds the query (Hauser ch.10). The search finds C and then D, at 0.371 m, and then reaches the cell of headings 0° to 175° beside it. Measured as plain numbers, that cell is 175° below the query:
350 - 175 = 175^\circ = 3.054 \text{ rad}
0.25 \times 3.054 = 0.764 \text{ m}
The gap of 0.764 m is more than the best so far, 0.371 m, so the cell is skipped, and with it E. The search ends at H (3.40 m, 320°), 0.199 m away. Wrong: E is nearer, at 0.120 m (Section 7.3).
Search with wrap-around. The heading 0° is the same as 360°, so the cell of headings 0° to 175° starts 10° above the query, across the top edge:
360 - 350 = 10^\circ = 0.175 \text{ rad}
0.25 \times 0.175 = 0.044 \text{ m}
Less than 0.371 m, so the cell is visited, and E, at 0.120 m, becomes the best. Measuring a cell’s distance the short way round the circle, and its points’ distances with the angular distance, is all that changes; we call this a nearest-neighbour search with wrap-around (G-2685)Nearest-neighbour search with wrap-around: A k-d tree search that measures a cell’s distance from the query the short way round the circle of headings, so a cell just across 0° is not skipped and the true nearest configuration is found. Explained in §8. Nearest neighbours when headings wrap.. LaValle §5.5.2 warns that the tree search must respect the places where the space wraps round, and Hauser ch.10 notes that headings need their own point-to-cell distance.
Figure 9 runs both searches. Watch the stage “plain search, step 3”, where the cell holding E is pruned as 0.764 m away, then “with wrap-around search, step 3”, where the same cell is 0.044 m away and E is found. The circle of the best distance so far wraps from the top edge to the bottom.

9. Uniform random rotations and directions


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A random heading must favour no direction: drawn evenly from 0° to 360°, every arc of 30° gets the same share, 1/12, wherever it lies. Directions and rotations in 3D need care: a uniform latitude angle crowds the poles, a point in a cube favours the corners; a normal sample scaled to length 1, the bread-slicer recipe and Shoemake’s recipe for 3D rotations are uniform.


9.1 What uniform means for headings
Sampling planners draw random configurations, so the random headings must not favour any direction. For the floor robot this is easy. Draw the heading from the continuous uniform distribution (G-467)Continuous uniform distribution U(a, b): A continuous variable spread evenly between a and b, with density 1/(b - a). Explained in: Uniform and Log-normal Distributions, §2. The uniform distribution from 0° to 360°, every value equally likely. Then any arc of 30° gets the same share of the draws, wherever on the circle it lies (notebook, 100,000 draws: 8.4 percent for 10° to 40°, 8.3 percent for 200° to 230°):
30 / 360 = 0.083
Equal shares for equal arcs, wherever they lie, is what uniform means for rotations. A uniform random rotation (G-2686)Uniform random rotation: A random rotation drawn so that every orientation is equally likely: turning the whole set of samples by any fixed rotation does not make some orientations more common; for headings, a draw evenly from 0° to 360°. Explained in §9.1 What uniform means for headings. makes every orientation equally likely: turning the whole set of samples by any fixed rotation must not make some orientations more common (LaValle §5.1.4, §5.2.2). The circle of headings has no favoured place, so the plain uniform draw is right. Directions and rotations in 3D, as for a drone or the gripper of an arm, are where the traps are.
9.2 Random directions
A uniform random direction (G-2689)Uniform random direction: A random unit vector drawn so that every direction is equally likely; a normal sample scaled to length 1 gives one, while a point in a square or cube scaled to length 1 favours the diagonals. Explained in §9.2 Random directions. is a unit vector (a vector of length 1) drawn so that every direction is equally likely: every patch of the circle, or of the sphere, of the same size gets the same share (LaValle §5.2.2).
Two traps and two fixes, with the shares from the notebook (Figure 10):

A point in a square, scaled to length 1. Draw x and y evenly from −1 to 1 and divide by the length. The square reaches 1.41 times as far along a diagonal as along an axis, so a thin wedge along a diagonal holds about twice the area, and diagonal directions come up more often: within 5° of a diagonal 16.2 percent of the time, within 5° of an axis 8.6 percent, against a fair share of 11.1 percent (LaValle §5.2.2 warns of this bias towards a cube’s corners).
A normal sample, scaled to length 1. Draw each coordinate from a normal distribution with the same spread. Its density depends only on the distance from the centre, so every direction is equally likely: 11.1 percent near the diagonals and 11.1 percent near the axes (LaValle §5.2.2).
On the sphere, a uniform latitude angle. Drawing the latitude evenly from −90° to 90° packs as many points into the short circles near the poles as into the long equator. The two caps above height 0.9 and below −0.9 hold 10 percent of the sphere’s surface but get 28.7 percent of the points.
On the sphere, a uniform height: the bread slicer. Drawing the height evenly from −1 to 1 and the longitude evenly from 0° to 360° is uniform, because slices of a sphere of equal thickness have equal crust area, like a loaf through a bread slicer (LaValle §5.2.2). The caps get 10.1 percent.

The caps by the two recipes, the height 0.9 being at latitude 64.2°:
\arcsin 0.9 = 64.2^\circ
\text{latitude: } 2 \times (90 - 64.2) / 180 = 0.287
\text{height: } 2 \times (1 - 0.9) / 2 = 0.1
The latitude recipe gives each degree of latitude the same share; the height recipe gives each slice of height the same share, which is right because equal slices have equal area.

Left, a point drawn evenly in the square from −1 to 1 and scaled to length 1: bumps on the diagonals, 16.2 percent within 5 degrees of a diagonal against 8.6 percent near an axis. Right, a normal sample scaled to length 1: even, 11.1 percent each, the fair share. Bottom: 1,500 points on the sphere from three samplers, orange where the height is above 0.9 or below −0.9 (two caps with 10 percent of the surface). Uniform latitude angle: 28.7 percent in the caps. Uniform height (bread slicer): 10.1 percent. The up arrow turned by Shoemake’s random rotations: 10.0 percent
9.3 Random rotations in 3D
A rotation in 3D, such as the orientation of a gripper, can be stored as four numbers h = (h_1, h_2, h_3, h_4) whose squares add up to 1, so h is a point on a sphere in four dimensions (LaValle §5.2.2):
h_1^2 + h_2^2 + h_3^2 + h_4^2 = 1
Uniform rotations are uniform points on that sphere, and the bread-slicer idea carries over one dimension up. Shoemake’s recipe (LaValle §5.2.2, eq. 5.15), with:

u_1, u_2, u_3 three numbers drawn evenly from 0 to 1;
h the four random numbers that describe the rotation.

h = (\sqrt{1 - u_1}\sin 2\pi u_2,
\sqrt{1 - u_1}\cos 2\pi u_2,
\sqrt{u_1}\sin 2\pi u_3,
\sqrt{u_1}\cos 2\pi u_3)
Check that the squares add up to 1. For u_1 = 0.3, u_2 = 0.6 and u_3 = 0.9 the recipe gives (−0.492, −0.677, −0.322, 0.443) (notebook). The squares of the first two entries, then of the last two:
0.242 + 0.458 = 0.700 = 1 - 0.3
0.104 + 0.196 = 0.300 = 0.3
0.700 + 0.300 = 1
The same steps in symbols, with s = 2\pi u_2, the first two entries squared:
(1 - u_1)\sin^2 s + (1 - u_1)\cos^2 s
= (1 - u_1)(\sin^2 s + \cos^2 s)
= 1 - u_1
The last two give u_1 the same way, and together:
(1 - u_1) + u_1 = 1
Check that it is uniform. Turn the arrow pointing straight up by 20,000 of these rotations. If every rotation is equally likely, the arrow’s tip lands evenly on the sphere, so the caps above height 0.9 should get 10 percent. The caps get 10.0 percent (notebook; Figure 10, bottom right). Drawing three angles evenly (turns about z, y and x, each from 0° to 360°) and turning the arrow puts 6.5 percent there, not 10: three uniform angles do not make a uniform rotation (notebook), as LaValle §5.2.2 warns.
10. Summary























































ToolAnswersOn our roomBroad phase and narrow phaseis this configuration free? cheaply1 exact test instead of 4 at (3.5, 3.2)Sweep and prunewhich boxes overlap?2 box tests instead of 10 pairsBounding-volume hierarchywhich bodies are near the robot?9 box tests among 25 bodiesSelf-collision pairswhich links can hit each other?1 pair for 3 links, 15 for 7Distance query, GJKhow far apart?clearance 0.75 m at the startEdge resolutionis this segment free?halving order: 5 checks instead of 21Angular distance and weighted metrichow far apart are two configurations?350° to 15°: 25°, not 335°Search with wrap-aroundwhich stored configuration is nearest?E at 0.120 m, not H at 0.199 mUniform rotations and directionsa random orientation that favours nonecaps get 10.0 percent, not 28.7

The three questions of the opening problem are answered on our room: (3.5, 3.2) is in collision, found with one exact test after the boxes, because only the table’s box overlaps the robot’s; the segment from (2, 2) to (4, 3.6) is not free, found at the fifth check in halving order, because the early checks spread evenly over the segment; and the nearest stored configuration to 350° is E at 15°, 0.120 m away, because the search measures headings the short way round.
Collision detection (G-2665)Collision detection: Deciding, yes or no, whether two bodies overlap, such as the robot’s disk and the table; planners call it thousands of times instead of building the obstacle region. Explained in §2.1 The yes-or-no question and what it costs. splits into a broad phase (G-2666)Broad phase: The first, cheap step of collision detection: wrap each body in a simple shape such as a box and keep only the pairs whose shapes overlap, so the costly exact test runs on few pairs. Explained in §2.2 Broad phase and narrow phase. with boxes whose sides run along x and y and a narrow phase (G-2667)Narrow phase: The second step of collision detection: the exact overlap test on the pairs the broad phase kept, such as the distance from the robot’s centre to the table compared with its 0.25 m radius. Explained in §2.2 Broad phase and narrow phase., so the costly exact test runs only on pairs whose boxes overlap.
Sweep and prune (G-2670)Sweep and prune: A broad phase that sorts the boxes by their left edge and sweeps along x, comparing each box only with the boxes it overlaps along x; it cuts the pairs tested, though long boxes that span the axis defeat it. Explained in §2.3 Sweep and prune. sorts the boxes along x, so each box is compared only with boxes it overlaps along x, but long boxes such as walls defeat a single axis.
A bounding-volume hierarchy (G-2671)Bounding-volume hierarchy (BVH): A tree of nested bounding volumes, each holding its two children’s down to one per body; a query skips every body inside a box that misses, so it needs about \log_2 n box tests for n bodies (9 among the room’s 25). Explained in §3.1 Why a tree of boxes. needs about \log_2 n box tests per query for n bodies, because a box that misses rules out everything inside it: about 13 tests for 10,000 bodies.
Self-collision (G-2672)Self-collision: Two links of the same robot overlapping, such as an arm’s third link folding back across its first; a configuration with a self-collision is not free, so planners test the robot’s own link pairs too. Explained in §4. Self-collision. checks only the pairs of links not joined by a joint, because joined links touch all the time.
A distance query (G-2674)Distance query: A geometric query that returns the shortest distance between two bodies, 0 if they overlap; it tells a planner how much room the robot has, not only whether it is free. Explained in §5.1 How far, not only whether. gives the clearance, the room to move; for convex bodies it is the distance from the origin to their Minkowski difference, which GJK (G-2678)GJK algorithm: The Gilbert-Johnson-Keerthi algorithm: it decides whether two convex shapes overlap, or how far apart they are, by searching their Minkowski difference for the origin using each shape’s farthest point in chosen directions, without building the difference. Explained in §5.2 The Minkowski difference and GJK. finds from the shapes’ farthest points in chosen directions.
Edge resolution (G-2679)Edge resolution (segment checking): Checking a straight path segment in C-space for collisions by testing points along it, spaced at most a chosen step apart; too long a step can miss a thin collision, too short a step wastes time. Explained in §6.1 A segment holds infinitely many configurations. checks points of a segment; too long a step misses the 0.403 m collision, and checking the middle point first, then the quarter points, finds it at check 5 instead of 21; with clearances, 9 checks prove the drive to the door free.
A metric (G-2681)Metric (distance function): A distance between points that is never negative, is 0 only between equal points, is the same both ways and obeys the triangle inequality; search trees rely on these rules to skip far regions safely. Explained in §7.1 The rules a distance must follow. must obey four rules, including the triangle inequality (G-2683)Triangle inequality: The rule that a detour through a third point is never shorter than going straight, d(p, q) \le d(p, r) + d(r, q); it is what lets a nearest-neighbour search skip a region farther than its best point. Explained in §7.1 The rules a distance must follow., because search trees prune on them; the angular distance (G-2684)Angular distance: The distance between two headings measured the short way round the circle, the smaller of \lvert \theta_1 - \theta_2 \rvert and 360° minus it, so 350° and 15° are 25° apart, not 335°. Explained in §7.2 The distance between two headings. and a weight of 0.25 m per radian give a metric for configurations with headings.
A nearest-neighbour search with wrap-around (G-2685)Nearest-neighbour search with wrap-around: A k-d tree search that measures a cell’s distance from the query the short way round the circle of headings, so a cell just across 0° is not skipped and the true nearest configuration is found. Explained in §8. Nearest neighbours when headings wrap. measures cells the short way round, so the cell across 0° is 0.044 m away, not 0.764 m, and the right neighbour is found.
A uniform random rotation (G-2686)Uniform random rotation: A random rotation drawn so that every orientation is equally likely: turning the whole set of samples by any fixed rotation does not make some orientations more common; for headings, a draw evenly from 0° to 360°. Explained in §9.1 What uniform means for headings. makes every orientation equally likely; a normal sample scaled to length 1, the bread slicer and Shoemake’s recipe are uniform, because they favour no direction, while a uniform latitude crowds the poles.

The robot’s planner can now test configurations and segments quickly, measure how far configurations are from each other, find the nearest stored one and draw random configurations evenly. Still missing: a planner that puts these together, drawing random configurations, joining each to its nearest neighbours with checked segments, and growing a route to the door: the sampling-based planners of a later chapter.

RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.title: Grid Path Planning: Wavefronts, Navigation Functions and Value Iteration
RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Partial derivatives and gradientsExplained in: Partial Derivatives and Gradients, §4. The gradient; Gradient descentGradient descent: Finding the lowest point of a function by repeated small steps downhill. Explained in: Gradient Descent from Scratch, §2. The idea; MemoizationMemoization: Storing the result of a function call and returning the stored result when the same input comes again. Explained in: Memoization in Backpropagation, §3. Memoization on the Fibonacci numbers; Breadth-first searchBreadth-first search (BFS): A search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ring; Dijkstra’s algorithmDijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §3.2 The algorithm: settle the nearest, update its neighbours; Backward and bidirectional searchBidirectional search: A forward search from the start and a backward search from the goal run in turn until some state has been expanded by both; the route is the smallest sum of the two costs over all states both reached, since the meeting state can be off the shortest route. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §8.2 Bidirectional search.
Leads to: D* replanningExplained in: Moving Through Unknown Maps: D* Replanning and Bug Algorithms, §3.2 Fixing them in order; Real-time heuristic search (LRTA*)Real-time heuristic search: Searching only a fixed, small number of states around the robot before each move, then moving and searching again; it bounds the thinking time per move at the cost of a possibly longer drive. Explained in: Moving Through Unknown Maps: D* Replanning and Bug Algorithms, §5.1 Learning the guesses: LRTA.
Compare with: Dijkstra’s algorithmDijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §3.2 The algorithm: settle the nearest, update its neighbours; Harmonic potentialsHarmonic potential: A potential field that is a harmonic function, held at 1 on every obstacle and 0 at the goal; it has no local minimum, so stepping downhill always reaches the goal, but it must be solved on a grid of the whole free space first. Explained in: Potential Fields, §6. A field with no local minima: harmonic potentials; Potential fieldsPotential field (artificial potential field): A height over the robot’s C-space that is lowest at the goal and rises near obstacles, built as an attractive bowl plus a repulsive hill round each obstacle; the robot reaches the goal by stepping downhill from wherever it is, with no grid and no search, but can stop in a local minimum. Explained in: Potential Fields, §2. The pull of the door: the attractive potential.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A route from A* serves one start, and a robot that slips off it must search again. Numbering every free cell with its distance to the door, in one pass from the door, gives the robot a move from any cell: walking downhill on those numbers reaches the door by the shortest route, wherever the robot finds itself.


So far the robot can find its shortest route to the door on its map, the room’s occupancy grid (G-2340)Occupancy grid: A grid map that stores in each cell a number between 0 and 1, such as the probability that the cell is occupied, instead of a hard 0 or 1; the standard grid map of robotics, since sensors are never sure. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §5.2 Bitmaps and occupancy grids of 0.5 m cells, 76 of them free. With moves to any of the 8 neighbouring cells, A* search (G-2577)A search:* Dijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid). Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.5 The algorithm finds the 3.414 m route from the start cell S to the door’s cell G after taking 9 cells off its open list.
What still breaks: the route is a list of cells for one start, and the robot does not stay on it. Its position is never exact: the corridor robotExplained in: Kalman Filter, §1. Overview missed by 0.27 m on average from its commands alone, and its beacon readings by 0.51 m, a whole cell. Figure 1 plays one such slip: the robot’s first move falls one cell short, and it lands in a cell the route does not contain.

One pass from the door, which numbers every free cell with its distance to the door, takes 76, and afterwards a robot in any cell knows its next move. Every number below is computed in the notebook RO-048-grid-planning-wavefronts-and-value-iteration.ipynb. This Note builds that pass and the ways to use and compute it:

numbering every cell from the door, ring by ring: the wavefront (Section 2);
which neighbours a cell has and what a move costs, which decide what the numbers mean (Section 3);
walking downhill on the numbers from any cell: the navigation function (Section 4);
computing the same numbers without a queue, by repeated sweeps: value iteration (Section 5);

2. Numbering every cell from the door: the wavefront


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Give the door’s cell 0, its free neighbours 1, their unnumbered neighbours 2, and so on. One breadth-first pass from the door numbers all 76 free cells with their fewest moves to the door; S gets 8.


The idea. The opening problem needs, for every cell the robot might land in, its distance to the door. Drop a stone into a pond at the door: the ripple reaches the cells next to the door first, then the cells next to those, ring after ring. If each cell writes down the ring that reached it, every cell knows how many moves it is from the door.
The standard term. Numbering the cells ring by ring outwards from the goal is wavefront propagation (G-2700)Wavefront propagation (wavefront planner): Numbering the free cells of a grid ring by ring outwards from the goal, each ring one move further, so every cell gets its fewest moves to the goal in one pass (8 for the room’s start cell); a breadth-first search from the goal, used when every move costs the same. Explained in §2. Numbering every cell from the door: the wavefront., and the program that does it is a wavefront planner (Choset slides, “The Wave-front Planner”; LaValle §8.2.3). Each ring is a wavefront: the cells first reached at the same number of moves.
The mechanism on our grid. We start with moves left, down, up and right only, the 4-connected grid (G-2544)4-connected grid: A grid made into a graph by joining each cell to the up to four cells that share a side with it (left, down, up, right); the simplest graph of a grid map, with every move the same length. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edges, whose cells are joined to the at most four cells that share a side with them. The steps (Choset slides; LaValle §8.2.3):

Give G the number 0 and put it in a list.
Take the oldest cell off the list.
Give each free neighbour without a number the taken cell’s number plus 1, and add it to the end of the list.
Go back to step 2 until the list is empty.

The list is a queue (G-2551)Queue (first in, first out): A list served in arrival order: new items join the back and the next item leaves from the front; as a search’s frontier it gives breadth-first search. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ring, so these steps are breadth-first search (G-2550)Breadth-first search (BFS): A search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ring run as a backward search (G-2583)Backward search: A search that starts at the goal and follows every move backwards until it reaches the start; it is cheaper when the goal’s side branches less, and run to the end it gives every state’s cost to the goal. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §8.1 Backward search, from the door, and run until every cell is reached instead of stopping at S.

A cell that never gets a number cannot reach the door at all (Choset slides: “0’s should only remain if unreachable regions exist”); our room has none.
The formal version. With:

W_k is the wavefront number k, the set of cells first reached after k moves, such as W_0 = \lbrace G \rbrace (curly brackets list the members of a set: here only G) and W_8, the 5 cells of ring 8, S among them;
\phi(x) is the number written in cell x, such as 8 for S.

Each wavefront is made of the free neighbours of the last one that have no number yet, and a cell’s number is the index of its wavefront (LaValle §8.2.3):
\phi(x) = k \quad \text{for every } x \text{ in } W_k
Each cell enters the list once and leaves it once, so the work grows in proportion to the number of cells, written O(n) in Big-O notation (G-2556)Big-O notation: A way to write how fast an algorithm’s work grows with the problem’s size, keeping only the fastest-growing part and dropping constant factors, such as O(V + E) for breadth-first search and O(b^d) for listing every path; it lets us compare methods without timing them. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §7.2 Big-O notation for n reachable cells (LaValle §8.2.3), 76 here. The numbers count moves along 4 directions, but our robot also moves diagonallyExplained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §2.1 Diagonal moves: the 8-connected grid, and a diagonal is longer than a straight move. What should a cell count then?
3. Which moves count: four or eight neighbours, moves or metres


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The numbers mean what the moves and their costs say: on the 4-connected grid S is 8 moves (4.0 m) from the door, and on the 8-connected grid 6 moves, but walking down those numbers can take 3.828 m. Counting metres instead, with Dijkstra’s algorithm run from the door, gives S its true 3.414 m.


The wavefront of Section 2 numbers each cell with its moves to the door, but the robot drives in metres. Two choices fix what a number means:

which cells are neighbours: the 4-connected grid, or the 8-connected grid (G-2564)8-connected grid: A grid made into a graph by joining each cell to all 8 cells around it: 4 straight moves of one cell side and 4 diagonal moves of 1.414 cell sides (0.707 m for 0.5 m cells), usually without cutting the corner of a blocked cell; it gives shorter, less jagged routes than a 4-connected grid. Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §2.1 Diagonal moves: the 8-connected grid, which joins each cell to all 8 cells around it (MR §10.4) and, on our grid, never lets a diagonal move cut the corner of a blocked cell;
what a move costs: one move each, or its length, 0.5 m straight and 0.707 m diagonal.
