Counting metres. To count metres, the pass must settle cells in order of their distance to the door, not of their moves, and that is Dijkstra’s algorithm (G-2565)Dijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §3.2 The algorithm: settle the nearest, update its neighbours run from the door until its priority queue is empty. The wavefront of Section 2 is the special case in which every move costs the same: then all cells of one ring are equally far and can be settled together, without a priority queue (LaValle §8.2.3). In the bottom panel of Figure 3, S’s number is 3.414 m, and the walk down the numbers is the 3.414 m route of A*.
The standard term. A cell’s number in metres, the length of the shortest route from that cell to the goal, is its cost-to-go (G-2701)Cost-to-go: The length of the shortest route from a state to the goal, such as 3.414 m from the room’s start cell to the door; stored for every state, it tells the robot how far it still has to go from wherever it is. Explained in §3. Which moves count: four or eight neighbours, moves or metres. (LaValle §2.3.1, §8.2.2). From here on we write it V(x):

x is a free cell;
V(x) is its cost-to-go, in m, such as 3.414 for S and 0 for G.

The cost-to-go of a cell is the true distance left that A*‘s heuristic (G-2570)Heuristic h: A cheap guess of the cost still to go from a state to the goal, such as 3.121 m from the start cell to the door; a search uses it to prefer states that look nearer the goal. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §2. A guess of the distance left: the heuristic only guesses: for S, the octile guess is 3.121 m and the cost-to-go 3.414 m. Every free cell now has its distance to the door; the robot still needs a rule that turns the numbers into moves.
4. Walking downhill: the navigation function


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

From any cell, step to the neighbour with the smallest move plus cost-to-go V, the cell’s shortest distance to the door; each step lowers V by exactly the move’s length, so the walk is as long as the start cell’s number: 3.414 m from S, 3.207 m from the cell the slip left the robot in. A number map with this property is a navigation function.


4.1 The numbers as a valley
The opening problem asks for a move from every cell. Picture each cell’s cost-to-go as a height: the door’s cell at height 0, S at 3.414, the corner by the cabinet at 11.121. The room becomes a valley whose lowest point is the door, and a ball dropped anywhere rolls to the door.

4.2 One step at a time, from any cell
The rule. A robot in a cell looks at its neighbours and steps to the one for which the move plus that neighbour’s number is smallest (LaValle §8.2.2, eq. 8.5). From S, with each move’s length and the neighbour’s cost-to-go (notebook):

The smallest, 3.414, is S’s own number, reached by two moves; we break the tie towards the neighbour with the smaller number, diagonally up and right.
Why the walk is the shortest route. S’s number is the length of its shortest route, and that route’s first move leads to a neighbour whose shortest route is the rest of it. With:

n is a neighbour of the cell x;
c(x, n) is the length of the move from x to n, 0.5 or 0.707 m;
\min means the smallest of the numbers that follow, here one for every neighbour n;
n^\ast is the neighbour the rule picks, diagonally up and right for S.

Our numbers first, then the same in symbols:
V(S) = \min(3.414, 3.414, 3.828, \dots)
V(x) = \min_{n} \big(c(x, n) + V(n)\big)
V(S) = 0.707 + 2.707 = 3.414
V(x) = c(x, n^\ast) + V(n^\ast)
So each step lowers the number by exactly the move just made. The walk from S passes through cells numbered 3.414, 2.707, 2.207, 1.707, 1.207, 0.5 and 0, and its moves add up to the drop from the first number to the last:
\text{walk} = 3.414 - 0 = 3.414 \text{ m}
\text{walk} = V(\text{start}) - V(G)
The same telescoping holds from every cell, because every cell’s number came from such a neighbour. When every move costs the same, as on the 4-connected grid of Section 2, the move adds the same amount everywhere, and the rule becomes “step to the neighbour with the lowest number” (Choset slides, “The Wavefront, Now What?”; LaValle §8.2.2). On our 8-connected grid the lowest-number rule happens to give shortest routes from all 75 cells (notebook), but only the rule with the move added is guaranteed to.

The slipped robot of Figure 1 no longer searches: its new cell’s arrow sends it on a 3.207 m route, the same route A* found by searching 7 cells. The navigation function answers the opening problem: one pass from the door, and every cell, on the route or off it, has its move.
The standard terms. A number map that guides the robot this way is a navigation function (G-2702)Navigation function: A number for every state that is 0 at the goal, infinite only where the goal cannot be reached, and lower at some neighbour of every other state, so it has one minimum, the goal; stepping to the neighbour with the smallest move plus number from any state leads to the goal, by the shortest route when the numbers are the cost-to-go. Explained in §4.2 One step at a time, from any cell. (LaValle §8.2.2). LaValle’s three conditions, on our map:

the goal has the value 0: V(G) = 0;
a cell from which the goal cannot be reached has the value infinity, and only such a cell: our room has none;
from every other cell, some move leads to a cell with a strictly lower value: true for all 75 cells (notebook), because every cell’s number was made from a neighbour’s number plus a move longer than 0.

The third condition says the valley of Figure 4 has one lowest point, the door, and no local minimum (G-1110)Local minimum: A point lower than everything around it, but not the lowest overall. Explained in: Gradient Descent from Scratch, §8. The shape of the loss function matters: no dent other than the goal where a walker could stop. A height map made by hand, such as a potential fieldPotential field (artificial potential field): A height over the robot’s C-space that is lowest at the goal and rises near obstacles, built as an attractive bowl plus a repulsive hill round each obstacle; the robot reaches the goal by stepping downhill from wherever it is, with no grid and no search, but can stop in a local minimum. Explained in: Potential Fields, §4. Why the robot stops: local minima, can have such dents. Walking downhill on a smooth valley is gradient descent (G-862)Gradient descent: Finding the lowest point of a function by repeated small steps downhill. Explained in: Gradient Descent from Scratch, §1. Overview; the grid’s arrows are its version on cells (LaValle §8.2.2).
A navigation function with its downhill rule is a feedback plan (G-2703)Feedback plan: A plan that names an action for every state the robot can be in, not one sequence for one start, so the robot’s measured state picks the action and a slip only changes the input; a navigation function with its downhill rule is one. Explained in §4.2 One step at a time, from any cell.: a plan that names an action for every state the robot can be in, instead of one sequence of actions for one start (LaValle §8.2.2). The plan is called feedback because the robot’s measured cell, fed back from its sensors, picks the action, so a slip changes the input, not the plan. A route from A* is not a feedback plan: off the route it says nothing.
A gotcha: shortest routes hug the obstacles. A shortest route bends round every corner as tightly as the grid allows, so a robot that follows it passes close to the furniture (Freiburg path planning, slide 42). Our grid already blocks every cell that furniture touches, which keeps the robot’s centre a quarter of a cell from it along the grid lines. Two common remedies take more room, both by treating the obstacles as bigger than they are (Freiburg path planning, slide 43): drop the free cells next to obstacles before numbering, or give those cells a higher move cost, so the numbers prefer open floor.
The numbers so far came from Dijkstra’s algorithm, which settles cells strictly in order of distance using a priority queue. The next section computes the same numbers with no order at all, which is the form that carries over to robots between cells.
5. Value iteration: the same numbers without a queue


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Start with 0 at the door and “unknown” everywhere else, then sweep over all cells, each taking the smallest move plus neighbour’s value, until a whole sweep changes nothing. On the room grid 8 sweeps give exactly Dijkstra’s numbers; no priority queue and no order are needed.


Why we need it. The numbers that sent the slipped robot to the door came from Dijkstra’s algorithm, which gets the cost-to-go, each cell’s shortest distance to the door, right because it settles cells in the right order, the nearest first. Keeping that order costs a priority queue, and some problems have no simple order at all, such as values stored between cells (Section 6) or moves whose result is uncertain. LaValle (§2.3.3) puts it this way: value iteration “extends easily to a much broader class of problems”, including continuous state spaces and planning with uncertain outcomes, while a Dijkstra-like order “may be inefficient or impossible in practice to maintain”.
The idea. Section 4.2 showed that each cell’s number equals the smallest move plus neighbour’s number. Turn that equation into a rule for fixing numbers: start from wrong numbers and let every cell repeatedly copy the best offer from its neighbours. Wrong numbers improve with every sweep, and once no cell can find a better offer, the numbers are the cost-to-go.
The standard term. Repeating, over all states, the update “value = smallest move cost plus the next state’s value” until the values stop changing is value iteration (G-2704)Value iteration: Computing every state’s cost-to-go by repeating, over all states, the update “value = smallest move cost plus the next state’s value” until no value changes; it needs no priority queue and no order, and it carries over to values between grid cells and to uncertain moves. Explained in §5. Value iteration: the same numbers without a queue. (LaValle §2.3.1, §2.3.2; Freiburg path planning, slide 40). The Reinforcement Learning (RL) Notes use the same update with rewards and with probabilities for where a move ends. With V(x), the cost-to-go of cell x in m, and the move lengths c(x, n) of Section 4.2:
V(x) \leftarrow \min_{n} \big(c(x, n) + V(n)\big)
The arrow means: replace the value on the left by the right side. Before the first sweep V(G) = 0 and every other value is infinity, written \infty: not yet known.
The mechanism on our grid. One sweep visits the free cells row by row, from the door’s wall down, left to right in each row, and updates each in place, so a cell already uses the values its neighbours received earlier in the same sweep (Sutton and Barto §4.1, §4.4). Figure 6 shows the values after each sweep. Watch two things:

frame “sweep 1”: 49 cells get a value, S already its final 3.414, because each row passes its values to the row below within the same sweep;
frame “sweep 3”: four values drop (orange), such as the cell x 2.0 to 2.5 m under the top wall, from 1.914 to 1.500.


Figure 6: Value iteration on the room grid, one frame per sweep; each cell shows its value in m (rounded to 0.01) and is coloured as in Figure 4; cells with no value yet are white. A sweep goes row by row from the top wall down, left to right. Blue outline: the cell got its first value in this sweep; orange outline: its value was lowered. Sweep 1 gives 49 cells a value, S 3.41; sweep 2 gives 11 more; sweep 3 lowers 4 values, such as 1.91 to 1.50 under the top wall; sweeps 3 to 7 lower 14 values in all. Sweep 8 changes nothing: every value equals the cost-to-go from Dijkstra’s algorithm
Why did the cell under the top wall first get 1.914? In sweep 2 it was visited before its right-hand neighbour had a value, so its best offer came diagonally, through a cell with 1.207:
0.707 + 1.207 = 1.914
In sweep 3 its right-hand neighbour already had 1.0, a shorter way in:
0.5 + 1.0 = 1.5
Sweep 8 changes nothing, and the 76 values equal Dijkstra’s (notebook).
Why the sweeps end at the right numbers. Two facts (LaValle §2.3.2):

A value is never too small. Every finite value is the length of some real route to the door, built move by move from G’s 0, and no route is shorter than the shortest.
After sweep k, every cell whose shortest route has at most k moves holds its exact value. The second cell of such a route has at most k - 1 moves left, so it was exact after sweep k - 1, and sweep k offers its value plus the first move.

The longest of the room’s shortest routes has 21 moves (notebook), so 21 sweeps always suffice and a 22nd confirms that nothing changes. Sweeps that each use only the values of the last sweep need exactly 22.
Updating in place, news can travel many cells in one sweep, and here 8 suffice. According to Sutton and Barto (§4.1), the in-place version “usually converges faster”, and the order of the sweep matters.
The price. Value iteration does more work than Dijkstra’s algorithm: 8 sweeps of 75 cells are 600 updates, against 76 cells settled once each (notebook). Dijkstra’s algorithm is value iteration that only touches the cells whose values can still change, in the order that makes each touch final (LaValle §2.3.3).
Value iteration pays for doing without that order. The next section needs exactly that freedom, because its values sit between the cells.
6. Between the cells: dynamic programming with interpolation


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The robot stands at (2, 1), not at a cell centre, and can drive at any angle. Storing values at the cell centres, blending the four around any point, and running value iteration with moves in 16 directions gives a cost-to-go between the cells; following it, the robot reaches the door’s cell after 3.564 m instead of 3.768 m by the grid’s cells.


6.1 The robot is between the cell centres
The problem, in numbers. The navigation function of Section 4, the door’s numbers the robot walks down, has a value at each cell centre and moves in 8 directions. But the robot stands at (2 m, 1 m), the corner of S, and can turn to any headingExplained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §4.4 Four ways to drive. To use the grid it must first drive 0.354 m to S’s centre and then follow 45° steps:
0.354 + 3.414 = 3.768 \text{ m}
To plan from where the robot really is, we need values at points between the centres.
The idea. A point between four cell centres takes a blend of their four values, each counted more the closer the point is to it. Draw the four centres as the corners of a square and the point inside: each corner’s share is the area of the rectangle on the far side of the point from that corner, so the nearest corner, with the largest far rectangle, counts most.
The standard term. The blend is bilinear interpolation (G-2706)Bilinear interpolation: Estimating a value at a point between four grid points as their weighted average, each weight the area of the rectangle on the far side of the point (linear interpolation along x, then along y); it fills in values between cell centres. Explained in §6.1 The robot is between the cell centres. (LaValle §8.5.2.1, eq. 8.59): linear interpolation (G-1092)Linear interpolation: Placing a percentile between two neighbouring sorted values, in proportion to its position; the pandas default. Explained in: Outlier Detection with the Percentile Method and Winsorization, §2.2 From percentiles to limits, placing a value between two neighbours in proportion to the distance, done once along x and once along y.
The mechanism on our numbers. Figure 7 takes the end of one 0.5 m move of the robot, at 67.5° from (2, 1): the point p = (2.191, 1.462). The four cell centres around p, with the cost-to-go of Section 6.2, are (1.75, 1.25) with 3.557, S’s centre (2.25, 1.25) with 3.338, (1.75, 1.75) with 3.122 and (2.25, 1.75) with 2.862. The formal version. With:

\alpha is how far across the square the point lies, from 0 at the left centres to 1 at the right ones, 0.8827 for p;
\beta is how far up, from 0 at the lower centres to 1 at the upper ones, 0.4239 for p;
V_{00}, V_{10}, V_{01} and V_{11} are the values at the bottom-left, bottom-right, top-left and top-right centres: 3.557, 3.338, 3.122 and 2.862.

V(p) = (1 - \alpha)(1 - \beta)\thinspace V_{00}
+ \thinspace\alpha (1 - \beta)\thinspace V_{10}
+ \thinspace(1 - \alpha)\beta \thinspace V_{01} + \alpha\beta\thinspace V_{11}
Why it holds: checks at easy points. At the bottom-left centre itself, \alpha = \beta = 0, and the first weight is 1 and the others 0, so the blend gives that centre’s own value. At the middle of the square, \alpha = \beta = 0.5, and every weight is 0.25, so the blend is the plain average. And the four weights always add up to 1, so a blend of four equal values gives that value back:
0.0676 + 0.5085 + 0.0497 + 0.3742 = 1
(1 - \alpha + \alpha)(1 - \beta + \beta) = 1
The robot can now read a value anywhere between four free centres. Where one of the four centres is a blocked cell, LaValle (§8.5.2.2) gives the point the value infinity, so no move ends there.
6.2 Value iteration with interpolation
The idea. Run the value iteration of Section 5 on the cell centres, but let each centre try moves in more than 8 directions. Each move ends between centres, and the bilinear blend of Section 6.1 gives the value at its end. The update is unchanged: the smallest move length plus value at the move’s end.
The standard term. Value iteration with values stored at sample points and blended in between is dynamic programming with interpolation (G-2705)Dynamic programming with interpolation: Value iteration with values stored only at sample points, such as cell centres, and blended in between, with moves in many directions; it gives a cost-to-go at every point, so a robot can plan from where it really stands and drive at any angle. Explained in §6.2 Value iteration with interpolation. (LaValle §8.5.2). The method is dynamic programming (G-652)Dynamic programming: Solving a problem by storing the answer to each overlapping sub-problem the first time it is computed and looking it up afterwards, so no work is repeated; memoization is one form of it. Explained in: Memoization in Backpropagation, §3.3 The memoized version, reusing each stored value instead of recomputing routes, on a continuous floor instead of a list of cells.
The mechanism on our grid. Every free centre tries 16 moves of 0.5 m, one every 22.5°; a centre within 0.5 m of the door’s centre may also go straight there (notebook). With:

x is a cell centre, or later any point of the floor;
u is one of the 16 directions;
x + 0.5u is the end of a 0.5 m move in direction u;
V(x + 0.5u) is the bilinear blend there.

V(x) \leftarrow \min_{u} \big(0.5 + V(x + 0.5u)\big)
The sweeps continue until no value changes by more than a millionth of a metre: 17 sweeps (notebook). S’s centre gets 3.338 m, below the grid’s 3.414 m, because S’s best move now leaves at 67.5°, between the grid’s 45° and 90°.
Why not Dijkstra’s algorithm here? A move’s value now depends on four stored values at once, and on where exactly the move ends, so no single neighbour settles a centre the way Dijkstra’s algorithm needs. LaValle (§8.5.2.3) shows a Dijkstra-like version can be built, with more bookkeeping; value iteration needs none.
6.3 The feedback plan between the cells
The values now exist between the cells, so the downhill rule of Section 4.2 works from any point: try the 16 moves, and take the one with the smallest 0.5 m plus the value at its end (LaValle §8.5.2.2, “Using G* as a navigation function”). The plan names a move for every point of the floor, not only for every cell: a feedback plan (G-2703)Feedback plan: A plan that names an action for every state the robot can be in, not one sequence for one start, so the robot’s measured state picks the action and a slip only changes the input; a navigation function with its downhill rule is one. Explained in §4.2 One step at a time, from any cell. over continuous positions, built by dynamic programming with interpolation.
Figure 8 lets the robot follow it from (2, 1). In the first frame, the 16 grey dots are the ends of the moves it tries; the orange one, at 67.5°, wins with the smallest total of the 16 (notebook):
0.5 + 3.164 = 3.664
The next best are 45° with 3.711 and 90° with 3.720. Then watch the robot cut between the cells instead of stepping along them.

The robot can now plan from anywhere on the floor and drive at any angle. The price is 17 sweeps of value iteration, and the values are still built from moves in a few fixed directions. Section 7 shows how far fixed directions put a grid’s distances off, and a one-pass method that is not tied to them.
7. A front that spreads in every direction: fast marching


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Dijkstra’s distances on a grid follow only the 8 grid directions, so in some directions they come out about 8 percent too long, however small the cells. The fast marching method lets a front spread over the floor at 1 m/s and takes each cell’s arrival time from two neighbours at once, so the front can cross the grid at any angle; its error shrinks as the cells shrink.


7.1 Why the grid’s distances are too long
The cost-to-go of Section 3, each cell’s shortest distance to the door, counts only routes made of the 8 grid moves. An open floor shows the error without obstacles in the way: there, a point 4 m across and 2 m up from the start is, in a straight line:
\sqrt{4^2 + 2^2} = 4.472 \text{ m}
The 8-connected grid must reach it by diagonals and straight moves: diagonals that cover 2 m across and 2 m up, 2.828 m long, then 2 m straight:
2.828 + 2.0 = 4.828 \text{ m}
The grid’s route is 8.0 percent too long. Smaller cells do not help: the same mix of diagonal and straight moves is needed at any cell size, so the error stays 8.0 percent (notebook). Sethian puts it this way: with Dijkstra’s method on a grid, “no matter how much you refine the mesh, you will still get stairstep patterns: you can never find the diagonal”.
In the room, on cells of 0.1 m, the 8-connected distance from the door’s cell centre to S’s centre is 3.180 m, while the shortest way round the blocked cells, a straight line to the corner of the blocked cells at (3, 3) and on to S’s centre, is 2.965 m (notebook).
7.2 Fast marching
The idea. Put a person with a watch at the centre of every cell, and let a front leave the door’s cell at 1 m/s in every direction, like a ripple on open water (Sethian). Each person writes down the time the front passes. The recorded time is the cell’s cost-to-go in seconds, and because the front moves through the open floor rather than along grid moves, it can arrive from any angle.
A program cannot let a front move, so it builds the times outwards from the door, smallest first, like the oil-depot fire of Dijkstra’s algorithmDijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §3.1 The fire picture (Sethian: “very closely related to Dijkstra’s method”). The one change: a cell’s time is worked out from two known neighbours at once, one across and one above or below, so the front can arrive between them on a slant.
The standard term. The method is the fast marching method (G-2707)Fast marching method: Dijkstra’s loop run on a grid with an update that takes a cell’s arrival time from two neighbours at once, one across and one up or down, so a front spreading from the goal can cross the grid at any angle; its distances get closer to the true ones as the cells shrink, unlike 8-connected Dijkstra’s. Explained in §7.2 Fast marching. (Sethian 1996). Its loop is Dijkstra’s: the cell with the smallest tentative time is accepted and never changed, and its neighbours’ tentative times are recomputed (Wikipedia, Fast marching method). Only the update differs.
Figure 9 runs both on the room, cut into cells of 0.1 m, from the door’s cell centre. The coloured area is where the front has arrived, coloured by arrival time; the lines are the front every 0.5 s, the cells reached at the same time, like the rings of Figure 2. Watch the shape of the lines in frame “t = 2.50 s”: straight sides and corners in the top panel, round arcs in the bottom one.

One frame per 0.25 s. Top: 8-connected Dijkstra, whose fronts are octagons with straight sides, because its distances follow only the 8 grid directions. Bottom: the fast marching method, whose fronts are round arcs. The last frame gives the arrival times at S’s centre: 3.180 s (Dijkstra) and 3.121 s (fast marching); the shortest way round the blocked cells is 2.965 m
The update on our numbers. At S’s 0.1 m cell, the neighbour to the right was reached at 3.0807 s and the one above at 3.0288 s (notebook). With:

a is the smaller arrival time of the cell’s left and right neighbours, 3.0807 s;
b is the smaller arrival time of its lower and upper neighbours, 3.0288 s;
h is the cell side, 0.1 m;
F is the front’s speed, 1 m/s;
T is the cell’s arrival time, in s.

The update (Wikipedia, Eikonal equation, numerical approximation), for F = 1:
T = \frac{a + b + \sqrt{2h^2 - (a - b)^2}}{2}
At S’s cell:
a + b = 6.1095
a - b = 0.0519
2h^2 - (a - b)^2 = 0.02 - 0.0027
= 0.0173
\sqrt{0.0173} = 0.1315
T = (6.1095 + 0.1315) / 2
= 3.1205 \text{ s}
When only one of the two is known, or they differ by at least h, the front came straight along one axis, and the update is the plain move: the smaller of a and b, plus h.
Why the update holds: a check at an easy front. Let a straight front cross the grid at 45°, reaching the left and the lower neighbour together, at 1.0 s. The cell’s centre lies a further half diagonal of a 0.1 m cell beyond the line through those two centres, 0.0707 m. Our numbers first, then the same steps in symbols:
(T - 1.0)^2 + (T - 1.0)^2 = 0.1^2
(T - a)^2 + (T - a)^2 = h^2
2(T - 1.0)^2 = 0.01
2(T - a)^2 = h^2
T - 1.0 = 0.0707
T - a = h / \sqrt{2}
T = 1.0707 \text{ s}
T = a + h / \sqrt{2}
The update gives exactly the front’s true arrival. The same holds for a straight front at any angle, because each of the two slopes is then the same from cell to cell; Dijkstra’s distances are exact only along the 8 grid directions. The first line is the equation the update solves, explained in Section 7.3.

Like Dijkstra’s algorithm, it accepts each cell once and keeps a heap of tentative times, so it takes about N \log N steps for N cells (Sethian).
7.3 The Eikonal equation
What equation does the update solve? Picture the arrival time T, the cost-to-go of Figure 4 measured in seconds, as a height over the floor: the valley of Figure 4, made smooth. The fronts of Figure 9 are its level lines, the points at one height, seen from above, as the rings of Figure 2 were: Figure 9 is a contour plot (G-468)Contour plot: A map of a surface seen from above, with lines joining points of equal height, so a 3D shape such as a loss bowl can be drawn and read on flat paper. Explained in: Partial Derivatives and Gradients, §1.1 Reading a contour map of the arrival-time surface.
Why the steepest slope is 1/F. The left half of Figure 10 shows the front at time T and a short time \Delta t later. The front moves at speed F, straight across itself, so the two lines are F\Delta t apart. Crossing that gap, the arrival time climbs by \Delta t:
\text{slope across the front} = \frac{\Delta t}{F\thinspace\Delta t}
= \frac{1}{F}
Across the front is the steepest way up, because along the front T does not change at all. The steepest slope of a function and its direction make its gradientExplained in: Partial Derivatives and Gradients, §4.3 The slope in any direction \nabla T (G-1295)Nabla (\nabla): The upside-down triangle \nabla, read “nabla” or “grad”; \nabla f means the gradient of f, the vector that collects all its partial derivatives. Explained in: Partial Derivatives and Gradients, §4.1 Collecting the partial derivatives: the arrow of its slopes along x and along y, whose length, written with bars, \lvert \nabla T \rvert, is the steepest slope (G-1888)Steepest ascent: The direction in which f increases fastest: the direction of the gradient; gradient descent steps the opposite way to go downhill fastest. Explained in: Partial Derivatives and Gradients, §4.3 The slope in any direction. So:
\lvert \nabla T \rvert = \frac{1}{F}
The standard term. The arrival time’s steepest slope equal to one over the front’s speed everywhere, with T = 0 on the goal, is the Eikonal equation (G-2708)Eikonal equation: The rule that the arrival time T of a front moving at speed F has steepest slope 1/F everywhere, written as the length of its gradient equals 1/F, with T = 0 where the front starts, the goal; its solution with F = 1 is the shortest distance, and fast marching solves its grid form. Explained in §7.3 The Eikonal equation. (Wikipedia, Eikonal equation; Sethian). With F = 1 m/s, T in seconds equals the distance to the goal in metres, so the Eikonal equation describes the true shortest distance.
A check on the open floor. From the start of Section 7.1, the arrival time at a point x m across and y m up is its straight-line distance, divided by F = 1. At the point (4, 2), T = 4.472 s, the square root of 20, and the gradient points straight away from the start, with slope 4 / 4.472 along x and 2 / 4.472 along y:
\lvert \nabla T \rvert^2 = \frac{4^2}{20} + \frac{2^2}{20}
= 0.8 + 0.2 = 1
On the grid. The right half of Figure 10 shows the update’s version: the slope along x is (T - a)/h, from the neighbour across; the slope along y is (T - b)/h, from the neighbour above or below. By Pythagoras’ rule, their squares add up to the square of the steepest slope:
\Big(\frac{T - a}{h}\Big)^2 + \Big(\frac{T - b}{h}\Big)^2 = \frac{1}{F^2}
Solving this for T gives the update of Section 7.2, and the 45° check there is this equation with a = b.

Figure 10: Left: the front at time T (dark blue) and at T + Δt (light blue), a distance F Δt apart (orange arrow), F being the front’s speed; T climbs Δt over a distance F Δt, so its steepest slope is Δt / (F Δt) = 1/F. Right: fast marching at S’s 0.1 m cell: the neighbour across (right) was reached at a = 3.0807 s, the neighbour above at b = 3.0288 s; the slope of T along x is (T − a)/h and along y is (T − b)/h, with h = 0.1 m; Pythagoras’ rule on the two slopes gives the grid equation ((T − a)/h)² + ((T − b)/h)² = 1/F², here T = 3.1205 s
Fast marching on a 4-connected stencil, using only the cells left, right, above and below, thus gives distances in every direction: the grid’s connectivity no longer limits the directions the front can take.

Wavefront propagation (G-2700)Wavefront propagation (wavefront planner): Numbering the free cells of a grid ring by ring outwards from the goal, each ring one move further, so every cell gets its fewest moves to the goal in one pass (8 for the room’s start cell); a breadth-first search from the goal, used when every move costs the same. Explained in §2. Numbering every cell from the door: the wavefront. numbers the cells ring by ring from the door, so each number is the cell’s fewest moves to the door: 8 for S on the 4-connected grid.
Counting moves on the 8-connected grid gives S 6 moves, but 16 of the 24 walks down those numbers are 3.828 m long, because a diagonal counts like a straight move; counting metres, with Dijkstra’s algorithm from the door, gives the cost-to-go (G-2701)Cost-to-go: The length of the shortest route from a state to the goal, such as 3.414 m from the room’s start cell to the door; stored for every state, it tells the robot how far it still has to go from wherever it is. Explained in §3. Which moves count: four or eight neighbours, moves or metres., 3.414 m for S.
Stepping to the neighbour with the smallest move plus cost-to-go lowers the number by exactly each move, so the walk from any cell is as long as its number; such a number map, 0 at the goal and with a lower neighbour everywhere else, is a navigation function (G-2702)Navigation function: A number for every state that is 0 at the goal, infinite only where the goal cannot be reached, and lower at some neighbour of every other state, so it has one minimum, the goal; stepping to the neighbour with the smallest move plus number from any state leads to the goal, by the shortest route when the numbers are the cost-to-go. Explained in §4.2 One step at a time, from any cell., and with its rule it is a feedback plan (G-2703)Feedback plan: A plan that names an action for every state the robot can be in, not one sequence for one start, so the robot’s measured state picks the action and a slip only changes the input; a navigation function with its downhill rule is one. Explained in §4.2 One step at a time, from any cell., a move for every state.
Value iteration (G-2704)Value iteration: Computing every state’s cost-to-go by repeating, over all states, the update “value = smallest move cost plus the next state’s value” until no value changes; it needs no priority queue and no order, and it carries over to values between grid cells and to uncertain moves. Explained in §5. Value iteration: the same numbers without a queue. gets the same numbers by sweeping “smallest move plus neighbour’s value” over all cells until nothing changes, 8 sweeps here, because a value is never too small and each sweep makes every cell exact whose shortest route has one more move; it does more work than Dijkstra (600 updates against 76) but needs no order.

Explained in §7.2 Fast marching. is Dijkstra’s loop with an update from two neighbours, so its front crosses the grid at any angle: 3.121 s at S on 0.1 m cells against Dijkstra’s 3.180, with an error that shrinks with the cells while Dijkstra’s stays 8 percent.

Likhachev, M. (Carnegie Mellon University), 16-350 Planning Techniques for Robotics, slides “Search Algorithms: Heuristics, Backward A*, Weighted A* Search”: 4-connected and 8-connected grids, www.cs.cmu.edu/~maxim/classes/robotplanning/lectures/heuristicsweightedsearch_16350_sp26.pdf

10. Key terms
Terms taught in this Note come first; linked terms are recaps, taught in the Note the link opens.

















































































































TermMeaningWavefront propagation (wavefront planner) (G-2700)Wavefront propagation (wavefront planner): Numbering the free cells of a grid ring by ring outwards from the goal, each ring one move further, so every cell gets its fewest moves to the goal in one pass (8 for the room’s start cell); a breadth-first search from the goal, used when every move costs the same. Explained in §2. Numbering every cell from the door: the wavefront.Numbering the free cells of a grid ring by ring outwards from the goal, each ring one move further, so every cell gets its fewest moves to the goal in one pass (8 for the room’s start cell); a breadth-first search from the goal, used when every move costs the same.Cost-to-go (G-2701)Cost-to-go: The length of the shortest route from a state to the goal, such as 3.414 m from the room’s start cell to the door; stored for every state, it tells the robot how far it still has to go from wherever it is. Explained in §3. Which moves count: four or eight neighbours, moves or metres.The length of the shortest route from a state to the goal, such as 3.414 m from the room’s start cell to the door; stored for every state, it tells the robot how far it still has to go from wherever it is.Navigation function (G-2702)Navigation function: A number for every state that is 0 at the goal, infinite only where the goal cannot be reached, and lower at some neighbour of every other state, so it has one minimum, the goal; stepping to the neighbour with the smallest move plus number from any state leads to the goal, by the shortest route when the numbers are the cost-to-go. Explained in §4.2 One step at a time, from any cell.A number for every state that is 0 at the goal, infinite only where the goal cannot be reached, and lower at some neighbour of every other state, so it has one minimum, the goal; stepping to the neighbour with the smallest move plus number from any state leads to the goal, by the shortest route when the numbers are the cost-to-go.Feedback plan (G-2703)Feedback plan: A plan that names an action for every state the robot can be in, not one sequence for one start, so the robot’s measured state picks the action and a slip only changes the input; a navigation function with its downhill rule is one. Explained in §4.2 One step at a time, from any cell.A plan that names an action for every state the robot can be in, not one sequence for one start, so the robot’s measured state picks the action and a slip only changes the input; a navigation function with its downhill rule is one.Value iteration (G-2704)Value iteration: Computing every state’s cost-to-go by repeating, over all states, the update “value = smallest move cost plus the next state’s value” until no value changes; it needs no priority queue and no order, and it carries over to values between grid cells and to uncertain moves. Explained in §5. Value iteration: the same numbers without a queue.Computing every state’s cost-to-go by repeating, over all states, the update “value = smallest move cost plus the next state’s value” until no value changes; it needs no priority queue and no order, and it carries over to values between grid cells and to uncertain moves.Bilinear interpolation (G-2706)Bilinear interpolation: Estimating a value at a point between four grid points as their weighted average, each weight the area of the rectangle on the far side of the point (linear interpolation along x, then along y); it fills in values between cell centres. Explained in §6.1 The robot is between the cell centres.Estimating a value at a point between four grid points as their weighted average, each weight the area of the rectangle on the far side of the point (linear interpolation along x, then along y); it fills in values between cell centres.Dynamic programming with interpolation (G-2705)Dynamic programming with interpolation: Value iteration with values stored only at sample points, such as cell centres, and blended in between, with moves in many directions; it gives a cost-to-go at every point, so a robot can plan from where it really stands and drive at any angle. Explained in §6.2 Value iteration with interpolation.Value iteration with values stored only at sample points, such as cell centres, and blended in between, with moves in many directions; it gives a cost-to-go at every point, so a robot can plan from where it really stands and drive at any angle.Fast marching method (G-2707)Fast marching method: Dijkstra’s loop run on a grid with an update that takes a cell’s arrival time from two neighbours at once, one across and one up or down, so a front spreading from the goal can cross the grid at any angle; its distances get closer to the true ones as the cells shrink, unlike 8-connected Dijkstra’s. Explained in §7.2 Fast marching.Dijkstra’s loop run on a grid with an update that takes a cell’s arrival time from two neighbours at once, one across and one up or down, so a front spreading from the goal can cross the grid at any angle; its distances get closer to the true ones as the cells shrink, unlike 8-connected Dijkstra’s.Eikonal equation (G-2708)Eikonal equation: The rule that the arrival time T of a front moving at speed F has steepest slope 1/F everywhere, written as the length of its gradient equals 1/F, with T = 0 where the front starts, the goal; its solution with F = 1 is the shortest distance, and fast marching solves its grid form. Explained in §7.3 The Eikonal equation.The rule that the arrival time T of a front moving at speed F has steepest slope 1/F everywhere, written as the length of its gradient equals 1/F, with T = 0 where the front starts, the goal; its solution with F = 1 is the shortest distance, and fast marching solves its grid form.Occupancy grid (G-2340)Occupancy grid: A grid map that stores in each cell a number between 0 and 1, such as the probability that the cell is occupied, instead of a hard 0 or 1; the standard grid map of robotics, since sensors are never sure. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §5.2 Bitmaps and occupancy gridsA grid map that stores in each cell a number between 0 and 1, such as the probability that the cell is occupied, instead of a hard 0 or 1; the standard grid map of robotics, since sensors are never sure.A* search (G-2577)A search:* Dijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid). Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.5 The algorithmDijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid).4-connected grid (G-2544)4-connected grid: A grid made into a graph by joining each cell to the up to four cells that share a side with it (left, down, up, right); the simplest graph of a grid map, with every move the same length. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edgesA grid made into a graph by joining each cell to the up to four cells that share a side with it (left, down, up, right); the simplest graph of a grid map, with every move the same length.Queue (first in, first out) (G-2551)Queue (first in, first out): A list served in arrival order: new items join the back and the next item leaves from the front; as a search’s frontier it gives breadth-first search. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ringA list served in arrival order: new items join the back and the next item leaves from the front; as a search’s frontier it gives breadth-first search.Breadth-first search (BFS) (G-2550)Breadth-first search (BFS): A search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ringA search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same.Backward search (G-2583)Backward search: A search that starts at the goal and follows every move backwards until it reaches the start; it is cheaper when the goal’s side branches less, and run to the end it gives every state’s cost to the goal. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §8.1 Backward searchA search that starts at the goal and follows every move backwards until it reaches the start; it is cheaper when the goal’s side branches less, and run to the end it gives every state’s cost to the goal.Big-O notation (G-2556)Big-O notation: A way to write how fast an algorithm’s work grows with the problem’s size, keeping only the fastest-growing part and dropping constant factors, such as O(V + E) for breadth-first search and O(b^d) for listing every path; it lets us compare methods without timing them. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §7.2 Big-O notationA way to write how fast an algorithm’s work grows with the problem’s size, keeping only the fastest-growing part and dropping constant factors, such as O(V + E) for breadth-first search and O(b^d) for listing every path; it lets us compare methods without timing them.8-connected grid (G-2564)8-connected grid: A grid made into a graph by joining each cell to all 8 cells around it: 4 straight moves of one cell side and 4 diagonal moves of 1.414 cell sides (0.707 m for 0.5 m cells), usually without cutting the corner of a blocked cell; it gives shorter, less jagged routes than a 4-connected grid. Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §2.1 Diagonal moves: the 8-connected gridA grid made into a graph by joining each cell to all 8 cells around it: 4 straight moves of one cell side and 4 diagonal moves of 1.414 cell sides (0.707 m for 0.5 m cells), usually without cutting the corner of a blocked cell; it gives shorter, less jagged routes than a 4-connected grid.Dijkstra’s algorithm (G-2565)Dijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §3.2 The algorithm: settle the nearest, update its neighboursA search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals).Heuristic h (G-2570)Heuristic h: A cheap guess of the cost still to go from a state to the goal, such as 3.121 m from the start cell to the door; a search uses it to prefer states that look nearer the goal. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §2. Explained in: Gradient Descent from Scratch, §8. Explained in: Gradient Descent from Scratch, §1. OverviewFinding the lowest point of a function by repeated small steps downhill.Linear interpolation (G-1092)Linear interpolation: Placing a percentile between two neighbouring sorted values, in proportion to its position; the pandas default. Explained in: Outlier Detection with the Percentile Method and Winsorization, §2.2 From percentiles to limitsPlacing a percentile between two neighbouring sorted values, in proportion to its position; the pandas default.Dynamic programming (G-652)Dynamic programming: Solving a problem by storing the answer to each overlapping sub-problem the first time it is computed and looking it up afterwards, so no work is repeated; memoization is one form of it. RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.title: Moving Through Unknown Maps: D* Replanning and Bug Algorithms
RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: A* searchA search:* Dijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid). Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.5 The algorithm; Admissible heuristicAdmissible heuristic: A heuristic that is never more than the true cost left from any state, h \le h^\ast; it makes f a lower bound on every route through a state, so the first route A* takes off the open list is the shortest. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §5.1 A guess that never overestimates; Growing obstacles by the robot’s radiusExplained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2.3 Growing the obstacles by the robot’s radius; Value iteration on a gridValue iteration: Computing every state’s cost-to-go by repeating, over all states, the update “value = smallest move cost plus the next state’s value” until no value changes; it needs no priority queue and no order, and it carries over to values between grid cells and to uncertain moves. Explained in: Grid Path Planning: Wavefronts, Navigation Functions and Value Iteration, §5. Value iteration: the same numbers without a queue.
Compare with: A* searchA search:* Dijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid). Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.5 The algorithm.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A plan is only as good as the map, and a box the map does not show makes the robot’s numbers wrong. Instead of searching again from scratch at every surprise, D* repairs just the numbers the box changes; with no time for a full search, real-time search moves after a few cells of thinking; with no map at all, bug algorithms follow the obstacle’s edge.


So far the robot can reach the door from any cell of its map: every free cell holds its cost-to-go (G-2701)Cost-to-go: The length of the shortest route from a state to the goal, such as 3.414 m from the room’s start cell to the door; stored for every state, it tells the robot how far it still has to go from wherever it is. Explained in: Grid Path Planning: Wavefronts, Navigation Functions and Value Iteration, §3. Which moves count: four or eight neighbours, moves or metres, its shortest distance to the door’s cell G, and the robot walks downhill on those numbersExplained in: Grid Path Planning: Wavefronts, Navigation Functions and Value Iteration, §4.2 One step at a time, from any cell, 3.414 m from the start cell S.
What still breaks: the numbers are only as right as the map. Someone has left a box, 1.0 m by 0.5 m, on the floor at x 2.0 to 3.0 m and y 2.0 to 2.5 m, across the robot’s route, and the map shows free floor there.
The robot’s sensor sees only the 8 cells around it, 0.5 m. Figure 1 plays what happens: after one move the robot sees the box, and its cell’s number, 2.707 m, is wrong, because the way round the box is 4.414 m.

Figure 1: The room’s 0.5 m grid (grey: blocked cells, with the true furniture outlined), the start cell S and the door’s cell G. The robot (black dot, drawn at the centre of its cell) follows the door’s numbers along its 3.414 m route; the box (dashed outline) stands on the route, but the map shows free floor there. After one move the box is 0.5 m away and the robot sees its two cells (brown): the route through them is blocked, and its cell’s number, 2.707 m, is wrong. A* from scratch searches 11 cells (light red) for a new route of 4.414 m; the robot reaches the door after 5.121 m, against the 3.414 m planned
The simplest fix is to run A* search (G-2577)A search:* Dijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid). Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.5 The algorithm again from the robot’s cell, here 11 cells, and to do that at every surprise. On a map of 0.1 m cells the robot sees the box piece by piece, plans again 7 times, and A* from scratch takes 596 cells off its open lists; a method that keeps and repairs its numbers takes 387 (notebook). Every number below is computed in the notebook RO-049-replanning-d-star-and-bug-algorithms.ipynb. This Note builds:

planning on a map that may be wrong: trust it, move, look, plan again, and why to plan from the door (Section 2);
D*, which repairs only the numbers a change makes wrong, and D* Lite (Section 3);
when repairing pays off, measured on finer maps (Section 4);
real-time search, LRTA* and RTAA*, for when there is no time to plan all the way to the door (Section 5);
bug algorithms, for a robot with no map at all (Section 6).

2. Planning on a map that may be wrong


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The robot treats every cell it has not seen blocked as free, plans, moves one cell, looks, and plans again when what it sees differs from its map. Planning from the door keeps the numbers right while the robot moves; only a change in the map makes some of them wrong.


2.1 Trust the map until it is wrong
The box in the opening is a cell the map gets wrong. The robot cannot wait for a perfect map, so it plans with the one it has: it treats every cell its map shows free, or has never seen, as free until a sensor shows otherwise (CMU incremental, slide 13; Koenig and Likhachev 2002).
Treating unseen cells as free is optimistic: the first plan is the shortest route that could exist, and every surprise can only make the route longer.
The robot then runs a loop (CMU incremental, slides 2 and 3):

plan a route to the door with the map as it stands;
move one cell along it;
look at the 8 cells around it and mark any blocked cell on the map;
if a marked cell changes the plan, plan again; go back to step 2.

Computing a new plan while moving, because the map, the robot’s position or the world has changed, is replanning (G-2711)Replanning: Computing a new plan while the robot is moving, because its map, its position or the world has changed, such as a box seen on the route; it keeps the robot on a route that is still possible. Explained in §2.1 Trust the map until it is wrong. (CMU incremental, slide 2). In Figure 1 the robot replanned once, at the cell x 2.5 to 3.0 m, y 1.5 to 2.0 m, and A* from scratch took 11 cells. A* keeps nothing from one search to the next: each search starts from scratch (Koenig and Likhachev 2002).
2.2 Why plan from the door
A search from the robot measures every number from the robot’s cell, so the numbers go stale the moment it moves. A search from the door measures every number to the door, and the door does not move: as the robot drives, those numbers stay right (CMU incremental, slide 8). The cost-to-goCost-to-go: The length of the shortest route from a state to the goal, such as 3.414 m from the room’s start cell to the door; stored for every state, it tells the robot how far it still has to go from wherever it is. Explained in: Grid Path Planning: Wavefronts, Navigation Functions and Value Iteration, §3. Which moves count: four or eight neighbours, moves or metres map the robot walks down is such a backward search (G-2583)Backward search: A search that starts at the goal and follows every move backwards until it reaches the start; it is cheaper when the goal’s side branches less, and run to the end it gives every state’s cost to the goal. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §8.1 Backward search, run from the door.
So the robot’s numbers go wrong only when the map changes, and then only the numbers whose shortest route ran through the change. Which numbers are those, and how can the robot fix only them?
3. Repairing the numbers: D*


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Each cell’s number should equal its lookahead, the smallest move plus neighbour’s number, and the box breaks that at only 5 cells. D* queues those cells and fixes them in order, raising the numbers that relied on the box and lowering them to the way round, until the robot’s cell is right: 12 steps take it from 2.707 to 4.414, and 68 numbers are never touched.


3.1 Which numbers the box makes wrong
The idea. In value iteration (G-2704)Value iteration: Computing every state’s cost-to-go by repeating, over all states, the update “value = smallest move cost plus the next state’s value” until no value changes; it needs no priority queue and no order, and it carries over to values between grid cells and to uncertain moves. Explained in: Grid Path Planning: Wavefronts, Navigation Functions and Value Iteration, §5. Value iteration: the same numbers without a queue each cell’s number came to equal the best offer from its neighbours: the smallest move plus neighbour’s number. The box breaks that equality only where an offer came through the box. To find the wrong numbers, each cell next to the box compares its number with its best offer now. With:

s is a cell, and n one of its neighbours;
g(s) is the number the cell holds, its cost-to-go to the door as last computed, in m;
c(s, n) is the length of the move from s to n: 0.5 m straight, 0.707 m diagonal, infinity if a box cell or the corner rule now forbids it;
\text{rhs}(s) is the cell’s lookahead, its best offer from its neighbours, in m (0 for G).

\text{rhs}(s) = \min_{n} \big(c(s, n) + g(n)\big)
The name rhs, “right-hand side”, is D* Lite’s (Koenig and Likhachev 2002). A cell whose number differs from its lookahead disagrees with what its neighbours now offer, so its number needs fixing (Koenig and Likhachev 2002).
On our numbers. The robot’s cell held 2.707: 0.5 m up into the box’s right cell, which held 2.207. With the box blocked, its offers are (notebook):





























Move from the robot’s cellMove (m)Neighbour’s number (m)Offer (m)left0.52.9143.414down0.53.2073.707diagonally down and left, to S0.7073.4144.121
The lookahead is the smallest, 3.414, not 2.707, so the robot’s cell disagrees with its lookahead. Four more cells do: the two box cells (lookahead infinity), the cell left of the robot (2.914 against a lookahead of 3.207) and the cell left of the box (2.621 against 2.914).
But even 3.414 is wrong: the offer from the cell on the robot’s left, 2.914, also ran through the box. The numbers must be fixed in the right order.
3.2 Fixing them in order
The mechanism. The cells that disagree with their lookahead wait in a priority queue (G-2568)Priority queue: A collection with two operations, insert an entry with a priority and remove the entry with the best priority (for Dijkstra’s algorithm, the smallest distance); it is what lets a search always pick its most promising vertex next. Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §5.1 Why a plain list is slow. The cell with the smallest key comes off first, and is fixed in one of two ways (Koenig and Likhachev 2002):

if its lookahead is smaller than its number, a shorter way has opened: the number falls to the lookahead and is final, like a vertex settled by Dijkstra’s algorithm (G-2565)Dijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §3.2 The algorithm: settle the nearest, update its neighbours;
if its lookahead is larger, its way has got longer: it cannot trust any old offer, which may itself have run through the change, so its number rises to infinity, and it goes back into the queue to fall to its new lookahead later.

After either change, every neighbour’s lookahead is recomputed, and any neighbour that disagrees joins the queue. The key orders the queue like A*‘s open listExplained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.1 g, h and f on the first step, so the cells on the robot’s side are fixed first. With:

h(s) is the octile distance (G-2571)Octile distance: The length of the shortest route between two cells of an 8-connected grid with no obstacles: diagonal moves while both the column and the row count shrink, then straight moves; with straight moves of length a and diagonals of length \ell it is \ell \min + a(\max - \min) of the column and row counts; a heuristic for 8-connected grids that never overestimates. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §2. A guess of the distance left: the heuristic between the robot’s cell and s, the guess of the distance between them, in m.

\text{key}(s) = \min\big(g(s), \text{rhs}(s)\big) + h(s)
Ties go to the smaller \min(g, \text{rhs}). The repair stops when the robot’s cell agrees with its lookahead and no queued cell has a smaller key than the robot’s cell (Koenig and Likhachev 2002). D* Lite also adds a correction to the keys each time the robot moves, so that keys made before and after a move stay comparable; in Figure 2 the queue is empty when the robot sees the box, so the correction does not change the order.
Figure 2 runs the repair one cell per frame, starting from the full number map, every cell’s cost-to-go before the box was seen. Watch the first six frames raise numbers to infinity, spreading down and left from the box, and then frame “7” start the falls: the cell left of the box finds a way round, 0.5 m up to a cell whose 2.414 never changed.

Figure 2: D* Lite repairing the door’s numbers after the robot, at x 2.5 to 3.0 m, y 1.5 to 2.0 m (black dot), sees the box’s two cells (brown); each cell shows its number, rounded to 0.01 m (grey: untouched). Orange outline: a cell whose number disagrees with its lookahead, waiting in the queue. Each frame takes one cell off the queue: a rise to infinity (red outline) or a fall to the cell’s lookahead (green outline). Steps 1 to 6 raise the box’s two cells, the robot’s cell, the cells left of and below the robot, and the cell left of the box; step 7 lowers the cell left of the box to 2.91; steps 8 to 12 raise and lower the cells on the way round. The last frame: the robot’s cell holds 4.41, equal to its lookahead, so the repair stops with 8 cells still queued, and the robot’s new route (blue) goes left round the box
The 12 steps, in order (notebook):

the box’s right cell rises from 2.207 to infinity;
the robot’s cell rises from 2.707 to infinity;
the box’s left cell rises from 2.414 to infinity;
the cell left of the robot rises from 2.914 to infinity;
the cell below the robot rises from 3.207, because its way ran through the robot’s cell;
the cell left of the box rises from 2.621, because its diagonal past the box’s corner is no longer allowed;
the cell left of the box falls to 2.914;
the cell below it, x 1.5 to 2.0 m, y 1.5 to 2.0 m, rises from 3.121;
S rises from 3.414;
the cell x 1.5 to 2.0 m, y 1.5 to 2.0 m falls to 3.414;
the cell left of the robot falls to 3.914;
the robot’s cell falls to 4.414, its lookahead: the repair stops.

Why 4.414 is right. Each fall adds one move to a number that is already right, back to a number the box never touched: the cell above the cell left of the box kept its 2.414. Our numbers first, then the same in symbols, for a chain of cells s_1 (the robot’s cell), s_2, s_3, s_4, s_5, each taking its number from the next:
g(s_1) = 0.5 + 3.914 = 4.414
g(s_1) = c(s_1, s_2) + g(s_2)
g(s_2) = 0.5 + 3.414 = 3.914
g(s_2) = c(s_2, s_3) + g(s_3)
g(s_3) = 0.5 + 2.914 = 3.414
g(s_3) = c(s_3, s_4) + g(s_4)
g(s_4) = 0.5 + 2.414 = 2.914
g(s_4) = c(s_4, s_5) + g(s_5)
The robot’s new number is the length of a real route round the box, and it equals what A* from scratch found, 4.414 m (notebook). The number is the shortest because the falls come off the queue in key order, the order that makes each settled number finalExplained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §3.3 Why the nearest unsettled vertex is final in Dijkstra’s algorithm (Koenig and Likhachev 2002).
Only 8 cells’ numbers changed, and 68 of the 76 were never touched (notebook). Eight cells are still queued when the repair stops, S among them: their numbers are wrong, but the robot does not need them unless it goes there.
3.3 The standard terms
Keeping the cost-to-go from a backward search and, when the sensed costs differ from the map, putting the affected cells back in the priority queue until the robot’s own cost-to-go is known again is D* (G-2713)D (dynamic A):** A replanner that keeps the cost-to-go from a backward search and, when sensed costs differ from the map, puts the affected cells back in a priority queue and fixes them until the robot’s own cost-to-go is right again; it repairs only the numbers a change affects instead of searching from scratch. Explained in §3.3 The standard terms., “dynamic A*”, published by Anthony Stentz in 1994 (LaValle §12.3.2; Stentz 1994; Wikipedia, D*). LaValle calls it “a dynamic version of the backward variant of Dijkstra’s algorithm”, and states that at any time the robot’s motions are optimal for the information it has.
The repair we ran is D* Lite (G-2714)D Lite:* A simpler algorithm with the same behaviour as D*, built on A*-like keys and a one-step lookahead (rhs) for every cell; current D* systems are typically based on it. Explained in §3.3 The standard terms., by Koenig and Likhachev (2002): it “implements the same navigation strategy as D* but is algorithmically different”, built on A*-like keys and the lookahead rhs, and it is shorter and simpler to analyse (Koenig and Likhachev 2002). Current systems are typically based on D* Lite rather than the original D* (Wikipedia, D*).
On this small grid, the repair took 12 cells and A* from scratch 11. The repair has to win somewhere to be worth it.
4. When repairing pays


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

On the 0.5 m grid repairing costs as much as searching again. On finer maps of the same room, where the box is seen piece by piece, D* Lite’s repairs cost 387 cells against 596 for A* from scratch, and a piece of the box behind the robot costs it nothing at all.


The opening problem asked for replanning that does not start over at every surprise. One box on a 76-cell grid is too small a test.
A real robot’s map has finer cells, and its sensor sees an obstacle bit by bit, so it replans many times. We cut the same room into cells of 0.25 m and 0.1 m, let the robot see 0.5 m round itself, and count, at every replan, the cells D* Lite, the repairing planner of Section 3, takes off its queue and the cells A* from scratch takes off its open list from the robot’s cell.
Here D* Lite starts, like A*, with no numbers: its first plan computes only the numbers it needs to reach S (notebook).

On the 0.5 m grid the single repair costs D* Lite more than in Figure 2, 19 cells, because its first plan computed only the numbers on the way from S, and the way round the box needs numbers it never computed. As the cells shrink, the saving grows: 387 against 596 replanning cells on 0.1 m cells. Koenig and Likhachev (2002) find the same trend on random maps, D* Lite’s “advantage seems to increase as the terrain gets larger”, and report earlier results in which D* beat repeated A* “by one order of magnitude or more”.
Figure 3 plays the 0.1 m drive. Watch the light red cells at each replan: in frame “move 3”, D* Lite’s first big repair (238 cells) costs more than A*‘s new search (125), because every number it raises must later fall again; in frame “move 4”, the next piece of the box costs D* Lite 44 cells and A* 125 again.

A* from scratch cannot know that and searches 17 cells each time. A repair touches only what a change affects; a fresh search pays for the whole route every time.
A gotcha. Searching from the door helps because only the robot moves. If the goal moves as well, numbers measured to the old goal are all wrong, and the CMU slides advise replanning from scratch in that case (CMU incremental, slide 9).
D* Lite still finishes a search before every move, up to the robot’s own cell. On a large map that can take longer than the robot can wait.
5. No time to plan to the door: real-time search


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Real-time search thinks about a fixed, small number of cells, moves, and thinks again, raising its guess of the distance wherever the guess proved too low. LRTA* looks one cell ahead and gets out of the pocket by the box after 4 raises, 9 moves, 5.121 m; RTAA* looks 4 cells ahead, 13 cells in 4 searches, 8 moves, 4.414 m.


5.1 Learning the guesses: LRTA*
The problem. Every method so far plans all the way to the door before the robot moves. On large terrains a search can take minutes, which “adds up to substantial idle times” (Koenig and Likhachev 2002). A robot that must keep moving needs a strict limit on how much it thinks per move (CMU real-time, slide 3).
The idea. Look only at the cells around the robot, step to the one that looks best, and remember what was learned. The robot’s guess of each cell’s distance to the door starts as the heuristic (G-2570)Heuristic h: A cheap guess of the cost still to go from a state to the goal, such as 3.121 m from the start cell to the door; a search uses it to prefer states that look nearer the goal. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §2. A guess of the distance left: the heuristic of A*, the octile distance. Real-time search runs from the robot towards the door, so here the guess is of the distance to the door; the h in D* Lite’s key of Section 3.2 guessed the distance to the robot, because D* Lite searches from the door. When every neighbour turns out worse than the guess at the robot’s cell promised, the guess was too low, and the robot raises it, so it does not come back here believing the same thing.
The standard term. Searching only a bounded number of cells around the robot before each move is real-time heuristic search (G-2715)Real-time heuristic search: Searching only a fixed, small number of states around the robot before each move, then moving and searching again; it bounds the thinking time per move at the cost of a possibly longer drive. Explained in §5.1 Learning the guesses: LRTA. (CMU real-time, slide 4). With a lookahead of one cell it is LRTA*, learning real-time A* (G-2716)LRTA (learning real-time A):** Real-time search that looks one move ahead: it raises the heuristic at the robot’s state to its best offer, the smallest move plus neighbour’s heuristic, and moves there; the raised guesses stay admissible and lead the robot out of dead ends. Explained in §5.1 Learning the guesses: LRTA. (Korf 1990; CMU real-time, slide 17). At each move (CMU real-time, slide 12):

set the guess at the robot’s cell to its best offer, the smallest move plus neighbour’s guess;
move to the neighbour that gives that smallest offer.

With:

s is the robot’s cell, and n one of its neighbours;
h(s) is the robot’s current guess of the distance from s to the door, in m, at first the octile distance: 3.121 m for S;
c(s, n) is the length of the move from s to n, 0.5 m straight or 0.707 m diagonal, as in Section 3.1.

h(s) \leftarrow \min_n \big(c(s, n) + h(n)\big)
The arrow means: replace the guess on the left by the right side.
Step 1 is the value iteration (G-2704)Value iteration: Computing every state’s cost-to-go by repeating, over all states, the update “value = smallest move cost plus the next state’s value” until no value changes; it needs no priority queue and no order, and it carries over to values between grid cells and to uncertain moves. Explained in: Grid Path Planning: Wavefronts, Navigation Functions and Value Iteration, §5. Value iteration: the same numbers without a queue update, done at one cell.
On our numbers. From S, two moves tie at 3.121: straight up, to a cell whose guess is 2.621, and diagonally up and right, to a cell whose guess is 2.414. Ties go to the smaller guess, as in A*Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.2 The smallest f first, ties to the smaller h, so the robot goes diagonally, into the pocket between the box and the table. There it sees the box, and its offers are (notebook):

Every offer is worse than the 2.414 the cell’s guess promised: the cell is a dent in the guesses, a local minimum (G-1110)Local minimum: A point lower than everything around it, but not the lowest overall. Explained in: Gradient Descent from Scratch, §8. The shape of the loss function matters, where a robot that only ever stepped to the lowest guess would stay forever (CMU real-time, slide 11). LRTA* raises the guess to 3.121 and moves left.
Figure 4 (left) plays the whole walk. Watch the orange outlines collect: 4 guesses rise (2.414 to 3.121, 2.621 to 3.328, 2.828 to 3.121, 2.621 to 2.914) until the guesses lead out round the box.

Why raising a guess is safe. The guesses start as an admissible heuristic (G-2578)Admissible heuristic: A heuristic that is never more than the true cost left from any state, h \le h^\ast; it makes f a lower bound on every route through a state, so the first route A* takes off the open list is the shortest. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §5.1 A guess that never overestimates, never above the true distance. The true distance from the pocket cell is its best move plus the true distance from there, and each true distance is at least its guess. With:

s is the pocket cell, the robot’s cell;
h^\ast(s) is its true distance to the door, 4.414 m, with the box known;
n^\ast is the first cell of its true shortest route, the cell to its left, whose true distance is 3.914 m and whose guess is 2.621 m.

Our numbers first, then the same in symbols:
h^\ast(s) = 0.5 + 3.914
h^\ast(s) = c(s, n^\ast) + h^\ast(n^\ast)
0.5 + 3.914 \ge 0.5 + 2.621
c(s, n^\ast) + h^\ast(n^\ast) \ge c(s, n^\ast) + h(n^\ast)
0.5 + 2.621 \ge 3.121
c(s, n^\ast) + h(n^\ast) \ge \min_n \big(c(s, n) + h(n)\big)
So the raised guess, 3.121, is still at most the true 4.414: the guesses stay admissible, and they also stay consistent (G-2580)Consistent heuristic (monotone heuristic): A heuristic that never falls by more than a move’s cost, h(n) \le c(n, n') + h(n'), with 0 at the goal (a triangle inequality); it keeps f from decreasing along a route, so A* with a closed list expands every state with its shortest g. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §6.2 The fix: a guess that never drops faster than the distance (CMU real-time, slide 14). LRTA* reaches the goal in a finite number of moves when every move costs more than 0, the map is finite with a route to the goal, and every move can be undone (CMU real-time, slide 15).
5.2 Looking further: RTAA*
LRTA* sees one cell ahead and learns one guess per move, so it found the pocket only by walking into it. Looking further, through more cells per move, lets each search learn many guesses at once (CMU real-time, slides 34 to 36).
The idea. Run A*Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.5 The algorithm from the robot’s cell, but stop after N cells have come off the open list. The best cell left on the open list, s, is where the robot heads. Every cell u that came off learns from s in one subtraction. With:

g(u) is A*‘s cost so far from the robot’s cell to u, in m;
f(s) is the smallest estimated total on the open list, the best cell’s cost so far plus its guess, in m.

h(u) \leftarrow f(s) - g(u)
The robot then moves along the found path towards s. The method is RTAA*, real-time adaptive A* (G-2717)RTAA (real-time adaptive A):** Real-time search that takes up to N states off an A* open list, sets each one’s heuristic to f(s) minus its cost so far, s being the best state left on the open list, and moves towards s; one subtraction per state keeps the guesses admissible. Explained in §5.2 Looking further: RTAA. (Koenig and Likhachev 2006; CMU real-time, slide 34). LRTA* with a lookahead of N cells would update the same cells by value iteration, which is more informed but slower; RTAA*‘s update is one pass (CMU real-time, slide 39).
On our numbers, with N = 4. The second search starts at the cell left of the robot’s pocket, x 2.0 to 2.5 m, y 1.5 to 2.0 m, after the box has been seen. The search takes off that cell, the pocket, the cell to its left and the cell below the pocket; the best cell left is the cell left of the box, 1.0 m away with a guess of 2.621 (notebook):
f(s) = 1.0 + 2.621 = 3.621
Each cell that came off gets the new guess: the best total minus its own cost so far.

Why the update is safe (CMU real-time, slide 38). Any route from the robot to the door that passes through u costs at least the shortest, and A* with an admissible heuristic has f(s) at most the shortest route’s length (the A* boundExplained in: A* and Heuristics, §5.2 Why the first route out is the shortest). With:
