So the new guess never exceeds the true distance. The whole drive takes 4 searches of at most 4 cells, 13 cells in all, and 8 moves, 4.414 m (notebook; Figure 4, right). Its first move, straight up from S, is not foresight: the box is still unseen, and every cell of the first search ties with the cell straight up at an estimated total of 3.121 m, so that cell happens to be the best one left on the open list. On a map this small such ties decide a lot: with N = 2 the drive is 5.828 m, and with N = 8 it is 5.121 m (notebook). Over many maps, a smaller lookahead gives longer drives but less thinking per search (Koenig and Likhachev 2006).
Both methods still need the robot’s grid map, with a guess stored for every cell they have visited.
6. No map at all: bug algorithms


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A robot that knows only where the door is and what it touches can still get there: head straight for the door, and follow the edge of whatever blocks the way. Bug 1 goes round the whole obstacle before leaving at the point nearest the door, 16.912 m; Bug 2 leaves as soon as it is back on the straight line to the door and nearer than where it hit, 4.885 m.


The problem. Every method so far needs a grid map: numbers, or at least guesses, for every cell. Put the robot in a room it has never seen, with the box where it was.
The robot knows two things: the direction and distance of the door, from a goal sensor, and the shape of an obstacle it touches, from a short-range sensor (LaValle §12.3.3). Everything else, the table too, is unknown.
The robot as a point. We follow the robot’s centre and grow every obstacle by the robot’s radius, 0.25 m, the grown obstacles (G-2652)Grown obstacle (inflated obstacle): An obstacle with every point within the robot’s radius added, its edges pushed out and its corners rounded; for a disk robot it is exactly the obstacle region, so the robot can be treated as a point (the table, 3.625 m², grows to 5.747 m² for a 0.25 m radius). Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2.3 Growing the obstacles by the robot’s radius of configuration space: then the centre may touch a grown obstacle’s edge but never cross it. The gap between the box and the table, 0.25 to 0.375 m, is narrower than the robot’s 0.5 m width, so the two grown shapes join into one obstacle, 11.702 m round (notebook).
The standard terms. A strategy that heads for the goal and follows the edge of any obstacle it meets, using only a goal sensor and contact, is a bug algorithm (G-2718)Bug algorithm: A strategy for a robot with no map that knows only the goal’s direction and what it touches: head for the goal, and follow the edge of any obstacle met until a rule says to leave (Bug 1: at the nearest point after a full loop; Bug 2: back on the straight start–goal line, nearer the goal). Explained in §6. No map at all: bug algorithms. (LaValle §12.3.3; Platt bugs). Our robot starts at (2, 1) and heads for the middle of the doorway, (3.6, 4.0), 3.4 m away; both algorithms below turn left when they hit, so the obstacle stays on the robot’s right.
Bug 1 (Lumelsky and Stepanov 1987; LaValle §12.3.3):

move straight towards the goal until it reaches the goal or hits an obstacle;
follow the obstacle’s whole edge back to the hit point, remembering the point nearest the goal;
return to that point along the edge, the shorter way, and go to step 1.

Bug 2 (LaValle §12.3.3; Platt bugs):

move along the start–goal line, the straight line from the start to the goal, until it reaches the goal or hits an obstacle;
follow the obstacle’s edge until it meets the start–goal line again at a point nearer the goal than the hit point;
leave the edge there and go to step 1.

Figure 5 runs both. Watch the hit point H, where both meet the obstacle after 0.850 m, then Bug 1’s full loop past C, the point nearest the door, against Bug 2’s early exit at L.

Figure 5: Bug 1 (top) and Bug 2 (bottom) in the room with no map: the robot’s centre (black dot) starts at (2, 1) and heads for the middle of the doorway, (3.6, 4.0). The box (brown) and the table (outline) are grown by the robot’s radius, 0.25 m (pale grey band); the gap between them is narrower than the robot, so the two grown shapes form one obstacle, 11.702 m round. Dashed: the start–goal line, from start to door. Both hit the obstacle at H, 0.850 m from the start, and turn left. Bug 1 goes once round the whole obstacle, passing C, the point nearest the door (0.755 m from it), returns to C the shorter way, 3.604 m, and leaves: 16.912 m. Bug 2 leaves at L, where it meets the start–goal line again 1.417 m from the door (H is 2.550 m from it): 4.885 m
Bug 1 on our numbers. The robot drives 0.850 m to H, 11.702 m round the obstacle, 3.604 m back to C, and 0.755 m from C to the door. To 4 decimals (notebook):
0.8500 + 11.7023 + 3.6043 + 0.7550
= 16.912 \text{ m}
Bug 1 knows that it has gone all the way round when the goal sensor’s reading repeats, and it can find the shorter way back because the readings tell it where it is (LaValle §12.3.3).
Bug 2 on our numbers. H is 2.550 m from the door. Bug 2 follows the edge for 2.619 m, to L on the start–goal line, 1.417 m from the door, and leaves:
0.8500 + 2.6187 + 1.4167
= 4.885 \text{ m}
How bad can each get? With:

d is the straight-line distance from start to goal, 3.4 m;
p_i is the length round obstacle i, here one obstacle with p = 11.702 m;
n_i is the number of times obstacle i‘s edge crosses the start–goal line, here 2, at H and L;
\sum_i adds up what follows over every obstacle i, here one obstacle only.

LaValle (§12.3.3) gives the longest each can drive. Bug 1 follows each edge at most one and a half times:
\text{Bug 1} \le d + \tfrac{3}{2}\sum_i p_i
= 3.4 + 17.553 = 20.953 \text{ m}
Bug 2 follows each edge at most half its length per crossing:
\text{Bug 2} \le d + \tfrac{1}{2}\sum_i n_i\thinspace p_i
= 3.4 + 11.702 = 15.102 \text{ m}
Our runs, 16.912 m and 4.885 m, stay inside both limits. Bug 2 is far shorter here, but not always: an obstacle whose edge crosses the start–goal line many times makes Bug 2 follow it piece after piece, each crossing adding to its bound (LaValle §12.3.3, Figure 12.23).
Bug 1 pays its long loop to see every point of the edge before choosing where to leave. Both assume the robot always knows its position exactly and moves exactly as commanded (Platt bugs).

LaValle, S. M. (2006). Planning Algorithms. Cambridge University Press. §12.3.2 “Stentz’s algorithm (D*)” and §12.3.3 “Planning in unknown continuous environments” (the Bug1 and Bug2 strategies). Free online: lavalle.pl/planning/node616.html, lavalle.pl/planning/node618.html, lavalle.pl/planning/node619.html and lavalle.pl/planning/node620.html (LaValle)

9. Key terms
Terms taught in this Note come first; linked terms are recaps, taught in the Note the link opens.





















































































TermMeaningReplanning (G-2711)Replanning: Computing a new plan while the robot is moving, because its map, its position or the world has changed, such as a box seen on the route; it keeps the robot on a route that is still possible. Explained in §2.1 Trust the map until it is wrong.Computing a new plan while the robot is moving, because its map, its position or the world has changed, such as a box seen on the route; it keeps the robot on a route that is still possible.D* (dynamic A*) (G-2713)D (dynamic A):** A replanner that keeps the cost-to-go from a backward search and, when sensed costs differ from the map, puts the affected cells back in a priority queue and fixes them until the robot’s own cost-to-go is right again; it repairs only the numbers a change affects instead of searching from scratch. Explained in §3.3 The standard terms.A replanner that keeps the cost-to-go from a backward search and, when sensed costs differ from the map, puts the affected cells back in a priority queue and fixes them until the robot’s own cost-to-go is right again; it repairs only the numbers a change affects instead of searching from scratch.D* Lite (G-2714)D Lite:* A simpler algorithm with the same behaviour as D*, built on A*-like keys and a one-step lookahead (rhs) for every cell; current D* systems are typically based on it. Explained in §3.3 The standard terms.A simpler algorithm with the same behaviour as D*, built on A*-like keys and a one-step lookahead (rhs) for every cell; current D* systems are typically based on it.Real-time heuristic search (G-2715)Real-time heuristic search: Searching only a fixed, small number of states around the robot before each move, then moving and searching again; it bounds the thinking time per move at the cost of a possibly longer drive. Explained in §5.1 Learning the guesses: LRTA.Searching only a fixed, small number of states around the robot before each move, then moving and searching again; it bounds the thinking time per move at the cost of a possibly longer drive.LRTA* (learning real-time A*) (G-2716)LRTA (learning real-time A):** Real-time search that looks one move ahead: it raises the heuristic at the robot’s state to its best offer, the smallest move plus neighbour’s heuristic, and moves there; the raised guesses stay admissible and lead the robot out of dead ends. Explained in §5.1 Learning the guesses: LRTA.Real-time search that looks one move ahead: it raises the heuristic at the robot’s state to its best offer, the smallest move plus neighbour’s heuristic, and moves there; the raised guesses stay admissible and lead the robot out of dead ends.RTAA* (real-time adaptive A*) (G-2717)RTAA (real-time adaptive A):** Real-time search that takes up to N states off an A* open list, sets each one’s heuristic to f(s) minus its cost so far, s being the best state left on the open list, and moves towards s; one subtraction per state keeps the guesses admissible. Explained in §5.2 Looking further: RTAA.Real-time search that takes up to N states off an A* open list, sets each one’s heuristic to f(s) minus its cost so far, s being the best state left on the open list, and moves towards s; one subtraction per state keeps the guesses admissible.Bug algorithm (G-2718)Bug algorithm: A strategy for a robot with no map that knows only the goal’s direction and what it touches: head for the goal, and follow the edge of any obstacle met until a rule says to leave (Bug 1: at the nearest point after a full loop; Bug 2: back on the straight start–goal line, nearer the goal). Explained in §6. No map at all: bug algorithms.A strategy for a robot with no map that knows only the goal’s direction and what it touches: head for the goal, and follow the edge of any obstacle met until a rule says to leave (Bug 1: at the nearest point after a full loop; Bug 2: back on the straight start–goal line, nearer the goal).Cost-to-go (G-2701)Cost-to-go: The length of the shortest route from a state to the goal, such as 3.414 m from the room’s start cell to the door; stored for every state, it tells the robot how far it still has to go from wherever it is. Explained in: Grid Path Planning: Wavefronts, Navigation Functions and Value Iteration, §3. Which moves count: four or eight neighbours, moves or metresThe length of the shortest route from a state to the goal, such as 3.414 m from the room’s start cell to the door; stored for every state, it tells the robot how far it still has to go from wherever it is.A* search (G-2577)A search:* Dijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid). Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.5 The algorithmDijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid).Backward search (G-2583)Backward search: A search that starts at the goal and follows every move backwards until it reaches the start; it is cheaper when the goal’s side branches less, and run to the end it gives every state’s cost to the goal. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §8.1 Backward searchA search that starts at the goal and follows every move backwards until it reaches the start; it is cheaper when the goal’s side branches less, and run to the end it gives every state’s cost to the goal.Value iteration (G-2704)Value iteration: Computing every state’s cost-to-go by repeating, over all states, the update “value = smallest move cost plus the next state’s value” until no value changes; it needs no priority queue and no order, and it carries over to values between grid cells and to uncertain moves. Explained in: Grid Path Planning: Wavefronts, Navigation Functions and Value Iteration, §5. Value iteration: the same numbers without a queueComputing every state’s cost-to-go by repeating, over all states, the update “value = smallest move cost plus the next state’s value” until no value changes; it needs no priority queue and no order, and it carries over to values between grid cells and to uncertain moves.Priority queue (G-2568)Priority queue: A collection with two operations, insert an entry with a priority and remove the entry with the best priority (for Dijkstra’s algorithm, the smallest distance); it is what lets a search always pick its most promising vertex next. Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §5.1 Why a plain list is slowA collection with two operations, insert an entry with a priority and remove the entry with the best priority (for Dijkstra’s algorithm, the smallest distance); it is what lets a search always pick its most promising vertex next.Dijkstra’s algorithm (G-2565)Dijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §3.2 The algorithm: settle the nearest, update its neighboursA search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals).Octile distance (G-2571)Octile distance: The length of the shortest route between two cells of an 8-connected grid with no obstacles: diagonal moves while both the column and the row count shrink, then straight moves; with straight moves of length a and diagonals of length \ell it is \ell \min + a(\max - \min) of the column and row counts; a heuristic for 8-connected grids that never overestimates. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §2. A guess of the distance left: the heuristicThe length of the shortest route between two cells of an 8-connected grid with no obstacles: diagonal moves while both the column and the row count shrink, then straight moves; with straight moves of length a and diagonals of length \ell it is \ell \min + a(\max - \min) of the column and row counts; a heuristic for 8-connected grids that never overestimates.Heuristic h (G-2570)Heuristic h: A cheap guess of the cost still to go from a state to the goal, such as 3.121 m from the start cell to the door; a search uses it to prefer states that look nearer the goal. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §2. A guess of the distance left: the heuristicA cheap guess of the cost still to go from a state to the goal, such as 3.121 m from the start cell to the door; a search uses it to prefer states that look nearer the goal.Local minimum (G-1110)Local minimum: A point lower than everything around it, but not the lowest overall. Explained in: Gradient Descent from Scratch, §8. The shape of the loss function mattersA point lower than everything around it, but not the lowest overall.Admissible heuristic (G-2578)Admissible heuristic: A heuristic that is never more than the true cost left from any state, h \le h^\ast; it makes f a lower bound on every route through a state, so the first route A* takes off the open list is the shortest. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §5.1 A guess that never overestimatesA heuristic that is never more than the true cost left from any state, h \le h^\ast; it makes f a lower bound on every route through a state, so the first route A* takes off the open list is the shortest.Consistent heuristic (monotone heuristic) (G-2580)Consistent heuristic (monotone heuristic): A heuristic that never falls by more than a move’s cost, h(n) \le c(n, n') + h(n'), with 0 at the goal (a triangle inequality); it keeps f from decreasing along a route, so A* with a closed list expands every state with its shortest g. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §6.2 The fix: a guess that never drops faster than the distanceA heuristic that never falls by more than a move’s cost, h(n) \le c(n, n') + h(n'), with 0 at the goal (a triangle inequality); it keeps f from decreasing along a route, so A* with a closed list expands every state with its shortest g.Grown obstacle (inflated obstacle) (G-2652)Grown obstacle (inflated obstacle): An obstacle with every point within the robot’s radius added, its edges pushed out and its corners rounded; for a disk robot it is exactly the obstacle region, so the robot can be treated as a point (the table, 3.625 m², grows to 5.747 m² for a 0.25 m radius). Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2.3 Growing the obstacles by the robot’s radiusAn obstacle with every point within the robot’s radius added, its edges pushed out and its corners rounded; for a disk robot it is exactly the obstacle region, so the robot can be treated as a point (the table, 3.625 m², grows to 5.747 m² for a 0.25 m radius).

RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.title: Potential Fields
RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Partial derivatives and gradientsExplained in: Partial Derivatives and Gradients, §4. The gradient; Gradient descentGradient descent: Finding the lowest point of a function by repeated small steps downhill. Explained in: Gradient Descent from Scratch, §2. The idea; Local minima and saddle pointsSaddle point: A flat point that curves up in one direction and down in another. Explained in: Optimizers in Deep Learning: Why Gradient Descent Needs Help, §5.5 Saddle points; Distance queries and GJKExplained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §5.2 The Minkowski difference and GJK.
Compare with: Navigation function and feedback planFeedback plan: A plan that names an action for every state the robot can be in, not one sequence for one start, so the robot’s measured state picks the action and a slip only changes the input; a navigation function with its downhill rule is one. Explained in: Grid Path Planning: Wavefronts, Navigation Functions and Value Iteration, §4.2 One step at a time, from any cell; Value iteration on a gridValue iteration: Computing every state’s cost-to-go by repeating, over all states, the update “value = smallest move cost plus the next state’s value” until no value changes; it needs no priority queue and no order, and it carries over to values between grid cells and to uncertain moves. Explained in: Grid Path Planning: Wavefronts, Navigation Functions and Value Iteration, §5. Value iteration: the same numbers without a queue; Rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT)Rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT): A sampling-based planner that grows a tree from the start: each round it draws a random configuration, steps the tree’s nearest node at most a fixed distance towards it and keeps the new node if the step is free, until the tree reaches the goal; it explores fast but its routes zig-zag. Explained in: Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees (RRT), §2.1 One step: sample, nearest node, steer, check.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A potential field (G-2740)Potential field (artificial potential field): A height over the robot’s C-space that is lowest at the goal and rises near obstacles, built as an attractive bowl plus a repulsive hill round each obstacle; the robot reaches the goal by stepping downhill from wherever it is, with no grid and no search, but can stop in a local minimum. Explained in §1. Overview. gives every placement of the robot a height that is lowest at the goal and rises near obstacles; the robot reaches the goal by stepping downhill from wherever it is, with no grid and no search. The catch is a dent: a low spot that is not the goal, where every step goes uphill.


So far the robot finds its way to the door on a grid. The wavefront (G-2700)Wavefront propagation (wavefront planner): Numbering the free cells of a grid ring by ring outwards from the goal, each ring one move further, so every cell gets its fewest moves to the goal in one pass (8 for the room’s start cell); a breadth-first search from the goal, used when every move costs the same. Explained in: Grid Path Planning: Wavefronts, Navigation Functions and Value Iteration, §2. Numbering every cell from the door: the wavefront gives every cell its distance to the door, so stepping to the neighbour with the lowest numberExplained in: Grid Path Planning: Wavefronts, Navigation Functions and Value Iteration, §4.2 One step at a time, from any cell always arrives, and D* (G-2713)D (dynamic A):** A replanner that keeps the cost-to-go from a backward search and, when sensed costs differ from the map, puts the affected cells back in a priority queue and fixes them until the robot’s own cost-to-go is right again; it repairs only the numbers a change affects instead of searching from scratch. Explained in: Moving Through Unknown Maps: D* Replanning and Bug Algorithms, §3.3 The standard terms repairs those numbers when a box appears. What still breaks: every cell is numbered before the robot moves. A grid of points 0.05 m apart, fine enough for the robot’s 0.25 m footprint, has 11,421 points in the room; a robot that also turns needs a number for every heading too.
This Note builds a potential field (G-2740)Potential field (artificial potential field): A height over the robot’s C-space that is lowest at the goal and rises near obstacles, built as an attractive bowl plus a repulsive hill round each obstacle; the robot reaches the goal by stepping downhill from wherever it is, with no grid and no search, but can stop in a local minimum. Explained in §1. Overview.: a height computed from where the robot is, from two things only: how far the door is, and how far the nearest obstacles are. The robot steps downhill, like a ball rolling on a landscape (MR §10.6.1). Figure 1 sends two robots of the disk footprintExplained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2.3 Growing the obstacles by the robot’s radius (radius 0.25 m) downhill on the same field at once. Watch the green robot from the start (2, 1) and the red one from (4.0, 0.5), between the table and the bottom wall, a second start chosen because from there the table stands between the robot and the door.

Figure 1: Animation: the room seen from above; two robots, drawn with their 0.25 m disk footprint, each step downhill on the same potential field. Green, from (2, 1): it rounds the table’s corner and reaches the doorway centre (3.6, 4.0) after 3.47 m of driving. Red, from (4.0, 0.5): it slides left under the table and stops at (3.60, 0.59), 3.41 m from the door, where no step goes downhill. The right panel counts the steps
In the last frame, the green robot is at the door after 3.47 m; the red one has stopped at (3.60, 0.59), still 3.41 m from the door, although nothing blocks the way round the table. The opening question of this Note: how can the robot pick each step from where it stands, why does the robot under the table stop, and how can it reach the door anyway? We answer it in steps:

the pull of the door, a bowl whose bottom is the door (Section 2);
the push of the obstacles, a hill round each one (Section 3);
why the robot under the table stops: a dent in the sum (Section 4);
shaking the robot out of the dent at random (Section 5);
a field built so that no dent can exist (Section 6);
a formula with no dent that needs no grid, and where it works (Section 7).

Every number below is computed in the notebook RO-050-potential-fields.ipynb.
2. The pull of the door: the attractive potential


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The attractive potential (G-2741)Attractive potential: The part of a potential field that pulls the robot to the goal: half the squared distance to the goal times a gain, \frac{1}{2}\zeta\Vert q - q_{\text{goal}}\Vert^2; minus its gradient points straight at the goal, like a spring. Explained in §2. The pull of the door: the attractive potential. is a bowl with its bottom at the door: half the squared distance to the door. Minus its gradient points straight at the door, so stepping downhill on the bowl alone drives the robot in a straight line.


The first part of the opening problem: which way should the robot at (2, 1) step, using only where it stands? Picture the floor bent into a bowl whose lowest point is the door. A ball put anywhere on it rolls towards the door. Figure 2 draws that bowl over the room, rolls the robot down it, then tilts the camera up until the bowl becomes its contour map (G-468)Contour plot: A map of a surface seen from above, with lines joining points of equal height, so a 3D shape such as a loss bowl can be drawn and read on flat paper. Explained in: Partial Derivatives and Gradients, §1.1 Reading a contour map: each ring is one height, as in a map of a hill.

Figure 2: Animation: the attractive potential drawn as a surface over the room’s floor, a bowl whose lowest point, 0, is the doorway centre (3.6, 4.0); the furniture is outlined on the surface only, because the bowl does not know it. The robot (green ball) at (2, 1), height 5.78, rolls straight down to the door. Then the camera tilts from the side to straight above: the surface becomes its contour map, rings of equal height round the door, with the straight path crossing them
The standard term. A height made from the distance to the goal is the attractive potential (G-2741)Attractive potential: The part of a potential field that pulls the robot to the goal: half the squared distance to the goal times a gain, \frac{1}{2}\zeta\Vert q - q_{\text{goal}}\Vert^2; minus its gradient points straight at the goal, like a spring. Explained in §2. The pull of the door: the attractive potential. (MR §10.6.1; Choset slides). The symbols, on the robot at the start:

q is the robot’s configuration (G-2286)Configuration: The list of numbers that fixes the position of every point of a robot, such as q = (x, y, \theta) = (2, 1, 0.524) for a floor robot or the joint angles (\theta_1, \theta_2) of a 2R arm; with it a planner treats the whole robot as one point. Explained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §2.1 The configuration: numbers that place every point, here the position (x, y) of its centre, in m: (2, 1) at the start; for the round robot the heading changes nothing;
q_{\text{goal}} is the doorway centre, (x_g, y_g) = (3.6, 4.0), in m;
\Vert q - q_{\text{goal}} \Vert is the straight-line distance from the robot to the door, in m: 3.4 m at the start;
\zeta (zeta) sets how steep the bowl is, 1 here, with no unit;
U_{\text{att}}(q) is the height at q, in m².

The height is half the squared distance to the door, times \zeta:
U_{\text{att}}(q) = \frac{1}{2}\thinspace\zeta\thinspace\Vert q - q_{\text{goal}} \Vert^2
At the start, the robot is 1.6 m left of the door and 3.0 m below it:
\Vert q - q_{\text{goal}} \Vert^2 = 1.6^2 + 3.0^2
= 2.56 + 9 = 11.56 \text{ m}^2
U_{\text{att}} = \frac{1}{2} \times 11.56 = 5.78 \text{ m}^2
Which way is downhill. The gradient (G-863)Gradient (of the loss): How fast the loss changes with each weight and bias, collected in one vector (the partial derivatives of the loss); it points in the direction in which the loss rises fastest. Explained in: Backpropagation, Part 1: What It Is, §1. Overview of a height is the vector of its slopes along x and along y; it points the way the height rises fastest, and minus the gradient points the way it falls fastest (the gradient on the contour mapExplained in: Partial Derivatives and Gradients, §4.2 The gradient as an arrow on the contour map). The slope along x, holding y at 1, by the power and chain rules, at the start:
U_{\text{att}} = \frac{1}{2}\big((x - 3.6)^2 + 9\big)
\frac{\partial U_{\text{att}}}{\partial x} = \frac{1}{2} \times 2\thinspace(x - 3.6)
= x - 3.6
= 2 - 3.6 = -1.6 \text{ m}
The same steps along y, holding x at 2:
\frac{\partial U_{\text{att}}}{\partial y} = y - 4.0
= 1 - 4.0 = -3.0 \text{ m}
In symbols:
\frac{\partial U_{\text{att}}}{\partial x} = \zeta\thinspace(x - x_g)
\frac{\partial U_{\text{att}}}{\partial y} = \zeta\thinspace(y - y_g)
\nabla U_{\text{att}} = \zeta\thinspace(q - q_{\text{goal}})
(Choset slides; MR §10.6.1.) At the start the gradient is (−1.6, −3.0), so minus the gradient is (1.6, 3.0): from the robot straight to the door, as long as the distance, 3.4 m. The pull grows with the distance, like a spring stretched between the robot and the door (MR §10.6.1; Choset slides).
One step downhill. Stepping a small multiple of minus the gradient is gradient descent (G-862)Gradient descent: Finding the lowest point of a function by repeated small steps downhill. Explained in: Gradient Descent from Scratch, §1. Overview (Choset slides; LaValle §8.4.1.2). With:

\alpha is the step factor, 0.01, with no unit; it plays the part of the learning rate (G-1068)Learning rate (\eta): How strongly each update changes the model; in gradient descent, the number the slope is multiplied by to get the step size. Explained in: Online Machine Learning, §5. The learning rate;
\nabla U is the gradient of the height at the robot, (−1.6, −3.0) m at the start;
q_{\text{new}} is the robot’s next position, in m.

q_{\text{new}} = q - \alpha\thinspace\nabla U
At the start:
q_{\text{new}} = (2, 1) - 0.01 \times (-1.6, -3.0)
= (2, 1) + (0.016, 0.030)
= (2.016, 1.030)
The step is 0.034 m long. We also cap every step at 0.05 m, because near an obstacle the slope gets very steep and an uncapped step could jump into it. Repeating the step until the robot is within 0.02 m of the door gives Figure 2: a straight line, the 3.4 m straight driveExplained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2.4 The room in C-space, and the drive to the door to the door, which happens to clear the table by 0.132 m.


                  
                  Extra 
                  
                

Here the gradient sets the robot’s velocity. If it set the robot’s acceleration instead, like a force on a ball with mass, the robot would roll past the door and back for ever, as a ball in a bowl without friction does; adding damping, a braking force that grows with speed, lets it settle (MR §10.6.1).


The bowl knows nothing about the furniture. From (4.0, 0.5), under the table, the straight line to the door runs into the table’s grown band 0.25 m above the robot, and the bowl would drive the robot into it. The obstacles must change the height too.
3. The push of the obstacles: the repulsive potential


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The repulsive potential (G-2742)Repulsive potential: The part of a potential field that pushes the robot away from one obstacle: zero beyond an influence distance, then growing without bound as the clearance shrinks, \frac{1}{2}\eta(1/d - 1/Q^\ast)^2; it keeps the robot from ever reaching the obstacle. Explained in §3. The push of the obstacles: the repulsive potential. is a hill round each obstacle: zero beyond 0.5 m of clearance, then growing without bound as the clearance shrinks to zero. Added to the bowl, it bends the green robot’s path round the table, 0.278 m clear of it; the red robot rolls under the table and stops.


The first part of the opening problem, continued: picking each step from where it stands, the robot under the table must not drive into the table. Picture a hill raised round every obstacle, steep close to it and flat a little way off. A ball rolling down the bowl then curves away from an obstacle it would hit.
The standard term. Each hill is a repulsive potential (G-2742)Repulsive potential: The part of a potential field that pushes the robot away from one obstacle: zero beyond an influence distance, then growing without bound as the clearance shrinks, \frac{1}{2}\eta(1/d - 1/Q^\ast)^2; it keeps the robot from ever reaching the obstacle. Explained in §3. The push of the obstacles: the repulsive potential. (MR §10.6.1; Choset slides). Each hill is computed from the robot’s clearance to one obstacle, its distance query (G-2674)Distance query: A geometric query that returns the shortest distance between two bodies, 0 if they overlap; it tells a planner how much room the robot has, not only whether it is free. Explained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §5.1 How far, not only whether answer: the distance from the robot’s body to that obstacle. The symbols, for one obstacle i:

d_i is the robot’s clearance to obstacle i, in m: the distance from the robot’s centre to the obstacle minus the radius 0.25 m; at (4.0, 0.5), 0.25 m to the table and 0.25 m to the bottom wall;
Q^\ast is the influence distance, 0.5 m: an obstacle farther than this does not push;
\eta (eta) sets how strongly an obstacle pushes, 0.02, in m⁴, so that the height comes out in m²;
U_{\text{rep}, i}(q) is obstacle i‘s hill at q, in m².

U_{\text{rep}, i} = \frac{1}{2}\thinspace\eta\thinspace\Big(\frac{1}{d_i} - \frac{1}{Q^\ast}\Big)^2
for d_i up to Q^\ast, and 0 beyond (Choset slides).
Checks at easy values. At the edge of the influence distance, d_i = 0.5 m, the fraction 1/d_i equals 1/Q^\ast, so the bracket is zero: the hill starts at height 0 with no step. At the robot under the table, d_i = 0.25 m:
U_{\text{rep}} = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.02 \times (4 - 2)^2
= 0.04 \text{ m}^2
At 0.1 m the hill is 0.64 m², and as d_i shrinks to 0 the term 1/d_i, and with it the hill, grows without bound: the robot can never roll into contact.
The push. The slope of the hill along the clearance, by the chain rule, at d_i = 0.25 m:
\frac{dU_{\text{rep}}}{dd} = 0.02 \times (4 - 2) \times \Big(-\frac{1}{0.25^2}\Big)
= 0.04 \times (-16) = -0.64 \text{ m}
The same in symbols:
\frac{dU_{\text{rep}}}{dd} = \eta\thinspace\Big(\frac{1}{d} - \frac{1}{Q^\ast}\Big)\Big(-\frac{1}{d^2}\Big)
The clearance grows fastest straight away from the obstacle’s nearest point, one metre of clearance per metre moved, so its gradient is the unit vector n_i pointing from that nearest point to the robot’s centre. So:
\nabla U_{\text{rep}, i} = -\eta\thinspace\Big(\frac{1}{d_i} - \frac{1}{Q^\ast}\Big)\frac{1}{d_i^2}\thinspace n_i
(Choset slides.) Minus this gradient, the push, points along n_i, away from the obstacle, with size 0.64 at a clearance of 0.25 m.
The whole field. The robot’s height U, in m², is the bowl plus one hill for each of the nine obstacles: the table, the cabinet, the two poles and five pieces of wall. The sign \sum adds up the nine hills, for i from 1 to 9:
U = U_{\text{att}} + \sum_{i=1}^{9} U_{\text{rep}, i}
and its gradient is the sum of their gradients (MR §10.6.1). At the start (2, 1) no obstacle is within 0.5 m, so the height is the bowl’s 5.78 m² and the first step is that of Section 2. Under the table, at (4.0, 0.5), the bowl gives
U_{\text{att}} = \frac{1}{2}\thinspace(0.4^2 + 3.5^2)
= \frac{1}{2} \times (0.16 + 12.25)
= 6.205 \text{ m}^2
and the table and the bottom wall each add 0.04 m²:
U = 6.205 + 0.04 + 0.04 = 6.285 \text{ m}^2
The two pushes, 0.64 down from the table and 0.64 up from the wall, cancel, so the first step is the bowl’s alone, up and a little left.

4. Why the robot stops: local minima


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Under the table the door’s pull, up, exactly balances the table’s push, down, so the gradient is zero and every step goes uphill: a local minimum (G-1110)Local minimum: A point lower than everything around it, but not the lowest overall. Explained in: Gradient Descent from Scratch, §8. The shape of the loss function matters of the field. Every start in the strip under the table between x = 2.95 and 5.25 m, 7.7 percent of the starts tried, rolls into it.


The second part of the opening problem: why did the red robot of Figure 3 stop at (3.60, 0.59)? Because the gradient there is zero: the door’s pull and the obstacles’ pushes cancel. At that point:

the robot is 3.407 m straight below the door, so the pull, minus the bowl’s gradient, is 3.407 m, straight up (Section 2);
its clearance to the table above is 0.15679 m, so the table pushes down;
its clearance to the bottom wall is 0.3432 m, so the wall pushes up, a little.

The size of the table’s push, minus its hill’s gradient, by the formula of Section 3, in m:
0.02 \times \Big(\frac{1}{0.15679} - 2\Big) \times \frac{1}{0.15679^2}
= 0.02 \times 4.378 \times 40.68
= 3.562
The wall’s push, the same way with 0.3432 m, is 0.155 m. Up and down balance: the pull plus the wall’s push equals the table’s push, in m:
3.407 + 0.155 = 3.562
A picture of the balance. Figure 4 cuts the field along the line x = 3.6 m, from the bottom wall’s band (y = 0.25 m) to the table’s band (y = 0.75 m). The bowl falls as the robot moves up, towards the door; the table’s hill rises as it nears the table. Their sum has a lowest point at y = 0.593 m, height 6.003 m²: a dent.

                  Key point 
                  
                

A randomized potential field (G-2744)Randomized potential field: A planner that follows a potential field downhill and, when stuck in a local minimum, takes random walks until it finds a lower point, then descends again, backtracking after many failed walks; it escapes local minima, at the price of long paths and many tuned settings. Explained in §5. Escaping by chance: randomized potential fields. descends until stuck, then takes a random walk (G-2745)Random walk: A path made of steps each chosen at random, with no memory of the steps before, such as moving x and y by 0.05 m up or down by coin tosses; it wanders about the square root of the number of steps times the step size. Explained in §5. Escaping by chance: randomized potential fields., a string of small random steps, until it finds a point lower than the local minimum, and descends again. From under the table it always reached the door in 200 runs, but drove 46 m (median) where the shortest route is 4.55 m.


The third part of the opening problem: how can the robot under the table reach the door anyway? The robot sits in the local minimum at (3.60, 0.59), height 6.003 m², and every small step goes uphill. Picture a marble stuck in a hollow of a tilted tray: shaking the tray bounces it about until it happens to clear the rim, and then it rolls on downhill.
The standard terms. A path made of steps each chosen at random, with no memory of the last, is a random walk (G-2745)Random walk: A path made of steps each chosen at random, with no memory of the steps before, such as moving x and y by 0.05 m up or down by coin tosses; it wanders about the square root of the number of steps times the step size. Explained in §5. Escaping by chance: randomized potential fields.. A planner that descends the potential, walks at random when stuck, then descends again is a randomized potential field (G-2744)Randomized potential field: A planner that follows a potential field downhill and, when stuck in a local minimum, takes random walks until it finds a lower point, then descends again, backtracking after many failed walks; it escapes local minima, at the price of long paths and many tuned settings. Explained in §5. Escaping by chance: randomized potential fields. planner (LaValle §5.4.3). The planner switches between three modes (LaValle §5.4.3, Figure 5.15):

Descend: gradient descent, as in Section 3, until the robot stops.
Random walk: each step moves x by 0.05 m up or down and y by 0.05 m up or down, each decided by a coin toss; a step into the obstacle region is thrown away and tried again. The walk ends as soon as the height is below the local minimum’s 6.003 m², or after a step limit drawn at random from 100 to 400 steps. Then back to Descend.
Backtrack: after 20 walks that all fall back into the same local minimum, restart from a point picked at random among the points of the earlier walks.

6. A field with no local minima: harmonic potentials


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Hold every obstacle at height 1 and the door at 0, and let every free point take the average of its neighbours: the result, a harmonic potential (G-2748)Harmonic potential: A potential field that is a harmonic function, held at 1 on every obstacle and 0 at the goal; it has no local minimum, so stepping downhill always reaches the goal, but it must be solved on a grid of the whole free space first. Explained in §6. A field with no local minima: harmonic potentials., has no local minimum, because an average is never below all its neighbours. Downhill from under the table reaches the door, but the heights must be solved on a grid of the whole room first.


The local minimum under the table came from adding a bowl and a hill; the random walks of Section 5 left it only by luck, after 46 m of driving. The third part of the opening problem, without luck: build a field with no local minimum at all. Picture the room as a metal plate whose obstacles are held hot and whose door is held cold. Heat flows from hot to cold until the temperatures stop changing. A cold spot inside the plate would draw heat from all sides and warm up, so in the settled plate the coldest place is the door, and from every point there is a way to somewhere colder.

The standard terms. The settled temperature obeys Laplace’s equation (G-2746)Laplace’s equation: The equation that a function’s bend along x plus its bend along y is zero everywhere inside a region, \partial^2\phi/\partial x^2 + \partial^2\phi/\partial y^2 = 0; on a grid it says each point is the average of its four neighbours, so its solutions have no local minima inside. Explained in §6. A field with no local minima: harmonic potentials.: its bend along x plus its bend along y is zero everywhere inside (the sum of the two second partial derivatives, the Laplacian, is zero). A function that obeys it is a harmonic function (G-2747)Harmonic function: A function that obeys Laplace’s equation, such as a settled temperature; its highest and lowest values lie on the boundary of its region, never inside, which is why it can guide a robot without local minima. Explained in §6. A field with no local minima: harmonic potentials. (LaValle §8.4.4.4; Wikipedia, Harmonic function).
From Laplace’s equation to the average. On a grid with spacing h, the bend along x at a point is how much its two neighbours along x rise above it, added and divided by h^2, and the same along y (Wikipedia, Discrete Laplace operator). Laplace’s equation sets the bend along x plus the bend along y to zero; multiplied by h^2, it says the four rises add up to zero. At (3.5, 3.6), with its height \phi (phi) not yet known and its neighbours’ heights 0.9429, 0.9336, 0.9482 and 0.9247:
(0.9429 - \phi) + (0.9336 - \phi)
+ (0.9482 - \phi) + (0.9247 - \phi) = 0
3.7494 - 4\phi = 0
\phi = 3.7494 / 4 = 0.93735
which rounds to the point’s settled 0.9374. The same steps in symbols, with:

\phi is the harmonic potential’s height at the point, with no unit, 0.9374 at (3.5, 3.6);
\phi_L, \phi_R, \phi_D, \phi_U are the heights of its left, right, lower and upper neighbours, 0.9429, 0.9336, 0.9482 and 0.9247;
h is the grid spacing, 0.05 m.

\frac{(\phi_L - \phi) + (\phi_R - \phi)}{h^2}
+ \frac{(\phi_D - \phi) + (\phi_U - \phi)}{h^2} = 0
\phi_L + \phi_R + \phi_D + \phi_U - 4\phi = 0
\phi = \frac{\phi_L + \phi_R + \phi_D + \phi_U}{4}
Why there is no local minimum. An average of four numbers is never below the smallest of them, and equals it only if all four are equal. So a point equal to the average of its neighbours always has a neighbour at least as low, and a strictly lower one unless all four are the same. A local minimum, a point lower than all its neighbours, cannot exist; the lowest value is on the boundary, at the door. No interior minimum is the minimum principle of harmonic functions (Wikipedia, Harmonic function; LaValle §8.4.4.4). In the room, the notebook checks it: of the 5,839 free points other than the door, every one has a strictly lower neighbour.

Explained in: Grid Path Planning: Wavefronts, Navigation Functions and Value Iteration, §5. Value iteration: the same numbers without a queue, which also sweeps until nothing changes. 7. One minimum by design: navigation functions


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A navigation function (G-2750)Navigation function (Rimon–Koditschek): A smooth field on free space with only one minimum, at the goal, the same top value on the whole boundary of free space and no flat stationary points; gradient descent on it reaches the goal from almost every start. Rimon and Koditschek gave a formula for worlds of disks, a disk-shaped free space with disk-shaped obstacles. Explained in §7. One minimum by design: navigation functions. in Rimon and Koditschek’s sense is a smooth field with a single minimum, at the goal, and the same top value, 1, on every obstacle’s edge. For a world of disks, a disk-shaped floor with disk-shaped obstacles, a formula with a knob κ gives one: with κ = 1 the robot under the table still stops in a local minimum; from κ = 2 it reaches the door.


The third part of the opening problem, without a grid: the harmonic field of Section 6 has no local minimum but needs the whole grid, while the bowl and hills of Section 3 need no grid but have a local minimum. A navigation function (G-2702)Navigation function: A number for every state that is 0 at the goal, infinite only where the goal cannot be reached, and lower at some neighbour of every other state, so it has one minimum, the goal; stepping to the neighbour with the smallest move plus number from any state leads to the goal, by the shortest route when the numbers are the cost-to-go. Explained in: Grid Path Planning: Wavefronts, Navigation Functions and Value Iteration, §4.2 One step at a time, from any cell on the grid, the wavefront’s numbers, already has the property we want: 0 at the goal and a lower neighbour everywhere else. Rimon and Koditschek asked for the same in a smooth field over free space, written as one formula.
The standard term. A navigation function (G-2750)Navigation function (Rimon–Koditschek): A smooth field on free space with only one minimum, at the goal, the same top value on the whole boundary of free space and no flat stationary points; gradient descent on it reaches the goal from almost every start. Rimon and Koditschek gave a formula for worlds of disks, a disk-shaped free space with disk-shaped obstacles. Explained in §7. One minimum by design: navigation functions. in the sense of Rimon and Koditschek is a field on free space that (LaValle §8.4.4.3; Choset slides):

is smooth, so it has a gradient everywhere;
has only one minimum, at the goal;
takes the same, highest value, 1, on the whole boundary of free space, so that every obstacle’s edge is equally high and the robot never reaches one;
has no flat stationary points: each one curves up or down in every direction, so none is a plateau where gradient descent cannot pick a direction.

Rule 2 does not forbid saddle points. In free space with holes, such as a room with furniture, a smooth field must have stationary points besides the goal (LaValle §8.4.4.3); saddles are harmless, because they catch the robot only from starts exactly on the lines that run into them.
A world made of disks. Rimon and Koditschek gave a formula for such a world: free space that is a disk (a ball in more dimensions) with disk-shaped obstacles inside it (Choset slides; LaValle §8.4.4.3). Our room is not one, so we redraw it as one, keeping the start under the table and the door:

the floor the robot’s centre may use is a disk of radius 3.3 m about (3.5, 2.0); it reaches 1.3 m below the room’s bottom wall, so this world is a stand-in, not the room;
the table, grown by the robot’s 0.25 m, is a disk of radius 1.3 m about (4.2, 1.9), close to the grown table’s size;
the two poles, grown by 0.25 m, are disks of radius 0.35 m about (1, 3) and (6, 0.8).

The formula. The symbols (Choset slides):

\gamma (gamma) is the squared distance from the robot to the door, in m²: at (4.0, 0.5), 12.41 m²;
\beta_0 is the room disk’s term, its radius squared minus the robot’s squared distance from its centre, in m²: 8.39 at (4.0, 0.5); it is 0 on the disk’s edge and positive inside;
\beta_i is obstacle i‘s term, the robot’s squared distance from its centre minus its radius squared, in m²: 0.31 for the table, 15.128 for the pink pole and 3.968 for the green pole at (4.0, 0.5); it is 0 on the obstacle’s edge and positive outside;
\beta is the product of all four, 156.1 m⁸ at (4.0, 0.5): 0 on every boundary of free space, positive inside it;
\kappa (kappa) is a knob, a number of 1 or more, 2 here;
\phi is now the navigation function’s height, with no unit; like the harmonic potential of Section 6 it is 0 at the goal and 1 on every boundary.

\phi = \frac{\gamma}{\big(\gamma^{\kappa} + \beta\big)^{1/\kappa}}
Checks at easy values. At the door, \gamma = 0, so \phi = 0: the lowest value. On any boundary, \beta = 0, so:
\phi = \frac{\gamma}{(\gamma^{\kappa})^{1/\kappa}} = \frac{\gamma}{\gamma} = 1
Inside free space \beta is positive, so the bottom of the fraction is larger than \gamma and \phi lies between 0 and 1. At the robot under the table, with \kappa = 2:
\phi = \frac{12.41}{\sqrt{12.41^2 + 156.1}}
= \frac{12.41}{\sqrt{154.0 + 156.1}}
= 12.41 / 17.61 = 0.705
Figure 10 draws this field as a surface, rolls the robot from under the table down it, then tilts to the contour map.

Figure 10: Animation: the Rimon–Koditschek navigation function, with its knob κ = 2, on the world of disks, drawn as a surface: the free disk of radius 3.3 m about (3.5, 2.0), the table as a disk of radius 1.3 m about (4.2, 1.9) and the two poles as disks of radius 0.35 m; heights run from 0 at the doorway centre (3.6, 4.0) to 1 on every boundary, and the area outside the free disk is drawn at 1. The red robot from (4.0, 0.5), height 0.705, rolls round the bottom of the table to the door. Then the camera tilts to the contour map
Why κ must be large enough. For small \kappa the obstacle term \beta dominates the bottom of the fraction and the formula has local minima of its own; for \kappa large enough the distance term wins and the only minimum left is the door (Choset slides, “for large enough κ, this is a navigation function”). Figure 11 raises \kappa step by step, with the robot from under the table each time.

Figure 11: Animation: the contour map of the navigation function on the world of disks (as in the last frame of Figure 10) for the formula’s knob κ = 1, 1.25, 1.5, 1.75, 1.9, 2, 3 and 4, with the path of the robot from (4.0, 0.5). For κ = 1 to 1.9 the robot stops in a local minimum left of the table (red star), at (1.76, 0.19) for κ = 1 and (1.73, 0.92) for κ = 1.9; from κ = 2 the local minimum is gone and it reaches the door. The height at the start grows with κ: 0.074 at κ = 1, 0.705 at κ = 2, 0.998 at κ = 4
In Figure 11 the local minimum moves up as \kappa grows and vanishes between 1.98 and 2 (notebook: the smallest \kappa that reaches the door from (4.0, 0.5) is 1.983). At \kappa = 2 the field has one minimum, the door, and three saddle points, one behind each obstacle, as rule 2 allows (notebook). The robot under the table reaches the door, which answers the third part of the opening problem without a grid, for the world of disks. Two limits remain:

Larger κ flattens the field. The height at the start is 0.074 for \kappa = 1, 0.705 for \kappa = 2, 0.974 for \kappa = 3, 0.998 for \kappa = 4 and 0.999993 for \kappa = 6: almost everything sits just below 1, and the slopes the robot follows become tiny.
Only disks. The formula holds for worlds of disks; other shapes must first be bent smoothly into a world of disks, which Rimon and Koditschek did for star-shaped obstacles. In a high-dimensional C-space the obstacles are known only through collision checks, so building such a bending is hard (LaValle §8.4.4.3; Choset slides).

The robot picks each step from where it stands by stepping down the potential field (G-2740)Potential field (artificial potential field): A height over the robot’s C-space that is lowest at the goal and rises near obstacles, built as an attractive bowl plus a repulsive hill round each obstacle; the robot reaches the goal by stepping downhill from wherever it is, with no grid and no search, but can stop in a local minimum. Explained in §1. Overview., so it needs no grid: from (2, 1) it reaches the door after 3.47 m; the robot under the table stops at (3.60, 0.59), 3.41 m from the door, because there the door’s pull up, 3.407, plus the wall’s push, 0.155, balances the table’s push down, 3.562.
The attractive potential (G-2741)Attractive potential: The part of a potential field that pulls the robot to the goal: half the squared distance to the goal times a gain, \frac{1}{2}\zeta\Vert q - q_{\text{goal}}\Vert^2; minus its gradient points straight at the goal, like a spring. Explained in §2. The pull of the door: the attractive potential., half the squared distance to the door, has minus its gradient pointing straight at the door, so alone it drives a straight line, the 3.4 m drive from (2, 1).
The repulsive potential (G-2742)Repulsive potential: The part of a potential field that pushes the robot away from one obstacle: zero beyond an influence distance, then growing without bound as the clearance shrinks, \frac{1}{2}\eta(1/d - 1/Q^\ast)^2; it keeps the robot from ever reaching the obstacle. Explained in §3. The push of the obstacles: the repulsive potential. is zero beyond 0.5 m of clearance and grows without bound at contact, so the robot never touches an obstacle: the green robot passes 0.278 m from the table instead of 0.132 m.
A local minimum (G-1110)Local minimum: A point lower than everything around it, but not the lowest overall. Explained in: Gradient Descent from Scratch, §8. The shape of the loss function matters appears where the pull meets an obstacle’s push head on; the starts that roll into it fill the strip under the table, 7.7 percent of the starts, so gradient descent alone fails there every time.
A randomized potential field (G-2744)Randomized potential field: A planner that follows a potential field downhill and, when stuck in a local minimum, takes random walks until it finds a lower point, then descends again, backtracking after many failed walks; it escapes local minima, at the price of long paths and many tuned settings. Explained in §5. Escaping by chance: randomized potential fields. escapes by a random walk (G-2745)Random walk: A path made of steps each chosen at random, with no memory of the steps before, such as moving x and y by 0.05 m up or down by coin tosses; it wanders about the square root of the number of steps times the step size. Explained in §5. Escaping by chance: randomized potential fields. until the height drops below the local minimum’s, so it always reached the door in 200 runs, but drove a median 46.1 m against the shortest 4.55 m, because random steps wander back and forth.
A harmonic potential (G-2748)Harmonic potential: A potential field that is a harmonic function, held at 1 on every obstacle and 0 at the goal; it has no local minimum, so stepping downhill always reaches the goal, but it must be solved on a grid of the whole free space first. Explained in §6. A field with no local minima: harmonic potentials. obeys Laplace’s equation (G-2746)Laplace’s equation: The equation that a function’s bend along x plus its bend along y is zero everywhere inside a region, \partial^2\phi/\partial x^2 + \partial^2\phi/\partial y^2 = 0; on a grid it says each point is the average of its four neighbours, so its solutions have no local minima inside. Explained in §6. A field with no local minima: harmonic potentials., so every free point is the average of its neighbours and none can be a local minimum; the robot under the table reaches the door in 5.61 m, after 5,000 sweeps of averaging over the whole grid.
A navigation function (G-2750)Navigation function (Rimon–Koditschek): A smooth field on free space with only one minimum, at the goal, the same top value on the whole boundary of free space and no flat stationary points; gradient descent on it reaches the goal from almost every start. Rimon and Koditschek gave a formula for worlds of disks, a disk-shaped free space with disk-shaped obstacles. Explained in §7. One minimum by design: navigation functions. has one minimum and the same top value on every boundary, so descent from almost every start reaches the goal; on a world of disks Rimon and Koditschek’s formula gives one once κ is large enough, here from κ = 2.

The robot can now reach the door from under the table, by luck, on a grid, or in a world of disks. Still missing: a planner that needs no grid, no tuned luck and no special shapes, and that works with only the collision checks and nearest neighbours of chapter RO-04; rapidly-exploring random treesRapidly-exploring random tree (RRT): A sampling-based planner that grows a tree from the start: each round it draws a random configuration, steps the tree’s nearest node at most a fixed distance towards it and keeps the new node if the step is free, until the tree reaches the goal; it explores fast but its routes zig-zag. Explained in: Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees (RRT), §2. Growing a tree from random samples: RRT grow a tree of random samples from the start instead.

RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.title: Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees (RRT)
RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Backward and bidirectional searchBidirectional search: A forward search from the start and a backward search from the goal run in turn until some state has been expanded by both; the route is the smallest sum of the two costs over all states both reached, since the meeting state can be off the shortest route. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §8.2 Bidirectional search; Checking a path segmentExplained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §6.2 Step size and order; MetricMetric (distance function): A distance between points that is never negative, is 0 only between equal points, is the same both ways and obeys the triangle inequality; search trees rely on these rules to skip far regions safely. Explained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §7.1 The rules a distance must follow; Nearest neighbours with wrap-aroundExplained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §8. Nearest neighbours when headings wrap.
Leads to: Kinodynamic RRTKinodynamic RRT: A rapidly-exploring random tree whose edges are motion primitives run through the system simulator: it samples a state, takes the nearest node, keeps the primitive that ends closest if its motion is free; every path it returns is drivable. Explained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §8. Growing a tree of drivable motions: kinodynamic RRT.
Compare with: Randomized potential fieldsRandomized potential field: A planner that follows a potential field downhill and, when stuck in a local minimum, takes random walks until it finds a lower point, then descends again, backtracking after many failed walks; it escapes local minima, at the price of long paths and many tuned settings. Explained in: Potential Fields, §5. Escaping by chance: randomized potential fields; Probabilistic roadmap (PRM)Probabilistic roadmap (PRM): A graph of random free configurations (milestones) joined by straight edges that pass a collision check, built once and then searched with A*; it describes the free space without building the obstacle region, so it scales to robots with many joints. Explained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §2.2 Phase 1 and phase 2: milestones and edges.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A rapidly-exploring random tree grows from the start by drawing random configurations and stepping the nearest node of the tree a short way towards each one; it needs no grid, only collision checks and nearest neighbours. Plain RRT finds a long route quickly; RRT* keeps rewiring the tree so the route shrinks towards the shortest; RRT-Connect grows a tree from each end and finds a route sooner.


So far the robot has met the room’s furniture with a potential field (G-2740)Potential field (artificial potential field): A height over the robot’s C-space that is lowest at the goal and rises near obstacles, built as an attractive bowl plus a repulsive hill round each obstacle; the robot reaches the goal by stepping downhill from wherever it is, with no grid and no search, but can stop in a local minimum. Explained in: Potential Fields, §1. Overview, a height it steps down from wherever it is. Under the table, at (4.0, 0.5), the robot stopped in a local minimum (G-1110)Local minimum: A point lower than everything around it, but not the lowest overall. Explained in: Gradient Descent from Scratch, §8. The shape of the loss function matters at (3.60, 0.59), and every fix had a price:

random walks got it out, after a median of 46.1 m of driving where the shortest route is 4.55 m;
a harmonic potential has no local minimum, but needs 29.2 million updates on a grid of the whole room first;
a navigation function works only in a world made of disks.

Grids do not scale. The room’s grid of points 0.05 m apart has 11,421 points; a robot that turns, with a heading every 1°, needs 4.1 million; an arm with six joints at 1° each needs 2.2 × 10¹⁵. LaValle’s example: 50 points along each of 10 axes is 50¹⁰ points, impossible to search (LaValle §5.4.3).
This Note grows a tree instead, from random samples, using only the two tests of chapter RO-04: is this configuration or segment free (collision checkingExplained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §6. Checking a path segment), and which stored configuration is nearest (nearest neighboursExplained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §8. Nearest neighbours when headings wrap). Figure 1 shows the three trees of this Note on the robot under the table; the red star is where the potential field left it.
Make interactive
Figure 1: Three planners from under the table (4.0, 0.5) to the doorway centre (3.6, 4.0), in the disk robot’s C-space (light grey: obstacles grown by 0.25 m). Red star: (3.60, 0.59), where gradient descent on the potential field stopped. Black dashed: the shortest route, 4.55 m. Left: RRT after 67 samples, route 6.08 m (green). Middle: RRT* after 2,000 samples, route 4.79 m. Right: RRT-Connect after 27 rounds, two trees (blue from the start, purple from the door), route 5.40 m
The opening question of this Note: how can the robot under the table find a route to the door without a grid, how close can that route get to the shortest, 4.55 m, and how soon can a first route appear? We answer it in steps:

one random sample at a time: the rapidly-exploring random tree (Section 2);
a tree that keeps shortening its routes: RRT* (Section 3);
two trees that run to meet each other: RRT-Connect (Section 4).

Every number below is computed in the notebook RO-051-rrt.ipynb.
2. Growing a tree from random samples: RRT


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Each round, RRT draws a random configuration, finds the tree’s nearest node, steps from it at most 0.5 m towards the sample and keeps the new node if the step is free. From under the table it reached the door after 67 samples with a route of 6.08 m; over 200 runs the median is 65 samples and 6.07 m, a third longer than the shortest route.


2.1 One step: sample, nearest node, steer, check
The first part of the opening problem: the robot under the table must get somewhere without a grid and without being stuck. Picture throwing darts at a map of the room. Wherever a dart lands, the nearest place the robot can already reach sends out a short branch towards it. Darts land all over the room, so branches reach out in every direction, round the table as easily as along it.
The standard terms. A planner that never builds the obstacle region or a grid, but draws random configurations and tests them only with collision checks, is a sampling-based planner (G-2760)Sampling-based planner: A motion planner that never builds the obstacle region or a grid, but draws random configurations and tests them with collision checks, joining the free ones into a tree or graph; it works in C-spaces with many dimensions, where grids are far too large. Explained in §2.1 One step: sample, nearest node, steer, check. (LaValle ch.5; MR §10.5). The tree it grows here is a rapidly-exploring random tree (G-2761)Rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT): A sampling-based planner that grows a tree from the start: each round it draws a random configuration, steps the tree’s nearest node at most a fixed distance towards it and keeps the new node if the step is free, until the tree reaches the goal; it explores fast but its routes zig-zag. Explained in §2.1 One step: sample, nearest node, steer, check., RRT for short (LaValle §5.5): a graph (G-2540)Graph: A set of vertices (points) joined by edges (lines), such as the room’s 76 free cells joined by 114 moves; it keeps only which places connect directly, so one search method works for maps, puzzles and any problem of states and moves. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edges of free configurations, its vertices, which we call nodes, joined by free straight edges, with exactly one path from the start to every node. One round has four moves (MR §10.5.1, Algorithm 10.3; CMU 16-350 slides):

Sample: draw a configuration evenly at random over the room’s floor.
Nearest node: find the tree’s nearest node (G-2762)Nearest node: The node of a planner’s tree closest to a new sample under the planner’s distance; RRT extends it, which makes the tree grow towards the largest empty regions. Explained in §2.1 One step: sample, nearest node, steer, check., the node closest to the sample, by a nearest-neighbour searchExplained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §8. Nearest neighbours when headings wrap.
Steer: move from the nearest node towards the sample, at most a step of 0.5 m; this step is the steer (G-2763)Steer (steering function): The step of a sampling-based planner that moves from a tree node towards a sample, at most a fixed distance (0.5 m here), stopping on the sample if it is closer; it keeps every new edge short enough to check. Explained in §2.1 One step: sample, nearest node, steer, check. function.
Check: test the new configuration and the edge to it; if both are free, add the node, with the nearest node as its parent (G-2576)Parent (back pointer): The vertex from which a search reached a vertex, stored with it during the search; following parents back from the goal gives the route. In A*, a cell’s parent changes whenever a shorter way in lowers its cost so far. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §4. Searching with a frontier and a visited list; if not, throw it away.

The first sample, on numbers. The tree starts as one node, the start (4.0, 0.5). The symbols:

q_{\text{rand}} is the sample, (1.395, 0.354), in m;
q_{\text{near}} is the tree’s nearest node, here the start (4.0, 0.5), in m;
\eta (eta) is the longest step, 0.5 m;
\Vert q_{\text{rand}} - q_{\text{near}} \Vert is the Euclidean distance (G-715)Euclidean distance: The straight-line distance between two points. Explained in: Handling Missing Data: KNN Imputer, §4.1 The Euclidean distance between them, in m;
q_{\text{new}} is the new node, in m.

The sample is 2.605 m left of the start and 0.146 m below it:
q_{\text{rand}} - q_{\text{near}} = (-2.605,\ -0.146)
\Vert q_{\text{rand}} - q_{\text{near}} \Vert= \sqrt{2.605^2 + 0.146^2}
= 2.609 \text{ m}
The sample is farther than 0.5 m, so the step goes 0.5 m along that direction:
q_{\text{new}} = (4.0,\ 0.5) + \frac{0.5}{2.609}\thinspace(-2.605,\ -0.146)
= (4.0,\ 0.5) + (-0.499,\ -0.028)
= (3.501,\ 0.472)
In symbols, steer moves at most \eta towards the sample, and stops on it if it is closer (LaValle §5.5.1; Karaman and Frazzoli 2011):
q_{\text{new}} = q_{\text{near}} + \frac{\eta}{\Vert q_{\text{rand}} - q_{\text{near}} \Vert}\thinspace(q_{\text{rand}} - q_{\text{near}})
when the sample is farther than \eta. Otherwise the new node is the sample itself:
q_{\text{new}} = q_{\text{rand}}
The check is edge resolution (G-2679)Edge resolution (segment checking): Checking a straight path segment in C-space for collisions by testing points along it, spaced at most a chosen step apart; too long a step can miss a thin collision, too short a step wastes time. Explained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §6.1 A segment holds infinitely many configurations with points at most 0.05 m apart. With \lceil \cdot \rceil rounding up to a whole number, the number of steps along the 0.5 m edge is:
\text{steps} = \lceil 0.5 / 0.05 \rceil = 10
so 11 points along the 0.5 m edge, each a test of the robot’s centre against the obstacles grown by 0.25 m. All 11 are free: the node (3.501, 0.472) joins the tree. The second sample, (3.215, 3.951), lands near the door; its nearest node is the new one, 3.49 m away, and the step of 0.5 m towards it ends at (3.46, 0.97), inside the table’s grown band. Rejected. One round adds at most one short edge, so the tree needs many rounds to reach the door.
