Explained in: Curse of Dimensionality, §2. What the curse of dimensionality isThe problems that appear when data has too many dimensions: lower performance and more computation.Collision detection (G-2665)Collision detection: Deciding, yes or no, whether two bodies overlap, such as the robot’s disk and the table; planners call it thousands of times instead of building the obstacle region. Explained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §2.1 The yes-or-no question and what it costsDeciding, yes or no, whether two bodies overlap, such as the robot’s disk and the table; planners call it thousands of times instead of building the obstacle region.Sampling-based planner (G-2760)Sampling-based planner: A motion planner that never builds the obstacle region or a grid, but draws random configurations and tests them with collision checks, joining the free ones into a tree or graph; it works in C-spaces with many dimensions, where grids are far too large. Explained in: Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees (RRT), §2.1 One step: sample, nearest node, steer, checkA motion planner that never builds the obstacle region or a grid, but draws random configurations and tests them with collision checks, joining the free ones into a tree or graph; it works in C-spaces with many dimensions, where grids are far too large.Continuous uniform distribution U(a, b) (G-467)Continuous uniform distribution U(a, b): A continuous variable spread evenly between a and b, with density 1/(b - a). Explained in: Uniform and Log-normal Distributions, §2. The uniform distributionA continuous variable spread evenly between a and b, with density 1/(b - a).Nearest neighbours (neighbours) (G-1306)Nearest neighbours (neighbours): The observations at the smallest distance from a given point; in KNN, the k training points closest to the query point, whose values or labels decide the prediction. Explained in: Handling Missing Data: KNN Imputer, §3.2 The k nearest neighboursThe observations at the smallest distance from a given point; in KNN, the k training points closest to the query point, whose values or labels decide the prediction.Edge resolution (segment checking) (G-2679)Edge resolution (segment checking): Checking a straight path segment in C-space for collisions by testing points along it, spaced at most a chosen step apart; too long a step can miss a thin collision, too short a step wastes time. Explained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §6.1 A segment holds infinitely many configurationsChecking a straight path segment in C-space for collisions by testing points along it, spaced at most a chosen step apart; too long a step can miss a thin collision, too short a step wastes time.Steer (steering function) (G-2763)Steer (steering function): The step of a sampling-based planner that moves from a tree node towards a sample, at most a fixed distance (0.5 m here), stopping on the sample if it is closer; it keeps every new edge short enough to check. Explained in: Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees (RRT), §2.1 One step: sample, nearest node, steer, checkThe step of a sampling-based planner that moves from a tree node towards a sample, at most a fixed distance (0.5 m here), stopping on the sample if it is closer; it keeps every new edge short enough to check.Graph (G-2540)Graph: A set of vertices (points) joined by edges (lines), such as the room’s 76 free cells joined by 114 moves; it keeps only which places connect directly, so one search method works for maps, puzzles and any problem of states and moves. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edgesA set of vertices (points) joined by edges (lines), such as the room’s 76 free cells joined by 114 moves; it keeps only which places connect directly, so one search method works for maps, puzzles and any problem of states and moves.Heuristic h (G-2570)Heuristic h: A cheap guess of the cost still to go from a state to the goal, such as 3.121 m from the start cell to the door; a search uses it to prefer states that look nearer the goal. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §2. A guess of the distance left: the heuristicA cheap guess of the cost still to go from a state to the goal, such as 3.121 m from the start cell to the door; a search uses it to prefer states that look nearer the goal.Connected component (of free space) (G-2656)Connected component (of free space): A piece of free space within which the robot can move from any configuration to any other without touching an obstacle; a path between two configurations exists only if both lie in the same component. Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §4.1 One piece or severalA piece of free space within which the robot can move from any configuration to any other without touching an obstacle; a path between two configurations exists only if both lie in the same component.Probability (G-1574)Probability: A number from 0 to 1 measuring how likely an event is; written P(A). Explained in: Empirical and Theoretical Probability, §2. What a probability measuresA number from 0 to 1 measuring how likely an event is; written P(A).Independent events (G-934)Independent events: Events where one happening does not change the probability of the other; for them the probability that both happen is the product of their probabilities. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Independent Events, §2. The definitionEvents where one happening does not change the probability of the other; for them the probability that both happen is the product of their probabilities.Product rule for independent events (G-1576)Product rule for independent events: For independent events, the probability that both happen is the product of their separate probabilities: P(A \cap B) = P(A) \times P(B). Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Independent Events, §2. The definitionFor independent events, the probability that both happen is the product of their separate probabilities: P(A \cap B) = P(A) \times P(B).Normal distribution (G-1343)Normal distribution: A symmetric, bell-shaped distribution: most values sit near the mean and they get rarer the further out we go; its mean and standard deviation set its centre and width. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution isA symmetric, bell-shaped distribution: most values sit near the mean and they get rarer the further out we go; its mean and standard deviation set its centre and width.Standard deviation (G-1871)Standard deviation: How far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n - 1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default). Explained in: Understanding Your Data: Seven First Questions, §7.1 Count, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximumHow far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n - 1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default).

RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.title: Manipulation Planning
RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Symbolic task planningSymbolic task planning: Choosing a sequence of actions that reaches a goal, from a description of the world in true-or-false facts such as “the cup is on the table”; it decides the order of steps (go to the table, pick up, go to the door, put down) that a route search alone cannot. Explained in: Symbolic Task Planning: STRIPS and PDDL, §2.1 Facts and states; Configuration spaceConfiguration space (C-space): The set of all configurations of a robot, one point per placement of the whole robot, such as a box of (x, y, \theta) whose top and bottom faces are the same headings for a floor robot; motion planning looks for paths through it. Explained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §2.2 The configuration space of the floor robot; Minkowski sumMinkowski sum: The set of all sums of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \oplus B, like sweeping one shape over the other; the obstacle region of a robot that keeps its heading is the obstacle’s Minkowski sum with the robot reflected through its centre. Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §3.2 Minkowski sum and difference; Lazy collision checkingLazy collision checking: Delaying an edge’s collision check until a candidate route uses it, deleting edges found to collide and searching again; it saves the checks of the many edges no route uses. Explained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §8. Lazy collision checking; Narrow passages and smarter samplingExplained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §6.2 Gaussian sampling and the bridge test; Probabilistic roadmap (PRM)Probabilistic roadmap (PRM): A graph of random free configurations (milestones) joined by straight edges that pass a collision check, built once and then searched with A*; it describes the free space without building the obstacle region, so it scales to robots with many joints. Explained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §2.2 Phase 1 and phase 2: milestones and edges.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

When a robot moves an object, the object is an obstacle while it stands and part of the robot while it is held, so the free space changes with each grasp and release. Manipulation planning splits the task into transit and transfer motions joined where both are possible; slow pushes move objects that cannot be held, and planning backwards from the goal with motions that slide along surfaces makes the result certain despite errors in the hand’s position.


So far the robot plans its own motion among obstacles that stay put. The probabilistic roadmap (G-2780)Probabilistic roadmap (PRM): A graph of random free configurations (milestones) joined by straight edges that pass a collision check, built once and then searched with A*; it describes the free space without building the obstacle region, so it scales to robots with many joints. Explained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §2.2 Phase 1 and phase 2: milestones and edges answers many trips in an unchanged room, and symbolic task planning (G-2600)Symbolic task planning: Choosing a sequence of actions that reaches a goal, from a description of the world in true-or-false facts such as “the cup is on the table”; it decides the order of steps (go to the table, pick up, go to the door, put down) that a route search alone cannot. Explained in: Symbolic Task Planning: STRIPS and PDDL, §1. Overview puts the steps of carrying a cup in order: go to the table, pick the cup up, carry it, put it down. “Pick up” is one step to the task planner, but the robot still has to move its arm to do it.
Manipulation needs an arm, so this Note leaves the room’s floor for the table top. We use the arm whose configuration (G-2286)Configuration: The list of numbers that fixes the position of every point of a robot, such as q = (x, y, \theta) = (2, 1, 0.524) for a floor robot or the joint angles (\theta_1, \theta_2) of a 2R arm; with it a planner treats the whole robot as one point. Explained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §2.1 The configuration: numbers that place every point, the numbers that place it, is its two joint angles: two links, 0.3 m and 0.2 m long, each turning about its joint, with the robot parked beside the table and the arm seen from the side. The shoulder is 0.1 m above the table top, and a suction gripper at the hand holds a cup by its lid while a wrist keeps the cup upright.
The task: move the cup, 6 cm wide and 8 cm tall, from spot A on the table to spot B, 0.24 m further on, with a bottle 0.14 m tall standing between them. What breaks is the cup itself, which is neither an obstacle that stays put nor a part of the robot:

planned as a fixed obstacle, the cup can never move;
planned as if it were not there, the cup goes wherever the hand goes. Figure 1 follows a route planned for the arm alone, 109.3 degrees of joint motion on which the arm touches nothing (notebook): the cup it carries sinks 1.7 cm into the table and passes through the bottle for 32.2 percent of the way.


Figure 1: Animation: the arm (blue link 1, orange link 2) carries the cup from spot A along a route planned for the arm alone, as if there were no cup (a probabilistic roadmap in the arm’s configuration space, seed 0, 109.3 degrees of joint motion). The robot’s top and the table are grey, the bottle green, spot B dashed. The arm touches nothing; the cup, drawn red while it overlaps something, sinks up to 1.7 cm into the table early on and passes through the bottle for 32.2 percent of the way; the dotted red line traces the cup’s bottom. Last frame: the cup at B
Two more problems wait. A cup without a lid cannot be held by suction at all, yet it still has to move. And the hand is never exactly where it is told to go: if its position is known only to within 1 cm, a cup holder at B that leaves 0.5 cm of play on each side will often be missed.
The opening question of this Note: how does the robot plan motions that move objects, by holding them or by pushing them, and still end with the cup where it must be? We answer it in steps:

carrying the cup: motions with and without the cup, and where they meet (Section 2);
moving the cup without holding it, by a slow push (Section 3);
placing the cup despite the hand’s error, by planning backwards from the goal (Section 4);
the software real robots use for all of this (Section 5).

2. Carrying the cup: transit and transfer


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The task has two kinds of motion: transit, with the hand empty and the cup an obstacle at its spot, and transfer, with the cup held and moving with the hand. Each has its own free space; the mode changes only at a configuration free in both, the grasp or the placing. Planning each motion in its own free space, with the PRM, moves the cup from A to B.


2.1 Two kinds of motion, two free spaces
The opening problem was that the cup is sometimes an obstacle and sometimes part of the robot. Which one depends on whether the hand holds it, so we split the task where that changes:

while the hand is empty, the arm moves and the cup stays where it stands, so the cup is an obstacle like the bottle;
while the hand holds the cup, the cup moves with the hand as if it were part of the arm, so it must not hit the table, the bottle or the arm’s own links.

A motion of the first kind is a transit (G-2801)Transit: A motion in which the robot moves and the object stays where it stands, so the object counts as an obstacle; for example the arm moving from home to the cup. Explained in §2.1 Two kinds of motion, two free spaces.: the robot moves while the object stays put. A motion of the second kind is a transfer (G-2802)Transfer: A motion in which the robot holds the object and the object moves as if attached to its hand, so the object counts as part of the robot and must not hit anything. Explained in §2.1 Two kinds of motion, two free spaces.: the object is held and moves as if attached to the robot’s hand (LaValle §7.3.2; Hauser ch.12, “Multi-modal motion planning”). Which of the two applies, together with where the object stands or how it is held, is the mode (G-2803)Mode (manipulation): Which kind of motion applies, transit or transfer, together with where the object stands or how it is held; each mode has its own free space. Explained in §2.1 Two kinds of motion, two free spaces. of the task (Hauser ch.12).
Each mode has its own free space. The arm’s configuration is its two joint angles, so its C-space is a square of angles from −180° to 180°, whose opposite edges are the same angles (cutting the torus into a squareExplained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §5.1 Cutting the torus into a square). Figure 2 draws the square three times, once per stage of the task, and colours every blocked configuration by what it hits: grey the table or the robot’s top, green the bottle, orange the cup in the way. Watch the orange part move: round the grasp in the first panel, where the links would hit the standing cup; at the top and bottom edges in the second, where the held cup would hit link 1; round the placing in the third.
Make interactive
Figure 2: The arm’s C-space, joint 1 across and joint 2 up, each from −180 to 180 degrees, in the three stages of the task; each blocked configuration is coloured by what it hits: grey the table or the robot’s top, green the bottle, orange the cup in the way. Left, transit with the cup standing at A: 49.4 percent free. Middle, transfer with the cup held under the hand: 42.3 percent free; the held cup closes extra bands at the top and bottom and widens the bottle’s region. Right, transit with the cup standing at B: 51.3 percent free. Black: home (90, 0) degrees; blue: the grasp at A (34.0, −144.1); red: the placing at B (23.2, −67.0)
The free share changes from 49.4 percent to 42.3 percent and then to 51.3 percent (notebook). A single free space for the whole task cannot exist, because the cup that blocks the arm in transit is part of the arm in transfer. Section 2.2 asks where one mode can hand over to the other.
2.2 Where the modes meet: transition configurations
A transit can end and a transfer begin only where both are possible: the hand on the cup’s lid, ready to lift, touching the cup but not overlapping it (LaValle §7.3.2). The joint angles that put the hand on the lid follow from the triangle of the two links and the line from the shoulder to the lid. Of its two solutions, elbow up and elbow down, only the elbow-up one is free (notebook):

the grasp at A: joint 1 at 34.0°, joint 2 at −144.1°, hand on the lid at (0.18, −0.02) m from the shoulder;
the placing at B: joint 1 at 23.2°, joint 2 at −67.0°, hand at (0.42, −0.02) m.

The grasp is free in the transit mode, because link 2 only touches the lid, and free in the transfer mode, because the held cup rests on the table without sinking in (notebook). A configuration that is free in two modes, where the task can switch from one to the other, is a transition configuration (G-2804)Transition configuration: A configuration that is free in two modes, such as the hand touching the cup’s lid, where a plan can switch from transit to transfer or back. Explained in §2.2 Where the modes meet: transition configurations. (Hauser ch.12; LaValle §7.3.2). In Figure 2, the blue grasp sits on the edge of the orange region in the first panel: one step further and link 2 would push into the cup.
The arm’s position at each moment follows from its two joint angles by adding the two links end to end, as the arm’s configuration (G-2286)Configuration: The list of numbers that fixes the position of every point of a robot, such as q = (x, y, \theta) = (2, 1, 0.524) for a floor robot or the joint angles (\theta_1, \theta_2) of a 2R arm; with it a planner treats the whole robot as one point. Explained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §2.1 The configuration: numbers that place every point showed with the hand at (0.260, 0.350) m for the angles (30°, 60°). With the transition configurations known, the three motions between them can be planned.
2.3 The plan: transit, transfer, transit
The plan has three legs, each in one mode, joined at the transition configurations (Hauser ch.12, “Simple Pick-and-Place”):

transit, with the cup standing at A, from home to the grasp;
grasp, then transfer, with the cup held, from the grasp to the placing;
release, then transit, with the cup standing at B, from the placing back home.

Each leg is an ordinary planning problem in its own free space, so the probabilistic roadmap (G-2780)Probabilistic roadmap (PRM): A graph of random free configurations (milestones) joined by straight edges that pass a collision check, built once and then searched with A*; it describes the free space without building the obstacle region, so it scales to robots with many joints. Explained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §2.2 Phase 1 and phase 2: milestones and edges plans it: 150 milestones (G-2781)Milestone: A free configuration kept as a vertex of a probabilistic roadmap, drawn at random; milestones are the places the roadmap’s routes pass through. Explained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §2.2 Phase 1 and phase 2: milestones and edges, random free configurations, each joined to its 10 nearest, with distances measured the short way round each joint (Hauser ch.12: “using your favorite C-space planner”). Figure 3 runs the plan. Watch the C-space on the right change at the two mode switches, and the path stay in the white free space of whichever mode is current.

Figure 3: Animation: the plan, transit, transfer, transit. Left: the arm, with the cup standing at A, then held under the hand, then standing at B. Right: the arm’s C-space of the current mode (coloured as in Figure 2) with the path so far. Leg 1, transit from home to the grasp, 169.0 degrees of joint motion (blue). At the grasp the cup is held and the C-space switches to the transfer mode. Leg 2, transfer over the bottle to the placing, 123.2 degrees (orange). At the placing the cup is let go and the C-space switches back. Leg 3, transit home, 99.2 degrees (green); earlier legs stay grey
The three roadmaps give routes of 169.0, 123.2 and 99.2 degrees of joint motion, all free in their modes (notebook). During the transfer, the bottom of the held cup rises to 0.076 m, 0.036 m above the bottle’s top at 0.04 m:
0.076 - 0.04 = 0.036 \text{ m}
So the cup clears the bottle that the route of Figure 1 dragged it through: the transfer was planned in the free space where the cup is part of the robot.
The formal version. The state of the task is the arm’s configuration together with the cup’s position, and the mode says which of the two free spaces applies (Hauser ch.12). A plan is a sequence of transit and transfer paths that alternate, each inside its mode’s free space, switching only at transition configurations (LaValle §7.3.2). Moving a robot and the objects it handles from where they are to where they should be is manipulation planning (G-2800)Manipulation planning: Planning the motions of a robot together with the objects it moves, as a sequence of transit and transfer motions joined at transition configurations, each planned in its own free space. Explained in §2.3 The plan: transit, transfer, transit. (LaValle §7.3.2). The symbolic plan’s “pick up” is now a transit that ends at a transition configuration, then a switch of mode. Every leg so far needed the cup to be held, though, and a cup without a lid cannot be.
3. Moving without grasping: pushing and the quasistatic assumption


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

An object that cannot be held can still be pushed. If the push is slow, speeding the object up takes a negligible force, so the forces on it balance at every moment: this quasistatic assumption makes the object move only while it is pushed, so where the hand stops decides where the object stops. Pushing the cup low makes it slide; pushing it more than 7.5 cm above the table tips it over.


3.1 Manipulation without a grasp
The opening’s second problem: a cup without a lid. A suction gripper holds an object only by a flat surface that seals (Hauser ch.12, “Suction grippers”), so the open cup cannot be held. The robot can still move it by touching it: pushing it along the table with the hand. Manipulating an object without grasping it, by pushing, tilting, throwing or squeezing it, is nonprehensile manipulation (G-2805)Nonprehensile manipulation: Moving an object without grasping it, by pushing, tilting, throwing or squeezing it, so a robot can move objects its gripper cannot hold. Explained in §3.1 Manipulation without a grasp. (LaValle §12.5.2; MR §12.3, which adds pushing a sofa and carrying glasses on a tray). Nonprehensile manipulation also handles objects too large to grasp or too heavy to lift (MR §12.3).
The task for this section: push the open cup 6 cm towards the robot, from A (centre at x = 0.18 m) to a spot C (x = 0.12 m). The plan is the hand’s motion: touch the cup’s right side, move 6 cm to the left, stop. For that to work, the cup must stop when the hand stops.
3.2 Why a slow push is predictable
Figure 4 pushes the cup three ways. In part 1, watch the cup slide with the hand at 0.05 m/s and stop with it at C; in part 3, watch it slide on past C after a push at 0.5 m/s.

Figure 4: Animation: the arm pushes the open cup (no lid) to the left, its hand touching the cup’s right side; the target spot C is dashed. Part 1, a slow push at 0.05 m/s, 4 cm above the table: the cup slides with the hand, the push equals the friction, 0.981 N, and speeding the cup up takes only 0.025 N; when the hand stops at C, the cup coasts 0.32 mm and stops at C. Part 2, a push at the rim, 8 cm up: the push’s torque about the cup’s left bottom corner, 0.981 × 0.08 = 0.0785 N m, beats the weight’s, 2.4525 × 0.03 = 0.0736 N m, so the cup tips over that corner and falls. Part 3, a fast push at 0.5 m/s, 4 cm up: the hand stops at C, and the cup slides on, slowed by friction, 3.2 cm past C
The cup’s numbers (the coefficient of friction is an assumed value for a cup on a table):

m is the cup’s mass, 0.25 kg;
g is the acceleration due to gravity, 9.81 m/s²;
\mu is the coefficient of friction between the cup and the table, 0.4, a ratio with no unit.

The cup presses on the table with its weight:
m g = 0.25 \times 9.81 = 2.4525 \text{ N}
The table’s friction can hold back at most \mu times the force pressing the two surfaces together (MR §12.2, Coulomb friction); that ratio is the coefficient of friction (G-2807)Coefficient of friction: The ratio of the largest friction force two surfaces can give to the force pressing them together, such as 0.4 for the cup on the table; it sets how hard a sliding object must be pushed. Explained in §3.2 Why a slow push is predictable.. With 0.4, every newton that presses the cup onto the table lets friction hold back at most 0.4 N. So the friction on the sliding cup is:
\mu m g = 0.4 \times 2.4525 = 0.981 \text{ N}
Why the forces balance. The force left over after friction speeds the cup up, by Newton’s second law (G-2809)Newton’s second law: The net force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration; it gives the force needed to change an object’s speed, which the quasistatic assumption neglects. Explained in §3.2 Why a slow push is predictable.: the net force on a body, all the forces on it added with their directions, equals its mass times its acceleration, how fast its speed changes (MR §8.1.1, eq. 8.4). With:

F_{\text{net}} is the net force on the cup, the push minus the friction, in N;
a is the cup’s acceleration, how fast its speed grows, in m/s².

F_{\text{net}} = m a
A slow push brings the cup from rest to 0.05 m/s in about 0.5 s:
a = 0.05 / 0.5 = 0.1 \text{ m/s}^2
F_{\text{net}} = 0.25 \times 0.1 = 0.025 \text{ N}
\text{share} = 0.025 / 0.981 = 0.0255
So speeding the cup up takes 2.5 percent of the friction force: the push almost exactly balances the friction at every moment. When the speeds and accelerations are so small that the force needed to change the speed can be ignored, the forces on the object balance at every instant; that is the quasistatic assumption (G-2806)Quasistatic assumption: The assumption that motions are slow enough for the force needed to change speeds to be ignored, so the forces on an object balance at every instant; a slowly pushed object then moves only while it is pushed. Explained in §3.2 Why a slow push is predictable. (MR §12.3, eq. 12.32).
Why the cup stops with the hand. When the hand stops, only friction acts on the cup, and it slows the cup down. With:

v is the cup’s speed when the hand stops, in m/s;
b is how fast friction slows it, in m/s²;
t is the time it takes to stop, in s;
d is the distance it slides on, in m.

By Newton’s second law, friction alone slows the cup by the friction force divided by the mass. After the fast push of part 3, the cup starts at 0.5 m/s:
b = 0.981 / 0.25 = 3.924 \text{ m/s}^2
t = 0.5 / 3.924 = 0.1274 \text{ s}
The speed falls steadily from 0.5 m/s to 0, so its average is half the start speed:
d = (0.5 / 2) \times 0.1274
= 0.0319 \text{ m}
The same steps in symbols:
b = \mu m g / m = \mu g
t = v / b
d = (v / 2)\thinspace t
= \frac{v^2}{2 b}
At 0.05 m/s, ten times slower, the distance is a hundred times smaller:
d = \frac{0.05^2}{2 \times 3.924} = 0.00032 \text{ m}
So the slow push of part 1 leaves the cup within 0.32 mm of where the hand stopped, while the fast push of part 3 overshoots C by 3.2 cm (notebook). Under the quasistatic assumption the cup moves only while it is pushed, so the plan only has to say where the hand goes, not how the cup speeds up and slows down (MR §12.3). The push’s height, though, decides whether the cup slides at all.
3.3 Where to push: slide or tip
Part 2 of Figure 4 pushes at the rim and the cup tips over instead of sliding. The cup can do one of three things under a push: stay put, slide, or tip over its front bottom corner, the left one when pushed to the left. Quasistatic analysis tests each for balance and keeps the one that balances (MR §12.3).
The turning effect of a force about a point is its torque (G-2808)Torque: The turning effect of a force about a point: the force times its distance from the point, measured square to the force’s line; comparing torques decides whether a pushed object tips. Explained in §3.3 Where to push: slide or tip.: the force times its distance from the point, measured square to the force’s line (MR §3.4). A door shows why the distance matters: the same push turns it more easily at the handle, far from the hinges, than close to them. Figure 5 marks the forces on the cup and their distances from the corner O.

The weight acts half the cup’s width from O and holds the cup down; the push acts at height p and turns it over. To slide, the push must reach the friction force, 0.981 N. Pushing 4 cm up:
\text{push: } 0.981 \times 0.04 = 0.0392 \text{ N m}
\text{weight: } 2.4525 \times 0.03 = 0.0736 \text{ N m}
The weight’s torque wins, so the cup slides flat. Pushing at the rim, 8 cm up:
\text{push: } 0.981 \times 0.08 = 0.0785 \text{ N m}

\mu m g is the friction force, 0.981 N, and m g the cup’s weight, 2.4525 N (Section 3.2);
p is the push’s height above the table, in m;

The cup slides without tipping if the push’s torque at the sliding force stays below the weight’s:
\mu m g\thinspace p \le m g\thinspace w / 2

A push below 7.5 cm slides the cup; a push above it tips the cup (MR §12.3, Exercise 12.23 asks the same of a pushed box). The robot’s plan for the open cup is now complete: touch the cup’s side 4 cm up, move the hand 6 cm to the left slowly, stop. A nonprehensile (G-2805)Nonprehensile manipulation: Moving an object without grasping it, by pushing, tilting, throwing or squeezing it, so a robot can move objects its gripper cannot hold. Explained in §3.1 Manipulation without a grasp. plan like this needs no grasp and, under the quasistatic assumption, no sensing while it runs; LaValle §12.5.2 shows even sequences of squeezes that turn a part to a known orientation without any sensor. Every plan so far, though, assumed that the hand goes exactly where it is told.
Another way to see it. Rest a metre stick on your two index fingers, one finger near the centre and one far from it, and slowly slide the fingers together. The stick never falls, and the fingers meet under its centre (MR §12.3, Example 12.10, the meter-stick trick). Testing each way the stick could slip for force balance, one at a time, shows why:

the finger farther from the centre carries less of the stick’s weight, so less friction, and the stick slides over it while it rides along on the other finger;
once the centre is halfway between the fingers, the stick slips on both, and the centre stays between them until they meet.

The analysis holds only for slow motion: move a finger fast and the stick falls, because the quasistatic assumption no longer holds (MR §12.3).
4. Placing despite errors: preimage planning


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A motion command whose direction can be off by up to 10 degrees surely reaches the goal only from a set of starts, its preimage. Sliding along the holder’s chamfers turns the preimage from a sliver 1 cm wide into a triangle 3 cm wide and 8.5 cm tall, so a hand known only to within 1 cm still places the cup. Planning backwards, each command must end inside the preimage of the next.


4.1 The error that breaks the placing
The opening’s third problem: the hand is never exactly where it is told. Say the robot knows the hand’s position only to within 1 cm either side, and any straight motion it commands may run up to 10 degrees off its direction (an error model of the kind preimage planning assumes, LaValle §12.5.1). Now B is a cup holder, so that the cup cannot be knocked over (Figure 6, left): two posts 2 cm tall, 7 cm apart at the bottom, each with a 45-degree chamfer 1 cm wide on its inner top corner. The 6 cm cup has 0.5 cm of play on each side.
Make interactive
Figure 6: The cup holder at B. Left, side view: the bottle, the two posts of the holder (purple) 1.5 cm thick and 2 cm tall, 7 cm apart at the bottom, each with a 45-degree chamfer, and the 6 cm cup above them; the black dot is the middle of the cup’s bottom. Right, the cup’s C-space: the cup becomes that point, and the posts, the bottle and the table grow by the cup’s shape (orange); the holder becomes a slot 1 cm wide at the bottom whose chamfers open to a mouth 3 cm wide, 2 cm above the table
To reason about the cup as a point, we use its C-space. The cup only moves, never turns, so as for the board of the Minkowski sum (G-2653)Minkowski sum: The set of all sums of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \oplus B, like sweeping one shape over the other; the obstacle region of a robot that keeps its heading is the obstacle’s Minkowski sum with the robot reflected through its centre. Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §3.2 Minkowski sum and difference, each obstacle grows by the cup’s shape reflected, and the cup becomes the point at the middle of its bottom (Figure 6, right). The gap between the posts shrinks by the cup’s width:
0.07 - 0.06 = 0.01 \text{ m}
So the slot is 1 cm wide, and the chamfers widen its mouth by 1 cm on each side, to 3 cm. A hand within 1 cm either side of the slot’s centre spans 2 cm, twice the slot, so aiming straight at the slot cannot be guaranteed to work.
4.2 The preimage of the holder
The command is “move down until stopped”. From a given start, every direction within 10 degrees of straight down is possible, so the start is good only if every one of them ends in the holder. Figure 7 draws five of those directions from one start, 0.8 cm right of the slot’s centre and 2 cm above the posts. In the stage “without sliding”, watch four of the five land on the chamfer and stop; in the stage “with sliding”, watch the same four slide down the chamfer into the slot.

Figure 7: Animation in the cup’s C-space near B (orange: the posts, bottle and table grown by the cup’s shape; the slot is 1 cm wide). The command “move down” may run up to 10 degrees off; five possible directions (260 to 280 degrees) are drawn from a start (black dot) 0.8 cm right of the slot’s centre and 2 cm above the posts. Without sliding, a touch outside the slot’s bottom fails: 1 of the 5 reaches the bottom, 4 stop on the chamfer (red). The preimage without sliding, the starts from which every direction ends in the holder (green), is a sliver at most 1 cm wide reaching 0.8 cm above the posts. With sliding, the chamfers guide all 5 into the slot. The preimage with sliding is a triangle 3 cm wide at the posts’ top and 8.5 cm tall. Last frame: a band 2 cm wide, every start the hand could be at, fits inside it 1.4 cm above the posts (green) but sticks out 5 cm above them (red)
The set of starts from which a motion command is sure to reach its goal, whatever error occurs, is the preimage (G-2811)Preimage: The set of starts from which a motion command is sure to reach its goal whatever error occurs; a command is safe to issue only from inside it. Explained in §4.2 The preimage of the holder. of the goal for that command (LaValle §12.5.1). Without sliding, the preimage is a sliver inside the slot, at most 1 cm wide and reaching only 0.8 cm above the posts (notebook): the robot would already have to be in the slot.
Sliding is what helps. On touching a surface, a moving object either sticks or slides along it. A motion that slides along a surface while touching it is a compliant motion (G-2810)Compliant motion: A motion that slides along a surface while touching it, guided by the surface, such as a cup sliding down a chamfer into its holder; it lets uncertain motions still reach a goal. Explained in §4.2 The preimage of the holder. (LaValle §12.5.1). Friction stops the sliding when the motion points nearly straight into the surface: with the coefficient of friction 0.4, sliding needs the motion to point more than 21.8 degrees away from straight into the surface, the angle whose tangent is 0.4, because the part of the motion along the surface must beat 0.4 times the part pressing into it (LaValle §12.5.1; MR §12.2):

on a chamfer, tilted 45 degrees, a motion within 10 degrees of straight down points 35 to 55 degrees away from straight into it, so the cup slides down the chamfer into the slot;
on the flat top of a post, a motion within 10 degrees of straight down points at most 10 degrees away from straight into it, so the cup sticks there and the placing fails.

With sliding, the preimage is a triangle 3 cm wide at the posts’ top and 8.5 cm tall (notebook). The flat tops of the posts, where the cup would stick, bound it on both sides.
4.3 How high the hand may start
A drop of height h drifts sideways by at most h times the tangent of 10 degrees. With:

h is the height of the start above the posts’ top, in m;
0.176 is the tangent of 10 degrees;
0.01 m is the hand’s error either side;
0.015 m is half the mouth’s width.

Every start in the hand’s 2 cm band lands inside the mouth, and slides into the slot, if the error plus the drift stays within half the mouth. For a start 2 cm up:
0.01 + 0.02 \times 0.176 = 0.0135 \text{ m}
0.0135 \le 0.015
so a 2 cm drop is safe. The highest safe start:
0.01 + 0.176\thinspace h \le 0.015
h \le 0.005 / 0.176 = 0.028 \text{ m}
The same steps in symbols, with:

e is the hand’s error either side, 0.01 m;
s is half the mouth’s width, 0.015 m;
\alpha is the largest error in the motion’s direction, 10 degrees.

e + h \tan \alpha \le s
h \le \frac{s - e}{\tan \alpha}
So the hand may start the drop anywhere up to 2.8 cm above the posts (notebook: 0.0284 m), as the green band of Figure 7, 1.4 cm up, shows. Without sliding, every start must land in the 1 cm slot itself:
0.01 + 0.176\thinspace h \le 0.005
which no height h meets, because the hand’s error alone, 0.01 m, is already more than 0.005 m.
4.4 Planning backwards from the goal
The drop works only if the motion before it ends inside the drop’s preimage, and the preimage fixes the goal of the previous motion: the transfer of Section 2.3, the motion with the cup held, must now end with the cup 1.4 cm above the posts, centred over the slot, not at a placing configuration that assumes a perfect hand. Choosing each command so that it ends inside the preimage of the next, starting from the goal and working backwards, is preimage planning (G-2812)Preimage planning: Planning a sequence of motion commands backwards from the goal, each command chosen to end inside the preimage of the next, so the sequence succeeds despite errors in motion and sensing. Explained in §4.4 Planning backwards from the goal. (LaValle §12.5.1, also called the LMT framework after Lozano-Pérez, Mason and Taylor). For the cup:

last command: move down until stopped, from the band 1.4 cm above the posts; its preimage is the triangle of Figure 7;
the command before: the transfer, planned with the roadmap, ending inside that band, so the hand’s 1 cm error is covered;
before that: the transit to the grasp.

Real pick-and-place software does the same with short fixed motions: it plans to a configuration just above the target and finishes with a straight move down a centimetre or two (Hauser ch.12, “Pre-grasp, post-grasp, pre-placement, and post-placement motions”). Hauser gives a second reason: the last centimetres before a grasp or a placing are a deep narrow passage (G-2793)Narrow passage: A thin part of free space that a route must cross, such as a gap only slightly wider than the robot; uniform random samples rarely land in it, so roadmaps tend to split on either side. Explained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §6.1 The tray robot: where uniform samples starve, a thin part of free space, for a sampling planner, and a fixed straight motion avoids sampling it. Computing preimages for general problems is hard (LaValle §12.5.1), so such fixed final motions are planned by hand, as here. The robot can now carry, push and place the cup; the last section shows the software that does this on real robots.
5. The software: MoveIt and OMPL


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

OMPL is a library of sampling-based planners, such as PRM and RRT, that by design knows nothing about robots or collisions. MoveIt is the robot-arm software around it: it keeps a model of the robot and its surroundings, checks every configuration the planner tries (including an object attached to the hand, which is the transfer mode), and turns the planner’s path into a timed trajectory.


The cup task of Sections 2 to 4 used a roadmap planner, a collision checker that knows whether the cup is held, and a model of the arm. Real robots get these pieces from two open-source packages.
OMPL (G-2814)OMPL (Open Motion Planning Library): A library of sampling-based planners, such as PRM and RRT, that by design has no collision checker or robot model, so it can be joined to any; MoveIt uses it by default. Explained in §5. The software: MoveIt and OMPL., the Open Motion Planning Library, is an open-source library (BSD licence, OMPL licence page) of sampling-based planners, among them PRM, RRT, EST and KPIECE, which work on abstractly defined spaces of configurations (OMPL). OMPL contains no collision checker and no drawing, on purpose, so that it can be joined to any of them (OMPL). Its PRM is the roadmap of Section 2 of the probabilistic roadmapsProbabilistic roadmap (PRM): A graph of random free configurations (milestones) joined by straight edges that pass a collision check, built once and then searched with A*; it describes the free space without building the obstacle region, so it scales to robots with many joints. Explained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §2.2 Phase 1 and phase 2: milestones and edges.
MoveIt (G-2813)MoveIt: Open-source motion-planning software for robot arms: it keeps a model of the robot and its surroundings, calls planners such as OMPL’s, checks collisions including carried objects, and times the result. Explained in §5. The software: MoveIt and OMPL. is motion-planning software for robot arms, free under the BSD licence (MoveIt home page); it uses OMPL’s planners as its default planners, through a plugin interface that also accepts others (MoveIt docs, “Motion Planning”). MoveIt keeps the planning scene (G-2815)Planning scene (MoveIt): MoveIt’s model of the world round the robot and of the robot’s state, including objects attached to the hand, which answers whether each configuration a planner tries is free. Explained in §5. The software: MoveIt and OMPL.: its model of the world round the robot and of the robot’s own state, including any object attached to, that is carried by, the robot (MoveIt docs, “The move_group node”). Figure 8 follows one request, the transfer of the cup, through MoveIt. Watch the planner and the planning scene take turns: the planner proposes configurations, the scene answers free or not.

Figure 8: Animation: one motion plan request followed through MoveIt, one box highlighted per frame. 1, the request: start at the grasp configuration, goal above the holder at B, the arm’s joints, the PRM planner. 2, request adapters before planning fix small problems, such as a start a hair outside a joint limit. 3, a planner from OMPL, here PRM; OMPL has no collision checker, so for every configuration it tries it asks MoveIt. 4, the planning scene answers: it checks the robot’s links against each other, against the table, the bottle and the holder, and the cup attached to the hand after the grasp. 5, back to the planner. 6, request adapters after planning add timing, keeping each joint within its speed and acceleration limits. 7, the trajectory goes to the arm’s controllers
Each piece of the cup task has its place in that pipeline (MoveIt docs, “Motion Planning”):

Transfer mode: after the grasp, the cup is added to the planning scene as an object attached to the hand, and collisions are checked with attached objects as well as between the robot’s own links, so every configuration the planner tries is checked in the transfer mode’s free space.
The planner: OMPL’s PRM or RRT plans each leg; the planner’s path has no timing.
Timing: an adapter after the planner turns the path into a trajectory that keeps each joint within its speed and acceleration limits.
Reuse: MoveIt can keep a PRM’s roadmap between requests, the multi-query (G-2786)Multi-query planner: A planner that invests time in a reusable description of the free space, such as a roadmap, so that many later problems in the same unchanged space are solved quickly. Explained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §3. Many trips on one roadmap: single-query and multi-query planners reuse of the probabilistic roadmaps; its lazy versions check edges again only as a route needs them, by lazy collision checking (G-2799)Lazy collision checking: Delaying an edge’s collision check until a candidate route uses it, deleting edges found to collide and searching again; it saves the checks of the many edges no route uses. Explained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §8. Lazy collision checking, which suits a scene that changes a little, such as a cup that has moved from A to B (MoveIt docs, “OMPL Planner”, persistent roadmaps).

MoveIt’s pick-and-place tutorial builds the task of Section 2 from stages: move to pick (a transit), approach and grasp, attach the object, lift, move to place (a transfer), lower and release, retreat (MoveIt docs, pick and place tutorial). Its lift and lower stages are the short final motions of Section 4.4.

Explained in §2.3 The plan: transit, transfer, transit.Planning the motions of a robot together with the objects it moves, as a sequence of transit and transfer motions joined at transition configurations, each planned in its own free space.Nonprehensile manipulation (G-2805)Nonprehensile manipulation: Moving an object without grasping it, by pushing, tilting, throwing or squeezing it, so a robot can move objects its gripper cannot hold. Explained in §3.1 Manipulation without a grasp.Moving an object without grasping it, by pushing, tilting, throwing or squeezing it, so a robot can move objects its gripper cannot hold.Coefficient of friction (G-2807)Coefficient of friction: The ratio of the largest friction force two surfaces can give to the force pressing them together, such as 0.4 for the cup on the table; it sets how hard a sliding object must be pushed. Explained in §3.2 Why a slow push is predictable.The ratio of the largest friction force two surfaces can give to the force pressing them together, such as 0.4 for the cup on the table; it sets how hard a sliding object must be pushed.Newton’s second law (G-2809)Newton’s second law: The net force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration; it gives the force needed to change an object’s speed, which the quasistatic assumption neglects. Explained in §3.2 Why a slow push is predictable.The net force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration; it gives the force needed to change an object’s speed, which the quasistatic assumption neglects.Quasistatic assumption (G-2806)Quasistatic assumption: The assumption that motions are slow enough for the force needed to change speeds to be ignored, so the forces on an object balance at every instant; a slowly pushed object then moves only while it is pushed. Explained in §3.2 Why a slow push is predictable.The assumption that motions are slow enough for the force needed to change speeds to be ignored, so the forces on an object balance at every instant; a slowly pushed object then moves only while it is pushed.Torque (G-2808)Torque: The turning effect of a force about a point: the force times its distance from the point, measured square to the force’s line; comparing torques decides whether a pushed object tips. Explained in §3.3 Where to push: slide or tip.The turning effect of a force about a point: the force times its distance from the point, measured square to the force’s line; comparing torques decides whether a pushed object tips.Preimage (G-2811)Preimage: The set of starts from which a motion command is sure to reach its goal whatever error occurs; a command is safe to issue only from inside it. Explained in §4.2 The preimage of the holder.The set of starts from which a motion command is sure to reach its goal whatever error occurs; a command is safe to issue only from inside it.Compliant motion (G-2810)Compliant motion: A motion that slides along a surface while touching it, guided by the surface, such as a cup sliding down a chamfer into its holder; it lets uncertain motions still reach a goal. Explained in §4.2 The preimage of the holder.A motion that slides along a surface while touching it, guided by the surface, such as a cup sliding down a chamfer into its holder; it lets uncertain motions still reach a goal.Preimage planning (G-2812)Preimage planning: Planning a sequence of motion commands backwards from the goal, each command chosen to end inside the preimage of the next, so the sequence succeeds despite errors in motion and sensing. Explained in §4.4 Planning backwards from the goal.Planning a sequence of motion commands backwards from the goal, each command chosen to end inside the preimage of the next, so the sequence succeeds despite errors in motion and sensing.OMPL (Open Motion Planning Library) (G-2814)OMPL (Open Motion Planning Library): A library of sampling-based planners, such as PRM and RRT, that by design has no collision checker or robot model, so it can be joined to any; MoveIt uses it by default. Explained in §5. The software: MoveIt and OMPL.A library of sampling-based planners, such as PRM and RRT, that by design has no collision checker or robot model, so it can be joined to any; MoveIt uses it by default.MoveIt (G-2813)MoveIt: Open-source motion-planning software for robot arms: it keeps a model of the robot and its surroundings, calls planners such as OMPL’s, checks collisions including carried objects, and times the result. Explained in §5. The software: MoveIt and OMPL.Open-source motion-planning software for robot arms: it keeps a model of the robot and its surroundings, calls planners such as OMPL’s, checks collisions including carried objects, and times the result.Planning scene (MoveIt) (G-2815)Planning scene (MoveIt): MoveIt’s model of the world round the robot and of the robot’s state, including objects attached to the hand, which answers whether each configuration a planner tries is free. Explained in §5. The software: MoveIt and OMPL.MoveIt’s model of the world round the robot and of the robot’s state, including objects attached to the hand, which answers whether each configuration a planner tries is free.Probabilistic roadmap (PRM) (G-2780)Probabilistic roadmap (PRM): A graph of random free configurations (milestones) joined by straight edges that pass a collision check, built once and then searched with A*; it describes the free space without building the obstacle region, so it scales to robots with many joints. Explained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §2.2 Phase 1 and phase 2: milestones and edgesA graph of random free configurations (milestones) joined by straight edges that pass a collision check, built once and then searched with A*; it describes the free space without building the obstacle region, so it scales to robots with many joints.Symbolic task planning (G-2600)Symbolic task planning: Choosing a sequence of actions that reaches a goal, from a description of the world in true-or-false facts such as “the cup is on the table”; it decides the order of steps (go to the table, pick up, go to the door, put down) that a route search alone cannot. Explained in: Symbolic Task Planning: STRIPS and PDDL, §1. OverviewChoosing a sequence of actions that reaches a goal, from a description of the world in true-or-false facts such as “the cup is on the table”; it decides the order of steps (go to the table, pick up, go to the door, put down) that a route search alone cannot.Configuration (G-2286)Configuration: The list of numbers that fixes the position of every point of a robot, such as q = (x, y, \theta) = (2, 1, 0.524) for a floor robot or the joint angles (\theta_1, \theta_2) of a 2R arm; with it a planner treats the whole robot as one point. Explained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §2.1 The configuration: numbers that place every pointThe list of numbers that fixes the position of every point of a robot, such as q = (x, y, \theta) = (2, 1, 0.524) for a floor robot or the joint angles (\theta_1, \theta_2) of a 2R arm; with it a planner treats the whole robot as one point.Milestone (G-2781)Milestone: A free configuration kept as a vertex of a probabilistic roadmap, drawn at random; milestones are the places the roadmap’s routes pass through. Explained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §2.2 Phase 1 and phase 2: milestones and edgesA free configuration kept as a vertex of a probabilistic roadmap, drawn at random; milestones are the places the roadmap’s routes pass through.Minkowski sum (G-2653)Minkowski sum: The set of all sums of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \oplus B, like sweeping one shape over the other; the obstacle region of a robot that keeps its heading is the obstacle’s Minkowski sum with the robot reflected through its centre. Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §3.2 Minkowski sum and differenceThe set of all sums of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \oplus B, like sweeping one shape over the other; the obstacle region of a robot that keeps its heading is the obstacle’s Minkowski sum with the robot reflected through its centre.Narrow passage (G-2793)Narrow passage: A thin part of free space that a route must cross, such as a gap only slightly wider than the robot; uniform random samples rarely land in it, so roadmaps tend to split on either side. Explained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §6.1 The tray robot: where uniform samples starveA thin part of free space that a route must cross, such as a gap only slightly wider than the robot; uniform random samples rarely land in it, so roadmaps tend to split on either side.Multi-query planner (G-2786)Multi-query planner: A planner that invests time in a reusable description of the free space, such as a roadmap, so that many later problems in the same unchanged space are solved quickly. Explained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §3. Many trips on one roadmap: single-query and multi-query plannersA planner that invests time in a reusable description of the free space, such as a roadmap, so that many later problems in the same unchanged space are solved quickly.Lazy collision checking (G-2799)Lazy collision checking: Delaying an edge’s collision check until a candidate route uses it, deleting edges found to collide and searching again; it saves the checks of the many edges no route uses. Explained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §8. RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.title: Planning with Motion Limits
RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Differential-drive kinematicsExplained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §5.2 The kinematic model; Nonholonomic constraintsNonholonomic constraint: A rule on velocities that does not follow from any equation on the pose, such as a wheel that cannot slide sideways; it limits which way a robot can move at each moment but not which poses it can reach. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §6. The robot cannot slide sideways; Breadth-first searchBreadth-first search (BFS): A search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ring; Configuration spaceConfiguration space (C-space): The set of all configurations of a robot, one point per placement of the whole robot, such as a box of (x, y, \theta) whose top and bottom faces are the same headings for a floor robot; motion planning looks for paths through it. Explained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §2.2 The configuration space of the floor robot; Obstacle region and free spaceFree space: All configurations at which the robot touches no obstacle, C_{\text{free}}, the C-space without the obstacle region; a planner looks for a path that stays inside it. Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle; Rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT)Rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT): A sampling-based planner that grows a tree from the start: each round it draws a random configuration, steps the tree’s nearest node at most a fixed distance towards it and keeps the new node if the step is free, until the tree reaches the goal; it explores fast but its routes zig-zag. Explained in: Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees (RRT), §2.1 One step: sample, nearest node, steer, check.
Leads to: Hybrid A*Hybrid A:* A* over grid cells and heading ranges in which each state keeps the exact pose that reached it most cheaply and every move is an arc the car can drive, such as six 1.5 m arcs per pose; its path is drivable, but because it drops other poses in the same cell it is not guaranteed to be the cheapest. Explained in: Hybrid A* and Path Smoothing, §2. Hybrid A: states with a heading, moves the car can drive; State lattice and control setExplained in: State Lattices and Motion Primitives, §3.2 The control set; Trajectory optimisationTrajectory optimisation: Finding the controls over time (and the duration, if free) that minimise a cost such as time or effort while the motion rules, the start and end states and every limit hold; it computes one good trajectory where a rule for every state would be too large. Explained in: Trajectory Optimisation, §2.2 The best trajectory: cost and constraints.
Compare with: Trajectory optimisationTrajectory optimisation: Finding the controls over time (and the duration, if free) that minimise a cost such as time or effort while the motion rules, the start and end states and every limit hold; it computes one good trajectory where a rule for every state would be too large. Explained in: Trajectory Optimisation, §2.2 The best trajectory: cost and constraints.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The planners so far assume the robot can stop dead and turn on the spot at any moment, but at speed it can do neither: from 0.6 m/s it needs 0.36 m to stop, and at 0.5 m/s its tightest turn is a circle of 0.5 m. Planning with motion limits puts the speed into the state and builds every path from motions the robot can really drive.


The differential-drive robotExplained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §3. The differential-drive robot of RO-001, at (2, 1) facing 30° in the room, already has several ways to plan a route to the door:

A* (G-2577)A search:* Dijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid). Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.5 The algorithm on the 0.5 m grid gives a 3.414 m route of straight moves with 45° corners;
the drive checked in C-spaceExplained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2.4 The room in C-space, and the drive to the door turns on the spot to 61.9° and drives a straight 3.4 m to the doorway;
the rapidly-exploring random treeRapidly-exploring random tree (RRT): A sampling-based planner that grows a tree from the start: each round it draws a random configuration, steps the tree’s nearest node at most a fixed distance towards it and keeps the new node if the step is free, until the tree reaches the goal; it explores fast but its routes zig-zag. Explained in: Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees (RRT), §2. Growing a tree from random samples: RRT (RRT) (G-2761)Rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT): A sampling-based planner that grows a tree from the start: each round it draws a random configuration, steps the tree’s nearest node at most a fixed distance towards it and keeps the new node if the step is free, until the tree reaches the goal; it explores fast but its routes zig-zag. Explained in: Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees (RRT), §2.1 One step: sample, nearest node, steer, check grows straight edges towards random samples.

All three join straight pieces at corners, and each assumes the robot can stop at any point and turn there on the spot. The assumption held while we only asked where the robot could be. The assumption breaks once the robot moves at a useful speed, because its motors have limits. We give our robot two:

each wheel turns at most fast enough for 0.6 m/s over the floor;
the forward speed changes by at most 0.5 m/s every second, the acceleration limit.

Figure 1 plays what the limits do to two of these plans. Watch the left panel first: the plan drives at the top speed, 0.6 m/s, straight at the doorway, whose door is now closed, and stops at 3.0 m along the line. The robot cannot stop in an instant, so it brakes from 3.0 m and still meets the door at 0.49 m/s. Then the right panel: at 0.5 m/s the robot reaches the first 45° corner of A*‘s route and turns as fast as it can, 1 rad/s; it swings 0.146 m to the right of the route, onto floor the route never checked.

Figure 1: Two plans driven with the robot’s real limits. Left, stopping: on the straight line to the closed door, with s the distance along the line, the plan cruises at 0.6 m/s and stops at s = 3.0 m (pale robot); braking at 0.5 m/s² the robot reaches the door at s = 3.117 m still at 0.49 m/s (red). Right, turning: on A*‘s route at 0.5 m/s the plan turns 45° at the corner (2.75, 1.75) on the spot (pale robot); turning at its limit of 1 rad/s the robot swings 0.146 m to the right of the route. The last frame holds both outcomes
Where do 1 rad/s and the 0.5 m circle come from? By the inverse kinematics (G-2295)Inverse kinematics (wheeled robot): Working out the wheel speeds that give a wanted linear and angular velocity, used by a controller to command the motors. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §4.5 Back again: the wheel speeds for a wanted motion of RO-001, the outer wheel runs faster than the robot by the turn rate times half the wheel separation. At 0.5 m/s only 0.1 m/s of wheel speed is left for turning. With:

v, the robot’s linear velocity (G-2291)Linear velocity v: How fast a robot’s reference point (for a differential drive, the middle of the axle) moves along its heading, in m/s; for a differential drive, the average of the two wheel speeds, so it sets how fast the robot advances. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §4.1 Why we describe motion by linear and angular velocity, 0.5 m/s;
\omega, its angular velocity (G-2292)Angular velocity \omega: How fast a robot’s heading changes, in rad/s, positive to the left; for a differential drive, the difference of the wheel speeds divided by the wheel separation. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §4.1 Why we describe motion by linear and angular velocity, the turn rate, in rad/s;
L, the wheel separation, 0.2 m;
v_{\max}, the top wheel speed, 0.6 m/s;
R, the turning radius (G-2293)Turning radius R: The distance from the point a robot is turning about (the instantaneous centre of curvature, ICC) to the robot’s reference point; R = v / \omega, so it says how tight a turn is. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §4.2 Why the robot turns about a point on its axle line, in m.

The outer wheel at its top speed, our numbers first, then the same steps in symbols:
0.5 + \omega \times 0.1 = 0.6
v + \omega L/2 = v_{\max}
\omega = 0.1 / 0.1 = 1 \text{ rad/s}
\omega = 2\thinspace(v_{\max} - v)/L
R = 0.5 / 1 = 0.5 \text{ m}
R = v / \omega
The numbers are RO-001’s: wheels at 0.6 and 0.4 m/s give 0.5 m/s, 1 rad/s and a circle of 0.5 m. With the 0.6 m/s limit, that circle is now the tightest one the robot can drive at 0.5 m/s.
The opening question of this Note: how does the robot plan a drive to the door that it can follow at speed, stopping in time and turning only as tightly as its wheels allow? We answer it in two parts:

stopping: put the speed into what the planner tracks (Section 2), find the states from which a crash can no longer be avoided (Section 3), and search the fastest safe drive (Section 6);
turning: find where the robot can get to in a short time (Section 4), build paths from a few drivable motions (Section 5), learn the shortest drivable paths (Section 7), and grow an RRT out of drivable motions (Section 8).

2. Speed is part of the state: phase space


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Whether the robot can still stop before the door depends on its position and its speed together, so the planner must track both. The pair (position, speed) is a point of the phase space (G-2820)Phase space: The space of a robot’s configurations together with their speeds, such as the pairs (position, speed) of a robot driving along a line; planning there lets a planner tell a robot that can still stop from one that cannot. Explained in §2.2 The state, its motion equations and the stopping distance.; planning there with the limits on how the speed can change is kinodynamic planning (G-2821)Kinodynamic planning: Planning a motion that avoids obstacles and also obeys limits on how the state can change, \dot{x} = f(x, u) with bounded inputs, such as a top speed and an acceleration limit; its plans can be driven as they are, without stops the robot cannot make. Explained in §2.3 Kinodynamic planning..


2.1 Why position is not enough
The stopping part of the opening problem starts with a simple question: at s = 2.8 m along the line to the closed door, is the robot safe? Figure 2 answers it with two robots at that same place, both braking as hard as they can. Watch robot A at 0.3 m/s stop at 2.89 m. Robot B, at 0.6 m/s, is at the same place but meets the door at 3.117 m still moving at 0.21 m/s.
The right panel of Figure 2 draws the same two runs in a new picture. Position along the line goes across and speed goes up, so each robot at each moment is one point. Robot A starts at (2.8 m, 0.3 m/s) and robot B at (2.8 m, 0.6 m/s). Braking moves each point down, because the speed falls, and to the right, because the robot still moves forward. A’s point reaches the speed 0 before the door; B’s point reaches the door, the dark red band, above 0.

Figure 2: Two robots at the same place, s = 2.8 m along the line to the closed door (s, the distance from the start), brake at 0.5 m/s² from time 0. Left: robot A at 0.3 m/s (green) stops at s = 2.89 m; robot B at 0.6 m/s (purple) reaches the door at s = 3.117 m still at 0.21 m/s (red). Right: the same runs as points in the plane of position s (across, 2.0 to 3.4 m) and speed v (up); braking moves each point down and to the right along a curve; the dark red band is the door, every s from 3.117 m on. The last frame holds both outcomes
The same position gives two different futures. So the planner must keep the speed as well as the position: the two numbers together decide what the robot can still do, in the same way that the heading (G-2284)Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading joined the position in RO-001.
2.2 The state, its motion equations and the stopping distance
For the drive along the line we track two numbers, and the robot changes them through one input:

s, the position along the line from the start (2, 1), in m;
v, the speed along the line, in m/s, from 0 to 0.6 m/s;
u, the acceleration the robot commands, in m/s², from −0.5 to 0.5.

The pair (s, v) is the state of the drive. A space of configurations and their speeds, such as these pairs, is the phase space (G-2820)Phase space: The space of a robot’s configurations together with their speeds, such as the pairs (position, speed) of a robot driving along a line; planning there lets a planner tell a robot that can still stop from one that cannot. Explained in §2.2 The state, its motion equations and the stopping distance. (Hauser ch.11; LaValle §14.1.3). The picture on the right of Figure 2 is the phase space of the straight drive, also called the phase plane because it has two numbers.
Speed grows at the rate u, and position at the rate v. In the dot notation (G-2296)Dot notation \dot{x}: A dot over a quantity means its rate of change per second (its derivative with respect to time), such as \dot{x} = 0.433 m/s; models of motion are written with it. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §5.2 The kinematic model of RO-001, where a dot means “rate of change per second”:
\dot{s} = v
\dot{v} = u
Equations like these, which give the rate of change of each number of the state from the state and the input, are called differential equations. For any robot we write them in one line (Hauser ch.11; MR §10.5), with:

\mathbf x, the state, such as (s, v), in bold so that it is not confused with the x coordinate;
u, the input, such as the acceleration;
f, the function that gives the rates from the state and the input, here (v, u).

\dot{\mathbf x} = f(\mathbf x, u)
The stopping distance. How much room does braking need? Braking at the full 0.5 m/s², the speed falls steadily to 0, so its average over the stop is half the starting speed. For robot B:

v, the speed when braking starts, 0.6 m/s;
a, the braking rate, the acceleration limit, 0.5 m/s²;
t, the time to stop, in s;
d, the distance travelled while stopping, in m.

Our numbers first, then the same steps in symbols:
t = 0.6 / 0.5 = 1.2 \text{ s}
t = v / a
d = (0.6 / 2) \times 1.2
d = (v / 2) \times t
d = 0.3 \times 1.2 = 0.36 \text{ m}
d = v^2 / (2a)
Robot B has this much room left before the door:
3.117 - 2.8 = 0.317 \text{ m}
less than the 0.36 m it needs (notebook). Robot A, at 0.3 m/s, needs only 0.09 m of the same 0.317 m.
2.3 Kinodynamic planning
The planners of chapter RO-04 searched the configuration space (G-2287)Configuration space (C-space): The set of all configurations of a robot, one point per placement of the whole robot, such as a box of (x, y, \theta) whose top and bottom faces are the same headings for a floor robot; motion planning looks for paths through it. Explained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §2.2 The configuration space of the floor robot: they asked only where the robot could be, and assumed it could move between any two nearby configurations. With motion limits, the planner searches the state space (G-2545)State space: All the states a problem can be in, joined by the moves between them, such as the robot’s 76 cells or the arrangements of a Rubik’s cube; it is a graph, so planning becomes finding a path from the start state to a goal state. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §2.2 Any problem of states and moves is a graph, all the states the problem can be in, here configurations with their speeds, and may only use motions that the motion equations produce with allowed inputs. Planning a path that respects both the obstacles and these limits on how the state can change is kinodynamic planning (G-2821)Kinodynamic planning: Planning a motion that avoids obstacles and also obeys limits on how the state can change, \dot{x} = f(x, u) with bounded inputs, such as a top speed and an acceleration limit; its plans can be driven as they are, without stops the robot cannot make. Explained in §2.3 Kinodynamic planning. (Hauser ch.11). The name was first used for planning with bounds on velocity and acceleration, as on our straight drive, and now covers any planning with such limits on how the state changes (LaValle §14.1.2.1).
Formally, with:

\mathbf x(t), the state at time t, such as (s, v) for the straight drive;
u(t), the input at time t, inside its allowed set, such as u between −0.5 and 0.5 m/s²;
X_{\text{free}}, the states that touch no obstacle;
\mathbf x_I, the start state, such as rest at the start: (0 m, 0 m/s);
X_G, the set of goal states, such as rest in front of the door;
T, the time the drive takes, in s.

a kinodynamic plan is a pair of curves \mathbf x(t) and u(t), for t from 0 to T, such that the four lines below hold (Hauser ch.11). The sign \in reads “is in”; for example, robot A’s state, (2.8 m, 0.3 m/s), is in X_{\text{free}}.
\mathbf x(t) \in X_{\text{free}} \text{ for every } t
\dot{\mathbf x}(t) = f(\mathbf x(t), u(t))
\mathbf x(0) = \mathbf x_I
\mathbf x(T) \in X_G
The first line keeps the robot off obstacles; the second allows only motions the robot can make. The rest of the Note builds such plans. First we need to know which states X_{\text{free}} really leaves out: robot B at 2.8 m touches nothing yet, but it is already lost.
3. States that are already lost: inevitable collision states


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Some states touch no obstacle yet cannot avoid one, because every input leads into the door; such states form the region of inevitable collision (G-2823)Region of inevitable collision (inevitable collision states): The free states from which every allowed input sooner or later leads into an obstacle, such as a robot at 0.6 m/s with only 0.317 m left before a wall when it needs 0.36 m to stop; it grows with the square of the speed, so fast robots must keep well out of it. Explained in §3.2 The region of inevitable collision.. On the straight drive the region holds every state whose stopping distance is longer than the room left, so it grows with the square of the speed.


3.1 Obstacles in phase space
Robot B of Figure 2 hit the door from a state that looked free. To see why, we first mark the states that are plainly forbidden. The door stops the disk at s = 3.117 m, whatever the speed: the obstacle region (G-2650)Obstacle region (C-obstacle): The set of all configurations at which the robot’s body touches or overlaps an obstacle, C_{\text{obs}}; drawing it in C-space lets a planner test a placement as one point, such as the disk robot’s centre (3.5, 3.2), which lies in it 0.2 m from the table. Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle of the line is every s from 3.117 m on. In the phase plane it becomes the band of every state (s, v) with that s and any speed v, the dark red band of Figures 2 and 3. The set of states whose configuration touches an obstacle, at any speed, is the obstacle region in phase space (G-2822)Obstacle region in phase space: Every state whose configuration touches an obstacle, at any speed, such as every (position, speed) from 3.117 m on in front of a closed door; a kinodynamic plan must stay out of it. Explained in §3.1 Obstacles in phase space. (LaValle §14.1.3). The top speed adds a second kind of limit: no state above 0.6 m/s is allowed (LaValle §14.1.3.1).
3.2 The region of inevitable collision

6. Searching the primitives systematically: lattice search


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

When every primitive changes the state by whole multiples of a fixed step, all reachable states fall on a regular grid, a lattice, and any graph search can explore it. On the straight drive, breadth-first search finds the fastest safe drive to the door: 7.0 s on a lattice with 0.5 s steps, against 6.2 s for the true best.


Section 3 told us where braking must start; it did not give the fastest drive that stops in front of the door. We search for it with primitives of the straight drive: every 0.5 s the robot accelerates at 0.5 m/s², coasts, or brakes at 0.5 m/s².

u, the acceleration, 0.5, 0 or −0.5 m/s²;

s' = s + v\thinspace\Delta t + \frac{1}{2}u\thinspace\Delta t^2

0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25 \text{ m/s}

7. The shortest drivable paths: Dubins and Reeds-Shepp curves


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

For a vehicle that cannot turn tighter than a circle of radius 0.5 m, the shortest path between two poses on an open floor is made of full-lock arcs and straight lines: at most three pieces from a list of six words when it only drives forward (Dubins path, G-2828)Dubins path (Dubins curve): The shortest path between two poses for a vehicle that drives forward only and turns no tighter than a given radius: at most three pieces, full-lock arcs and a straight line, one of the words LSL, RSR, LSR, RSL, LRL, RLR; it is the best forward drive on an empty floor. Explained in §7.1 Dubins paths: forward only., at most five pieces with two reversals when it may reverse (Reeds-Shepp path, G-2829)Reeds-Shepp path (Reeds-Shepp curve): The shortest path between two poses for a vehicle that turns no tighter than a given radius but may also reverse: at most five full-lock arcs and straight pieces with at most two reversals, from 48 words in nine families; planners use it to join two poses exactly with a drivable path. Explained in §7.2 Reeds-Shepp paths: with reverse.. Both ignore obstacles, so planners use them to connect nearby poses.


7.1 Dubins paths: forward only
The robot at (2, 1) facing 30° at 0.5 m/s must reach the pose in front of the door, (3.6, 3.5) facing 90°, without stopping. What is the shortest path it can drive, if we forget the furniture for a moment?
When our robot keeps moving forward at 0.5 m/s, it moves like a car that drives forward only and cannot turn tighter than a circle of radius 0.5 m. At rest our robot could spin on the spot instead, and its shortest path would then be turn, drive straight, turn (MR §13.3.3); at speed it cannot.
Dubins proved in 1957 that the shortest path is made of at most three pieces, each an arc of the tightest circle or a straight line (MR §13.3.3, Theorem 13.11). Write L for a full left turn, R for a full right turn and S for straight; a path is then a three-letter word (MR §13.3.3). Why only six words?

Three letters from L, S and R give 27 words.
Two equal letters in a row are one piece, so we drop them, which leaves 12.
A word that starts or ends with S cannot be shortest: turning first and then going straight is never longer than going straight and turning later. Dubins’s theorem lists only words that turn at both ends (MR §13.3.3, Theorem 13.11). Six words are left: LSL, RSR, LSR, RSL, LRL and RLR.
