Distances that ignore the motion limits can badly misjudge which pose is near (MR §10.5; Hauser ch.11). Section 8 meets this problem again.
7.3 Using them in a planner: a drivable steer
Dubins and Reeds-Shepp paths are exact but blind to obstacles; planners are aware of obstacles but need drivable pieces. The two meet in the planner’s steer (G-2763)Steer (steering function): The step of a sampling-based planner that moves from a tree node towards a sample, at most a fixed distance (0.5 m here), stopping on the sample if it is closer; it keeps every new edge short enough to check. Explained in: Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees (RRT), §2.1 One step: sample, nearest node, steer, check, the step that moves from one configuration towards another, in RO-051 along a straight line. For a car the steer must return a drivable path that ends exactly on the target pose, or report that it cannot; such a steer is a local planner (G-2782)Local planner: The fast method a sampling planner uses to try to join two configurations, usually the straight segment; it proposes one simple motion without searching round obstacles, and a collision check reports whether that motion is free. Explained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §2.2 Phase 1 and phase 2: milestones and edges, the fast method that tries to join two configurations with one simple motion (Hauser ch.11; MR §10.5). The Reeds-Shepp path is a natural choice (Hauser ch.11; MR §10.5), and Hybrid A*‘s shot to the goalExplained in: Hybrid A* and Path Smoothing, §4. The Reeds-Shepp shot to the goal uses it to reach a parking pose exactly.
One way to use it turns any free route of straight pieces into a drivable path (MR §13.3.3). Take a route that is free but has corners, such as A*‘s: here three straight pieces from the start round the table’s left side to the pose in front of the door. Join its two ends with a Reeds-Shepp path. If that path hits an obstacle, cut the route at its middle, take the route’s pose there (its point, facing along the route), and join each half the same way. Repeat on every half that fails. Figure 10 runs it; watch the red tries fail and the green ones stay.

Figure 10: Turning a free route of three straight pieces (black, dotted) into a drivable path with Reeds-Shepp pieces for the tightest circle of 0.5 m. Each try joins two poses of the route (black arrows): red when the path hits an obstacle grown by 0.25 m (orange), green when it is free. Try 1, start to goal, L+ S+ L+ 2.992 m, hits the grown table; try 2, the first half, is free; try 3, the second half, hits; tries 4 and 5, the two quarters, are free. Last frame: the drivable path (blue), 3 pieces, 3.893 m, with 3 reversals
Five tries give a drivable path of three pieces, 3.893 m, with 3 reversals (notebook). Halving always ends for a car that can reverse, because the route has some free space around it, the car can follow any path as closely as we like by shuffling, and the Reeds-Shepp paths between ever closer poses become ever shorter, so they stay near the route (MR §13.3.3). The result is drivable, but its three reversals mean three stops, and this method needs reverse. For the robot that keeps moving forward we need a planner that builds paths out of the forward primitives themselves.
8. Growing a tree of drivable motions: kinodynamic RRT


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The kinodynamic RRT grows a tree whose every edge is a primitive run through the simulator: it samples a state, takes the nearest tree node, tries the primitives from it and keeps the one that comes closest, if its motion is free. Every path in the tree is drivable by construction; in the room it reaches the goal region in front of the door with 8 primitives, 3.0 m, at 0.5 m/s without a stop.


The RRTRRT:* RRT with two extra moves per round: the new node takes as parent the nearby node that gives it the shortest route from the start, and nearby nodes are rewired through it when that is shorter; its route converges to the shortest as samples grow. Explained in: Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees (RRT), §2.1 One step: sample, nearest node, steer, check grows a tree from the start towards random samples, each new edge a straight step towards the sample. For our moving robot a straight edge is the problem we started with: it may ask for a sideways move or a turn on the spot. The fix keeps the RRT’s loop and changes only how an edge is made (MR §10.5; LaValle 1998):

Sample a state at random; one time in ten, take the goal pose instead, a goal bias (G-2764)Goal bias: The small probability (0.05 here) with which a sampling-based planner uses the goal itself as its next sample, so the tree keeps trying to reach the goal; too large a bias makes it greedy, too small leaves it wandering. Explained in: Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees (RRT), §2.4 The algorithm and the goal bias of 0.1, to pull the tree towards it.
Find the nearest node (G-2762)Nearest node: The node of a planner’s tree closest to a new sample under the planner’s distance; RRT extends it, which makes the tree grow towards the largest empty regions. Explained in: Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees (RRT), §2.1 One step: sample, nearest node, steer, check to the sample, by RO-038’s distance, which counts 0.25 m for each radian of turn.
In place of the straight steer, run each of the three primitives of Section 5 from that node through the simulator, and keep the one whose end comes closest to the sample.
If its whole motion stays in free space, add its end as a new node, with the primitive as the edge; otherwise throw it away.
Stop when a new node lands in the goal region.

An RRT whose edges are simulated motions is a kinodynamic RRT (G-2832)Kinodynamic RRT: A rapidly-exploring random tree whose edges are motion primitives run through the system simulator: it samples a state, takes the nearest node, keeps the primitive that ends closest if its motion is free; every path it returns is drivable. Explained in §8. Growing a tree of drivable motions: kinodynamic RRT. (LaValle §14.4.3; Hauser ch.11). Figure 11 runs it in the room, with the obstacles grown by the robot’s radius. Watch the first frames: the red cross is the sample, the black dot the nearest node, the grey arcs the three primitives tried, the thick one the closest, green if kept and red if thrown away. Then the frames jump 15 iterations at a time.

Figure 11: The kinodynamic RRT in the room (seed 4), from (2, 1) facing 30° at 0.5 m/s, obstacles grown by 0.25 m (orange). In each of the first 12 frames: the sample (red cross and arrow), the nearest tree node (black dot), the three primitives tried from it (grey), and the one that ends closest to the sample, green when free and added, red when it would hit an obstacle and is thrown away. Later frames jump 15 iterations. The goal region (purple dashed circle): within 0.25 m and 25° of (3.6, 3.5) facing 90°. Last frame: after 221 iterations, 147 of them thrown away, the tree has 75 nodes and the path to the goal region (blue) is 8 primitives, 3.0 m
After 221 iterations, 147 of them thrown away, the tree has 75 nodes and a node lies in the goal region: 0.243 m from (3.6, 3.5), facing 73° (notebook). Its path is 8 primitives, 3.0 m: left, left, right, right, left, right, straight, left. Each is a 0.5 m/s motion with a turn rate of at most 1 rad/s, so the robot drives it without a stop, and it passes left of the table where the Dubins path of Figure 8 went through it. The run shown is typical: over 20 seeds, 18 reached the goal region within 4000 nodes, with a median of 76.5 nodes and a median path of 3.375 m (notebook).
Three details explain the method’s behaviour:

A goal region, not a goal pose. Chains of fixed primitives almost never land exactly on one pose, so the tree aims at a small region around it (Hauser ch.11). A drivable steer, such as the Reeds-Shepp path of Section 7.3, can then join the last node to the exact pose.
Many throw-aways. Choosing the primitive that comes closest often points it into an obstacle; 147 of 221 tries were thrown away. The Modern Robotics book keeps instead the closest free one (MR §10.5.1.3).
The distance misleads. RO-038’s distance prefers a node beside the sample, which, as Section 7.2 showed, may be a whole loop away for a robot that cannot reverse. A distance closer to the true driving distance makes the tree grow better, and finding one is a known difficulty of kinodynamic RRT (MR §10.5; Hauser ch.11).

The kinodynamic RRT answers the turning part of the opening question: it plans in the room with only motions the robot can drive at speed. Its path is not the shortest, and random sampling gives a different path each run.

Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §5.3 Why we predict the path step by stepOne step of predicting motion: hold the rates fixed for a short time \Delta t and add rate times \Delta t to each quantity; repeated, it traces a path, more accurately the smaller \Delta t is.Kinematic model (G-2297)Kinematic model: Equations that give how a robot’s configuration changes from its speed inputs alone, ignoring masses and forces, such as \dot{x} = v\cos\theta, \dot{y} = v\sin\theta, \dot{\theta} = \omega; used to predict motion at low speed. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §5.2 The kinematic modelEquations that give how a robot’s configuration changes from its speed inputs alone, ignoring masses and forces, such as \dot{x} = v\cos\theta, \dot{y} = v\sin\theta, \dot{\theta} = \omega; used to predict motion at low speed.Breadth-first search (BFS) (G-2550)Breadth-first search (BFS): A search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ringA search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same.Metric (distance function) (G-2681)Metric (distance function): A distance between points that is never negative, is 0 only between equal points, is the same both ways and obeys the triangle inequality; search trees rely on these rules to skip far regions safely. Explained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §7.1 The rules a distance must followA distance between points that is never negative, is 0 only between equal points, is the same both ways and obeys the triangle inequality; search trees rely on these rules to skip far regions safely.Steer (steering function) (G-2763)Steer (steering function): The step of a sampling-based planner that moves from a tree node towards a sample, at most a fixed distance (0.5 m here), stopping on the sample if it is closer; it keeps every new edge short enough to check. Explained in: Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees (RRT), §2.1 One step: sample, nearest node, steer, checkThe step of a sampling-based planner that moves from a tree node towards a sample, at most a fixed distance (0.5 m here), stopping on the sample if it is closer; it keeps every new edge short enough to check.Local planner (G-2782)Local planner: The fast method a sampling planner uses to try to join two configurations, usually the straight segment; it proposes one simple motion without searching round obstacles, and a collision check reports whether that motion is free. Explained in: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM), §2.2 Phase 1 and phase 2: milestones and edgesThe fast method a sampling planner uses to try to join two configurations, usually the straight segment; it proposes one simple motion without searching round obstacles, and a collision check reports whether that motion is free.Goal bias (G-2764)Goal bias: The small probability (0.05 here) with which a sampling-based planner uses the goal itself as its next sample, so the tree keeps trying to reach the goal; too large a bias makes it greedy, too small leaves it wandering. Explained in: Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees (RRT), §2.4 The algorithm and the goal biasThe small probability (0.05 here) with which a sampling-based planner uses the goal itself as its next sample, so the tree keeps trying to reach the goal; too large a bias makes it greedy, too small leaves it wandering.Nearest node (G-2762)Nearest node: The node of a planner’s tree closest to a new sample under the planner’s distance; RRT extends it, which makes the tree grow towards the largest empty regions. Explained in: Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees (RRT), §2.1 One step: sample, nearest node, steer, checkThe node of a planner’s tree closest to a new sample under the planner’s distance; RRT extends it, which makes the tree grow towards the largest empty regions.

RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.title: Hybrid A* and Path Smoothing
RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Gradient descentGradient descent: Finding the lowest point of a function by repeated small steps downhill. Explained in: Gradient Descent from Scratch, §2. The idea; A* searchA search:* Dijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid). Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.5 The algorithm; Admissible heuristicAdmissible heuristic: A heuristic that is never more than the true cost left from any state, h \le h^\ast; it makes f a lower bound on every route through a state, so the first route A* takes off the open list is the shortest. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §5.1 A guess that never overestimates; Dubins and Reeds-Shepp pathsExplained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §7. The shortest drivable paths: Dubins and Reeds-Shepp curves; Motion primitives and lattice searchMotion primitive: A short motion the robot can drive, usually one input held for a fixed time, such as full left at 0.5 m/s for 0.75 s; planners chain primitives so that every path they build is drivable. Explained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §5. A few motions to build with: motion primitives and a system simulator.
Compare with: State lattice and control setExplained in: State Lattices and Motion Primitives, §3.2 The control set.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A route found on a grid joins cell centres with sharp corners and ignores which way the car faces, so a car that cannot turn on the spot cannot drive it. Hybrid A* searches the same grid, but every step is an arc the car can drive and every state keeps its exact pose; a short smoothing pass then removes needless steering.


The robot can already plan on a grid. A* (G-2577)A search:* Dijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid). Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.5 The algorithm finds the shortest route through a grid of cells, guided by a guess of the distance left. The robot can also build motions it can drive: short pieces of the turning circle, the motion primitives (G-2826)Motion primitive: A short motion the robot can drive, usually one input held for a fixed time, such as full left at 0.5 m/s for 0.75 s; planners chain primitives so that every path they build is drivable. Explained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §5. A few motions to build with: motion primitives and a system simulator, and the shortest drivable path between two poses when reversing is allowed, the Reeds-Shepp path (G-2829)Reeds-Shepp path (Reeds-Shepp curve): The shortest path between two poses for a vehicle that turns no tighter than a given radius but may also reverse: at most five full-lock arcs and straight pieces with at most two reversals, from 48 words in nine families; planners use it to join two poses exactly with a drivable path. Explained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §7.2 Reeds-Shepp paths: with reverse.
This Note plans for a car, so the world changes from the room to a parking lot: a car parks, and a car cannot spin on the spot. A car steers its front wheels and turns about a point on the line of its rear axle; how far it can steer sets the radius of its tightest circle (car-like robots, RO-003; MR §13.3.1). Our car:

is 4.0 m long and 1.8 m wide, with its rear axle 0.75 m from the rear bumper;
has 2.5 m between its axles;
cannot drive a circle tighter than 5 m, measured at the middle of the rear axle.

We describe the car by its pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading: the position of the middle of its rear axle and its heading (G-2284)Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, the direction it faces.
The lot is 24 m by 24 m (Figure 1). A lower lane runs along the bottom wall; a middle row of six parked cars separates it from an upper lane; the two lanes meet at the right end. Along the top wall, nine bays 2.5 m wide hold parked cars, except one. The car starts in the lower lane at (2, 3), facing along x (0°). The car must back into the empty bay, nose out, ending at (12, 23) facing down (−90°).
What breaks is the grid route. Figure 1 runs A* on 1 m cells and lets the car follow the result. Watch the green car leave the start and turn as hard as it can towards the blue route:

Figure 1: The lot with 1 m cells (grey: cells that touch a parked car or a wall), the A* route of 33.31 m through cell centres (blue dots), the target bay (orange dashed) and the goal pose (orange outline, nose down). The car (green) follows the route at 1 m/s, steering towards the route point 2 m ahead and never tighter than its 5 m circle; its rear axle leaves a dark green trail. Last frame: after 4.05 m its body (red) overlaps the third parked car of the middle row
The car hits a parked car after 4.05 m. The route fails in three ways:

it was planned for a point, while the car is 4.0 m long and 1.8 m wide;
it has 8 corners, where it turns by 45° or 90° within one cell, and the car’s tightest turn is a 5 m circle;
its last move heads up the bay (90°), nose first, while the goal is nose out (−90°).

This Note builds a planner whose every step the car can drive:

Hybrid A*: A* whose states carry a heading and whose moves are arcs the car can drive (Section 2);
the two guesses of the cost left that keep its search small (Section 3);
a shot to the goal along a Reeds-Shepp path, which lands exactly on the goal (Section 4);
smoothing, which takes the corners out of a route, and why it cannot rescue the grid route but does improve Hybrid A*‘s path (Section 5).

2. Hybrid A*: states with a heading, moves the car can drive


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Hybrid A* runs A* on the cells of the grid, but each state also has a heading, and each move is an arc of 1.5 m that the car can drive. Each cell and heading range keeps the cheapest exact pose that reached it, so the path is drivable from end to end.


2.1 Six arcs from every pose
The grid route failed because its moves were jumps between cell centres. The fix is to let the search move only the way the car moves. A* that searches over the grid’s cells, but whose states carry a heading and an exact pose and whose moves are arcs the car can drive, is Hybrid A* (G-2840)Hybrid A:* A* over grid cells and heading ranges in which each state keeps the exact pose that reached it most cheaply and every move is an arc the car can drive, such as six 1.5 m arcs per pose; its path is drivable, but because it drops other poses in the same cell it is not guaranteed to be the cheapest. Explained in §2.1 Six arcs from every pose. (Dolgov et al. 2008).
From any pose the car can drive forward or in reverse, and steer full left, straight, or full right. Each of these six choices, held for 1.5 m, is a short arc of the 5 m circle or a straight piece: six of RO-054’s motion primitives (G-2826)Motion primitive: A short motion the robot can drive, usually one input held for a fixed time, such as full left at 0.5 m/s for 0.75 s; planners chain primitives so that every path they build is drivable. Explained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §5. A few motions to build with: motion primitives and a system simulator, short motions the car can drive, each one input held for a fixed length. Junior, the Stanford car that used this planner in the 2007 DARPA Urban Challenge, chose between forward and reverse moves of different steering in the same way (Dolgov et al. 2008). Figure 2 draws them from the start.
Make interactive
Figure 2: The first expansion: the six arcs of 1.5 m from the start pose (2, 3), facing 0°. The three forward arcs (blue) end at (3.478, 3.223) facing +17.2°, (3.500, 3.000) facing 0° and (3.478, 2.777) facing −17.2°; the cells they end in are shaded blue. The three reverse arcs (red) are blocked: after the straight reverse arc the body (red outline) pokes through the left wall
Two numbers fix the arcs. A turning arc follows the 5 m circle, so it turns the heading by the arc length divided by the radius (the arc ruleExplained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.3 Why angles are measured in radians, RO-001):
\frac{1.5}{5} = 0.3 \text{ rad}
= 17.2^\circ
The arc is 1.5 m long so that every move leaves its cell: a cell of 1 m is at most 1.414 m across, its diagonal. Modern Robotics asks the same of its grid planner for wheeled robots: the cells as large as possible, but every motion must move the robot out of its cell (MR §10.4.2).
Where an arc ends follows from the pose and the circle, as RO-054’s system simulator (G-2825)System simulator: The module that works out where an input takes the robot, by stepping its motion equations forward, such as 75 Euler steps of 0.01 s; planners call it to turn inputs into motions they can check for collisions. Explained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §5. A few motions to build with: motion primitives and a system simulator works it out. For the left arc from the start, with:

x and y the start position, (2, 3) m;
\theta the start heading, 0 rad;
\rho the radius of the circle, 5 m;
\Delta\theta the turn of the arc, 0.3 rad;
x' and y' the end position, in m.

Numbers first, then the same in symbols:
x' = 2 + 5 \times (\sin 0.3 - \sin 0)
= 2 + 5 \times 0.29552 = 3.478
y' = 3 - 5 \times (\cos 0.3 - \cos 0)
= 3 + 5 \times 0.04466 = 3.223
x' = x + \rho\thinspace(\sin(\theta + \Delta\theta) - \sin\theta)
y' = y - \rho\thinspace(\cos(\theta + \Delta\theta) - \cos\theta)
The steering for that circle is the car’s largest steering angle. With 2.5 m between the axles it is the angle whose tangent is 2.5 divided by 5 (MR §13.3.1, eq. 13.16):
\tan^{-1}(2.5 / 5) = 26.6^\circ
2.2 A state is a cell and a heading range
A* needs states it can recognise again. Hybrid A* uses the grid’s cells for that: 1 m cells centred on whole metres, and the heading cut into 72 ranges of 5° (Dolgov et al. used 5°; it is also Nav2’s default). A state is a cell plus a heading range, but it stores the car’s exact pose inside them (Dolgov et al., Fig. 2). Figure 2 shades the cells the forward arcs end in: the left and right arcs both end in the cell centred on (3, 3), in different heading ranges, so they are two states.
Then the search is A*Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.5 The algorithm, step for step. Each state has three numbers:

g, its cost so far (G-2574)Cost so far g (g-value): The length of the best route found so far from the start to a state; A* lowers it whenever a shorter way into the state turns up. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.1 g, h and f on the first step, the cost of the best way found to it, in m;
h, a guess of the cost left from it to the goal, in m;
f, its estimated total cost (G-2575)Estimated total cost f (f-value): The cost so far plus the heuristic, f = g + h: the length of the best route through a state if the guess were exact; A* expands the open state with the smallest f. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.1 g, h and f on the first step, their sum, in m.

f = g + h
The state with the smallest f comes off the open list (G-2547)Frontier (open list): The vertices a search has reached but not yet expanded, waiting to be taken off one at a time; which one comes off next is what makes one search differ from another. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §4. Searching with a frontier and a visited list, the states reached but not yet expanded, and is expanded by driving its six arcs. Each arc is checked along its length, every 0.25 m, for the body touching a parked car or a wall (as in checking a path segmentExplained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §6.2 Step size and order), with the body grown by 0.1 m on every side as a safety margin (a grown body makes the check conservative, MR §10.9).
The first expansion, with the guess h of Section 3, the larger of two guesses of the distance left:













































ArcEnd poseCell, heading rangeg (m)h (m)f (m)forward, left(3.478, 3.223), 17.2°(3, 3), 15°1.532.31433.814forward, straight(3.500, 3.000), 0°(4, 3), 0°1.531.31432.814forward, right(3.478, 2.777), −17.2°(3, 3), 345°1.532.31433.814reverse (all three)x about 0.5———blocked by the wall
The straight arc has the smallest f, so it is expanded next. The search goes on like this until it reaches the goal.
2.3 Why one pose per state, and what it costs
Without states the search would be a tree of arcs, and trees explode. Every pose has six children, so after five arcs there are six to the fifth power arc ends:
6^5 = 7776
Yet those 7,776 ends fall into only 455 different cells and heading ranges (notebook, obstacles ignored). Many ends are nearly the same pose. Figure 3 shows three of them: left then right, right then left, and straight then straight all end facing 0° inside the cell centred on (5, 3).
Make interactive
Figure 3: Three two-arc drives from the start: left then right (blue) ends at (4.955, 3.447), right then left (purple) at (4.955, 2.553), straight then straight (orange) at (5.000, 3.000). All three end facing 0° inside the cell centred on (5, 3) (orange). Hybrid A* keeps only one of the three poses
Hybrid A* treats poses in one cell and heading range as the same state, as if each pose were rounded to its cell: a new arrival is kept only if its cost so far is lower than the pose already stored there; otherwise it is dropped. The three drives of Figure 3 cost the same, so the first one stored stays.
Merging keeps the search finite, but it has a price. The dropped poses are real, different positions; the best route might have passed through one of them. So Hybrid A* is not guaranteed to find the least-cost path (Dolgov et al. 2008: “not guaranteed to find the minimal-cost solution, due to its merging of continuous-coordinate states that occupy the same cell”). What it does guarantee is a path made only of arcs the car can drive.
2.4 What a path costs
Distance alone would let the car reverse as much as it likes. Dolgov et al. penalise driving in reverse and switching between forward and reverse. We use:

each metre forward costs 1;
each metre in reverse costs 2 (Nav2’s default reverse penalty);
each switch between forward and reverse, which means a stop, adds 2 m.

The search stops when a state lands in the goal’s cell with a heading within 10° of the goal heading. Run this way, with the guess of Section 3, the search expands 1,949 states and stops 0.54 m and 5° from the goal (Figure 4): it reached the right cell, but not the exact pose.
Make interactive
Figure 4: Zoom on the target bay after Hybrid A* without the shot of Section 4: the path (blue) and the car where the search stopped (green), 0.54 m and 5° from the goal pose (orange outline); the goal’s cell is shaded orange
The arcs turn the heading in steps of 17.2°, and no whole number of such steps from 0° makes exactly −90°, so an arc-only search cannot end exactly on the goal. Section 3 makes the search smaller; Section 4 makes it land exactly.
3. Two guesses of the cost left


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Hybrid A* is guided by the larger of two guesses of the cost left: the length of the shortest Reeds-Shepp path, which knows the car must turn but not where the parked cars are, and the grid distance, which knows the parked cars but not the turning. Each covers the other’s blind spot.


The search of Section 2 expands 1,949 states to cross the lot, and how many it expands depends on its guess of the cost left. The guess must never overestimate the cost left, or A* can stop on a dearer path (admissible heuristicsAdmissible heuristic: A heuristic that is never more than the true cost left from any state, h \le h^\ast; it makes f a lower bound on every route through a state, so the first route A* takes off the open list is the shortest. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §5. Why A returns the shortest route: admissible heuristics, G-2578)Admissible heuristic: A heuristic that is never more than the true cost left from any state, h \le h^\ast; it makes f a lower bound on every route through a state, so the first route A* takes off the open list is the shortest. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §5.1 A guess that never overestimates. The closer the guess comes to the true cost, the fewer states A* expands (a closer guess takes fewer cellsExplained in: A* and Heuristics, §5.3 A closer guess takes fewer cells). From the start, the path Hybrid A* finds costs 50.8 (Section 4). Figure 5 draws what three cheap guesses imagine.
Make interactive
Figure 5: Three guesses of the distance left from the start (green) to the goal (orange): the straight line (grey, dotted), 22.36 m; the shortest Reeds-Shepp path (purple), 27.31 m, which first backs up to turn and then drives through the middle row of parked cars; the shortest grid route (blue), 33.31 m, around the end of the middle row but with corners and no heading
The straight line. The first guess is the Euclidean distance (G-715)Euclidean distance: The straight-line distance between two points. Explained in: Handling Missing Data: KNN Imputer, §4.1 The Euclidean distance from the start to the goal, which is 10 m along x and 20 m along y away:
\sqrt{10^2 + 20^2} = \sqrt{500}
= 22.36 \text{ m}
The straight line ignores both the parked cars and the heading.
The Reeds-Shepp length. The shortest path of a car that may reverse, between two poses on an empty floor, is a Reeds-Shepp path (G-2829)Reeds-Shepp path (Reeds-Shepp curve): The shortest path between two poses for a vehicle that turns no tighter than a given radius but may also reverse: at most five full-lock arcs and straight pieces with at most two reversals, from 48 words in nine families; planners use it to join two poses exactly with a drivable path. Explained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §7.2 Reeds-Shepp paths: with reverse, made of arcs of the tightest circle and straight pieces: 27.31 m from the start. The Reeds-Shepp length knows the car must turn round to arrive nose out. The Reeds-Shepp length ignores the parked cars, so it can never be longer than the real path: it is the shortest of all drivable paths, and the real path is one of them (Dolgov et al. call it the non-holonomic-without-obstacles heuristic).
The grid distance. Dijkstra’s algorithm (G-2565)Dijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §3.2 The algorithm: settle the nearest, update its neighbours, run once from the goal cell over the free cells, gives every cell its distance to the goal along the grid: 33.31 m from the start cell, the route of Figure 1. The grid distance knows the middle row blocks the way, but it ignores the heading (Dolgov et al.’s holonomic-with-obstacles heuristic).
The larger of the two. Dolgov et al. show that neither guess overestimates the cost, so their larger value does not either, and at every state it is at least as close to the true cost as each of them. Run without the shot of Section 4, and stopping as in Section 2.4:






























Guess hAt the start (m)States expandedstraight line22.362,318Reeds-Shepp length27.312,006grid distance33.312,011larger of Reeds-Shepp and grid33.311,949
In this lot the gain is modest, because the long way round the middle row dominates. In open lots, where the heading matters most, Dolgov et al. measured a far larger gain: 21,515 states with the straight line and 1,465 with the Reeds-Shepp length; in a maze with dead ends, the Reeds-Shepp length alone expanded 68,730 states and the larger of the two only 10,588.
The search is now guided, but it still stops in the goal’s cell rather than on the goal, 0.54 m away, after 1,949 expansions.
4. The Reeds-Shepp shot to the goal


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Every few expansions, Hybrid A* tries the shortest Reeds-Shepp path from the pose it is expanding to the exact goal. When that path hits nothing, the search is done: it ends exactly on the goal, after 312 expansions instead of 1,949.


The arcs of Section 2 can only approach the goal in steps of 1.5 m and 17.2°. A Reeds-Shepp path lands exactly on any pose, but knows nothing of obstacles. Hybrid A* combines them: from time to time it takes the pose it is expanding, computes the Reeds-Shepp path from there to the goal, and checks that path for collisions like an arc. If it is free, the path is complete (Dolgov et al. 2008). RO-054 uses Reeds-Shepp paths the same way, as a drivable steerExplained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §7.3 Using them in a planner: a drivable steer: the step that joins two poses with a drivable path, or reports that it cannot.
This extra child is the analytic expansion (G-2841)Analytic expansion (Reeds-Shepp shot): An extra child that Hybrid A* tries every few expansions: the shortest Reeds-Shepp path from the pose being expanded to the exact goal, kept if it hits nothing; it lets the search end exactly on the goal and much sooner (312 expansions instead of 1,949 in the parking lot). Explained in §4. The Reeds-Shepp shot to the goal., here the Reeds-Shepp shot: “analytic” because the path comes from a formula, not from a search. Trying it at every expansion would waste time far from the goal, where it nearly always hits something. So it is tried once every N expansions, more often as the goal comes nearer (Dolgov et al.; Nav2’s analytic expansion ratio). We use:

d, the straight-line distance from the pose to the goal, in m;
N, the number of expansions between two shots, at least 1.

N = \lfloor d / 3 \rfloor
where the brackets keep the whole part. At the start:
N = \lfloor 22.36 / 3 \rfloor = 7
and within 3 m of the goal, every expansion tries a shot.
Figure 6 runs the whole search. Watch the tree of arcs grow along the lower lane and round the end of the middle row, and the red dashed shots that hit parked cars, until a green one gets through.

Figure 6: Hybrid A* with the shot, one frame per expansion for the first ten, then several per frame. Each expansion takes the pose with the smallest estimated total cost f, cost so far plus guess (orange arrow) and drives its six arcs: kept arcs blue (forward) or purple (reverse), arcs into a cell and heading range that already holds a cheaper pose grey, arcs that hit something red. Red dashed: a Reeds-Shepp shot that hits a parked car. At expansion 312 the shot is free (green). Last frame: the whole path, 39.42 m, with one switch from forward to reverse
Of 64 shots tried, 63 hit something. The free one starts at (9.40, 14.67) in the upper lane, facing 206.3°: the car has driven past the bay. From there the shot backs into the bay in one move: reverse with full right steering, reverse straight, reverse with a little left steering, 9.418 m in all. The path is 20 forward arcs, then the shot. Its cost, with the rules of Section 2.4:
20 \times 1.5 = 30.0
2 \times 9.4176 = 18.835
30.0 + 18.835 + 2 = 50.835
The 2 at the end is the one switch from forward to reverse. The path is 39.42 m long:
30.0 + 9.418 = 39.42 \text{ m}
The path ends exactly on the goal, and the car’s body never comes closer than 0.16 m to a parked car. The shot cut the search from 1,949 expansions to 312. What is left is the steering: the arcs only steer full left, straight or full right.
5. Smoothing the path


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Smoothing moves each point of a path a little towards its found position and a little towards its two neighbours, again and again, which rounds corners. Smoothing cannot turn a grid route into one a car can drive, but it removes needless steering from Hybrid A*‘s path, as long as it keeps the turns within the 5 m circle and the body away from the parked cars.


5.1 The smoothing rule
Hybrid A*‘s path steers only full left, straight or full right, and switches between them in jumps: Dolgov et al. found such paths “drivable, but can contain unnatural swerves that require unnecessary steering”. The grid route of Figure 1 is worse: it turns 90° at one point. The simplest remedy is to pull the corners in.
Write the found points as x_i and the smoothed points as y_i, both positions in the plane, numbered along the path. At the start each y_i equals its x_i. Two wishes pull against each other (Dolgov et al. 2008, smoothness term; Nav2 smoother):

each smoothed point should stay near its found point;
each smoothed point should stay near its neighbours, which straightens the path.

The first wish alone leaves the path as found; the second alone pulls all points together onto the straight line between the two ends, which are held fixed. Think of a rubber band laid along the route and tied at both ends: it pulls every point towards its neighbours, and pins near the found points stop it snapping straight. Weighting the two and stepping downhill is gradient descent (G-862)Gradient descent: Finding the lowest point of a function by repeated small steps downhill. Explained in: Gradient Descent from Scratch, §1. Overview. With:

x_i, found point i, in m;
y_i, smoothed point i, in m, starting at x_i;
\alpha, the data weight, how hard a point is pulled back to its found position, 0.5;
\beta, the smoothing weight, how hard it is pulled towards its neighbours, 0.1;
E, the weighted squared errors that involve point i, in m²;
E', the slope of E as y_i changes, in m.

Take the 90° corner of the grid route at (16, 7), between (15, 7) and (16, 8), and look at its x coordinate y alone; the found value is 16 and the neighbours’ x values are 15 and 16. The weighted squared errors, their slope at the start, and half a step down the slope, then the same in symbols:
E = 0.5\thinspace(16 - y)^2
+\ 0.1\thinspace\big((y - 15)^2 + (16 - y)^2\big)
E' = -1.0\thinspace(16 - y)
+\ 0.2\thinspace\big((y - 15) - (16 - y)\big)
E'(16) = 0 + 0.2 \times 1 = 0.2
y \leftarrow 16 - 0.2 / 2 = 15.9
E = \alpha\thinspace(x_i - y_i)^2
+\ \beta\thinspace\big((y_i - y_{i-1})^2 + (y_{i+1} - y_i)^2\big)
E' = -2\alpha\thinspace(x_i - y_i)
-\ 2\beta\thinspace(y_{i+1} + y_{i-1} - 2y_i)
y_i \leftarrow y_i - E' / 2
= y_i + \alpha\thinspace(x_i - y_i)
+\ \beta\thinspace(y_{i+1} + y_{i-1} - 2y_i)
The y coordinate moves the same way, from 7 to 7.1, so the corner point moves to (15.9, 7.1), into the inside of the turn. One pass over all points is a sweep; the sweeps repeat until the points stop moving, and the two end points never move. Rounding corners after planning is a standard step: Modern Robotics recommends smoothing the jerky motions of grid and sampling planners afterwards (MR §10.8). Smoothing a path this way is path smoothing (G-2842)Path smoothing: Moving the points of a found path, sweep after sweep, a little towards their found places and a little towards their neighbours, y_i \leftarrow y_i + \alpha(x_i - y_i) + \beta(y_{i+1} + y_{i-1} - 2y_i); it rounds corners and removes needless steering, but on its own it knows nothing of obstacles, the turning circle or the goal heading. Explained in §5.1 The smoothing rule..
5.2 Smoothing the grid route
Can smoothing rescue the grid route of Figure 1? Figure 7 tries, first with data weight 0.5 and smoothing weight 0.1, then with the data weight set to 0.

Figure 7: Smoothing the grid route sweep by sweep: grey, the route as found; blue, after the sweep; red dots, points where the car’s body, facing along the path, overlaps a parked car or a wall. With data weight 0.5 and smoothing weight 0.1 the route settles after 20 sweeps, barely changed: its tightest turn is a circle of 0.69 m. With data weight 0 the points slide towards each other; after 11,292 sweeps the route is the straight line from the start to the bay, through the middle row
With the data weight 0.5 the route settles after 20 sweeps. How sharp a turn is can be read from its curvature: the change of direction at a point divided by the length of the step into it (Dolgov et al.). The 90° corner turns 1.571 rad within a 1 m step:
\frac{1.571}{1} = 1.571 \text{ per m}
After smoothing, the sharpest turn is 1.453 per m, a circle of radius:
\frac{1}{1.453} = 0.69 \text{ m}
The car needs 5 m. The body still overlaps something at 25 of the 31 points, and the route still ends heading up the bay, nose first. With the data weight 0 nothing pulls the points back, so the route becomes the straight line between its fixed ends, and it runs through the middle row. Smoothing only rounds what the planner found; it knows nothing of the car’s size, its turning circle or the goal heading. So the planner itself must know the car, as Hybrid A* does.
5.3 Smoothing Hybrid A*‘s path
Hybrid A*‘s path is drivable, so smoothing only has to make it better without breaking it. We take a point every 0.5 m and smooth the forward drive and the reverse drive separately. Three rules keep the path drivable (Dolgov et al.’s cost has the same three concerns):

the first two and last two points of each drive stay fixed, so the start, the goal and the switch from forward to reverse keep their position and their heading;
a third pull moves a point away from an obstacle while its body is closer than 0.3 m (Dolgov et al.’s obstacle term), at a tenth of the distance missing;
where the smoothed path would turn tighter than the 5 m circle, those points and their neighbours are held where Hybrid A* put them, and the drive is smoothed again (a simple stand-in for Dolgov et al.’s curvature term).

We use Nav2’s weights: data weight 0.2 and smoothing weight 0.3. Figure 8 shows the forward drive, sweep by sweep, with its steering angle along the way.

Figure 8: Smoothing the forward drive of Hybrid A*‘s path, sweep by sweep. Left: the drive round the end of the middle row, as found (grey) and after the sweep (green); black dots are points held where Hybrid A* put them. Right: the steering angle along the 30 m drive, as found (grey) and after the sweep (green); the angle of 26.6° is full lock. The jumps from straight to full lock become gradual, and the short straight piece inside the long left turn, at about 21 m, flattens. Last frame: settled after 49 sweeps; total steering movement 100° instead of 133°
The smoothed forward drive:

turns its front wheels 100° in total, adding up every change of steering angle along the drive, instead of 133°, so the swerves are smaller;
still steers at most 26.6°, so it stays within the 5 m circle;
keeps its body at least 0.19 m from the parked cars instead of 0.16 m.

Two long turns, from 12.0 to 20.5 m and from 23.0 to 30.0 m along the drive, stay as found: both are at full lock already, and smoothing pulls a turn inwards, tighter than the car can drive. The reverse drive into the bay stays as found too: its turns are at full lock and its middle piece is already straight. Dolgov et al. smooth with a curvature penalty and then add finer points between the smoothed ones, which gives steering that changes gradually all along.

RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.title: State Lattices and Motion Primitives
RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Checking a path segmentExplained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §6.2 Step size and order; Motion primitives and lattice searchMotion primitive: A short motion the robot can drive, usually one input held for a fixed time, such as full left at 0.5 m/s for 0.75 s; planners chain primitives so that every path they build is drivable. Explained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §5. A few motions to build with: motion primitives and a system simulator.
Compare with: Hybrid A*Hybrid A:* A* over grid cells and heading ranges in which each state keeps the exact pose that reached it most cheaply and every move is an arc the car can drive, such as six 1.5 m arcs per pose; its path is drivable, but because it drops other poses in the same cell it is not guaranteed to be the cheapest. Explained in: Hybrid A* and Path Smoothing, §2. Hybrid A: states with a heading, moves the car can drive.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A state lattice fixes the car’s states to whole-metre points and a few headings, and fixes its moves in advance so that every move ends exactly on another lattice state. Plain A* then finds the cheapest path the lattice holds, ends exactly on the goal, and checks each move by looking up the map cells it sweeps, listed before planning.


The car of Hybrid A* and path smoothingExplained in: Hybrid A* and Path Smoothing, §1. Overview can already back into its bay. Hybrid A* (G-2840)Hybrid A:* A* over grid cells and heading ranges in which each state keeps the exact pose that reached it most cheaply and every move is an arc the car can drive, such as six 1.5 m arcs per pose; its path is drivable, but because it drops other poses in the same cell it is not guaranteed to be the cheapest. Explained in: Hybrid A* and Path Smoothing, §2.1 Six arcs from every pose, A* over cells and heading ranges whose moves are arcs the car can drive, finds a 39.42 m path after 312 expansions. We keep the same lot and the same car: 4.0 m by 1.8 m, its tightest circle 5 m, starting at (2, 3) facing 0° and backing into the bay at (12, 23) facing −90°.
What still breaks shows in RO-055’s search:

The arcs never land on the goal. Each arc turns the heading by 17.2°, and no whole number of 17.2° steps from 0° makes −90°. Without the Reeds-Shepp shot the search expanded 1,949 states and stopped 0.54 m and 5° from the goal.
The cheapest path is not promised. Poses that fall in the same cell and heading range are merged and all but one dropped, so the cheapest path may be among the dropped ones (Dolgov et al. 2008).
Every move is worked out during the search. The search drove 1,866 arcs through the car’s motion equations and checked the body at 7 places along each.

This Note fixes all three at once by designing the moves before planning:

why moves that are not designed never land on the same point twice (Section 2);
moves that end exactly on lattice points, the control set (Section 3);
the cells each move sweeps, worked out once (Section 4);
A* on the lattice, and how its path compares with Hybrid A*‘s (Section 5).

2. Why fixed moves never close up


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

If the car repeats Hybrid A*‘s full-left arc of 1.5 m, it never returns to the same point: one lap of the 5 m circle is 20.94 arcs, not a whole number. Moves whose lengths do not fit the geometry make endless different states; moves designed to fit a grid make a finite graph.


RO-055’s first problem was that the arcs never land exactly on the goal. The cause is general (LaValle §14.2.2.3), and the simplest case shows it: the car steers full left and keeps driving arcs of 1.5 m round its 5 m circle. One lap is the circumference:
2\pi \times 5 = 31.416 \text{ m}
31.416 / 1.5 = 20.94 \text{ arcs}
Figure 1 plays it. Watch the end points of the arcs: after 21 arcs the car is round once more, but not on the start.

Figure 1: The car drives full-left arcs of 1.5 m round its 5 m circle, one arc per frame. Blue dots: ends of the arcs of lap 1; orange: lap 2; purple: lap 3. After 21 arcs (1.00 laps) the end of the 21st arc lies 0.084 m past the start; after 63 arcs (3.01 laps) there are 64 different end points, none repeated. Last frame: a quarter-turn move of the same circle, 7.85 m long (green squares), is back on the start after 4 moves
Twenty-one arcs turn the car by:
21 \times 0.3 = 6.3 \text{ rad}
6.3 - 2\pi = 0.0168 \text{ rad}
so the end of the 21st arc lies 0.0168 rad of the circle past the start, along the 5 m circle:
0.0168 \times 5 = 0.084 \text{ m}
Every lap shifts by the same amount, so the ends never meet: after 63 arcs there are 64 different points. Because the lap is not a whole number of arcs, the ends keep filling the circle, and the search graph they make has no end of states (LaValle §14.2.2.3). Hybrid A* copes by merging nearby poses into cells; that is exactly the merging that cost it the promise of the cheapest path.
The last frame of Figure 1 shows the other way out. A quarter turn of the same circle is 7.85 m:
\frac{\pi}{2} \times 5 = 7.854 \text{ m}
Four such moves bring the car back exactly to the start. A move whose length is chosen to fit the geometry lands on the same few points over and over.
RO-054 met this good case in its straight drive: with speed changes held for a fixed time, positions and speeds fell on a regular grid, and the lattice search (G-2827)Lattice search: Graph search over states that the primitives keep on a regular grid, such as positions every 0.0625 m and speeds every 0.25 m/s when the robot accelerates, coasts or brakes every 0.5 s; any graph search then finds the best plan on that grid. Explained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §6. Searching the primitives systematically: lattice search searched it. For the car we can choose the grid first and then design the moves to fit it. The states are:

positions on whole metres, (x, y) = (2, 3), (2, 4), and so on;
headings in steps of 45°: 0°, 45°, 90°, up to 315°.

A regular grid of states, joined only by moves the vehicle can drive that end exactly on other states of the grid, is a state lattice (G-2855)State lattice: A regular grid of states, such as positions on whole metres and headings in steps of 45 deg, joined only by drivable moves that end exactly on other states of the grid; no states need merging, so plain A* finds the cheapest path the lattice holds. Explained in §2. Why fixed moves never close up. (Pivtoraiko, Knepper and Kelly 2009). Its states are exactly the lattice points, so nothing needs merging, and a search over it is plain A*. What remains is to find the moves.
3. Moves that end on the lattice: the control set


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A turn on the 5 m circle alone ends between lattice points, but a short straight piece before and after the arc can be sized so that the move ends exactly on one. The moves from each heading, worked out once and copied to every state, are the lattice’s control set.


3.1 A 45° turn that lands on a lattice point
Section 2 asked for moves that land on lattice points. Start from (0, 0) facing 0° and turn left by 45° on the 5 m circle. The arc alone ends at (3.536, 1.464): between lattice points, as in Figure 2.
Make interactive
Figure 2: Building the 45° left turn. Grey dots: lattice points, 1 m apart. Red dashed: the arc alone, which ends at (3.536, 1.464), between points. Orange, blue, orange: a straight piece of 0.929 m, the 45° arc of the 5 m circle (3.927 m), and a straight piece of 0.757 m along 45°, which end exactly on (5, 2) facing 45°
Add a straight piece before the arc, along 0°, and one after it, along 45°, and choose their lengths so that the end is a lattice point. With:

\rho, the radius of the circle, 5 m;
\phi, the turn, 45°;
a, the length of the straight piece before the arc, in m;
b, the length of the straight piece after it, in m;
X and Y, the lattice point we aim for, (5, 2) in m.

The arc alone ends at (3.5355, 1.4645), and driving along 45° adds the same amount to x and to y, 0.7071 m for every metre. The y coordinate gives b; the x coordinate, which gains the same 0.5355 m from the second straight piece, then gives a. Numbers first, then in symbols:
1.4645 + 0.7071\thinspace b = 2
b = 0.5355 / 0.7071 = 0.757 \text{ m}
a + 3.5355 + 0.5355 = 5
a = 0.929 \text{ m}
Y = \rho\thinspace(1 - \cos\phi) + b \sin\phi
X = a + \rho \sin\phi + b \cos\phi
The move is 5.613 m long:
0.929 + 3.927 + 0.757 = 5.613 \text{ m}
and every part of it is drivable: straight, then the 5 m circle, then straight. Pivtoraiko et al. solve the same problem with smoother curves whose steering changes gradually; straight-arc-straight moves are the simplest that land exactly.
3.2 The control set
The other moves are found the same way (notebook). From a state facing 0° (Figure 3, left):

straight 1 m, ending on (1, 0);
turn 45° left or right, ending on (5, 2) or (5, −2);
turn 90° left or right, a quarter of the 5 m circle, ending on (5, 5) or (5, −5) with no straight pieces needed.

From a state facing 45° (Figure 3, right), the straight move is a diagonal of 1.414 m to (1, 1), and the 45° turns end on (2, 5) and (5, 2). Each move also exists in reverse: the same shape mirrored, driven backwards, which also ends on a lattice point.
Make interactive
Figure 3: The control set. Left: the 10 moves from a state facing 0°: straight 1 m, 45° turns to (5, ±2) and 90° turns to (5, ±5), forward (blue) and in reverse (purple). Right: the 6 moves from a state facing 45°: the 1.414 m diagonal and 45° turns to (2, 5) and (5, 2), forward and in reverse. Every move ends on a lattice point (grey dots) with a heading that is a multiple of 45°
The moves work like toy bricks made to snap only onto studs: whatever order they are joined in, each ends on a stud, here a lattice point. The moves from one heading, designed once before any planning, are the lattice control set (G-2856)Lattice control set: The moves from each heading of a state lattice, designed once before planning so that each ends exactly on a lattice state, such as 10 moves from 0 deg (straight, 45 deg and 90 deg turns, forward and reverse); copied to every state during the search, and its size is the branching factor. Not the same as a vehicle’s control set of speed and turn-rate pairs. Explained in §3.2 The control set., the canonical set of repeating moves of Pivtoraiko et al. The lattice control set is not the set of every speed and turn-rate pair a vehicle can produce, such as the diamond of the room robotExplained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §5. A few motions to build with: motion primitives and a system simulator. Each move is a motion primitive (G-2826)Motion primitive: A short motion the robot can drive, usually one input held for a fixed time, such as full left at 0.5 m/s for 0.75 s; planners chain primitives so that every path they build is drivable. Explained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §5. A few motions to build with: motion primitives and a system simulator, a short drivable motion, chosen so that it ends on the lattice. The number of moves from a state is the search’s branching factor (G-2555)Branching factor b: The number of choices at each step of a search, such as 4 moves on a 4-connected grid or 18 turns of a Rubik’s cube; level d of a search tree holds up to b^d nodes, so it sets how fast the tree grows. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §7.1 Counting the work: 10 from the four headings along the axes, 6 from the four diagonal headings.
The diagonal headings get their own moves because a move designed for 0° does not stay on the lattice when turned by 45°: (5, 2) turned by 45° is not a pair of whole numbers. Turning by 90° does keep whole numbers, so the set for 0° serves 90°, 180° and 270°, and the set for 45° serves the other diagonals (Hauser ch. 11 makes the same split into axis-aligned and diagonal moves).
3.3 Copying a move to any state
The lattice repeats: a move that joins two lattice states also joins every other pair arranged the same way (Pivtoraiko et al., §2.1). So during the search a move is turned to the state’s heading and added to its position (Hauser ch. 11). With:

(x, y), the state’s position, in m;
\theta, its heading;
(\Delta x, \Delta y), where the move ends when it starts from (0, 0) facing 0°, in m;
(x', y'), where it ends from the state, in m.

The lattice path of Section 5 turns left by 45° from (17, 9) facing 90°; the 0° move ends on (5, 2); the cosine of 90° is 0 and its sine is 1:
x' = 17 + 0 \times 5 - 1 \times 2 = 15
y' = 9 + 1 \times 5 + 0 \times 2 = 14
x' = x + \Delta x \cos\theta - \Delta y \sin\theta
y' = y + \Delta x \sin\theta + \Delta y \cos\theta
The move ends on (15, 14), facing 135°: a lattice state again. So each move is built once, as an “action template”, and replicated at every state the search reaches (CMU 16-350 slides). The moves are in place; each still has to be checked against the parked cars.
4. Checking a move by look-up: the swept cells


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Because every move starts on a lattice point, the cells of a fine map that the car’s body sweeps during the move are the same at every state, shifted. The cells can be listed once per move, and checking a move during the search is looking up whether any of those cells is occupied.


Hybrid A* checked its body at 7 places along every arc, during the search. On the lattice that work can move to before the search. Take a fine map of the lot in cells of 0.1 m, each marked occupied if its centre lies inside a parked car or outside the lot. During a move, the car’s body (grown by RO-055’s safety margin of 0.1 m) passes over a set of these cells, the move’s swept cells (Pivtoraiko et al., §3.3; CMU 16-350 case study). Figure 4 drives the 90° left turn from (12, 3), the turn the lattice path takes round the end of the middle row; watch the blue cells pile up behind the body.

Figure 4: The 90° left turn from (12, 3) facing 0°, driven step by step: blue, the map cells of 0.1 m that the car’s body, grown by 0.1 m, has swept so far; grey, the map cells inside parked cars; green, the body. Last frame: all 3,260 swept cells; no blue cell is grey, so the move is free
Lattice points are whole metres, exactly 10 map cells apart, so a move’s swept cells at another state are the same list shifted by whole cells. The 64 lists, one per move and start heading, are worked out once; during the search, checking a move is reading the map at its listed cells. The whole search of Section 5 made 5,192 such look-ups and drove no arc through the motion equations, where Hybrid A* drove 1,866 arcs and checked each at 7 places. Pivtoraiko et al. write that adding up the cells a move sweeps “is typically much more efficient than simulating the motion of the system”. The moves and their checks are ready; what is left is the search itself.
5. Searching the lattice with A*


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A* over lattice states (with RO-055’s costs and guess) finds a 42.93 m path to the exact goal pose after 629 expansions, and no other path in the lattice is cheaper. The path is longer than Hybrid A*‘s 39.42 m because 8 headings and fixed turns are coarse; finer lattices close the gap.


5.1 The search
With states, moves and checks in place, the search is A* (G-2577)A search:* Dijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid). Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.5 The algorithm as in RO-034. Its costs and guess are RO-055’s: each metre forward costs 1 and each metre in reverse 2, each switch between them adds 2 m, and the guess h of the cost left is the larger of the Reeds-Shepp length and the grid distanceExplained in: Hybrid A* and Path Smoothing, §3. Two guesses of the cost left. A state is a lattice point, a heading and the direction of the last move, so that a switch can be charged. Figure 5 runs it.

Figure 5: A* on the state lattice. Grey dots: lattice points. Each expansion takes the state with the smallest estimated total cost f, cost so far plus guess (orange arrow) and copies the control set there: moves whose swept cells touch a parked car or a wall red, moves to a state already reached more cheaply grey dotted, kept moves blue (forward) or purple (reverse). One frame per expansion for the first eight, then several per frame. Expansion 629 takes the goal state off the open list. Last frame: the path, 42.93 m, ending exactly on the goal with one switch to reverse
The path drives 10 m straight along the lower lane, turns 90° left round the end of the middle row, drives 1 m, makes two 45° left turns into the upper lane, drives 3 m past the bay, then backs in with a reverse 90° turn and 2 m reverse straight. Its forward and reverse lengths:
10 + 7.854 + 1 + 2 \times 5.6133 + 3
= 33.0806 \text{ m forward}
7.854 + 2 = 9.854 \text{ m in reverse}
Its length and its cost:
33.0806 + 9.854 = 42.93 \text{ m}
33.0806 + 2 \times 9.854 + 2 = 54.79
The path ends exactly on (12, 23) facing −90°, without any shot, because the goal is a lattice state. Its body stays at least 0.25 m from the parked cars.
Is it the cheapest path the lattice holds? The lattice has no merged states, so A* with a guess that never overestimates returns the cheapest path in it (admissible heuristicsAdmissible heuristic: A heuristic that is never more than the true cost left from any state, h \le h^\ast; it makes f a lower bound on every route through a state, so the first route A* takes off the open list is the shortest. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §5. Why A returns the shortest route: admissible heuristics, G-2578)Admissible heuristic: A heuristic that is never more than the true cost left from any state, h \le h^\ast; it makes f a lower bound on every route through a state, so the first route A* takes off the open list is the shortest. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §5.1 A guess that never overestimates. As a check, the same search with no guess at all, Dijkstra’s algorithm (G-2565)Dijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §3.2 The algorithm: settle the nearest, update its neighbours, expands 1,620 states and finds the same cost, 54.79. Pivtoraiko et al. state both properties: a search of the lattice finds the best path in the lattice, and as the lattice is made finer its best path can approach the best path of the real car (Pivtoraiko et al., §3.1).
5.2 The lattice against Hybrid A*
Figure 6 puts the two paths side by side.
Make interactive
Figure 6: The lattice path (blue, 42.93 m) and Hybrid A*‘s path from RO-055 (green, 39.42 m) on the same lot, from the same start to the same goal. The lattice path drives straight to x = 12 before its 90° turn and swings wider into the upper lane








































Hybrid A* (with the shot)State lattice, 8 headingsExpansions312629Path length39.42 m42.93 mCost50.83554.79Ends on the goalthrough the Reeds-Shepp shotexactly, by designCheapest possible in its own graphno (poses merged)yesMoves checked during the search1,866 arcs driven, 7 checks each5,192 look-ups of swept cells
The lattice path is 3.51 m longer:
42.93 - 39.42 = 3.51 \text{ m}
The lattice is cheapest among its own moves, and its moves are coarse: only 8 headings, and turns of 45° or 90° with straight pieces attached. Hybrid A*‘s arcs can stop turning at any multiple of 17.2°, and its final Reeds-Shepp shot can take any shape. Lattices used in practice are finer: Nav2’s lattice planner ships a control set with 16 headings by default, and CMU’s car Boss planned its parking manoeuvres in the 2007 DARPA Urban Challenge on a lattice with 32 headings and 36 moves per state (CMU 16-350 case study). Finer lattices find shorter paths but branch more, so their searches need the good guesses of RO-055: for Boss, 2,019 states expanded with the larger of two guesses, against 26,108 and 124,794 with either guess alone (CMU 16-350 case study).
The car can now plan into the bay with every move checked in advance and every state exact.
6. Summary



































Hybrid A*State latticeStatescells and heading ranges, each holding a pose anywhere insidelattice points and 8 headings, exactlyMoves6 arcs of 1.5 m, driven during the search10 or 6 moves designed once, ending on lattice pointsCollision checkbody at 7 places per arc, during the searchlook-up of the swept cells, listed onceGoalneeds the Reeds-Shepp shotreached exactlyGuaranteenone on costcheapest path in the lattice

The lattice solves RO-055’s three problems: its path ends exactly on (12, 23) facing −90° without a shot, Dijkstra confirms its cost of 54.79 is the cheapest the lattice holds, and its search checks moves by 5,192 look-ups instead of driving 1,866 arcs; the price is a path of 42.93 m against 39.42 m, because 8 headings are coarse.
Moves held for a fixed length do not close up, so a graph built from them has no end of states: one lap of the 5 m circle is 20.94 arcs of 1.5 m, so the arc ends drift by 0.084 m each lap.
A state lattice (G-2855)State lattice: A regular grid of states, such as positions on whole metres and headings in steps of 45 deg, joined only by drivable moves that end exactly on other states of the grid; no states need merging, so plain A* finds the cheapest path the lattice holds. Explained in §2. Why fixed moves never close up. is a regular grid of states joined only by drivable moves that end exactly on other states, so no states need merging and plain A* applies.
A 45° turn lands on (5, 2) when straight pieces of 0.929 m and 0.757 m are added round the arc, because their lengths can be solved for from where the arc alone ends, (3.536, 1.464).
The lattice control set (G-2856)Lattice control set: The moves from each heading of a state lattice, designed once before planning so that each ends exactly on a lattice state, such as 10 moves from 0 deg (straight, 45 deg and 90 deg turns, forward and reverse); copied to every state during the search, and its size is the branching factor. Not the same as a vehicle’s control set of speed and turn-rate pairs. Explained in §3.2 The control set., the moves from each heading designed once, is copied to every state by turning and shifting, because a regular lattice looks the same from every state; its size, 10 or 6 here, is the branching factor.
The map cells a move’s body sweeps are the same at every state up to a shift of whole cells, so they are listed once and collision checking becomes a look-up.

The car now has a planner whose path is exact and cheapest within its lattice. Still missing: every planner so far plans in a parking lot or a room; driving between places in a city plans on a road network instead, which route planning on road graphsExplained in: Route Planning on Road and Route Graphs, §1. Overview covers next.
