RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.title: Route Planning on Road and Route Graphs
RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Graphs and state spacesState space: All the states a problem can be in, joined by the moves between them, such as the robot’s 76 cells or the arrangements of a Rubik’s cube; it is a graph, so planning becomes finding a path from the start state to a goal state. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §2.2 Any problem of states and moves is a graph; Dijkstra’s algorithmDijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §3.2 The algorithm: settle the nearest, update its neighbours; A* searchA search:* Dijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid). Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.5 The algorithm; Admissible heuristicAdmissible heuristic: A heuristic that is never more than the true cost left from any state, h \le h^\ast; it makes f a lower bound on every route through a state, so the first route A* takes off the open list is the shortest. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §5.1 A guess that never overestimates; Backward and bidirectional searchBidirectional search: A forward search from the start and a backward search from the goal run in turn until some state has been expanded by both; the route is the smallest sum of the two costs over all states both reached, since the meeting state can be off the shortest route. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §8.2 Bidirectional search; MetricMetric (distance function): A distance between points that is never negative, is 0 only between equal points, is the same both ways and obeys the triangle inequality; search trees rely on these rules to skip far regions safely. Explained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §7.1 The rules a distance must follow.
Compare with: HeuristicHeuristic h: A cheap guess of the cost still to go from a state to the goal, such as 3.121 m from the start cell to the door; a search uses it to prefer states that look nearer the goal. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §2. A guess of the distance left: the heuristic.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Across a city, a robot or a car plans on a graph of roads whose edges cost travel time, and the search loop is A* as before. What decides how much of the map the search looks at is the heuristic: on a Chicago street graph of 1628 intersections, one trip takes 1526 intersections off the open list with no heuristic, 1229 with the straight line at the top speed and 108 with 16 landmarks, while a contraction hierarchy, which adds shortcuts before any search, takes 159.


The robot can already plan its way to the door of its room. A* (G-2577)A search:* Dijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid). Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4.5 The algorithm on the room’s 0.5 m grid takes 9 cells off its open list (G-2547)Frontier (open list): The vertices a search has reached but not yet expanded, waiting to be taken off one at a time; which one comes off next is what makes one search differ from another. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §4. Searching with a frontier and a visited list, the cells reached but not yet expanded, where Dijkstra’s algorithm takes 54, because a heuristic (G-2570)Heuristic h: A cheap guess of the cost still to go from a state to the goal, such as 3.121 m from the start cell to the door; a search uses it to prefer states that look nearer the goal. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §2. A guess of the distance left: the heuristic, a cheap guess of the distance left, points it at the door.
Past the door, the trips get longer. A delivery robot, or a car, must cross a city: from a street corner in the south-west of the map of Figure 1 to one near the lake shore in the north-east, 4.6 km apart as the crow flies. Three things break:

Size. The map covers 4.9 km by 5.0 km; cut into 0.5 m cells like the room, it would be 96 million cells, against the room’s 112.
Roads. A car may not drive across a block. The car keeps to the streets, in the allowed direction, and in the right lane.
Time. A trip is judged by how long it takes, not how long it is: the fastest route is 7047 m long and takes 492.8 s, while the shortest, 6717 m, takes 573.1 s (notebook).

Roads fix the size: the map shrinks to its 1628 intersections and the streets between them. The search effort is what is left. Figure 1 runs the same trip four ways, 40 intersections per frame in every panel: watch the red dots, the intersections taken off the open list, fill most of the map in the two top panels and stay close to the route in the two bottom ones.

Figure 1: The same trip on the Chicago street graph, from the green dot in the south-west to the green dot in the north-east, searched four ways with travel-time costs. 40 intersections are taken off the open list per frame in every panel; a panel that has finished holds its last frame. Top left: Dijkstra’s algorithm (heuristic 0), 1526 intersections. Top right: A* with the straight line to the goal at the top speed limit, 88.5 km/h, 1229. Bottom left: A* with 16 landmarks (purple diamonds), 108. Bottom right: a contraction hierarchy, a search up from the start (red) and one up from the goal (blue), 67 + 92 = 159. All four return the same 492.8 s route (blue line)
All four searches return the same route. In the first three the search loop is the same and only the heuristic, the guess of the time left, changes, and with it the work: from 1526 intersections to 108. The fourth adds shortcuts to the graph before any search and takes 159. This Note builds the four, on a small town first and then on the Chicago map:

why route planning is a level of its own, above the planners of the room (Section 2);
the road network as a graph of intersections and one-way edges, and of lanes (Section 3);
travel time as the cost of a road (Section 4);
the first heuristic in seconds, the straight line at the top speed, and why it is loose (Section 5);
a tight heuristic from stored travel times to a few landmarks (Section 6);
contraction hierarchies, which add shortcuts so that a search only climbs to more important roads, and a heuristic built from them (Section 7).

2. Why route planning is its own level


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A car’s drive cannot be planned as one problem from the destination down to the steering angle. Planning is split into levels; the top one, route planning, picks the roads and lanes on a map of the road network and leaves every detail of the motion to the levels below.


The first thing that breaks is size. The room’s planners worked on every free cell and every heading; across the city, the same detail means 96 million cells, other cars, traffic lights and lane markings, for a drive of 8 minutes.
The idea. A taxi driver does not plan every turn of the steering wheel before leaving. First the driver decides the roads: west on this street, onto the expressway, off at the river. Only while driving does the driver decide when to change lane, whether to stop at a light, and how hard to brake. Each decision uses the one above it and adds detail.
Planning for self-driving cars is split the same way, because driving is hard to model as a single optimisation problem (Tübingen L12 slides; Paden et al. 2016). Figure 2 shows the levels.

Figure 2: The planning levels of a self-driving car, from the destination at the top to the steering, throttle and brake at the bottom. The route planner turns the destination and a map of the road network into a route; the behaviour layer picks a manoeuvre (follow the lane, stop, yield, change lane) from what the car sees; the motion planner turns the manoeuvre into a path or trajectory; the controller follows it. Each level works coarser than the one below it
The standard term. Finding the best way from where the vehicle is to the destination on a map of the road network, by time or by distance, is route planning (G-2870)Route planning (mission planning): Finding the best way from where a vehicle is to its destination on a map of the road network, by travel time or by distance, such as the 492.8 s route across the Chicago map; the top level of planning, which picks the roads and lanes and leaves the motion to the levels below. Explained in §2. Why route planning is its own level., also called mission planning (Tübingen L12 slides). Route planning is the top level of Figure 2:

the route planner chooses the roads and lanes;
the behaviour layer chooses manoeuvres, such as stopping at a stop line or changing lane;
the motion planner finds a path or a trajectory that carries out the manoeuvre, with the planners of this chapter;
the controller turns it into steering, throttle and brake.

Earlier levels work with coarser pictures of the world (Tübingen L12 slides). A route planner never sees a parked car; the motion planner never sees the whole city.
Robots do the same. A delivery robot in a building can plan on a fixed graph of waypoints, such as corridor junctions and doors, the room’s door among them, and leave the last few metres to a free-space planner such as A* on the room’s grid (Nav2 Route Server). A fixed graph of points a robot may travel between, made by hand or by a program from the map, is a route graph (G-2872)Route graph: A fixed graph of points a robot may travel between, such as corridor junctions and doors, made by hand or by a program from the map; a robot plans its long trips on it and leaves the last metres to a free-space planner. Explained in §2. Why route planning is its own level. (Nav2 Route Server). On route graphs, Dijkstra’s algorithm alone is fast enough: 0.232 ms on average on a graph of 10,000 nodes and 44 ms on a million (Nav2 Route Server). A road graph of Western Europe has 18 million intersections (Geisberger et al. 2008), and there the search effort matters.
The route planner needs the road network as a graph; the next section builds one.
3. Roads as a graph


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Intersections are the vertices and road segments the edges of a road graph, and a one-way street is an edge that goes one way only, so road graphs are directed. When the route must say which lane to be in, each lane segment becomes a vertex of its own, joined to the next segment and to the lanes beside it.


Section 2 left the route planner a map of the road network; this section turns it into the graph (G-2540)Graph: A set of vertices (points) joined by edges (lines), such as the room’s 76 free cells joined by 114 moves; it keeps only which places connect directly, so one search method works for maps, puzzles and any problem of states and moves. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edges, points joined by lines, that a search needs. A road map is the next step up from the room, with roads instead of free floor, so we leave the room for a town.
3.1 Intersections, road segments and one-way streets
A small town. We follow every step by hand on a town of 11 intersections, small enough to check each number (Figure 3). A driver at S wants to reach T. The town has three kinds of road:

a bypass north of the town, from N to M and on to L, at 80 km/h;
the main road, which joins S to the town and the town to T and to the bypass, at 50 km/h;
the old town, B, C, E and F, at 30 km/h; the street from F to C is one-way, northbound.

Every position is measured in one map frame: metres east and north of the map’s south-west corner.
The room’s moves went both ways; the street from F to C does not. Explained in §3.1 Intersections, road segments and one-way streets. (Tübingen L12 slides). A two-way street becomes two edges, one each way, so the town’s 13 streets are 25 edges: 12 two-way streets give 24, and the one-way street gives 1 (notebook). Road networks are directed graphs (Tübingen L12 slides).
A real road graph. The saved graph has 1670 intersections and 3946 streets; we keep the 1628 intersections from which every other one can be reached, joined by 3857 edges, and 1409 of those edges are one-way streets (notebook). 3.2 Lane graphs
A road graph has one vertex per intersection, so it cannot say which lane the car should be in. The lane matters before a turn. In Figure 5 a car in the right lane that must turn left at the junction has to change to the left lane first, and it cannot do so at the last metre.
The idea. Cut every lane into short pieces and make each piece a vertex. Join a piece to the piece that follows it in the same lane, and to the pieces beside it that the car may change into.

Figure 5: A lane graph on a two-lane road heading east. Each lane is cut into pieces, the vertices a1 and a2 (right lane), b1 and b2 (left lane), s (straight on after the junction) and l (the left turn). Blue arrows join a piece to the next piece in the same lane; orange dashed arrows join pieces a car may change between, at a penalty. To turn left from a1, the route must cross to the left lane: a1, b1, b2, l or a1, a2, b2, l
The standard terms. One piece of one lane, with its left and right borders, is a lanelet (G-2875)Lanelet: One short piece of one lane, given by its left and right borders, as used by the Lanelet2 map format; the vertex of a lane graph. Explained in §3.2 Lane graphs. (Lanelet2 routing). A graph whose vertices are lanelets is a lane graph (G-2874)Lane graph: A graph whose vertices are lane segments (lanelets), joined to the next segment in the same lane and to the neighbouring lanes a vehicle may change into; it lets a route say which lane to be in, for example before a left turn. Explained in §3.2 Lane graphs.. Its edges are of two kinds (Lanelet2 routing):

succeeding: from a lanelet to the next one in the same lane, such as a1 to a2;
left and right: to a neighbouring lanelet the car may change into, such as a1 to b1; a lane change adds a penalty to the cost, so a route changes lane only when that pays.

Lanes beside each other that may not be changed between, such as two lanes with a solid line between them, get no lane-change edge. The graph is also built for one kind of road user: a bicycle’s lane graph includes cycle lanes that a car’s does not (Lanelet2 routing).
To turn left from a1 in Figure 5, a route must include a lane change: a1, b1, b2, l or a1, a2, b2, l. A route planner that runs on a lane graph returns a list of lane IDs; the Autoware software for self-driving cars groups them into sections of road, each with the lanes the car may change between (Autoware mission planner).
The graph is ready, at the level of roads or of lanes. Its edges still need a cost, and length is not the one a driver cares about.
4. Travel time as the edge cost


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The cost of a road is the time it takes: its length divided by its speed limit. With that cost, the fastest route in the town runs 3300 m by the bypass in 197.1 s, while the shortest, 2500 m through the old town, takes 252.0 s.


Section 3 left the edges of the road graph without a cost. In the room, a move cost its length, and the weighted graph (G-2563)Weighted graph (edge cost): A graph in which every edge carries a number, its cost, such as a move’s length in metres (0.5 m straight, 0.707 m diagonal); the cost of a path is the sum of its edge costs, so the cheapest route need not have the fewest edges. Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §2.2 Edge costs: the fewest moves is not the shortest of the room’s grid gave each edge its length in metres. On roads, the same choice picks the wrong route.
The problem on numbers. From S to T, the straight way through the old town is 2500 m; the way round by the bypass is 3300 m. By length, the old town wins. But the old town’s streets allow 30 km/h and the bypass 80 km/h.
The idea. A driver judges a route by the time it takes. Driving a street at its speed limit takes its length divided by that speed, so each edge gets that time as its cost (Rhodes COMP 372; Tübingen L12 slides). A speed in km/h becomes m/s by dividing by 3.6, because 1 km is 1000 m and 1 h is 3600 s. For the bypass from N to M, 1500 m at 80 km/h:
80 \text{ km/h} = 80 / 3.6
= 22.22 \text{ m/s}
\text{time} = 1500 / 22.22
= 67.5 \text{ s}
With:

\ell, the length of the street, in m (1500 m from N to M);
v, its speed limit, in m/s (22.22 m/s);
c, the cost of its edge, in s (67.5 s).

c = \ell / v
The standard term. An edge cost equal to the time it takes to drive the edge, here its length divided by its speed limit, is a travel-time edge cost (G-2876)Travel-time edge cost: The cost of a road edge given as the time to drive it, its length divided by its speed limit, such as 1500 m at 80 km/h = 67.5 s; with it a search finds the fastest route, which can be longer than the shortest. Explained in §4. Travel time as the edge cost. (Tübingen L12 slides; Freiburg L3). Figure 6 labels every street of the town with it, and draws both routes.

5. A heuristic in seconds: the straight line at the top speed


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Divide the straight-line distance to the goal by the highest speed limit on the map: no route can be shorter than the straight line or faster than the top speed, so the guess never overestimates. But most roads are much slower than the top speed, so the guess is loose: in Chicago it averages 0.41 of the true time, and A* still takes off 1229 of the trip’s intersections.


Section 4 left A* without a heuristic for travel time. The room’s straight-line and octile distances are in metres; the costs are now in seconds, and A* adds the two, so a heuristic in metres cannot be used.
5.1 The bound and why it holds
The idea. The time left from an intersection is at least the time it would take to drive the straight line to the goal at the fastest speed anywhere on the map. For the town, the fastest speed is the bypass’s 80 km/h, 22.22 m/s. From S, 2500 m from T as the crow flies:
h(S) = 2500 / 22.22
= 112.5 \text{ s}
With:

u, an intersection;
\delta(u), the straight-line distance from u to the goal T, in m (2500 m from S);
v_{\max}, the highest speed limit on the map, in m/s (22.22 m/s in the town);
h(u), the heuristic at u, in s (112.5 s at S).

h(u) = \delta(u) / v_{\max}
This heuristic is the straight-line distance over the top speed (Freiburg L3; Rhodes COMP 372).
Why it never overestimates. Take the fastest route from S, five streets of 500, 400, 1500, 400 and 500 m. Driving each street at the top speed instead of its own limit can only make it faster, and no route is shorter than the straight line:
\text{time} = 36 + 28.8 + 67.5 + 28.8 + 36
= 197.1
\ge 3300 / 22.22
= 148.5
\ge 2500 / 22.22
= 112.5
= h(S)
The same steps for any route from u to the goal, with:

\ell_i, the length of street i of the route, in m;
v_i, its speed limit, in m/s, never above v_{\max};
\sum_i, the sum over the streets of the route (five terms for the route from S, one per street).

\text{time} = \sum_i \ell_i / v_i
\ge \sum_i \ell_i / v_{\max}
\ge \delta(u) / v_{\max}
= h(u)
The second line holds because every v_i is at most v_{\max}; the third because the streets of a route together are never shorter than the straight line between its ends. So the heuristic is admissible (G-2578)Admissible heuristic: A heuristic that is never more than the true cost left from any state, h \le h^\ast; it makes f a lower bound on every route through a state, so the first route A* takes off the open list is the shortest. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §5.1 A guess that never overestimates: it never overestimates, and A* returns the fastest route. The heuristic is also consistent (G-2580)Consistent heuristic (monotone heuristic): A heuristic that never falls by more than a move’s cost, h(n) \le c(n, n') + h(n'), with 0 at the goal (a triangle inequality); it keeps f from decreasing along a route, so A* with a closed list expands every state with its shortest g. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §6.2 The fix: a guess that never drops faster than the distance, for the same reason applied to one edge at a time (Freiburg L3).
Rhodes College’s Memphis exercise uses the same bound with 65 miles per hour, the highest speed limit of any Memphis road (Rhodes COMP 372).
5.2 Why the bound is loose
A heuristic that never overestimates is safe; how much work it saves depends on how close it comes to the truth: of two admissible heuristics, the one that is never smaller, which dominates (G-2579)Dominance (of heuristics): One admissible heuristic dominates another when it is at least as large at every state; being closer to the true cost, it makes A* expand fewer states (the octile distance dominates the straight line). Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §5.3 A closer guess takes fewer cells the other, takes fewer vertices off the open list. At S it guesses 112.5 s for a true 197.1 s. 6. Landmarks: lower bounds from stored travel times


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Store, once, the exact travel times between a few landmark vertices and every other vertex; since a detour through the goal is never faster than the fastest way to a landmark, the stored times give a lower bound on the time left that knows about the roads. With 16 landmarks, A* takes off 108 of the Chicago trip’s intersections instead of 1229.


The straight line of Section 5 knows nothing about the roads: at B it guessed 67.5 s where the true time is 156.0 s. A better guess needs the roads, but the exact time left differs for every goal: computing it before each search is too slow, and storing it for every pair of vertices takes too much memory (Red Blob, differential heuristics).
6.1 The triangle inequality on travel times
The idea. Pick one vertex, L at the east edge of the town, and compute the fastest time from every vertex to it, once, with one Dijkstra run backwards from L. Then use it for any goal. From B, one way to reach L is to drive to T first and then on to L. That way can never beat the fastest way from B to L (Figure 9). With the stored times, 193.8 s from B to L and 46.8 s from T to L (notebook):
\text{time}(B, T) + 46.8 \ge 193.8
\text{time}(B, T) \ge 193.8 - 46.8
= 147.0 \text{ s}

Figure 9: The landmark bound at B. The fastest times from B to the landmark L, 193.8 s, and from T to L, 46.8 s, are stored (purple). The fastest time from B to the goal T is what the search does not know (blue, dashed; the true value is 156.0 s). Driving B to T to L is one way of reaching L, so it is never faster than the fastest way: time(B, T) + 46.8 ≥ 193.8, so time(B, T) ≥ 147.0 s
The guess at B rises from 67.5 s to 147.0 s; the truth is 156.0 s. The rule used is the triangle inequality (G-2683)Triangle inequality: The rule that a detour through a third point is never shorter than going straight, d(p, q) \le d(p, r) + d(r, q); it is what lets a nearest-neighbour search skip a region farther than its best point. Explained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §7.1 The rules a distance must follow, a detour through a third point is never shorter than going straight, here for fastest travel times instead of distances (Red Blob, differential heuristics; Freiburg L3).
The formal version. With:

u, the vertex the search is at (B above);
t, the goal (T);
L, a landmark (L);
\text{time}(x, y), the fastest travel time from x to y, in s;
h_L(u), the heuristic at u from landmark L, in s (147.0 s at B).

The steps, as above with numbers:
\text{time}(u, t) + \text{time}(t, L) \ge \text{time}(u, L)
\text{time}(u, t) \ge \text{time}(u, L) - \text{time}(t, L)
h_L(u) = \text{time}(u, L) - \text{time}(t, L)
On a directed graph the trip into a landmark and the trip out of it can differ, so each landmark stores both, and a second bound comes from driving L to u to t (Freiburg L3):
\text{time}(u, t) \ge \text{time}(L, t) - \text{time}(L, u)
The heuristic takes the larger of the two bounds, and 0 if both are negative. Both lines are lower bounds, so the heuristic is admissible. The landmark heuristic is also consistent (Freiburg L3). On the edge from A to N, 28.8 s, the stored times to L are 141.3 s from A and 112.5 s from N:
141.3 \le 28.8 + 112.5
141.3 - 46.8 \le 28.8 + 112.5 - 46.8
94.5 \le 28.8 + 65.7
The same steps for any edge from u to w with travel time c:
\text{time}(u, L) \le c + \text{time}(w, L)
h_L(u) \le c + h_L(w)
The first line is the triangle inequality again; the second subtracts \text{time}(t, L) from both sides.
The standard terms. A vertex chosen in advance whose travel times to and from every other vertex are stored is a landmark (G-2877)Landmark (route planning): A vertex chosen in advance whose fastest travel times to and from every other vertex are computed once and stored; by the triangle inequality the stored times give a lower bound on the time between any two vertices. Not the sensed landmark of localisation. Explained in §6.1 The triangle inequality on travel times. in route planning; it is a vertex of the graph, not an object the robot senses, as a landmark (G-2342)Landmark: An object the robot can detect reliably and tell apart from the others, such as a coloured pole or a door; its known position in the map lets readings of it fix the robot’s pose. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §6.1 Why extract features is in localisation. A* with the largest landmark bound as its heuristic is ALT (G-2878)ALT (A, landmarks, triangle inequality; differential heuristic):* A* whose heuristic is the largest lower bound from a few landmarks, time(u, L) − time(t, L) and time(L, t) − time(L, u); it never overestimates and follows the roads, so on the Chicago map 16 landmarks cut a trip from 1229 vertices taken off to 108. Explained in §6.1 The triangle inequality on travel times., for A*, landmarks and the triangle inequality (Goldberg and Harrelson 2005). The bound is also called the differential heuristic, because it takes the difference of two stored costs (Red Blob, differential heuristics).
6.2 The search with a landmark
The bound at B is now close to the truth. Figure 10 runs A* with it on the town; watch B through the frames: it goes onto the open list and is never taken off.

A* takes off S, A, N, M, D and T, 6 vertices, only the fastest route. B, in the old town, stays on the open list: its f = 96.0 + 147.0 = 243.0 s is above the route’s 197.1 s
With the landmark, B’s estimated total cost is:
f(B) = 96.0 + 147.0

which is above the route’s 197.1 s, so A* finishes before B comes off: 6 vertices against 7 with the straight line and 10 with Dijkstra, all with the 197.1 s route (notebook).
One landmark does not help everywhere. At M the bound is only 1.8 s, while the straight line gives 28.8 s and the truth is 64.8 s (notebook): from M the fastest way to L does not pass T, so the detour through T says little. A landmark gives a tight bound when it lies behind the goal, as seen from the vertex, or before the vertex, as seen from the goal (Freiburg L3; Goldberg and Harrelson 2005). No single landmark is behind every goal, so ALT keeps several landmarks and takes the largest bound (Red Blob, differential heuristics).

On a road graph of 1.6 million vertices with travel-time costs, A* with landmarks, searching from both ends, took 12 ms where bidirectional (G-2584)Bidirectional search: A forward search from the start and a backward search from the goal run in turn until some state has been expanded by both; the route is the smallest sum of the two costs over all states both reached, since the meeting state can be off the shortest route. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §8.2 Bidirectional search Dijkstra took 340 ms (UW CSE 421 L7).
Landmarks keep the search near the route, but the search still walks the route itself, intersection by intersection. A long route passes thousands of vertices, such as the 3,617 of a route from Glasgow to London (mjt CH), and A* takes every one of them off its open list.
7. Contraction hierarchies: shortcuts over unimportant roads


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Rank the vertices from least to most important and remove them in that order, adding a shortcut whenever a removed vertex lay on the only fastest way between two of its neighbours. A query then runs two searches, from the start and from the goal, that only climb to higher ranks and meet at the top, which the shortcuts make enough: 67 + 92 intersections on the Chicago trip.


ALT of Section 6 still takes off its open list every intersection of the route and some around it: 108 on the Chicago trip, whose route has 42, and the route grows with the trip. Long trips need a search that skips most of the small roads.
7.1 Why skip small roads
The idea. Drivers use small streets near the start and the goal, bigger roads farther away, and motorways in between (Freiburg L6). On the town trip, only S and T are on small roads; the middle of the route is the bypass. A search would be faster if, away from the ends, it looked only at important roads.
A rule such as “far from the ends, use only motorways” is fast but can miss the fastest route; navigation devices used rules of that kind for years (Freiburg L6). Contraction hierarchies keep the idea and lose nothing: they add shortcuts so that skipping a vertex never loses a route.
7.2 Contracting a vertex: shortcuts
The idea. Put the vertices in an order, least important first: in the town, the old town (E, F, B, C), then the ends (S, T, L), the junctions (A, D) and the bypass last (N, M). Remove them one at a time. Before removing a vertex, look at every way through it, from a neighbour u in to a neighbour w out:

if the way through it is the only fastest way from u to w, add a direct edge from u to w with the same time;
if another way from u to w, avoiding the vertex, is no slower, add nothing.

The standard terms. Removing a vertex while keeping every fastest time between the vertices left is node contraction (G-2879)Node contraction: Removing a vertex from a graph while keeping every fastest time between the vertices left, by adding a shortcut for each way through it that nothing else matches; the step that builds a contraction hierarchy. Explained in §7.2 Contracting a vertex: shortcuts. (Geisberger et al. 2008). The direct edge it adds is a shortcut (G-2880)Shortcut (contraction hierarchies): A direct edge from u to w added when a contracted vertex v lay on the only fastest way u → v → w, with that way’s time, such as A → C, 120 s, for A → B → C; it lets a search skip v and is unpacked back into the original edges. Explained in §7.2 Contracting a vertex: shortcuts.. The other way is found by a Dijkstra run from u that may not use the vertex being contracted (Freiburg L6; Geisberger et al. 2008). For each way through the vertex (orange), a search that avoids the vertex looks for another way that is no slower (purple, dashed). None: a shortcut (green) with the way’s time. After every vertex has gone, each has a rank, its place in the order, and the graph to search is the original edges plus the shortcuts: the contraction hierarchy (G-2882)Contraction hierarchy (CH): A road graph whose vertices have been contracted one by one in order of importance, so each has a rank, plus the shortcuts added; a query runs two searches, from the start and back from the goal, that only climb to higher ranks and meet near the top, so on large maps it looks at a few hundred vertices. Explained in §7.2 Contracting a vertex: shortcuts., CH (Geisberger et al. 2008).
Why contraction keeps every fastest time. Each contraction keeps every fastest time between the vertices that remain: a fastest route through the removed vertex either has a shortcut of the same time or another way that is no slower (Freiburg L7). In the town, after B is gone, A to C still takes 120 s, by the shortcut. Applying this once per vertex, the times in the final graph equal those of the original (Freiburg L7).
The order decides the speed, not the answer. Any order gives correct routes; a good order adds few shortcuts and gives short searches (Freiburg L6; mjt CH). A common order prefers vertices whose contraction adds fewer edges than it removes, and spreads the contractions evenly over the map by counting neighbours already contracted (Geisberger et al. 2008). On a road graph of Western Europe, 18,029,721 vertices, the first rule alone gave queries that took 1791 vertices off; adding the count of contracted neighbours cut that to 403 (Geisberger et al. 2008). The Chicago hierarchy uses those two rules and adds 5509 shortcuts to its 3857 edges (notebook).
7.3 The query: two searches that only climb
The idea. Search from the start and, backwards, from the goal, as in bidirectional search (G-2584)Bidirectional search: A forward search from the start and a backward search from the goal run in turn until some state has been expanded by both; the route is the smallest sum of the two costs over all states both reached, since the meeting state can be off the shortest route. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §8.2 Bidirectional search, but let each search follow only edges that lead to a higher rank. Each climbs towards the important roads, and they meet near the top (Geisberger et al. 2008). Figure 13 runs it on the town; the bottom of each frame redraws the vertices at the height of their rank.

Figure 13: Queries on the contracted town. Top: the town; bottom: the same vertices raised to their rank (0 for E at the bottom, 10 for M at the top), with the edges and shortcuts (green) between them. The search from the start (red) and the search back from the goal (blue) take one vertex off in turn and follow only edges that climb; purple: taken off by both. S to T: they meet at M, 132.3 + 64.8 = 197.1 s, after 8 take-offs. S to C: the cheapest vertex taken off by both is A, 36 + 120 = 156 s, by the shortcut A → C, which unpacks to A, B, C on the map
On the town trip, the search from S climbs S, A, N, M, and the search back from T climbs T, D, L, M. M is taken off by both:
132.3 + 64.8 = 197.1 \text{ s}
the fastest time, after 8 take-offs, against Dijkstra’s 10. Each search stops once the smallest cost on its open list is at least the best route found so far, as no later vertex can give a faster one (Geisberger et al. 2008). The answer is the smallest sum over all vertices taken off by both (Freiburg L6), as in bidirectional search: for S to C three vertices qualify, A with 156 s, N with 213.6 s and M with 221.1 s, and A wins (Figure 13, last frame).
Why climbing is enough. Follow the ranks along the fastest town route S-A-N-M-D-T:























VertexSANMDTRank4791085
The ranks rise to M, the most important vertex on the route, and then fall. So the route is a climb from S to M, found by the search from S, and a climb from T to M, found by the search from T. A route whose ranks dip in the middle is also covered: the dip’s vertex was contracted before its two neighbours, and a shortcut, or another way of the same time, bridges it. On S to C, B (rank 2) lies between A (rank 7) and C (rank 3), and the shortcut A → C bridges it; unpacking the shortcut gives back A, B, C (Freiburg L7; Geisberger et al. 2008).
On real maps. On the Chicago trip the two searches take off 67 and 92 intersections, 159 in all, and over 200 random trips 90.0 on average, against 861.1 for Dijkstra and 51.6 for 16 landmarks (notebook). On a city map, the hierarchy and the landmarks are close. The hierarchy pays on large maps: on Western Europe’s 18 million vertices, a query took 403 vertices off and ran in 183 µs (Geisberger et al. 2008), and on the United Kingdom’s 3,478,051 vertices a query visited 3968 + 3113 of them (mjt CH).
7.4 CH-Potentials: the hierarchy as a heuristic
A contraction hierarchy is built for one set of costs. Traffic changes the times, and forbidden turns or other rules change which routes are allowed; A* handles such changes easily, because only its costs and moves change, but it is only as fast as its heuristic (Strasser and Zeitz 2021). CH-Potentials (G-2883)CH-Potentials: A heuristic for A* taken from a contraction hierarchy, which estimates the time left tightly; it keeps A*‘s flexibility for traffic and turn rules while using the hierarchy’s speed. Explained in §7.4 CH-Potentials: the hierarchy as a heuristic. take the heuristic for A* from a contraction hierarchy: the hierarchy’s fast queries give A* tight estimates of the time left, while A* keeps its flexibility (Strasser and Zeitz 2021). Here the heuristic is built from the road network’s own hierarchy.
From no heuristic to the straight line to landmarks, the A* loop never changed; only the heuristic did, and with it the work, from 1526 intersections to 108. CH-Potentials take the same step once more: the hierarchy itself becomes the heuristic.

Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edgesOne point of a graph, such as one free cell of the room or one waypoint; the places a search moves between.Edge (graph) (G-2542)Edge (graph): A link between two vertices of a graph, such as one 0.5 m move between two free cells that share a side; it says the search can go directly from one vertex to the other. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edgesA link between two vertices of a graph, such as one 0.5 m move between two free cells that share a side; it says the search can go directly from one vertex to the other.Weighted graph (edge cost) (G-2563)Weighted graph (edge cost): A graph in which every edge carries a number, its cost, such as a move’s length in metres (0.5 m straight, 0.707 m diagonal); the cost of a path is the sum of its edge costs, so the cheapest route need not have the fewest edges. Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §2.2 Edge costs: the fewest moves is not the shortestA graph in which every edge carries a number, its cost, such as a move’s length in metres (0.5 m straight, 0.707 m diagonal); the cost of a path is the sum of its edge costs, so the cheapest route need not have the fewest edges.Dijkstra’s algorithm (G-2565)Dijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §3.2 The algorithm: settle the nearest, update its neighboursA search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals).Admissible heuristic (G-2578)Admissible heuristic: A heuristic that is never more than the true cost left from any state, h \le h^\ast; it makes f a lower bound on every route through a state, so the first route A* takes off the open list is the shortest. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §5.1 A guess that never overestimatesA heuristic that is never more than the true cost left from any state, h \le h^\ast; it makes f a lower bound on every route through a state, so the first route A* takes off the open list is the shortest.Consistent heuristic (monotone heuristic) (G-2580)Consistent heuristic (monotone heuristic): A heuristic that never falls by more than a move’s cost, h(n) \le c(n, n') + h(n'), with 0 at the goal (a triangle inequality); it keeps f from decreasing along a route, so A* with a closed list expands every state with its shortest g. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §6.2 The fix: a guess that never drops faster than the distanceA heuristic that never falls by more than a move’s cost, h(n) \le c(n, n') + h(n'), with 0 at the goal (a triangle inequality); it keeps f from decreasing along a route, so A* with a closed list expands every state with its shortest g.Dominance (of heuristics) (G-2579)Dominance (of heuristics): One admissible heuristic dominates another when it is at least as large at every state; being closer to the true cost, it makes A* expand fewer states (the octile distance dominates the straight line). Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §5.3 A closer guess takes fewer cellsOne admissible heuristic dominates another when it is at least as large at every state; being closer to the true cost, it makes A* expand fewer states (the octile distance dominates the straight line).Triangle inequality (G-2683)Triangle inequality: The rule that a detour through a third point is never shorter than going straight, d(p, q) \le d(p, r) + d(r, q); it is what lets a nearest-neighbour search skip a region farther than its best point. Explained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §7.1 The rules a distance must followThe rule that a detour through a third point is never shorter than going straight, d(p, q) \le d(p, r) + d(r, q); it is what lets a nearest-neighbour search skip a region farther than its best point.Landmark (G-2342)Landmark: An object the robot can detect reliably and tell apart from the others, such as a coloured pole or a door; its known position in the map lets readings of it fix the robot’s pose. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §6.1 Why extract featuresAn object the robot can detect reliably and tell apart from the others, such as a coloured pole or a door; its known position in the map lets readings of it fix the robot’s pose.Bidirectional search (G-2584)Bidirectional search: A forward search from the start and a backward search from the goal run in turn until some state has been expanded by both; the route is the smallest sum of the two costs over all states both reached, since the meeting state can be off the shortest route. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §8.2 Bidirectional searchA forward search from the start and a backward search from the goal run in turn until some state has been expanded by both; the route is the smallest sum of the two costs over all states both reached, since the meeting state can be off the shortest route.

RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.title: Trajectory Optimisation
RO/navigation/06-grid-sampling-and-car-l.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Gradient descentGradient descent: Finding the lowest point of a function by repeated small steps downhill. Explained in: Gradient Descent from Scratch, §2. The idea; Kinodynamic planning and phase spaceKinodynamic planning: Planning a motion that avoids obstacles and also obeys limits on how the state can change, \dot{x} = f(x, u) with bounded inputs, such as a top speed and an acceleration limit; its plans can be driven as they are, without stops the robot cannot make. Explained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §2.3 Kinodynamic planning.
Compare with: Motion primitives and lattice searchMotion primitive: A short motion the robot can drive, usually one input held for a fixed time, such as full left at 0.5 m/s for 0.75 s; planners chain primitives so that every path they build is drivable. Explained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §5. A few motions to build with: motion primitives and a system simulator.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A path says where the robot goes; a trajectory also says when, and with which commands. Trajectory optimisation writes the commands over time as a list of numbers and improves the list with gradients until the robot ends where it should, within its limits, at the least cost: the robot reaches the door pose in 6.18 s, against 8.08 s for stopping and turning along a route.


The robot can already find its way to the door. The planners of this chapter give it a route round the table, and planning with motion limitsExplained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §5. A few motions to build with: motion primitives and a system simulator gives it drivable motions built from fixed pieces: arcs, straight runs and speed changes that respect how fast its wheels can turn and how fast it can speed up. Fixed pieces have a price: on a straight 3.0 m drive from rest to rest, a lattice searchLattice search: Graph search over states that the primitives keep on a regular grid, such as positions every 0.0625 m and speeds every 0.25 m/s when the robot accelerates, coasts or brakes every 0.5 s; any graph search then finds the best plan on that grid. Explained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §6. Searching the primitives systematically: lattice search over such pieces, with steps of 0.5 s, drives it in 7.0 s, while the true least time is 6.2 s: speed up at the limit, cruise at the top speed, brake.
The drive the robot needs is not straight. The robot starts at rest at (2.0, 1.0) facing 30°, and must stop at the door pose, (3.6, 3.5) facing 90°, just below the door. Its limits are those of the same robot: a disk of radius 0.25 m, each wheel at most 0.6 m/s, its forward speed changing by at most 0.5 m/s every second. Three things stand in the way:

The table. The straight line from start to door pose, 2.968 m long, passes 0.185 m from the table’s corner; the disk needs 0.25 m, so it would hit the table by 0.065 m (notebook).
The turns. The robot faces 30° at the start, the line runs at 57.4°, and the door pose faces 90°.
The timing. A route says where to drive, not how fast at each moment. Following a route with one corner, at (3.0, 3.3), and stopping to turn at the corner takes 8.08 s (notebook).

Figure 1 plays the stop-and-turn drive and the drive this Note finds side by side, with a clock: watch the grey robot stop at the corner to turn while the blue one keeps moving round the table’s corner.

Figure 1: Two drives from rest at (2.0, 1.0) facing 30° to rest at the door pose (3.6, 3.5) facing 90°, past the table, one frame per 0.2 s. Grey: stop and turn, along a route with one corner at (3.0, 3.3): turn on the spot, drive, stop, turn, drive, stop, turn: 8.08 s. Blue: the least-time trajectory found in this Note: 6.18 s. Each robot is a disk of radius 0.25 m with a line for its heading; the dotted line round the table is the band the disk’s centre must stay out of; the pale circle is the door pose. The last frame holds at 8.08 s
The blue drive arrives 1.90 s sooner. The blue robot never stops: it turns towards the door while it speeds up, runs at the 0.6 m/s limit, passes the table’s corner with no room to spare, and turns to face the door as it brakes. No fixed set of pieces had to contain that motion; it was computed. This Note builds that computation:

what a trajectory is, and the problem of finding the best one (Section 2);
turning commands over time, which are functions, into a list of numbers (Section 3);
single shooting: simulate the drive, measure the miss, adjust the commands (Section 4);
multiple shooting: the same with the drive cut into pieces (Section 5);
collocation: no simulation, the motion rules written as equations at points (Section 6);
iLQR and DDP, which use the robot’s model to take much better steps (Section 7);
the other family, indirect methods, and Pontryagin’s principle (Section 8).

2. From a path to a trajectory


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A trajectory gives the robot’s state at every moment, and the commands that produce it. Finding the best trajectory means choosing the commands over time that minimise a cost, here the time or the effort, while the robot obeys its motion rules, starts and ends where it must, and keeps its limits.


The opening drive failed on timing as much as on the table: a route says where to drive, and the robot still needs to know how fast to go and how hard to turn at each moment.
2.1 What a trajectory is
The idea. A path is a line on the floor. A trajectory is the same line with a clock on it: where the robot is at 1 s, at 2 s, at 3 s, how fast it goes and how it is turning. Figure 2 shows the drive of Figure 1 this way: the dots, one every 0.5 s, are far apart where the robot is fast and close together where it speeds up or brakes.
Make interactive
Figure 2: The least-time drive as a trajectory. Left: its path from the start (2.0, 1.0) to the door pose (3.6, 3.5), with a dot every 0.5 s and the time written at 2, 3, 4 and 5 s; the robot arrives at 6.18 s. Dots far apart mean the robot is fast. Right: its forward speed v over time: up at 0.5 m/s² for 1.2 s, along the 0.6 m/s limit (dashed), and down at 0.5 m/s² at the end
To describe the robot at one moment we need four numbers, its state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §4.1 State: from one number to many, everything about the robot that matters for what happens next, and two commands, its control inputs (G-2298)Control input u: The numbers we choose to drive a robot, such as u = (v, \omega); the model turns them into motion. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §5.2 The kinematic model. With their values at the start:

x, y, the position of the robot’s centre, in m (2.0 and 1.0);
\theta, its heading, the direction it faces, in rad (30°, 0.524 rad);
v, its forward speed, in m/s (0 at the start);
a, the acceleration, how fast v changes, in m/s² (a control input);
\omega, the turn rate, how fast \theta changes, in rad/s (a control input).

The rules that say how the state changes are the robot’s kinematic model (G-2297)Kinematic model: Equations that give how a robot’s configuration changes from its speed inputs alone, ignoring masses and forces, such as \dot{x} = v\cos\theta, \dot{y} = v\sin\theta, \dot{\theta} = \omega; used to predict motion at low speed. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §5.2 The kinematic model, plus one line that makes the speed change only through the acceleration. A dot over a symbol means how fast that quantity changes, per second:
\dot x = v \cos\theta
\dot y = v \sin\theta
\dot \theta = \omega
\dot v = a
The speed is part of the state, not a command, because the robot cannot change its speed at once: at most 0.5 m/s every second (the acceleration limitExplained in: Planning with Motion Limits, §2.2 The state, its motion equations and the stopping distance).
The wheel limit. Each wheel turns at most 0.6 m/s. With the wheel separation L = 0.2 m, the wheel speedsExplained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §4.5 Back again: the wheel speeds for a wanted motion for a forward speed v and turn rate \omega are, with:

v_R, v_L, the right and left wheel speeds, in m/s;
L, the wheel separation, 0.2 m.

v_R = v + \omega L / 2
v_L = v - \omega L / 2
Both must stay at most 0.6 m/s. Driving at 0.5 m/s:
0.5 + \omega \times 0.1 \le 0.6
\omega \le 1 \text{ rad/s}
and at rest the robot can spin at up to 6 rad/s. Turning costs speed: the faster the robot drives, the slower it can turn.
The standard term. A description of the robot’s state at every moment of a time interval, together with the controls that produce it, is a trajectory (G-2886)Trajectory: The state of a robot at every moment of a time interval, together with the controls that produce it, such as the 6.18 s drive to the door pose; unlike a path, it says when the robot is where and how it is commanded. Explained in §2.1 What a trajectory is. (Kelly 2017; Lynch and Park §10.7).
2.2 The best trajectory: cost and constraints
Among all the trajectories that take the robot from the start to the door pose, we want the best one. “Best” needs a number, the cost. This Note uses two costs:

least time: the duration T, in s; the opening drive asks for it;
least effort in a fixed time: drive to the door pose in exactly 8 s, as gently as possible, with the effort defined below. A gentle drive is easier on the motors and the wheels’ grip, and least effort in a fixed time is a standard first example: a cart that swings a pole upright with the motor force squared, added up over the swing, as small as possible (Kelly 2017).

With:

T, the duration of the drive, in s (8 s for the effort problem);
J, the effort, in m²/s³: the acceleration squared plus 0.01 times the turn rate squared, added up over the drive, so that turning at 1 rad/s counts like speeding up at 0.1 m/s²; squaring makes large commands cost much more than small ones, so the drive comes out smooth (Kelly 2017).

J = \int_0^T \big(a^2 + 0.01\thinspace\omega^2\big)\thinspace dt
The \int sign adds up the quantity after it over every moment from 0 to T, the area under its curve (G-957)Integration: Finding the area under a curve by adding up infinitely many thin strips. Explained in: Probability Density Function and the CDF of a Continuous Variable, §3. Area under the curve is probability.
The rules the trajectory must obey are its constraints (G-456)Constraint: A condition the solution must satisfy; in SVM, y_i (w^T x_i + b) \geq 1 for every training point. Explained in: The Mathematics of SVM: Hard Margin, §4.2 One constraint for both classes, conditions every acceptable answer must meet:

the motion rules of Section 2.1, at every moment;
the start, (2.0, 1.0) facing 30° at rest, and the end, (3.6, 3.5) facing 90° at rest;
the limits at every moment: both wheels at most 0.6 m/s, the acceleration between −0.5 and 0.5 m/s², the speed at least 0;
the table: the disk’s centre at least 0.25 m from it.

Constraints of the first kind come from the robot’s model, the second fix its ends, and the third and fourth hold along the whole drive. Finding the controls over time, and the duration if it is free, that minimise the cost while every constraint holds is trajectory optimisation (G-2887)Trajectory optimisation: Finding the controls over time (and the duration, if free) that minimise a cost such as time or effort while the motion rules, the start and end states and every limit hold; it computes one good trajectory where a rule for every state would be too large. Explained in §2.2 The best trajectory: cost and constraints. (Kelly 2017; Lynch and Park §10.7). In symbols (Lynch and Park §10.7), with:

\mathbf{x}, the state, the four numbers (x, y, \theta, v), at the start (2.0, 1.0, 0.524, 0);
\mathbf{u}, the controls, the two numbers (a, \omega);
f, the four motion rules of Section 2.1, which give how fast each state number changes.

\text{find } a(t), \omega(t), T
\text{minimising } T \text{ or } J
\text{with } \dot{\mathbf{x}} = f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u})
\mathbf{x}(0) = \text{start}
\mathbf{x}(T) = \text{door pose}
\text{and the limits at every } t
Why one trajectory, not a rule for every state. The best possible answer would be a policy (G-1512)Policy: The agent’s rules for which action to take. Explained in: Types of Machine Learning, §5.1 Agent, environment, policy and reward: the best controls from every state the robot could be in. A policy needs a value for every state, and the states grow fast with their number: a walking robot with 10 joints has a state of 20 numbers, an angle and a turning speed for each joint, and the cost of covering every state grows exponentially with that number (Kelly 2017). Even our 4-number state, cut into 5 cm, 5° and 0.05 m/s steps, gives 140 positions across the room, 80 along it, 72 headings and 13 speeds:
140 \times 80 \times 72 \times 13
= 10483200 \text{ states}
for one room. Trajectory optimisation gives up on every state and finds one good trajectory, from this start to this goal, which needs far less computation (Kelly 2017). The price is that it answers only for this start: a robot pushed off the trajectory needs a new one, or a controller that brings it back.
The problem is stated. But a(t) and \omega(t) are functions, with a value at every one of infinitely many moments, and a computer can only search over a list of numbers.
3. Turning functions into numbers: transcription


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Cut the drive into short intervals and keep a few numbers per interval: the controls, or the controls and the states. The trajectory problem becomes a problem of choosing a list of numbers: the 8 s drive with 30 intervals has 60 control numbers.


Section 2 left the controls as functions of time, with infinitely many values to choose.
The idea. A film is a list of still pictures, 24 every second, and the eye fills in between. A drive can be described the same way: cut the 8 s into 30 intervals of 0.267 s and hold the acceleration and the turn rate constant in each. The two functions become 30 pairs of numbers, 60 in all (Figure 3).
Make interactive
Figure 3: The controls of the 8 s least-effort drive (found in Section 4) as a list of numbers. The 8 s are cut into 30 intervals of 0.267 s, and in each the acceleration a (top) and the turn rate ω (bottom) are held constant: 30 + 30 = 60 numbers. The acceleration falls in nearly a straight line from 0.27 to −0.27 m/s²: speed up, then brake
The standard terms. Turning a trajectory optimisation problem, whose unknowns are functions, into a problem whose unknowns are a finite list of numbers is transcription (G-2888)Transcription: Turning a trajectory optimisation problem, whose unknowns are functions of time, into one whose unknowns are a finite list of numbers, such as 60 control values for an 8 s drive cut into 30 intervals, so that an optimiser can search over them. Explained in §3. Turning functions into numbers: transcription. (Kelly 2017). The result is an optimisation over a list of numbers: choose the numbers to minimise a cost, subject to equations and inequalities that may be curved, such as the cosine in \dot x = v \cos\theta (Kelly 2017).
There are three ways to pick the numbers (Lynch and Park §10.7):

the path only, and work out the controls from it; this does not work for our robot, which has 2 controls for its 3 position numbers x, y, \theta (Lynch and Park §10.7), so most paths cannot be driven;
the controls only, and find the states by simulating the motion rules: shooting (Section 4);
the controls and the states, and make the motion rules hold between them as equations: collocation (Section 6).

Discretising first and optimising after is what makes all of these methods direct; the other family, indirect methods, comes in Section 8 (Kelly 2017). The list of numbers is ready; the next question is how to improve it.
4. Single shooting: simulate, measure the miss, adjust


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Guess the controls, simulate the drive, measure how far it ends from the goal, and change the controls against the gradient of that miss; repeat. On the straight drive each step cuts the miss to a quarter, and on the room drive 60 numbers reach the door pose in 73 iterations, but an early control moves the end far more than a late one, which makes long drives hard.


Section 3 turned the controls into numbers. Shooting keeps only those numbers as unknowns and finds the states by simulation.
4.1 Fire, see where it lands, adjust: one number by hand
The idea. To hit a target with a cannon, fire, see where the ball lands, change the launch speed and fire again (Kelly, cannon). A drive works the same way: choose the controls, simulate the drive, and see where it ends.
We start with the straight drive, which has one number to choose. The robot must cover 3.0 m along a line in 10 s, from rest to rest: speed up at a for 5 s, then brake at a for 5 s. With:

a, the acceleration, in m/s², the one number we choose (first guess 0);
s_{\text{end}}, the distance covered after 10 s, in m;
e, the miss, s_{\text{end}} minus the 3.0 m wanted, in m.

After 5 s the speed is 5a. The distance in each half follows from constant acceleration:
\text{first half} = a \times 5^2 / 2
= 12.5\thinspace a
\text{second half} = 5a \times 5 - a \times 5^2 / 2
= 12.5\thinspace a
s_{\text{end}} = 25\thinspace a
The braking takes the speed from 5a back to 0, so every shot stops; only the distance can miss.
The miss and its slope. The first shot, a = 0, does not move: it misses by 3.0 m. To improve it we use gradient descent (G-862)Gradient descent: Finding the lowest point of a function by repeated small steps downhill. Explained in: Gradient Descent from Scratch, §1. Overview: take the squared miss as the cost and step against its slope. With:

e, the miss, 25a - 3, in m;
C, the cost, the squared miss, e^2;
\eta, the learning rate (G-1068)Learning rate (\eta): How strongly each update changes the model; in gradient descent, the number the slope is multiplied by to get the step size. Explained in: Online Machine Learning, §5. The learning rate, the size of each step, 0.0006.

The slope of the squared miss is twice the miss, and the miss grows by 25 m for every 1 m/s² of a, so by the chain rule (G-371)Chain rule: To differentiate a function of a function, multiply the outer derivative by the inner derivative. Explained in: The Derivative of the Sigmoid Function, §2. Two rules we need the slope of C with respect to a is
\frac{dC}{da} = 2e \times 25
= 50\thinspace e
The first step, from a = 0 with e = -3:
\frac{dC}{da} = 50 \times (-3)
= -150
a = 0 - 0.0006 \times (-150)
= 0.09
The second shot ends short again:
s_{\text{end}} = 25 \times 0.09
= 2.25 \text{ m}
e = 2.25 - 3
= -0.75 \text{ m}
Figure 4 fires the shots one per frame; watch the red miss shrink.

Figure 4: Single shooting with one number, the acceleration a, on the straight drive: speed up at a for 5 s, brake at a for 5 s, ending 25a metres along. Each frame fires one shot (blue: distance along the line over time; earlier shots pale), measures the miss at 10 s against the target 3.0 m (dashed; the miss in red), and steps a against the slope of the squared miss, 50 times the miss, with step size 0.0006. a goes 0, 0.09, 0.1125, 0.1181, 0.1195; the miss 3.0, 0.75, 0.1875, 0.0469, 0.0117 m
Each step cuts the miss to a quarter: 3.0, 0.75, 0.1875, 0.0469 m (notebook). The quarter follows from one step, with e_{\text{new}} the miss after it:
e_{\text{new}} = 25\thinspace(a - 0.0006 \times 50\thinspace e) - 3
= 25\thinspace(a - 0.03\thinspace e) - 3
= (25a - 3) - 0.75\thinspace e
= e - 0.75\thinspace e
= 0.25\thinspace e
The shots close in on the a that makes the miss 0:
a = 3 / 25
= 0.12 \text{ m/s}^2
which reaches 0.6 m/s at 5 s, exactly the robot’s top speed.
The standard terms. Keeping only the controls (and the start) as unknowns, finding the trajectory by one simulation from the start, and adjusting the controls until the end meets the goal is single shooting (G-2890)Single shooting (direct shooting): Trajectory optimisation that keeps only the controls as unknowns, finds the trajectory by one simulation from the start, and adjusts the controls until the end meets the goal; simple, but an early control moves the end far more than a late one. Explained in §4.1 Fire, see where it lands, adjust: one number by hand., also called direct shooting (Kelly 2017; Kelly, cannon). The gap between where a simulation ends and where it must end is a defect (G-2891)Defect: The gap between where a simulation or an integration rule says the trajectory should be and where the unknowns put it, such as a shot ending 1.048 m short of the door pose; the solver drives every defect to 0. Explained in §4.1 Fire, see where it lands, adjust: one number by hand. (Kelly, cannon); the solver drives every defect to 0.
4.2 Shooting the drive to the door
The room drive has 60 numbers instead of one, and turning makes the motion rules curved. The loop is the same:

guess the 60 controls; our first shot faces the goal and speeds up and brakes too gently, ending 1.048 m short (notebook);
simulate the drive from the start, in steps of 0.067 s;
measure the miss at the end and how far the drive breaks a limit or enters the table’s band;
change all 60 controls at once, using how each miss and each broken limit changes with each control;
repeat until nothing misses and nothing is broken.

Each simulation step uses a fourth-order Runge–Kutta step, a more accurate version of the Euler step (G-2299)Euler step: One step of predicting motion: hold the rates fixed for a short time \Delta t and add rate times \Delta t to each quantity; repeated, it traces a path, more accurately the smaller \Delta t is. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §5.3 Why we predict the path step by step that samples the motion rules four times per step (Kelly 2017).
The table that lists how every miss changes with every control is the Jacobian (G-980)Jacobian: The table (matrix) of all first partial derivatives of a function with several inputs and outputs, one row per output and one column per input, J_{ij} = \partial f_i/\partial x_j; it shows how every output changes with every input near a point. Explained in: The Jacobian and Gradients of Matrices, §4.2 The formula: every partial derivative in one grid. Plain gradient descent would step down the slope of the cost; we use SciPy’s least-squares solver, a Gauss–Newton method, which uses the Jacobian to aim each step at the point where the misses, treated as straight lines, would all be 0, and so needs far fewer steps (Virtanen et al. 2020). The misses and broken limits are added to the cost, squared and weighted, and the weight is raised from 100 to 1,000,000 so that by the end they must be 0: such penalty terms are the usual way to add constraints to shooting (Tedrake, Underactuated ch. 10). Figure 5 runs it; watch the end of the blue drive close on the door pose.

Figure 5: Single shooting of the 8 s least-effort drive to the door pose, one solver iteration per frame (thinning out after the first 12). Each frame is one simulation from the start with the current 60 controls (blue; the 4 before it pale), and the red line is the miss at the end. 4.3 The long lever of the first control
Single shooting worked here, but it has a weakness that grows with the length of the drive. A control early in the drive acts on everything after it; a late control acts on little. On the straight drive with two numbers, a_1 for the first 5 s and a_2 for the last 5 s, the first half covers 12.5\thinspace a_1 as in Section 4.1 and ends at the speed 5a_1, which the second half keeps adding for 5 s:
s_{\text{end}} = 12.5\thinspace a_1 + 5a_1 \times 5 + 12.5\thinspace a_2
= 37.5\thinspace a_1 + 12.5\thinspace a_2
The first number moves the end 3 times as far as the second. On the room drive, 0.1 rad/s more turn rate in the first interval moves the end 0.079 m, and the same change in the last interval moves it about 0.0001 m (notebook): a turn early on swings the whole rest of the drive round.
So the solver must balance numbers whose effects differ by orders of magnitude, and on long or sensitive problems the steps go wrong; this is a property of the problem, not of the program (Tedrake, Underactuated ch. 10). Limits along the way are also awkward, because the states are not unknowns: every limit is a long chain of simulation back to the controls (Kelly 2017). Single shooting suits problems with simple controls and few path constraints, such as spacecraft, and can fail on harder ones (Kelly 2017; Kelly, cannon). The fix is to shorten the lever.
5. Multiple shooting: shorter pieces, joined up


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Cut the drive into pieces, simulate each from its own start state, and make those start states unknowns too, with a defect at every join that must close. Each control then acts on one short piece: on the room drive with 5 pieces, the first turn rate’s lever falls from 0.079 m to 0.008 m, and the same drive is found in 80 iterations.


Section 4.3 ended on the long lever: in single shooting, the first control moves the end of an 8 s drive ten times as far as the same change within a 1.6 s piece.
The idea. Instead of one long shot, fire several short ones. Cut the 8 s into 5 pieces of 1.6 s. Guess where the robot is at the start of each piece, its full state, and simulate each piece from there with its own 6 intervals of controls. At first the pieces do not meet; the solver moves both the controls and the start states until each piece ends exactly where the next one starts (Kelly 2017; Kelly, cannon). Figure 6 runs it; watch the red gaps between the coloured pieces close.

The drive is cut into 5 pieces of 1.6 s (colours); each is simulated from its own start state (dot), an unknown, first placed on the stop-and-turn route. Red lines are the defects: the gap between a piece’s end and the next piece’s start, and the miss at the door pose. The largest first gap is 0.477 m; after 80 iterations every gap is 0 and the drive is the one single shooting found
The standard term. Shooting with the trajectory cut into segments, each simulated from its own start state, which is an unknown, with a defect at every join constrained to 0, is multiple shooting (G-2892)Multiple shooting (parallel shooting): Shooting with the trajectory cut into segments, each simulated from its own start state, which is also an unknown, with a defect at every join constrained to 0; each control then acts on one short piece, which makes it more robust than single shooting. Explained in §5. Multiple shooting: shorter pieces, joined up., also called parallel shooting (Kelly 2017).
What changes. The unknowns are now the 60 controls plus 4 start states of 4 numbers, 76 in all, with 4 joins of 4 defects each plus the 4 numbers of the end that must close. In exchange:

each control acts only within its piece: 0.1 rad/s more turn rate in the first interval moves the end of its 1.6 s piece by 0.008 m, against 0.079 m for the end of the full drive (notebook);
the pieces are small problems that can be solved in parallel (Kelly, cannon);
multiple shooting is much more robust than single shooting on hard problems: it converges where single shooting fails (Kelly 2017; Kelly, cannon).

On our short drive both converge: multiple shooting takes 80 iterations to single shooting’s 73, from a first guess with gaps of up to 0.477 m, and ends on the same drive with the same effort, 0.217 (notebook). Shorter pieces mean shorter levers; at the limit, every interval is its own piece, and the states at every point are unknowns. Then nothing needs to be simulated at all.
6. Direct collocation: the motion rules as equations at points


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Make the states and the controls at a row of points in time all unknowns, and require between each pair of neighbours that the change in state equals the trapezoid-rule area under its rate of change, so nothing is simulated and limits are simple. Checked on the straight drive, it approaches the known 6.2 s as the points get closer; on the room drive it finds the least time to the door pose, 6.18 s.


Section 5 shortened the pieces of multiple shooting; at one interval per piece every state is an unknown, and the motion rules can be written as equations instead of being simulated (Tedrake, Underactuated ch. 10).
6.1 States at points instead of a simulation
Mark 31 points in time across the drive, 0.267 s apart for the 8 s drive. At each point, the state (4 numbers) and the controls (2 numbers) are unknowns: 186 numbers. Between neighbouring points, the motion rules must hold approximately: the change in each state between the two points must equal how fast it was changing, averaged over the two points, times the time between them. The solver moves all the points at once until every one of those equations holds (Kelly 2017).
The standard terms. Transcription in which the states and the controls at a set of points are all unknowns and the motion rules are enforced as constraints between them is direct collocation (G-2893)Direct collocation: Transcription in which the states and controls at a row of points in time are all unknowns and the motion rules are enforced as equations between neighbouring points; nothing is simulated, so limits along the way are easy to add. Explained in §6.1 States at points instead of a simulation. (Kelly 2017; Tedrake, Underactuated ch. 10). The points are the knot points (G-2895)Knot point (collocation point): One of the points in time at which collocation keeps the state and controls as unknowns, such as 31 points 0.267 s apart over an 8 s drive; more knot points make the solution more accurate. Explained in §6.1 States at points instead of a simulation., also called collocation points, and each equation that ties neighbouring knot points together through the motion rules is a collocation constraint (G-2894)Collocation constraint (trapezoidal): The equation that ties neighbouring knot points through the motion rules; in trapezoidal collocation the change in state equals the time step times the average of the rates at the two points, x_{k+1} - x_k = \frac{h}{2}(f_k + f_{k+1}). Explained in §6.2 The trapezoid rule by hand. (Kelly 2017).
6.2 The trapezoid rule by hand
The equation between neighbours comes from the area under a straight line. On the straight drive, the first interval of the least-time collocation with 10 intervals lasts 0.6364 s, and in it the speed rises in a straight line from 0 to 0.3182 m/s at 0.5 m/s² (notebook). The distance covered is the area under the speed, a trapezoid (here with one side 0, a triangle) (Figure 7):
\text{distance} = 0.6364 / 2 \times (0 + 0.3182)
= 0.1013 \text{ m}
Make interactive
Figure 7: The trapezoid rule on the first interval of the straight drive, 0.6364 s long (10 intervals of the least-time collocation). The speed rises in a straight line from 0 at knot k to 0.3182 m/s at knot k + 1; the distance covered is the area under it (orange), 0.6364 / 2 × (0 + 0.3182) = 0.1013 m, exactly what speeding up at 0.5 m/s² for 0.6364 s gives
Constant acceleration gives the same distance, so here the rule is exact, because the speed changes in a straight line:
0.5 \times 0.5 \times 0.6364^2 = 0.1013 \text{ m}
The same rule written for every state of the robot, with:

\mathbf x_k, the state at knot point k (four numbers);
\mathbf u_k, the controls at knot point k (two numbers);
h, the time between knot points, in s (0.267 s for the 8 s drive);
f_k, the rates of change at knot point k, the four motion rules of Section 2.1 evaluated at \mathbf x_k and \mathbf u_k.

\mathbf x_{k+1} - \mathbf x_k = \frac{h}{2}\thinspace(f_k + f_{k+1})
This equation is the collocation constraint of trapezoidal collocation (Kelly 2017, eq. 3.2). The rule assumes the rates change in a straight line between knot points, which makes each state a parabola between them; where the true rates bend, it is only approximate (Kelly 2017).

Limits are simple here because the states are unknowns: the wheels, the speed and the table are checked at every knot point and halfway between neighbours, with no simulation in between (Kelly 2017). Collocation suits problems with complicated controls and path constraints (Kelly 2017).
Least time. Now we make the duration T an unknown and the cost, T itself, with a tiny cost on the controls added so that the turn rate does not wander where the time does not care. For this problem we use a solver that keeps every constraint exactly, SciPy’s SLSQP, a sequential quadratic programming solver: gradient-based methods of this kind find a locally best trajectory when the first guess is close to one (Lynch and Park §10.7).
